ECON-NL-EASY-1.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-EASY-1.q: In the circular flow of income and expenditure, why does total income equal total expenditure?
options: Every dollar spent by a buyer becomes income for a seller
Government sets income equal to spending
ECON-NL-EASY-1.feedback: Income equals expenditure because one person's spending becomes another person's income.

ECON-NL-EASY-2.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-EASY-2.q: If households spend $500 billion buying goods and services, what happens to sellers' income in the basic income-expenditure logic?
options: It only rises if taxes fall
ECON-NL-EASY-2.feedback: Spending by buyers becomes income for sellers, so seller income rises by the same amount.

ECON-NL-EASY-3.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-EASY-3.q: GDP measures which two sides of economic activity?
ECON-NL-EASY-3.feedback: GDP can be measured as total income or total expenditure because those two sides are linked.

ECON-NL-EASY-5.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
options: The value of final goods and services produced domestically during a period
The total value of all used goods sold in a year
The total income earned only by government workers
The total amount of money printed by the central bank
ECON-NL-EASY-5.feedback: GDP is the market value of final goods and services produced within a country during a period.

ECON-NL-EASY-6.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-EASY-6.q: A newly produced car sold to a household is counted in GDP because it is:
options: A final good produced in the current period
A used good resold in the current period
ECON-NL-EASY-6.feedback: Newly produced final goods are counted in GDP.

ECON-NL-EASY-7.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
ECON-NL-EASY-7.q: Why are intermediate goods usually not counted separately in GDP?
options: Their value is included in the final good.
They are not produced by firms
ECON-NL-EASY-7.feedback: Counting intermediate goods separately would double count their value.

ECON-NL-EASY-9.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-EASY-9.q: Which purchase is not counted in current GDP?
options: Buying a used textbook from another student
Buying a new laptop made domestically
ECON-NL-EASY-9.feedback: Used goods were counted when first produced, so resale does not count in current GDP.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-100.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-100.q: A student says GDP can be measured by adding up either total income or total expenditure. Why is that true?
options: Each buyer’s spending becomes a seller’s income
GDP only counts income earned by households, not spending
The government adjusts income until it equals spending
Exports and imports must always be equal
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-100.feedback: The income and expenditure approaches match because each dollar spent becomes income to someone else.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-102.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-102.q: Which example best shows the income-expenditure identity in action?
options: A firm sells a $40 meal and the restaurant receives $40 in revenue
A used car is resold and counted twice in GDP
A government transfer payment raises GDP directly
A household saves money under a mattress
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-102.feedback: The restaurant sale shows spending by the buyer becoming income to the seller.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-104.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-104.q: Which transaction is counted in U.S. GDP?
options: A U.S. company buys shares of another company
A U.S. household buys a used refrigerator
A German tourist pays for a hotel room in Florida
A U.S. citizen buys a used car from a neighbor
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-104.feedback: The hotel service is produced in the United States, so it counts in U.S. GDP.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-106.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-106.q: A laptop produced last year is sold used this year for $700. How does this affect this year's GDP?
options: GDP rises only if the laptop was imported
GDP does not rise from the used-good sale
GDP rises by the original price
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-106.feedback: Used goods are not counted in current GDP because they were counted when first produced.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-107.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-107.q: A homeowner pays a contractor $12,000 to renovate a kitchen. Why is this counted in GDP?
options: It is a market service produced during the current period
It is counted only if paid in cash
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-107.feedback: Paid renovation work is current market production and is counted in GDP.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-108.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-108.q: Which item would be excluded from GDP because it is non-market production?
options: A person mowing their own lawn
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-108.feedback: Unpaid work performed for yourself is generally not counted in GDP.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9016.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9016.q: A U.S. firm earns profits from a factory located in Vietnam. Why is this not part of U.S. GDP?
options: GDP counts production within U.S. borders, not income earned abroad by U.S. residents
Profits are excluded from GDP because GDP measures wage income rather than business income earned by firms
Foreign production enters U.S. GDP when the resulting goods or services are eventually sold to U.S. consumers
GDP assigns production to the owner's home country rather than to the country where the production occurs
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9016.feedback: GDP is domestic production. Income earned abroad relates more to national income measures, not U.S. GDP.

ECON-NL-HARD-200.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-HARD-200.q: A firm produces $600,000 of final output. It pays $350,000 in wages, $100,000 in rent, $50,000 in interest, and keeps $100,000 in profit. What does this example show about GDP measurement?
options: Expenditure on output and income earned from production both equal $600,000
Only wages count in GDP, so GDP is $350,000
Profit is excluded from GDP, so GDP is $500,000
GDP cannot be measured from income
ECON-NL-HARD-200.feedback: The value of final output equals the income generated in producing it: wages, rent, interest, and profit all add to $600,000.

ECON-NL-HARD-201.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-HARD-201.q: Suppose expenditure GDP is $22 trillion. Income data show $13 trillion in wages, $3 trillion in rent and interest, $4 trillion in profit, and $2 trillion in other production income. What do these figures show?
options: The income and expenditure approaches both measure GDP at $22 trillion.
The income approach measures $20 trillion because other production income is excluded.
The expenditure approach measures $24 trillion because other production income is added again.
The figures cannot be compared because wages are excluded from the income approach.
ECON-NL-HARD-201.feedback: The income categories sum to $22 trillion, matching expenditure GDP. The two approaches measure the same current domestic production from different sides.

ECON-NL-HARD-202.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
ECON-NL-HARD-202.q: Why would counting both the sale of flour to a bakery and the sale of bread to consumers overstate GDP?
options: It counts the flour twice—alone and inside the bread price
It would exclude the baker's labor income
It would treat bread as an import
It would make income less than expenditure by definition
ECON-NL-HARD-202.feedback: Intermediate goods are already embodied in the final good, so counting both creates double counting.

ECON-NL-HARD-203.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-HARD-203.q: A U.S. company produces $2 million of software in Ireland and sells it to customers in Europe. How does this affect U.S. GDP?
options: It does not count in U.S. GDP
It counts in U.S. GDP because the firm is U.S.-owned
It counts as U.S. government purchases
It counts only if the software is downloaded in the U.S.
ECON-NL-HARD-203.feedback: GDP is based on production within a country's borders, not ownership of the firm.

ECON-NL-HARD-204.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-HARD-204.q: A Canadian company produces cars in Tennessee and sells them to U.S. households. How are those cars treated in U.S. GDP?
options: They count because they were produced inside the United States
They do not count because the company is foreign-owned
They count only as transfer payments
ECON-NL-HARD-204.feedback: GDP counts production within national borders, regardless of whether the producer is domestically or foreign owned.

ECON-NL-HARD-206.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-HARD-206.q: A household pays $2,000 for illegal services and $2,000 for legal market services. Which statement best explains the GDP issue?
options: Legal services count; hidden or illegal production is often missed
Both are always fully counted because all services are visible
Neither counts because services are excluded from GDP
Only illegal activity counts because it is current production
ECON-NL-HARD-206.feedback: GDP aims to count market production, but illegal or hidden activity is often excluded or poorly measured.

ECON-NL-HARD-207.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-HARD-207.q: A restaurant buys $300 of ingredients and receives $900 from customers for meals, including $100 in tips. Ignoring other complications, how much final restaurant service enters GDP?
ECON-NL-HARD-207.feedback: The $300 of ingredients are intermediate inputs. The full $900 customer payment, including the $100 in tips, is final expenditure on restaurant service.

ECON-NL-ELITE-300.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-ELITE-300.q: A country reports $18T in consumption, $5T in investment, $6T in government purchases, $4T in exports, and $5T in imports. Separately, income data show $20T in wages, $4T in rents and interest, and $4T in profits plus other production income. What is the best conclusion?
options: The expenditure and income approaches both imply GDP of $28T
The expenditure approach implies $38T while income implies $28T
Imports should be added, so GDP is $38T
Income cannot be used to measure GDP

ECON-NL-ELITE-301.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-ELITE-301.q: A student argues that total spending must exceed total income because consumers sometimes borrow to spend. What is the best correction?
options: Borrowed spending still becomes sellers’ income
Borrowed spending is excluded from GDP
Income only counts wages, so the student is correct
ECON-NL-ELITE-301.feedback: Borrowing can finance spending, but the expenditure still becomes income for producers.

ECON-NL-ELITE-302.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-ELITE-302.q: A firm produces $1M of output, sells $800,000 to customers, and adds $200,000 to inventory. It pays $600,000 in wages, $100,000 in rent, $100,000 in interest, and has $200,000 in profit. Which statement is correct?
options: GDP rises by $1M and income generated also totals $1M
GDP rises only by $800,000 because inventories are unsold
GDP rises by $1.2M because inventory is added to sales
ECON-NL-ELITE-302.feedback: Unsold output is inventory investment, so all $1M counts; income payments also total $1M.

ECON-NL-ELITE-303.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
ECON-NL-ELITE-303.q: A mill sells $180 of flour made from $70 of current domestic grain. A baker uses all the flour in $310 of bread sold to households. What are the baker’s value added and GDP across the full domestic chain?
options: $130 at the bakery; $310 across the chain
$240 at the bakery; $560 across the chain
$310 at the bakery; $310 across the chain
$130 at the bakery; $490 across the chain
ECON-NL-ELITE-303.feedback: The baker adds 310 - 180 = 130. Summing domestic value added gives 70 + (180 - 70) + 130 = 310, equal to the final sale. Intermediate sales cannot be added again.

ECON-NL-ELITE-304.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-ELITE-304.q: A U.S. household buys a new $30,000 car built in Mexico, while a Mexican household buys a new $40,000 car built in Michigan. What is the net effect on U.S. GDP from these two transactions?
ECON-NL-ELITE-304.feedback: Only the car produced in Michigan counts in U.S. GDP. The imported car affects consumption and imports but not domestic production.

ECON-NL-ELITE-305.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-ELITE-305.q: Which transaction is most likely counted in current GDP?
options: A homeowner pays a licensed contractor to build a new deck
A homeowner builds a deck alone using leftover materials already owned
A household buys shares in a construction company
A collector resells an antique table
ECON-NL-ELITE-305.feedback: Paid current market production counts. Financial transactions, used-good sales, and unpaid household production generally do not.

ECON-NL-ELITE-306.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
ECON-NL-ELITE-306.q: A firm imports $500,000 of parts, adds $300,000 of domestic labor and capital services, and sells the final good domestically for $800,000. What is the contribution to domestic GDP?
ECON-NL-ELITE-306.feedback: Only domestic value added counts in domestic GDP. Imported inputs are not domestic production.

ECON-NL-ELITE-307.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-ELITE-307.q: A country produces only two goods. In 2025 it produces 100 meals at $20 and 50 laptops at $1,000. It imports 10 additional laptops at $900 each for households. What domestic production value is counted in GDP?
ECON-NL-ELITE-307.feedback: GDP counts domestic production: 100($20) + 50($1,000) = $52,000. Imported laptops are not domestic production.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9001.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9001.q: A domestic assembler sells $420,000 of new equipment, using $150,000 of imported parts and $90,000 of current domestic components. A clerk adds all three values as domestic GDP. What correction reconciles final spending with domestic value added?
options: $270,000 total domestic GDP, including $180,000 at assembly
$420,000 total domestic GDP, including $330,000 at assembly
$510,000 total domestic GDP, including $420,000 at assembly
$180,000 total domestic GDP, excluding the domestic component makers
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9001.feedback: Final spending of 420,000 less imported inputs of 150,000 yields 270,000 domestic value added. Assembly contributes 420,000 - 150,000 - 90,000 = 180,000; domestic component makers contribute the remaining 90,000. Do not count their output twice.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9002.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9002.q: A firm imports $200,000 of components, adds $150,000 of domestic labor and capital services, and sells the final product domestically for $350,000. How much does this production add to domestic GDP?
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9002.feedback: Only domestic value added counts in domestic GDP. Imported components are not domestic production.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9003.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9003.q: A workshop sells $560 of new furniture after buying $140 of domestic lumber. Its wage bill is $250 and rent plus interest is $90. With no other costs or taxes, which value-added and profit account is consistent?
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9003.feedback: Value added is final output less intermediate lumber: 560 - 140 = 420. Of that, wages and rent/interest absorb 340, leaving profit of 80. Subtracting wages when computing value added would remove income generated by production.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9009.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9009.q: A renovation business bills households $96,000, including $24,000 of imported fixtures. It also brokers an old building for a $6,000 fee; the building sells for $310,000. Ignoring other inputs, what current domestic production and counting rule follow?
options: $78,000; count domestic renovation value and the new brokerage service
$388,000; the old building becomes current output when sold
$102,000; imported fixtures count because households bought them
$72,000; services attached to used assets must also be excluded
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9009.feedback: Domestic renovation value is 96,000 - 24,000 = 72,000. The current brokerage service adds 6,000, while the old building itself is not new output. Total current domestic production is 78,000.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9010.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9010.q: A production audit reports $74 million of final sales and $6 million of new inventories. Domestic production income is $51 million in wages, $9 million in rent and interest, and unreported profit. With no imports, taxes or depreciation adjustments, which result closes both accounts?
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9010.feedback: Current production includes the unsold 6 million, giving expenditure GDP of 80 million. Wages and rent/interest total 60 million, so residual profit is 20 million. Sales alone omit inventory investment.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9011.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9011.q: A used machine changes hands for $40,000 through a broker charging $2,000. A new domestic machine worth $28,000 is produced but remains unsold. An analyst counts only the $40,000 resale as this year’s GDP. What is the corrected contribution?
options: $2,000: unsold output cannot count until purchased
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9011.feedback: The resale transfers an existing asset; the newly produced brokerage service counts. The unsold new machine is inventory investment when produced. Thus current GDP includes 2,000 + 28,000 = 30,000.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9020.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9020.q: A household pays $30 for a restaurant meal, including $5 of sales tax. How should this be interpreted for GDP?
options: Count the final service; the tax is not government purchases
Only the pre-tax $25 counts because taxes are never linked to GDP
Only the $5 tax counts as government purchases
Nothing counts because meals are services
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9020.feedback: GDP counts the market value of final goods and services; taxes do not turn the meal into government purchases.

ECON-NL-EASY-4.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-EASY-4.q: If total expenditure in an economy is $20 trillion, what is total income in the basic GDP accounting identity?
ECON-NL-EASY-4.feedback: In the basic circular-flow logic, total expenditure equals total income.

ECON-NL-EASY-8.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
ECON-NL-EASY-8.q: A bakery buys flour for $20 and sells bread for $50. What value is counted in GDP from the final bread sale?
ECON-NL-EASY-8.feedback: GDP counts the final good, so the bread sale counts as $50.

ECON-NL-HARD-205.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-HARD-205.q: A firm buys steel for $80, adds labor and capital services, and sells a machine for $230 to another firm. If the machine is newly produced and used in production, how much does GDP increase?
ECON-NL-HARD-205.feedback: The newly produced machine is a final capital good, so its full market value of $230 is counted.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-101.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-101.q: Suppose firms sell $900 billion of final goods and households, firms, government, and foreigners buy all of it. What should total income from producing those goods equal?
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-101.feedback: Total expenditure on final output becomes total income earned from producing that output.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-103.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-103.q: If total income generated by current production is $18 trillion, what is total expenditure on that production?
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-103.feedback: In GDP accounting, total income and total expenditure are two ways of measuring the same economic activity.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-105.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-105.q: A farmer sells wheat to a miller for $100. The miller sells flour to a baker for $160. The baker sells bread to consumers for $250. How much is added to GDP?
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-105.feedback: GDP counts the final bread sale of $250, not each intermediate transaction separately.

ECON-EC-EASYBOSS-17004.q: Which transaction would be counted in U.S. GDP?
options: A new car produced and sold in the United States this year
A used car resold from one household to another
A parent cooking dinner at home
A stock purchase through a brokerage account
ECON-EC-EASYBOSS-17004.feedback: GDP counts newly produced final goods and services within a country during a period.

ECON-EC-EASYBOSS-17005.q: Which of these items is included in current GDP: a new laptop, a used bike, a homemade dinner, or a stock purchase?
ECON-EC-EASYBOSS-17005.feedback: The new laptop is newly produced and sold in a market. Used goods, home production, and stock trades are not counted the same way.

options: Final domestic production during a period
The total value of all used goods sold this year
The total value of all financial transactions
The amount of money held by households
ECON-EC-EASYBOSS-17010.feedback: GDP measures the market value of final goods and services produced within a country during a period.

ECON-EC-EASYBOSS-17011.q: Why is a tire sold to a car manufacturer usually not counted separately in GDP when the final car is sold?
options: Counting tire and car double counts production
The tire was not produced in a market
ECON-EC-EASYBOSS-17011.feedback: GDP counts final goods to avoid double counting intermediate goods already included in the final product's value.

ECON-EC-EASYBOSS-17013.q: Why does total income equal total expenditure for the economy as a whole?
ECON-EC-EASYBOSS-17013.feedback: For the economy as a whole, spending by buyers becomes income for sellers.

ECON-EC-EASYBOSS-17014.q: If one person’s spending is another person’s income, does every transaction increase GDP?
options: No; GDP counts current final production
Yes, every financial transaction raises GDP
Yes, all used goods sales raise GDP again
ECON-EC-EASYBOSS-17014.feedback: Income and expenditure are two sides of transactions, but GDP only counts current production of final goods and services.

ECON-EC-EASYBOSS-17022.q: Why is GDP usually studied in macroeconomics rather than microeconomics?
options: It measures total production for the economy as a whole
It measures one firm's output only
It measures only one household's choices
It tracks only one product's demand curve
ECON-EC-EASYBOSS-17022.feedback: GDP measures aggregate production for the whole economy, which makes it a macroeconomic measure.

ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2000.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2000.q: Why can GDP be measured as both total income and total expenditure?
options: Because every dollar spent by a buyer becomes income for a seller
Because income is always higher than spending
Because prices do not affect GDP
ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2000.feedback: GDP can be measured either way because one person's spending becomes another person's income.

ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2001.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2001.q: A household spends $500 at a local repair shop. In the income-expenditure flow, what happens to the repair shop?
ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2001.feedback: The household's expenditure becomes income for the repair shop.

ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2002.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2002.q: If total expenditure on final goods and services is $18 trillion, what should total income equal in the basic GDP identity?
ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2002.feedback: Total income equals total expenditure, so both are $18 trillion.

ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2003.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2003.q: An economist asks which item belongs in GDP. Which one counts?
options: A newly produced washing machine sold to a household
A used washing machine resold online
A gift from one household to another
ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2003.feedback: GDP counts newly produced final goods and services.

ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2004.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2004.q: Why is a used car sale usually not counted in current GDP?
options: The car was counted when it was first produced
Cars are never counted in GDP
ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2004.feedback: Used goods are not current production, so they are not counted again.

ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2005.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2005.q: A bakery buys flour for $40 and sells bread to consumers for $100. How much is counted in GDP from the final bread sale?
ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2005.feedback: GDP counts the value of the final good, which is the $100 bread sale.

P52B-S3-GDPM-B2-001.q: Which transaction is included in current-year GDP?
options: A used refrigerator resold by its owner.
A household purchase of corporate stock.
An unpaid repair performed by the homeowner.
A newly produced refrigerator purchased by a household.
P52B-S3-GDPM-B2-001.commonError: Counting asset transfers, used goods, or unpaid household work as current production.
P52B-S3-GDPM-B2-001.feedback: GDP includes newly produced final goods and services, not transfers of existing assets or unpaid household production.

P52B-S3-GDPM-B2-002.q: A bakery buys flour for $2 and sells bread to a household for $5. How much does the bread transaction add to GDP if the flour was produced this year?
options: $5, because the final sale already includes the flour’s value.
$7, because both the flour and bread sales are added.
$3, because only the bakery’s value added counts and the flour is excluded everywhere.
$2, because intermediate goods are the only production counted.
P52B-S3-GDPM-B2-002.commonError: Double counting an intermediate input and the final product.
P52B-S3-GDPM-B2-002.feedback: Counting the $5 final bread sale captures the value of the flour and the bakery’s value added without double counting.

P52B-S3-GDPM-B2-003.q: Why does total income equal total expenditure in the national accounts?
options: Government legally requires national income to equal national expenditure each year.
Each transaction is spending for a buyer and income for a seller.
Households always spend every dollar of income and never save financial assets.
Imports are recorded as both domestic production income and domestic expenditure.
P52B-S3-GDPM-B2-003.commonError: Treating the accounting identity as a behavioral claim that everyone spends all income.
P52B-S3-GDPM-B2-003.feedback: The same transaction is recorded from two sides: one party’s expenditure is another party’s income.

P52B-S3-GDPM-B3-001.q: A domestic firm produces a machine this year but does not sell it until next year. How is the machine treated this year?
options: It is excluded until a customer buys it next year.
It is counted as household consumption this year.
It is counted as inventory investment in this year’s GDP.
It is counted only if the firm imports the parts.
P52B-S3-GDPM-B3-001.commonError: Assuming unsold output is not counted until the final sale.
P52B-S3-GDPM-B3-001.feedback: Newly produced unsold goods enter inventories, which are counted as investment in the year of production.

P52B-S3-GDPM-B3-002.q: A U.S.-owned factory located in Mexico produces a car. Which statement is correct for U.S. GDP?
options: The car is included because the factory has a U.S. owner.
The car is included only if sold to a U.S. resident.
The car is counted as U.S. government production.
The car is excluded because it was produced outside the United States.
P52B-S3-GDPM-B3-002.commonError: Using ownership instead of location to define domestic product.
P52B-S3-GDPM-B3-002.feedback: GDP is based on production within a country’s borders, regardless of the producer’s nationality.

P52B-S3-GDPM-B3-003.q: A homeowner buys paint for $200 and paints the house without pay. What enters GDP?
options: The $200 market purchase of paint, but not the unpaid painting service.
Both the paint and an imputed value for the homeowner’s labor.
Only the homeowner’s labor because it creates the final service.
Neither the paint nor the labor because the house already existed.
P52B-S3-GDPM-B3-003.commonError: Excluding a purchased input because the final service is unpaid, or imputing all household labor.
P52B-S3-GDPM-B3-003.feedback: The market purchase of paint is counted, while unpaid household labor generally is not recorded in GDP.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9101.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9101.q: A firm produces $400 million of output, sells $340 million, and adds $60 million to inventory. Income paid to workers, lenders, landlords, and owners totals $400 million. What is GDP under the expenditure and income approaches?
options: GDP is $400M by both expenditure and income logic
GDP is $340M because only sold goods count
GDP is $460M because inventory adds to sales twice
GDP is $60M because only unsold goods are investment
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9101.feedback: Inventory investment counts, so expenditure GDP is $400M. Income generated is also $400M.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9102.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9102.q: A U.S. company produces $700 million of output abroad, while a foreign company produces $600 million of output inside the United States. How much is counted in U.S. GDP?
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9102.feedback: U.S. GDP counts production inside U.S. borders, regardless of ownership.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9107.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9107.q: A final good sells for $500 after using $180 of imported inputs. All remaining production occurs domestically, including $120 of domestic intermediate production. How much does the good add to domestic GDP across all domestic stages?
options: $500 because the final sale includes imported input value.
$180 because only the imported input is counted.
$440 because the domestic intermediate value is added again.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9107.feedback: Domestic value added across all domestic stages is $500 − $180 = $320. The $120 of domestic intermediate production is included once within that total rather than counted again.

ECON-NL-GDP-COUNTING-RULES-5002.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-GDP-COUNTING-RULES-5002.q: GDP counts goods and services that are:
options: Final, newly produced, and produced within the country
Used, resold, and produced long ago
ECON-NL-GDP-COUNTING-RULES-5002.feedback: GDP counts current production of final goods and services within a country's borders.

ECON-NL-GDP-COUNTING-RULES-5003.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-GDP-COUNTING-RULES-5003.q: A used car is resold this year. Why is the vehicle's sale price excluded from current GDP?
options: It was counted when first produced
ECON-NL-GDP-COUNTING-RULES-5003.feedback: Used goods are not current production.

ECON-NL-INCOME-EXPENDITURE-IDENTITY-5000.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-INCOME-EXPENDITURE-IDENTITY-5000.q: In GDP accounting, why does total income equal total expenditure?
options: Because one person's spending becomes another person's income
Because government sets income equal to spending
Because wages are excluded from GDP
ECON-NL-INCOME-EXPENDITURE-IDENTITY-5000.feedback: Every transaction has a buyer and seller, so expenditure becomes income.

ECON-NL-INCOME-EXPENDITURE-IDENTITY-5001.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-INCOME-EXPENDITURE-IDENTITY-5001.q: If a customer spends $100 at a business, what happens to the business in the income-expenditure flow?
ECON-NL-INCOME-EXPENDITURE-IDENTITY-5001.feedback: The customer's spending is the business's income.

ECON-NL-INTERMEDIATE-VS-FINAL-GOODS-5004.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
ECON-NL-INTERMEDIATE-VS-FINAL-GOODS-5004.q: Why are intermediate goods not counted separately in GDP?
options: Their value is included in the final good.
ECON-NL-INTERMEDIATE-VS-FINAL-GOODS-5004.feedback: Counting intermediate goods separately would double count their value.

ECON-NL-INTERMEDIATE-VS-FINAL-GOODS-5005.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
ECON-NL-INTERMEDIATE-VS-FINAL-GOODS-5005.q: Flour sold to a bakery is usually considered what kind of good?
ECON-NL-INTERMEDIATE-VS-FINAL-GOODS-5005.feedback: The flour is used to produce bread, so it is an intermediate good.

ECON-NL-GDP-COUNTING-RULES-6001.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
ECON-NL-GDP-COUNTING-RULES-6001.q: Which transaction counts in current GDP?
options: A newly built apartment rented to tenants
ECON-NL-GDP-COUNTING-RULES-6001.feedback: Newly produced housing services count; used goods and financial transfers do not add current production.

ECON-NL-INCOME-EXPENDITURE-IDENTITY-6000.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
ECON-NL-INCOME-EXPENDITURE-IDENTITY-6000.q: If total expenditure on final goods is $21 trillion, what should total income from producing those goods be?
ECON-NL-INCOME-EXPENDITURE-IDENTITY-6000.feedback: Total income and total expenditure are two sides of the same GDP activity.

ECON-NL-INTERMEDIATE-VS-FINAL-GOODS-6002.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
ECON-NL-INTERMEDIATE-VS-FINAL-GOODS-6002.q: A mill sells flour to a bakery for $50, and the bakery sells bread for $120. What final value is counted if using final-goods accounting?
ECON-NL-INTERMEDIATE-VS-FINAL-GOODS-6002.feedback: Final-goods accounting counts the bread sale, not the intermediate flour separately.

ECON-NL-EASY-10.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
ECON-NL-EASY-10.q: Which of the following is one of the four components of GDP expenditure?
ECON-NL-EASY-10.feedback: Consumption is one of the four expenditure components of GDP.

ECON-NL-EASY-11.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
ECON-NL-EASY-11.feedback: GDP expenditure is consumption plus investment plus government purchases plus net exports.

ECON-NL-EASY-13.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
ECON-NL-EASY-13.feedback: Net exports equal exports minus imports.

ECON-NL-EASY-14.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.

ECON-NL-EASY-14.feedback: Household spending on goods and services is consumption.

ECON-NL-EASY-15.feedback: Business spending on capital goods is investment.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-111.feedback: Government spending on goods and services is counted as government purchases.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-114.feedback: Business purchases of new capital goods are investment.

Only the payment of pension benefits

PM2B1-GDPC-M-002.q: A developer completes a new apartment building that will be rented to households. How is the construction classified?

PM2B1-GDPC-M-003.q: Why are imports subtracted in C + I + G + X − M?

To force exports and imports to carry opposite accounting signs
To remove foreign production already embedded in domestic spending
Because imported goods provide no value to domestic buyers
PM2B1-GDPC-M-003.commonError: Treats the subtraction of imports as a claim that imported goods are inherently harmful or absent from spending.
PM2B1-GDPC-M-003.feedback: Imports are subtracted because imported final spending may already appear in C, I, or G and foreign production must not enter domestic GDP.

ECON-NL-ELITE-310.commonError: Excluding unsold current production instead of counting it as inventory investment.
ECON-NL-ELITE-310.q: A firm produces $500M in goods, sells $450M, and unintentionally accumulates $50M in inventories. Which GDP component includes the unsold goods?
ECON-NL-ELITE-310.feedback: Inventory accumulation is counted as investment, even when unplanned.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9008.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9008.q: A firm produces $10M of goods in December but sells $7M in December and $3M in January. How should the $3M be treated for December GDP?
options: It counts as inventory investment in December
It counts as consumption in December
It is subtracted from December GDP
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9008.feedback: Goods produced but not sold are counted as inventory investment in the period produced.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9021.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9021.q: A firm buys a new domestically produced machine for $1M and a share of stock in another company for $1M. What is the direct effect on GDP?
options: GDP rises $1M; the stock purchase is financial
GDP rises by $2M because both are investments
GDP does not change because firms made both purchases
GDP rises only from the stock purchase
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9021.feedback: Economic investment in GDP means new capital goods, not financial asset purchases.

ECON-NL-HARD-210.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
ECON-NL-HARD-210.q: A government sends $1,000 unemployment checks to households, and households spend the full amount on groceries. What is the GDP effect?
options: The transfer is excluded; grocery purchases count as consumption
Both the transfer and groceries count, so GDP rises by $2,000
Neither counts because government is involved
Only the transfer counts as government purchases
ECON-NL-HARD-210.feedback: Transfer payments are not purchases of current goods and services, but later household spending can count as consumption.

ECON-NL-HARD-211.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
ECON-NL-HARD-211.q: A U.S. household buys a $40,000 car produced in Germany. In U.S. GDP accounting, what happens?
options: Consumption rises $40,000 and net exports fall $40,000; GDP is unchanged
Consumption rises and GDP rises by $40,000
Investment rises and imports are ignored
Government purchases rise and GDP is unchanged
ECON-NL-HARD-211.feedback: Imported consumer goods enter consumption but are subtracted through imports in net exports, so domestic GDP does not rise.

PM2B1-GDPC-H-001.commonError: Adds financial transfers, used goods, or imported production to domestic GDP.
PM2B1-GDPC-H-001.feedback: The domestic machine adds $5,000 of business investment. The imported laptop is offset by imports, and the benefit check is a transfer rather than a purchase of current output.

PM2B1-GDPC-H-002.commonError: Treats only machines as investment and misses new homes or inventory changes.
PM2B1-GDPC-H-002.feedback: GDP records the $6 million of goods produced this year. Selling $4 million of goods produced last year changes inventories but does not add new current production.

PM2B1-GDPC-H-003.q: A city buys $3 million of domestic buses and sends $2 million in transfers. Recipients spend $1.5 million on imported services. What is the direct increase in domestic GDP?
PM2B1-GDPC-H-003.commonError: Adds financial transfers, used goods, or imported production to domestic GDP.
PM2B1-GDPC-H-003.feedback: The $3 million of domestic buses is government purchases. Transfers do not enter GDP directly, and the recipients

PM2B1-GDPC-H-004.q: A domestic software firm exports $4 million of services, imports $1.5 million of servers, and adds $0.5 million of current domestic output to inventory. What is the direct contribution to domestic GDP?
PM2B1-GDPC-H-004.commonError: Treats the subtraction of imports as a claim that imported goods are inherently harmful or absent from spending.
PM2B1-GDPC-H-004.feedback: The $4 million export and $0.5 million of inventory are current domestic production. The imported servers do not add domestic production, so the direct contribution is $4.5 million.

ECON-NL-ELITE-308.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
ECON-NL-ELITE-308.q: Consumption is $9T, investment is $3T, government purchases are $4T, exports are $2T, and imports are $3T. Then households buy $1T more imported goods, with no change in domestic production. What happens to measured GDP?
options: It rises by $1T because consumption rises
It falls by $1T because imports rise
It rises by $2T because trade increases
ECON-NL-ELITE-308.feedback: Imported consumption raises C but lowers NX by the same amount, so domestic GDP is unchanged.

ECON-NL-ELITE-309.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
ECON-NL-ELITE-309.q: A government spends $100B hiring workers to build bridges and also sends $100B in Social Security payments. If recipients spend all Social Security payments on current domestic goods, what is the maximum direct GDP increase described?
ECON-NL-ELITE-309.feedback: Bridge spending is government purchases, and household spending from transfers can count as consumption. The transfer itself is not counted separately.

options: The condo is investment; the property tax is not current output
The condo is consumption and the tax is government purchases
ECON-NL-ELITE-312.feedback: New residential construction is investment. A tax payment is not itself government purchase of a final good or service.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9000.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9000.q: An economy reports C = 46, G = 13, exports = 9, imports = 11, and GDP = 72, all in billions. A separate inventory report records 4 billion of new unsold output. What investment total reconciles the accounts, and how should the inventory figure be treated?
options: I = 15; the 4 of inventories is included within that total
I = 19; add inventories after solving the identity
I = 7; subtract inventories twice to avoid unsold output
I = 37; imports should be added when solving for investment
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9000.feedback: The expenditure identity gives I = 72 - 46 - 13 - 9 + 11 = 15. Inventory investment is one part of I, leaving 11 in other investment; it is not an extra addition after reconciliation.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9004.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9004.q: A government purchases $18 million of new domestic flood barriers and pays $12 million in household benefits. options: $37 million; benefits and recipient purchases both count
$28 million; imported purchases count only in C
$18 million; spending financed by benefits is excluded
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9004.feedback: The benefit payment itself is a transfer. Recipient purchases enter C = 7 + 3 = 10; M = 3 removes the imported goods. G = 18, so domestic GDP rises 18 + 10 - 3 = 25 million, without counting the transfer again.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9012.commonError: Excluding unsold current production instead of counting it as inventory investment.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9012.q: At the start of a year, a producer has $8 million of goods made last year. It produces $30 million this year and sells $34 million, leaving $4 million in inventory. With unchanged prices, no imports and all sales to final users, which GDP account is correct?

$34 million: sales determine the production year
$38 million: add beginning inventories to new output
$42 million: add beginning inventories to final sales
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9012.feedback: Inventory investment is the change in stock: 4 - 8 = -4. Sales of 34 plus inventory investment of -4 equal current production of 30. Selling previously produced goods does not create output again.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9017.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.

Fall $4 billion; imports are subtracted without adding their spending
Remain unchanged; every correction associated with imports cancels
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9017.feedback: C rises by 8 billion and M by 6 billion. The net 2-billion increase is the newly measured domestic service. Subtracting imports removes foreign production, not the associated domestic activity.

PM2B1-GDPC-MB-002.commonError: Treats the subtraction of imports as a claim that imported goods are inherently harmful or absent from spending.
PM2B1-GDPC-MB-002.feedback: Imports are subtracted because imported final spending may already appear in C, I, or G and foreign production must not enter domestic GDP.

PM2B1-GDPC-MB-003.q: Which pair is classified as investment in GDP accounting?
options: A pension payment plus a household appliance purchase
An imported restaurant meal plus a tax refund
A new home plus added business inventories
A used home plus a corporate bond purchase
PM2B1-GDPC-MB-003.commonError: Treats only machines as investment and misses new homes or inventory changes.
PM2B1-GDPC-MB-003.feedback: GDP investment includes business fixed investment, residential construction, and changes in inventories.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9100.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9100.q: C = $12 trillion, I = $3 trillion, G = $4 trillion, exports = $2 trillion, and imports = $3 trillion. Households then buy $1 trillion more of imported goods, with no change in domestic production. What is final GDP?
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9100.feedback: Initial GDP = 12 + 3 + 4 + (2 - 3) = 18. Imported consumption raises C and lowers NX equally, so GDP stays 18.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9106.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9106.q: A household buys a new domestically built house for $300,000, a used car for $20,000, and $10,000 of imported furniture. What directly adds to domestic GDP?
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9106.feedback: The new domestic house counts as residential investment. Used car resale and imported furniture do not add to domestic GDP.

PM2B1-GDPC-LB-001.q: Households buy $3 million of domestic services and $2 million of imports; firms buy $4 million of domestic machinery and $2 million of stock; government buys $5 million of domestic bridges and sends $1 million in transfers; exporters sell $2 million abroad. What is GDP from these transactions?
PM2B1-GDPC-LB-001.commonError: Adds financial transfers, used goods, or imported production to domestic GDP.
PM2B1-GDPC-LB-001.feedback: Domestic services add $3 million, domestic machinery adds $4 million, bridges add $5 million, and exports add $2 million. Imports, stock purchases, and transfers add no domestic production directly, so GDP is $14 million.

ECON-NL-GDP-COMPONENTS-IDENTITY-5006.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
ECON-NL-GDP-COMPONENTS-IDENTITY-5006.q: Which equation correctly states the expenditure approach to GDP?
ECON-NL-GDP-COMPONENTS-IDENTITY-5006.feedback: GDP equals consumption plus investment plus government purchases plus net exports.

ECON-NL-GDP-COMPONENTS-IDENTITY-5007.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
ECON-NL-GDP-COMPONENTS-IDENTITY-5007.q: A household buying groceries is counted under which GDP component?
ECON-NL-GDP-COMPONENTS-IDENTITY-5007.feedback: Household spending on goods and services is consumption.

ECON-NL-IMPORTS-EXPORTS-NX-5008.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
ECON-NL-IMPORTS-EXPORTS-NX-5008.feedback: Net exports are exports minus imports.

ECON-NL-IMPORTS-EXPORTS-NX-5009.commonError: Treats the subtraction of imports as a claim that imported goods are inherently harmful or absent from spending.
ECON-NL-IMPORTS-EXPORTS-NX-5009.q: Why are imports subtracted after imported spending may appear in C, I, or G?
options: To remove foreign production from domestic GDP
To erase the buyer’s spending from every account
Because exports must always exceed imports
ECON-NL-IMPORTS-EXPORTS-NX-5009.feedback: Imports are subtracted because imported final spending may already appear in C, I, or G and foreign production must not enter domestic GDP.

ECON-NL-INVENTORY-INVESTMENT-5010.commonError: Excluding unsold current production instead of counting it as inventory investment.
ECON-NL-INVENTORY-INVESTMENT-5010.q: Unsold goods produced this year are counted as:
ECON-NL-INVENTORY-INVESTMENT-5010.feedback: Goods produced but not sold are counted as inventory investment.

ECON-NL-INVENTORY-INVESTMENT-5011.commonError: Counts a government transfer as government purchases before any recipient buys output.
ECON-NL-INVENTORY-INVESTMENT-5011.q: Does a government benefit payment enter G when it is sent?
options: Yes; every government payment enters G
Yes; but only if the household saves it
No; it is a transfer, not a purchase of current output
ECON-NL-INVENTORY-INVESTMENT-5011.feedback: Transfers redistribute income and are excluded from G; a later purchase can enter the appropriate spending component.

ECON-NL-GDP-COMPONENTS-IDENTITY-6003.commonError: Classifies by the buyer label instead of the economic transaction.
ECON-NL-GDP-COMPONENTS-IDENTITY-6003.q: A firm buys a newly produced domestic machine. How is this expenditure classified in the GDP identity?
options: Classify the machine as business investment
Treat the final machine as an intermediate input and omit it
Classify the domestic machine purchase as a government transfer
Subtract the machine as an import even though it is domestic
ECON-NL-GDP-COMPONENTS-IDENTITY-6003.feedback: Classify final spending by household consumption, business/residential investment, government purchases, or net exports.

ECON-NL-IMPORTS-EXPORTS-NX-6004.commonError: Infers output growth directly from nominal GDP growth.
ECON-NL-IMPORTS-EXPORTS-NX-6004.q: The expenditure identity reports current-dollar spending. Which measure helps determine whether higher spending reflects higher prices or greater output?
ECON-NL-IMPORTS-EXPORTS-NX-6004.feedback: Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production.

ECON-NL-INVENTORY-INVESTMENT-6005.commonError: Treats only machines as investment and misses new homes or inventory changes.
ECON-NL-INVENTORY-INVESTMENT-6005.q: Current production remains unsold and enters inventory investment. Which GDP-measurement rule explains why it still counts?
options: Inventory is treated as a transfer from the firm
Foreign production is added before subtracting every import
Current final production is counted when produced
Used goods are counted again whenever later resold
ECON-NL-INVENTORY-INVESTMENT-6005.feedback: Because the goods were produced this period, they count in current GDP; the unsold amount is recorded as inventory investment.

ECON-NL-EASY-16.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.

ECON-NL-EASY-17.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
ECON-NL-EASY-17.feedback: Real GDP uses constant base-year prices to remove the effect of price changes.

ECON-NL-EASY-18.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.

It holds prices constant so the comparison focuses on changes in output.

P52B-S2-RVNGDP-E-001.feedback: Real GDP uses constant prices to separate changes in quantities from changes in the price level.

PM2B1-RNGDP-E-001.q: Quantity is unchanged, but the current price of the only final good falls. With the same base year, what happens?

Nominal GDP is unchanged while real GDP falls
PM2B1-RNGDP-E-001.commonError: Infers output growth directly from nominal GDP growth.
PM2B1-RNGDP-E-001.feedback: Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production.

PM2B1-RNGDP-E-002.q: The base-year price is $10 and current production is 8 units. What is current real GDP?
PM2B1-RNGDP-E-002.commonError: Mixes current and base-year prices while valuing current output.
PM2B1-RNGDP-E-002.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-115.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-115.q: Suppose an economy produces only 10 bikes. In year 1, each bike sells for $100. In year 2, the economy still produces 10 bikes but each sells for $120. What happens?

Real GDP rises, but nominal GDP is unchanged
Both nominal and real GDP must fall
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-115.feedback: Nominal GDP rises because prices rise, while real GDP is unchanged because output did not change.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-117.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-117.q: Which situation would cause real GDP to rise?
options: Prices rise while output stays the same
Output rises while base-year prices are used
The CPI rises while production is unchanged
Used goods are resold more often
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-117.feedback: Real GDP rises when actual production rises, not merely when prices rise.

P52B-S2-RVNGDP-M-001.q: An economy produces exactly the same quantities of every final good in two years, but current prices change. Using fixed base-year prices, which statement must be true?

Real GDP must rise because some current prices changed.

P52B-S2-RVNGDP-M-001.feedback: With quantities unchanged, valuing both years at the same base-year prices leaves real GDP unchanged.

P52B-S2-RVNGDP-M-002.q: Two years have the same nominal GDP, but the second year has a higher GDP deflator. Which year has higher real GDP?

P52B-S2-RVNGDP-M-002.commonError: Assuming equal nominal GDP implies equal real output despite different price levels.
P52B-S2-RVNGDP-M-002.feedback: Real GDP equals nominal GDP divided by the price index. With equal nominal GDP, the year with the lower deflator has higher real GDP.

PM2B1-RNGDP-M-001.q: Current output is 20 units, the current price is $9, and the base-year price is $6. What are nominal and real GDP?
PM2B1-RNGDP-M-001.commonError: Mixes current and base-year prices while valuing current output.
PM2B1-RNGDP-M-001.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

PM2B1-RNGDP-M-002.q: Real GDP rises from $100 billion to $110 billion. What is the percentage growth rate?
PM2B1-RNGDP-M-002.commonError: Uses the new level rather than the initial real-GDP level as the percentage-growth denominator.
PM2B1-RNGDP-M-002.feedback: Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.

ECON-NL-HARD-213.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
ECON-NL-HARD-213.q: Nominal GDP rises from $20T to $22T while real GDP rises from $18T to $18.9T. What is the best interpretation?

ECON-NL-HARD-213.feedback: Real GDP rose 5%, while nominal GDP rose 10%, so both output and prices likely increased.

ECON-NL-HARD-216.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
ECON-NL-HARD-216.q: An economy produces only apples. Quantity rises from 1,000 to 1,100 and price rises from $2 to $3. What happens to nominal and real GDP using the first year as base?
options: Nominal GDP rises by more than real GDP
Real GDP rises by more than nominal GDP
Nominal GDP falls while real GDP rises
ECON-NL-HARD-216.feedback: Nominal GDP reflects both higher quantity and higher price, while real GDP only reflects higher quantity.

P52B-S2-RVNGDP-H-001.q: Nominal GDP falls 2 percent while the GDP deflator falls 5 percent. What is the best approximate conclusion?
P52B-S2-RVNGDP-H-001.commonError: Adding nominal and price changes instead of separating them.
P52B-S2-RVNGDP-H-001.feedback: Approximate real GDP growth equals nominal GDP growth minus inflation in the deflator: −2% − (−5%) = about 3%.

P52B-S2-RVNGDP-H-002.q: Base-year prices are $4 for books and $10 for meals. This year the economy produces 120 books and 30 meals. What is this year’s real GDP?
P52B-S2-RVNGDP-H-002.commonError: Using current prices or adding quantities without base-year valuation.

PM2B1-RNGDP-H-001.q: Nominal GDP grows 18% while the GDP deflator grows 10%. To one decimal place, what is the exact real-GDP growth implied by the ratio of the indexes?
PM2B1-RNGDP-H-001.commonError: Uses the new level rather than the initial real-GDP level as the percentage-growth denominator.
PM2B1-RNGDP-H-001.feedback: Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.
PM2B1-RNGDP-H-001.roundingRule: Round real-GDP growth to one decimal place.

PM2B1-RNGDP-H-002.q: An accountant divides current nominal GDP of $864 billion by a deflator of 120 and reports real GDP of $7.2 billion. Last year real GDP was $640 billion. Which correction and growth rate are right?

PM2B1-RNGDP-H-002.feedback: An index with base 100 requires dividing by 120/100, not 120: 864/1.2 = 720. Real growth is (720 - 640)/640 = 12.5%. The deflator’s level is not the output growth rate.
PM2B1-RNGDP-H-002.roundingRule: Round real-GDP growth to one decimal place.

ECON-NL-ELITE-313.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
ECON-NL-ELITE-313.q: Nominal GDP rises from $25T to $30T. The GDP deflator rises from 100 to 120. What happens to real GDP?
ECON-NL-ELITE-313.feedback: Initial real GDP = 25. New real GDP = 30 / 1.20 = 25. Real GDP is unchanged.

ECON-NL-ELITE-314.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
ECON-NL-ELITE-314.q: An economy produces 20 units at $5 in the base year. This year it produces 25 units at $8. What are nominal GDP and real GDP this year?
ECON-NL-ELITE-314.feedback: Nominal GDP uses current price: 25 x 8 = 200. Real GDP uses base price: 25 x 5 = 125.

ECON-NL-ELITE-315.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
ECON-NL-ELITE-315.q: Real GDP rises 5% while nominal GDP rises 15.5%. A report calls the full nominal increase output growth. What price change and correction follow?
options: Deflator is unchanged; the two growth rates use different units
ECON-NL-ELITE-315.feedback: The price-index ratio is 1.155/1.05 = 1.10. Thus the deflator rises 10%, while the stated real production increase remains 5%. Price and quantity growth combine multiplicatively.

ECON-NL-ELITE-316.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
ECON-NL-ELITE-316.q: If nominal GDP is $36T and real GDP is $30T, then the GDP deflator indicates:
options: The price level is 20% above the base-year level
The price level is 20% below the base-year level
Real output is 120% higher than nominal output
ECON-NL-ELITE-316.feedback: GDP deflator = 36/30 x 100 = 120, meaning prices are 20% above the base-year level.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9005.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9005.q: A country’s nominal GDP is $468 billion and its deflator is 130. Next year real GDP rises 10%, but nominal GDP is $475.2 billion. Which new deflator and interpretation reconcile these facts?
options: 120; real output rises while the domestic price level falls
132; nominal and real growth must move together
145.2; add real growth to the old deflator
120; the lower deflator proves real production fell
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9005.feedback: Initial real GDP is 468/1.30 = 360. It grows to 396; the new deflator is 475.2/396 × 100 = 120. Output grew despite a decline in the price index from 130 to 120.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9006.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9006.q: A workshop economy makes pumps and repair visits. Base prices are $40 and $20. Current quantities are 60 pumps and an unreported number of visits; current prices are $50 and $30. Current nominal GDP is $6,000. What real GDP and deflator follow?
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9006.feedback: Pumps account for 60 × 50 = 3,000 nominal dollars, leaving 3,000/30 = 100 visits. At base prices real GDP is 60 × 40 + 100 × 20 = 4,400. The deflator is 6,000/4,400 × 100 ≈ 136.4.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9007.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9007.q: Two new domestic goods have current prices of $12 and $30 and base prices of $10 and $20. Output of the first is 80 units; total real GDP is $2,400. A report calls $2,400 current nominal GDP. What is the correct nominal total and source of the difference?
options: $3,360; recover 80 units of the second good and value both at current prices
$2,880; raise all real output by the first good’s price increase
$2,400; real and nominal GDP use the same quantities, so they are equal
$4,320; current prices must be applied to the dollar value of real GDP
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9007.feedback: Base-price output of the first good is 800, leaving 1,600/20 = 80 units of the second. Nominal GDP is 80 × 12 + 80 × 30 = 3,360. The same quantities have different values at different price vectors.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9013.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9013.q: Nominal GDP grows 8% and the GDP deflator grows 12.5%. Population is unchanged. Which conclusion best evaluates the claim that average real production rose?
options: Real GDP per person falls 4%; nominal growth does not establish output growth
Real GDP per person falls 4.5%; subtracting rates gives an exact result
Real GDP per person rises 8%; population did not change
Real GDP per person rises 20.5%; combine both positive rates
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9013.feedback: The real-output ratio is 1.08/1.125 = 0.96, a 4% fall. With population fixed, real GDP per person falls by the same proportion. Nominal output rose only because the price increase exceeded the real contraction.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9018.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9018.q: An economy produces 50 units at $10 in year 1 and 60 units at $12 in year 2. Using year 1 as base, what are year 2 nominal GDP, real GDP, and the GDP deflator?
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9018.feedback: Nominal GDP = 60 x 12 = 720. Real GDP = 60 x 10 = 600. Deflator = 720/600 x 100 = 120.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9022.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9022.q: Nominal GDP rises 32% over two years. Real GDP rises 10% in the first year and is unchanged in the second. The deflator started at 125. Which final deflator and cumulative price change follow?
options: 152.5; subtracting growth rates gives an exact 22% price rise
150; the domestic price level rose 50% during these two years
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9022.feedback: Real GDP’s cumulative factor is 1.10. The price factor is 1.32/1.10 = 1.20, giving deflator 125 × 1.20 = 150. A level of 150 is 50% above the base year, but only 20% above the initial 125.

ECON-NL-HARD-214.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
ECON-NL-HARD-214.q: If nominal GDP is $30T and real GDP is $25T, what is the GDP deflator?
ECON-NL-HARD-214.feedback: GDP deflator = nominal GDP / real GDP x 100 = 30/25 x 100 = 120.

ECON-NL-HARD-215.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
ECON-NL-HARD-215.q: An economy produces 100 units at $5 in year 1 and 110 units at $6 in year 2. Using year 1 as the base year, what is year 2 real GDP?
ECON-NL-HARD-215.feedback: Real GDP uses base-year prices, so year 2 real GDP = 110 x $5 = $550.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9103.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9103.q: A statistical office reports nominal GDP of $715 billion with a deflator of 130, followed by $756 billion with a deflator of 140. Which real-output comparison is consistent, to one decimal place?

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9014.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9014.q: Two regions report real GDP per person of $44,000 and $40,000. In the first, output per hour is $40 and annual hours per resident are 1,100; in the second they are $50 and 800. Which comparison is supported without assigning a value to leisure?

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9015.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9015.q: After a storm, rebuilding adds $12 million of current production while lost business activity reduces other current production by $5 million. Destroyed existing buildings were worth $30 million. Which GDP and welfare statement is defensible?

GDP is $23 million lower because destroyed wealth is subtracted from current production
GDP is $12 million higher; lost current production is irrelevant
GDP is $37 million higher because rebuilding replaces the destroyed stock
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9015.feedback: The change in current production is 12 - 5 = 7 million. Destruction of existing wealth is a separate loss, not a negative item of current production. Higher measured GDP therefore does not establish higher well-being.

P52A-CPI-M-001.commonError: Using the dollar increase rather than the basket-cost ratio.

P52A-CPI-M-002.q: An index moves from 175 to 189. A report calls the 14-point rise “14 percent inflation.” Which correction uses the proper comparison?

P52A-CPI-M-005.q: A fixed basket has two meals at a base price of $4 each and one fare at $12. Meal prices rise 10%; the fare is unchanged. What CPI results, with the base set to 100?

110; use the price change of the only item that rose
140; the meal expenditure weight is the inflation rate
104; meals had 40% of base basket spending

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9026.commonError: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.

Unchanged; the first year’s full indexation guarantees this forever
About 2.9% lower; a later price decline reduces purchasing power
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9026.feedback: The cumulative wage factor is 27/25 = 1.08 and cumulative price factor is 525/500 = 1.05. Their ratio is 1.02857, giving about 2.9% more purchasing power. Use cumulative levels instead of adding annual rates.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9027.commonError: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.
