PM2B3-PROD-E-001.feedback: Point A shows output per worker of 28.53, so that is the productivity value read from the graph.

PM2B3-PROD-E-002.q: Two factories produce 1,000 units. Factory A uses 100 labor hours and Factory B uses 125. Which factory has higher labor productivity?
options: They have equal productivity because output is equal
Productivity cannot be compared without the product price
PM2B3-PROD-E-002.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-E-002.feedback: Factory A produces 10 units per labor hour (1,000/100), versus 8 for Factory B (1,000/125), so A is more productive.

PM2B3-PROD-E-003.q: A plant produces 10 percent more output with the same labor hours. What happens to output per labor hour?
options: It rises only if the number of workers also rises
PM2B3-PROD-E-003.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-E-003.feedback: With labor hours unchanged, a 10% increase in output raises output per labor hour by 10%.

PM2B3-PROD-E-004.q: A business uses more labor hours but produces the same amount of output. What happens to labor productivity?
options: It becomes equal to total output
PM2B3-PROD-E-004.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-E-004.feedback: With output fixed, adding labor hours increases the denominator, so output per labor hour falls.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-147.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-147.q: A country wants to raise living standards. Why is raising productivity more important than simply working more hours forever?
options: Higher worker output supports higher income per person
Working hours are the same as net exports
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-147.feedback: Sustained living-standard gains come from producing more output per worker.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-148.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-148.q: If two countries have the same number of workers but one produces twice as much output, the key difference is likely:
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-148.feedback: More output with the same labor means higher productivity.

PM2B3-PROD-M-001.q: Using GROWTH-01, moving from point A to point B raises output per worker by approximately how much?
PM2B3-PROD-M-001.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-M-001.feedback: Output per worker rises from 28.53 at A to 36.37 at B: 36.37−28.53=7.84.

PM2B3-PROD-M-002.q: A firm produces 1,200 units in 100 hours, then 1,320 units in the same 100 hours. What is the productivity increase?
PM2B3-PROD-M-002.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-M-002.feedback: Productivity rises from 12 units/hour (1,200/100) to 13.2 (1,320/100), a 10% increase.

PM2B3-PROD-M-003.q: Two economies have the same output per person, but workers in Economy X work fewer hours per person. What is the strongest inference?
options: The economies must have identical technology
Economy X necessarily has more natural resources
Economy X has higher output per hour worked
Economy X must have lower output per worker
PM2B3-PROD-M-003.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-M-003.feedback: The same output per person produced in fewer hours means more output per hour worked.

PM2B3-PROD-M-004.q: Output grows 12 percent while total labor hours grow 4 percent. What happens to labor productivity?
options: It cannot change unless population changes
PM2B3-PROD-M-004.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-M-004.feedback: Productivity is output divided by labor hours; output grew faster than labor hours, so it rises.

ECON-NL-HARD-246.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-HARD-246.q: Output rises from 10,000 units to 12,000 units while labor rises from 100 workers to 150 workers. What happens to productivity?
options: It falls from 100 units per worker to 80 units per worker
It rises from 100 units per worker to 120 units per worker
It stays at 100 units per worker
ECON-NL-HARD-246.feedback: Initial productivity is 100; new productivity is 12000/150 = 80, so productivity falls.

ECON-NL-HARD-247.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-HARD-247.q: A country raises total output by adding more workers, but output per worker does not rise. What is the best conclusion?
options: GDP may rise without much gain in productivity or living standards
Real GDP per person must double
Productivity must rise because output rose
ECON-NL-HARD-247.feedback: More workers can raise total output without raising output per worker.

PM2B3-PROD-H-001.q: GROWTH-01 becomes flatter as capital per worker rises. After moving from A to B, what should be expected from another equal increase in capital per worker, holding other factors constant?
options: A smaller additional gain in output per worker than the A-to-B gain
A larger gain because the economy is richer
No further output gain is possible
PM2B3-PROD-H-001.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-H-001.feedback: The curve is flatter to the right, so an equal additional amount of capital produces a smaller marginal output gain than A-to-B.

PM2B3-PROD-H-002.q: Output rises 30 percent while labor hours rise 20 percent. To one decimal place, what is the exact increase in output per labor hour?
PM2B3-PROD-H-002.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-H-002.feedback: Productivity changes by (1.30/1.20)−1 = 8.3% when output rises 30% and labor hours rise 20%.
PM2B3-PROD-H-002.roundingRule: Compute 1.30 ÷ 1.20 − 1 and round to one decimal place.

PM2B3-PROD-H-003.q: Output per worker rises, but output per labor hour is unchanged. Which explanation is consistent with both facts?
options: The labor force must have shrunk to zero
Average hours worked per worker increased
Every worker became more productive per hour
PM2B3-PROD-H-003.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-H-003.feedback: If output per worker rises while output per hour is unchanged, each worker must be working more hours on average.

PM2B3-PROD-H-004.q: Total output falls 2 percent while labor hours fall 5 percent. To one decimal place, what happens to labor productivity?
PM2B3-PROD-H-004.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-H-004.feedback: Productivity changes by (0.98/0.95)−1 ≈ 3.2%, so it rises.
PM2B3-PROD-H-004.roundingRule: Compute 0.98 ÷ 0.95 − 1 and round to one decimal place.

ECON-NL-ELITE-345.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-ELITE-345.q: Output rises from 50,000 to 60,000 while labor hours rise from 10,000 to 12,500. What happens to productivity?
options: It falls from 5 to 4.8 units per hour
It rises from 5 to 6 units per hour
It stays at 5 units per hour
It rises from 4.8 to 5 units per hour

ECON-NL-ELITE-346.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-ELITE-346.q: A country's output per worker rises from $80,000 to $92,000. What is the percentage increase in productivity?
ECON-NL-ELITE-346.feedback: Increase = 12,000 on a base of 80,000, so productivity rises by 15%.

ECON-NL-ELITE-347.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-ELITE-347.q: Two countries have the same real GDP, but Country A has half as many workers as Country B. What must be true?
options: Country A has higher output per worker
Country A has lower real GDP per worker by definition
ECON-NL-ELITE-347.feedback: Producing the same output with fewer workers means higher productivity.

ECON-NL-ELITE-348.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-ELITE-348.q: A country raises output by increasing labor force participation, but output per worker falls. What is the most precise conclusion?
options: Total production rose, but productivity declined
Real GDP cannot rise when productivity falls
ECON-NL-ELITE-348.feedback: More workers can raise total output even while output per worker falls.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9050.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9050.q: A plant initially produces 24,000 units using 20 workers who each work 100 hours. Next period, 24 workers each work 80 hours and produce 25,344 units. Which comparison is correct?
options: Output per worker falls 12%; output per hour rises 10%
Both productivity measures rise 5.6%, matching total output
Output per worker rises 10%; output per hour falls 12%
Output per hour is unchanged because the plant hired more workers
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9050.feedback: Per-worker output falls from 1,200 to 1,056, or 12%. Total hours fall from 2,000 to 1,920; hourly output rises from 12 to 13.2, or 10%. Changes in hours per worker make the productivity measures diverge.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9051.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9051.q: An economy initially produces $90 billion using 3 billion labor hours. A plan targets $108 billion while limiting total hours to 3.2 billion. What hourly productivity and increase over the initial level are required?
options: $30 per hour, with no productivity gain
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9051.feedback: Initial productivity is 90/3 = 30 dollars per hour. The target requires 108/3.2 = 33.75, or 12.5% more. Output growth alone overstates the needed productivity increase because hours also expand.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9052.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9052.q: Two countries have equal real GDP per person, but one works far fewer hours per person. What can be inferred?
options: The country with fewer hours likely has higher output per hour
They must have identical productivity per hour
The country with more hours must be richer
Real GDP per person cannot be compared
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9052.feedback: Equal output per person with fewer hours implies greater output per hour.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9053.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9053.q: A country’s real GDP rises 6% while employment rises 10%. Population is unchanged. Which assessment separates average material output from output per worker?
options: Output per person rises 6%; output per worker falls about 3.6%
Both fall about 3.6% because productivity declined
Output per person falls 4%; subtract employment growth from GDP growth
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9053.feedback: With population fixed, GDP per person rises 6%. Output per worker changes by 1.06/1.10 - 1 ≈ -3.6%. A productivity decline does not imply that average output per resident also declined.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9066.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9066.q: Output per worker rises from $50,000 to $55,000, but real GDP per resident stays at $30,000. What must happen to the employed share of residents, assuming the measures cover the same output?
options: It falls from 60% to about 54.5%, offsetting the productivity rise
It rises from 60% to 66%, reinforcing the productivity rise
It stays at 60% because output per resident is unchanged
It falls from 50% to 45%, because wages determine employment shares
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9066.feedback: Workers/residents equals output/resident divided by output/worker. The share changes from 30,000/50,000 = 60% to 30,000/55,000 ≈ 54.5%. This accounting result does not identify why the employment share fell.

PM2B3-PROD-L-001.q: In GROWTH-01, two otherwise similar economies begin at A and B. Each receives the same small addition to capital per worker. Which conclusion is best supported by the graph?
options: Point A has the larger marginal output gain; convergence is not guaranteed

Both economies must receive exactly the same output gain whenever capital increases by the same amount
Point A is guaranteed to overtake point B even if institutions and technology differ

PM2B3-PROD-L-001.feedback: The graph is steeper at A, so the same small capital addition yields a larger marginal output gain there; this alone does not guarantee convergence.

PM2B3-PROD-L-002.q: A plant automates part of production. Output rises 18 percent while labor hours fall 5 percent. To one decimal place, what happens to output per labor hour?
PM2B3-PROD-L-002.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.

PM2B3-PROD-L-002.roundingRule: Compute 1.18 ÷ 0.95 − 1 and round to one decimal place.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.q: An economist asks for the core driver of long-run living standards. What is the best answer?
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.feedback: Long-run living standards depend heavily on productivity.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.q: Why does higher productivity raise living standards?
options: Workers can produce more goods and services per unit of labor
Workers automatically work fewer hours with no tradeoff

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3008.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3008.q: A factory produces 4,800 units using 600 labor hours. What is productivity?
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3008.feedback: Productivity = output / labor hours = 4,800 / 600 = 8 units per hour.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3009.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3009.feedback: Productivity is output per unit of labor input.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3010.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3010.q: Output rises, but labor input rises even faster. What happens to productivity?
options: Productivity is unchanged by labor input
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3010.feedback: If labor rises faster than output, output per unit of labor falls.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3011.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3011.q: Output rises from 1,000 to 1,200 while labor hours rise from 100 to 150. What happens to productivity?
options: It falls from 10 to 8 units per hour
It rises from 10 to 12 units per hour
It stays at 10 units per hour
It rises from 8 to 10 units per hour
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3011.feedback: Initial productivity is 1,000/100 = 10. New productivity is 1,200/150 = 8.

PM2B3-PROD-EB-001.q: A factory produces 900 units in 90 labor hours. What is labor productivity?
PM2B3-PROD-EB-001.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-EB-001.feedback: Labor productivity is output divided by labor hours: 900/90 = 10 units per labor hour.

PM2B3-PROD-EB-002.q: In GROWTH-01, which point has both lower capital per worker and lower output per worker?
options: Both points have the same capital per worker
Neither point lies on the production curve
PM2B3-PROD-EB-002.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-EB-002.feedback: Point A is lower on both axes, so it has lower capital per worker and lower output per worker.

PM2B3-PROD-EB-003.q: A company hires more workers and total output rises, but output per labor hour does not change. What happened to labor productivity?
options: It became equal to output per worker automatically
It rose because total output rose
PM2B3-PROD-EB-003.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-EB-003.feedback: Output and labor hours increased in the same proportion, leaving output per labor hour unchanged.

PM2B3-PROD-FB-004.q: Use the displayed GROWTH-01 coordinates. Moving from A to B doubles capital per worker. Approximately how much does output per worker rise, and what is consistent with the curve’s shape?
options: 7.84%; the numerical output increase is already a percentage
27.5%; the same further capital increase would add less output
27.5%; each further equal capital increase must add more output
PM2B3-PROD-FB-004.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-FB-004.feedback: The graph gives output 28.53 at A and 36.37 at B. The increase is 7.84/28.53 × 100 ≈ 27.5%. The flattening curve shows diminishing marginal gains from equal additional capital, holding other inputs fixed.

PM2B3-PROD-FB-005.q: A factory targets 300,000 units of output and productivity of 12.5 units per labor hour. How many labor hours can it use and still meet that productivity target?
PM2B3-PROD-FB-005.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-FB-005.feedback: Required labor hours equal output divided by target productivity: 300,000/12.5 = 24,000 hours.

PM2B3-PROD-FB-006.q: Economy A produces 480 billion units with 24 billion labor hours; Economy B produces 420 billion units with 20 billion labor hours. Which has higher labor productivity?
options: Economy A, because its total output is larger
They have equal productivity because both use billions of hours
Economy B, because it uses more labor hours
Economy B, at 21 units per hour versus 20 for Economy A
PM2B3-PROD-FB-006.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-FB-006.feedback: Economy A produces 20 units/hour (480/24), while B produces 21 (420/20), so B is higher.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9118.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9118.q: Boss Audit: Output rises from 200,000 to 260,000 while labor hours rise from 20,000 to 25,000. What happens to productivity?
options: It rises from 10 to 10.4 units per hour

PM2B3-PROD-LB-001.q: Output grows 25 percent while labor hours grow 20 percent. To one decimal place, what is the exact productivity growth rate?
PM2B3-PROD-LB-001.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-LB-001.feedback: Productivity changes by (1.25/1.20)−1 ≈ 4.2%, not by the simple difference in growth rates.
PM2B3-PROD-LB-001.roundingRule: Compute 1.25 ÷ 1.20 − 1 and round to one decimal place.

PM2B3-PROD-LB-002.q: GROWTH-01 shows A at lower capital per worker on the steeper portion of the curve and B farther to the right where the curve is flatter. What is the strongest productivity interpretation?
options: Equal capital additions must create identical output gains at every point on the curve
Output per worker is higher at A than at B even though A has less capital
The graph proves that every low-capital economy must eventually converge regardless of its other conditions
Equal new capital likely adds more output near A than near B
PM2B3-PROD-LB-002.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-PROD-LB-002.feedback: Because the curve is steeper near A, an equal new capital addition is expected to add more output per worker near A.

ECON-NL-PRODUCTIVITY-CALCULATION-5036.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
options: Output per unit of labor input
ECON-NL-PRODUCTIVITY-CALCULATION-5036.feedback: Productivity measures output per unit of labor.

ECON-NL-PRODUCTIVITY-CALCULATION-5037.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-PRODUCTIVITY-CALCULATION-5037.q: If output is 500 and labor hours are 100, productivity is:

ECON-NL-PRODUCTIVITY-CALCULATION-6018.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-PRODUCTIVITY-CALCULATION-6018.q: Output is 2,400 units and labor input is 300 hours. What is productivity?

ECON-NL-EASY-50.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-EASY-50.feedback: Physical capital includes tools, machines, buildings, and equipment used in production.

ECON-NL-EASY-51.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
ECON-NL-EASY-51.feedback: Human capital is the knowledge and skill workers bring to production.

ECON-NL-EASY-52.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
ECON-NL-EASY-52.feedback: Natural resources are inputs into production supplied by nature.

ECON-NL-EASY-53.commonError: Confusing better production methods with more labor or more machines.
options: The market basket used for CPI
ECON-NL-EASY-53.feedback: Technological knowledge is know-how about production methods.

ECON-NL-EASY-54.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
ECON-NL-EASY-54.q: If workers receive better training, which productivity factor has increased?

ECON-NL-EASY-55.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-EASY-55.q: If a firm gives workers better machines, which productivity factor has increased?
ECON-NL-EASY-55.feedback: Better machines increase physical capital per worker.

ECON-NL-EASY-56.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
options: Each added unit of capital contributes less extra output
ECON-NL-EASY-56.feedback: Diminishing returns means extra capital still helps, but by smaller amounts as capital accumulates.

ECON-NL-EASY-57.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-EASY-57.q: The catch-up effect suggests that poorer countries may grow faster because:
options: They can get larger gains from additional capital
ECON-NL-EASY-57.feedback: Poorer countries may have less capital, so new capital can produce larger gains.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-149.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-149.q: A new irrigation machine allows farmers to grow more crops with the same labor. Which productivity factor improved most directly?
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-149.feedback: Better production methods and equipment raise productivity.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-150.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-150.q: A nation invests heavily in worker training and apprenticeship programs. Which factor of productivity is most directly increased?
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-150.feedback: Training and education increase human capital.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-151.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-151.q: A country discovers large deposits of rare minerals used in manufacturing. Which productivity factor increased?

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-152.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-152.q: A factory adds more machines for each worker. What should happen to output per worker, other things equal?
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-152.feedback: More physical capital per worker generally raises productivity.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-153.commonError: Confusing better production methods with more labor or more machines.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-153.q: Which example best illustrates technological knowledge?
options: A new production process that uses fewer inputs per unit of output
A higher CPI for imported goods
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-153.feedback: Technological knowledge means knowing better ways to produce.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-154.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-154.q: Diminishing returns imply that if a country keeps adding capital while labor stays fixed:
options: Each additional unit of capital eventually adds smaller increases in output
Each additional unit of capital adds larger increases forever
Capital stops being counted in GDP
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-154.feedback: Diminishing returns means extra capital becomes less productive as more of it is added.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-155.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-155.q: Why might poorer countries experience faster growth than richer countries, other things equal?
options: Scarce capital can earn higher returns in poorer countries
Inflation forces poor countries to grow
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-155.feedback: The catch-up effect occurs because capital may be especially productive where it is scarce.

ECON-NL-HARD-249.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-HARD-249.q: A country buys more machines, improves schools, and adopts better production software. Which productivity factors are increasing?
ECON-NL-HARD-249.feedback: Machines raise physical capital, schools raise human capital, and software/process improvements reflect technological knowledge.

ECON-NL-HARD-250.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-HARD-250.q: Two countries have similar workers and technology, but one has far more equipment per worker. Which difference most directly explains higher productivity?
ECON-NL-HARD-250.feedback: More equipment per worker generally raises output per worker.

ECON-NL-HARD-251.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-HARD-251.q: A country with strong education but weak roads, ports, and electricity may still struggle with productivity because it lacks:
ECON-NL-HARD-251.feedback: Infrastructure is part of the physical capital that helps workers produce efficiently.

ECON-NL-HARD-252.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
ECON-NL-HARD-252.q: A new farming method raises output per acre without increasing land, labor, or machinery. Which factor is most directly responsible?
ECON-NL-HARD-252.feedback: A better method of production is technological knowledge.

ECON-NL-HARD-253.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
ECON-NL-HARD-253.q: Which example best illustrates human capital rather than technological knowledge?
options: Workers complete advanced training in machine repair
A firm invents a new production algorithm
ECON-NL-HARD-253.feedback: Training workers increases human capital; an invention or method itself is technological knowledge.

ECON-NL-HARD-254.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
ECON-NL-HARD-254.q: Why does capital deepening eventually face limits if technology and human capital do not improve?
options: Each extra machine adds less output as capital accumulates
Output per worker must become zero
ECON-NL-HARD-254.feedback: Diminishing returns limit the gains from adding more capital alone.

ECON-NL-HARD-255.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-HARD-255.q: A poor country has little capital per worker. A new investment project adds basic equipment to farms and factories. Why might returns be high?
options: Because capital is scarce, the marginal product of additional capital can be large
Because diminishing returns never exist in poor countries
Because inflation makes machines cheaper in real terms
ECON-NL-HARD-255.feedback: The catch-up effect comes from high returns to capital where capital is scarce.

ECON-NL-ELITE-349.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-ELITE-349.q: A government gives firms tax incentives to buy machines, funds technical colleges, and expands broadband infrastructure. Which productivity factors are targeted?
ECON-NL-ELITE-349.feedback: Machines are physical capital, technical colleges build human capital, and broadband supports technological/infrastructure capacity.

ECON-NL-ELITE-350.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-ELITE-350.q: Which change most clearly increases human capital rather than physical capital?
options: Workers complete coding and equipment-maintenance training
ECON-NL-ELITE-350.feedback: Training raises worker knowledge and skills, which is human capital.

ECON-NL-ELITE-351.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-ELITE-351.q: A country has abundant natural resources but weak education, poor infrastructure, and unstable property rights. What is the best growth interpretation?
options: Resources need skills, capital, technology, and institutions
Natural resources guarantee high living standards
Education is irrelevant if resources are abundant
GDP must equal natural resource value
ECON-NL-ELITE-351.feedback: Natural resources help, but productivity also depends on skills, capital, technology, and institutions.

ECON-NL-ELITE-352.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-ELITE-352.q: A new algorithm lets firms produce the same output with fewer machines and workers. Which factor best explains the improvement?
ECON-NL-ELITE-352.feedback: A better production method is technological knowledge.

ECON-NL-ELITE-353.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-ELITE-353.q: A country doubles its capital stock, but output rises by less than double. Which concept is most directly illustrated?
ECON-NL-ELITE-353.feedback: Diminishing returns means additional capital raises output, but by less and less as capital accumulates.

ECON-NL-ELITE-354.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-ELITE-354.q: A poor country receives basic tractors for farms that previously used hand tools. A rich country adds another advanced tractor to farms already full of equipment. Which investment likely has the higher marginal return?
options: The poor country's investment, because capital is scarcer
The rich country's investment, because diminishing returns never apply
ECON-NL-ELITE-354.feedback: Capital tends to have higher marginal returns when it is scarce.

ECON-NL-ELITE-355.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-ELITE-355.q: Which statement best connects diminishing returns and the catch-up effect?
options: Scarce capital has high returns, which fall as capital accumulates
Poor countries grow slower because every new unit of capital has zero return
Rich countries grow faster because diminishing returns help them
Catch-up occurs because inflation is lower in rich countries
ECON-NL-ELITE-355.feedback: The catch-up effect relies on high returns to scarce capital, but diminishing returns eventually reduce those gains.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9054.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9054.q: A factory adds machinery but productivity barely changes. After operator training, output rises with the same machines and labor hours. A manager concludes that machines have no productive value. Which interpretation best fits both stages?
options: Training helped realize the value of complementary capital; the first stage did not show that machines were useless
Training proves all earlier spending on machines should be subtracted from GDP
The later gain must be more physical capital because worker skills are unchanged by training
The data prove training raises output equally in every factory, regardless of equipment
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9054.feedback: The second stage changes human capital while holding physical inputs fixed. Its effect can reflect complementarity between skills and machinery. A weak result before training does not identify a zero contribution from capital.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9055.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9055.q: A country discovers oil but has weak courts, low education, and poor infrastructure. Why might productivity remain low?
options: Resources alone do not guarantee high productivity
Oil is not a natural resource
Education matters only in service economies
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9055.feedback: Natural resources can help, but productivity depends on several complementary factors.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9056.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9056.q: Two plants initially use the same machines and hours. Plant A adopts a freely available scheduling method and raises output 8%. Plant B trains operators without changing its method and raises output 8%. What can be inferred about productivity sources?
options: A changed technological knowledge and B human capital; equal output gains do not make the mechanisms identical
Both added physical capital because output rose without more labor hours
Both changed natural resources because the gain has the same size
A’s gain is human capital and B’s is technology solely because both involve information
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9056.feedback: A new production method is technological knowledge; skills acquired by workers are human capital. Equal measured gains do not identify a common mechanism or prove the two interventions would have equal effects elsewhere.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9057.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9057.q: A country builds ports, roads, and power grids while also expanding vocational education. Which factors are increased?
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9057.feedback: Infrastructure is physical capital; vocational education builds human capital.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9058.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9058.q: With labor, skills and technology fixed, output at 10, 20 and 30 identical machines is 100, 160 and 200 units. A planner predicts that 40 machines must yield 260. Which assessment follows from the observed pattern?
options: The successive gains are 60 and 40; continued diminishing marginal returns would put the next gain below 40
The observed average gain is 50, so 40 machines must yield exactly 250
The capital stock doubled once, proving output must double at 40 machines
The last gain was 40, so every later ten machines must add exactly 40
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9058.feedback: Equal capital increments add 60 then 40 units while other inputs are fixed. If the diminishing-returns pattern continues, the next increment adds less than 40; the table alone does not supply an exact future output level.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9059.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9059.q: A low-capital economy gets basic tools and output jumps sharply. Later, additional tools add smaller gains. Which pattern is this?
options: Catch-up effect followed by diminishing returns
CPI substitution bias followed by inflation
Frictional unemployment followed by cyclical unemployment
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9059.feedback: Capital is highly productive when scarce, but additional capital eventually yields smaller gains.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9065.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9065.q: A poor country and a rich country both add $1,000 of capital per worker. Why might the poor country gain more output per worker?
options: Poor countries do not face diminishing returns
The CPI is lower in poor countries
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9065.feedback: The catch-up effect depends on higher marginal returns to capital where capital is scarce.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3012.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3012.feedback: Physical capital is the equipment and structures used to produce goods and services.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3013.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3013.q: If workers receive better machinery, what should happen to productivity, other things equal?
options: It no longer depends on output
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3013.feedback: Better machinery usually allows workers to produce more output per hour.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3014.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3014.q: A business has 10 workers and 20 machines. It adds 10 more machines while employment stays the same. What has increased?
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3014.feedback: More machines with the same number of workers means more physical capital per worker.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3015.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3015.q: Two countries use similar machines, but one invests heavily in worker education and training. Which productivity factor differs most?
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3015.feedback: Education and training build human capital—the knowledge and skills workers bring to production.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3016.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3016.q: A country expands technical training and apprenticeship programs. Which productivity factor increases most directly?
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3016.feedback: Training programs increase worker skills, which raises human capital.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3017.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3017.q: Two factories use the same machines, but one has better-trained workers. Why might that factory produce more?
options: Its workers have more human capital
It has more natural resources by definition
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3017.feedback: Better-trained workers can use tools and processes more effectively.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3018.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3018.q: Which item is a natural resource used in production?
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3018.feedback: Natural resources are inputs supplied by nature, such as land, water, minerals, and oil.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3019.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3019.q: A new drilling method allows firms to extract more oil with the same workers and equipment. Which factor changed most directly?
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3019.feedback: A better method of production is technological knowledge.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3020.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3020.q: A country discovers large copper deposits but lacks skilled workers and roads. What is the best interpretation?
options: Resources help, but skills and capital also matter
Natural resources alone guarantee high living standards
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3020.feedback: Natural resources are useful, but they work best alongside skills, infrastructure, and technology.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3021.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3021.q: A factory keeps the workforce fixed and adds identical machines. Each new machine raises output by less than the previous one. What principle is shown?
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3021.feedback: With other inputs fixed, each additional unit of capital eventually adds less output.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3022.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3022.q: A worker with no tools gains a hammer and becomes much more productive. A worker with ten hammers gains an eleventh and barely improves. What does this show?
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3022.feedback: The extra hammer matters more when capital is scarce.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3023.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3023.q: Capital per worker doubles, but output per worker rises by only 25%. What does that suggest?
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3023.feedback: Output rose less than proportionally to capital, which is consistent with diminishing returns.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3024.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
options: Scarce capital can produce faster catch-up growth
Growth rates are unrelated to capital
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3024.feedback: The catch-up effect occurs when capital-scarce economies can gain more from new investment.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3025.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3025.q: Why might a poor country gain more from one additional machine than a rich country?
options: Scarcer capital can have a higher marginal return
The rich country cannot use machines
The poor country has no workers
Machines count only in poor countries
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3025.feedback: Capital tends to have a higher marginal product when it is scarce.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3026.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3026.q: Country A has very little capital per worker and Country B has abundant capital per worker. If each receives the same new equipment, which country may grow faster from that addition?
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3026.feedback: Country A may gain more because capital is scarcer there.

PM2B3-SRC-EB-001.q: A worker receives a new machine that raises output with the same labor time. Which productivity input increased most directly?
PM2B3-SRC-EB-001.commonError: Treats every increase in capital as producing the same output gain.
PM2B3-SRC-EB-001.feedback: Providing a new machine increases physical capital per worker; with labor time unchanged, that can raise output per worker.

PM2B3-SRC-EB-002.q: In GROWTH-01, why does an equal small addition to capital have greater output potential near point A than near point B?
options: Point A has more output per worker than B
The curve is vertical near B
Capital has no relationship to output near A
The curve is steeper near A
PM2B3-SRC-EB-002.commonError: Treats every increase in capital as producing the same output gain.
PM2B3-SRC-EB-002.feedback: The curve is steeper near A, so an equal small capital addition produces a larger additional output per worker there.

PM2B3-SRC-EB-003.q: A new production method lets the same workers and machines produce more output. Which source of productivity improved?
PM2B3-SRC-EB-003.commonError: Confuses technological knowledge with merely owning more machines.
PM2B3-SRC-EB-003.feedback: Technology raises the efficiency with which available inputs are transformed into output.

PM2B3-SRC-FB-004.q: GROWTH-01 is upward sloping but becomes flatter as capital per worker rises. Which concept is represented by that shape?
options: A fixed level of productivity at all capital levels
PM2B3-SRC-FB-004.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
PM2B3-SRC-FB-004.feedback: An upward-sloping curve that becomes flatter means capital still raises output per worker, but each additional unit adds less: diminishing returns to capital.

PM2B3-SRC-FB-005.q: A low-capital country buys machinery, but workers lack training and firms cannot reliably obtain electricity. Why might catch-up remain limited?
options: Physical capital works with human capital, infrastructure, and other complementary inputs
Catch-up requires natural resources and nothing else
More machines always guarantee convergence regardless of other conditions
Human capital matters only after a country becomes rich
PM2B3-SRC-FB-005.commonError: Treats every increase in capital as producing the same output gain.
PM2B3-SRC-FB-005.feedback: Catch-up is limited because capital works with skills, reliable infrastructure, and institutions; machinery alone cannot overcome missing complements.

PM2B3-SRC-FB-006.q: Two countries add the same number of machines. One also improves worker training and production methods. Why can its productivity gain be larger?
options: Machines reduce productivity whenever training also rises
Human capital and technology affect only total population
Natural resources must fall when technology improves
Capital can complement human capital and technological knowledge
PM2B3-SRC-FB-006.commonError: Treats worker knowledge and skills as physical equipment.
PM2B3-SRC-FB-006.feedback: Training and better production methods complement machines, so the same equipment can generate a larger productivity gain.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9119.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9119.q: Boss Audit: A country improves schools but has no reliable electricity, roads, or legal protection for investors. What limits growth?
options: Skills need capital, infrastructure, and reliable institutions
Legal institutions matter only for unemployment
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9119.feedback: Productivity depends on complementary factors, not education alone.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9120.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9120.q: Two equal additions to capital per worker produce output gains of 9 and 6 with skills and technology fixed. A later 9-unit gain occurs after a new production method is introduced. Does that last observation refute diminishing returns to capital?
options: No; the first two gains compare capital with other inputs fixed, while technology changed in the third

options: Unemployed divided by labor force times 100
Unemployed divided by adult population times 100
Not in labor force divided by employed times 100
ECON-NL-EASY-62.feedback: The unemployment rate is unemployed workers divided by the labor force.

ECON-NL-EASY-63.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
ECON-NL-EASY-63.q: The labor force participation rate is calculated as:
options: Labor force divided by adult population times 100
Unemployed divided by labor force times 100
ECON-NL-EASY-63.feedback: Labor force participation measures the share of adults in the labor force.

ECON-NL-EASY-67.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-EASY-67.q: A person with a paid job is classified as:
ECON-NL-EASY-67.feedback: A person with a paid job is employed.

ECON-NL-EASY-68.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-EASY-68.q: A person without a job who has actively looked for work in the last four weeks is classified as:
ECON-NL-EASY-68.feedback: Someone without a job who is actively looking is unemployed.

ECON-NL-EASY-69.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-EASY-69.q: A retired person who is not looking for work is classified as:
ECON-NL-EASY-69.feedback: People not working and not looking for work are not in the labor force.

ECON-NL-EASY-70.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
ECON-NL-EASY-70.q: A discouraged worker is usually counted as:
ECON-NL-EASY-70.feedback: Discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed because they are not actively looking for work.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-163.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-163.q: If 2 million unemployed workers become discouraged and stop looking for work, what happens immediately to the measured unemployment rate?
options: It rises because discouraged workers become unemployed
It falls because they leave the labor force
It is unchanged because employment rises
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-163.feedback: Discouraged workers leave the labor force, which can lower the measured unemployment rate.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-165.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-165.q: A parent who stays home full-time and is not seeking paid work is classified as:
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-165.feedback: Someone not working and not looking for paid work is not in the labor force.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-166.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-166.q: A person works one hour for pay during the survey week while looking for full-time work. How is the person classified?
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-166.feedback: A person who does any paid work during the survey period is counted as employed.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-167.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-167.q: A worker without a job sends out applications during the last four weeks. How is the worker classified?
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-167.feedback: Actively looking for work while jobless means the person is unemployed.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-168.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-168.q: A discouraged worker wants a job but stopped searching because they believe no jobs are available. How is this worker classified in official unemployment statistics?
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-168.feedback: Discouraged workers are not in the labor force because they are not actively searching.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-169.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-169.q: Which classification is most likely to make the unemployment rate understate labor market weakness?
options: Counting discouraged workers as not in the labor force
Counting active job seekers as unemployed
Counting unemployed workers in the labor force
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-169.feedback: Discouraged workers are excluded from unemployment, which can hide labor market weakness.

ECON-NL-HARD-260.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
ECON-NL-HARD-260.q: An economy has 180 million employed, 12 million unemployed, and 68 million not in the labor force. What are the unemployment rate and labor force participation rate?
ECON-NL-HARD-260.feedback: Labor force = 192M; unemployment = 12/192 = 6.25%; adult population = 260M; participation = 192/260 = 73.85%.

ECON-NL-HARD-261.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
ECON-NL-HARD-261.q: An economy has 95 employed, 5 unemployed, and 50 not in the labor force. Ten people who were not in the labor force begin looking for work but do not find jobs. What is the new unemployment rate?
ECON-NL-HARD-261.feedback: Unemployed rises to 15 and labor force rises to 110, so unemployment = 15/110 = 13.6%.

ECON-NL-HARD-262.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
ECON-NL-HARD-262.q: An economy has 100 employed and 20 unemployed. Five unemployed workers find jobs, while five others stop looking. What happens to the unemployment rate?
options: It falls because unemployment decreases and the labor force shrinks
It stays unchanged because ten workers changed status
ECON-NL-HARD-262.feedback: Unemployed falls to 10 and labor force falls to 115, so the unemployment rate falls from 16.7% to about 8.7%.

ECON-NL-HARD-263.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
ECON-NL-HARD-263.q: If the unemployment rate falls because many jobless workers stop searching, what is the best interpretation?
options: Measured unemployment fell, but the labor market may not have improved
ECON-NL-HARD-263.feedback: A falling unemployment rate can be misleading if discouraged workers leave the labor force.

ECON-NL-HARD-265.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-HARD-265.q: A person has no job, wants work, is available, but has not searched in six weeks because they think no jobs exist. How is this person classified and why does it matter?
options: Outside the labor force; this can understate labor-market weakness
Unemployed; all jobless people are counted
Structurally employed; skills do not matter
ECON-NL-HARD-265.feedback: Without active search, discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed, which can understate weakness.

ECON-NL-HARD-266.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-HARD-266.q: A worker has a part-time job but wants full-time work. How is the worker officially classified?
options: Employed, even though the situation may show underemployment
Unemployed because the worker wants more hours
Not in the labor force because the job is part time
Discouraged because the worker is dissatisfied
ECON-NL-HARD-266.feedback: Part-time workers are counted as employed, even when they would prefer full-time work.

ECON-NL-HARD-267.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-HARD-267.q: Which case creates the biggest problem for interpreting the official unemployment rate?
options: A large increase in discouraged workers
A worker voluntarily switches jobs and searches for one week
A student works part time by choice
ECON-NL-HARD-267.feedback: Discouraged workers are excluded from measured unemployment, hiding some labor market distress.

ECON-NL-HARD-268.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
ECON-NL-HARD-268.q: A laid-off engineer searches actively for work in the same field. A retired teacher does not want work. A discouraged factory worker wants work but stopped searching. Who is counted as unemployed?
options: The engineer and discouraged factory worker
ECON-NL-HARD-268.feedback: Only jobless people actively searching are counted as unemployed.

ECON-NL-HARD-269.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-HARD-269.q: Why does the official unemployment rate miss some labor market pain?
options: It misses discouraged workers and involuntary part-time work
It counts all adults as unemployed
ECON-NL-HARD-269.feedback: The unemployment rate is useful but misses discouraged workers and underemployment.

ECON-NL-ELITE-360.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
ECON-NL-ELITE-360.q: An economy has 155 million employed, 9 million unemployed, and 96 million not in the labor force. What are the unemployment rate and labor force participation rate?
ECON-NL-ELITE-360.feedback: Labor force = 164M; unemployment = 9/164 = 5.49%; adult population = 260M; participation = 164/260 = 63.08%.

ECON-NL-ELITE-361.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
ECON-NL-ELITE-361.q: An economy has 120 employed, 8 unemployed, and 72 not in the labor force. Four unemployed workers find jobs, and six people outside the labor force begin searching but do not find work. What is the new unemployment rate?
ECON-NL-ELITE-361.feedback: New employed = 124, unemployed = 10, labor force = 134. Unemployment = 10/134 = 7.46%.

ECON-NL-ELITE-362.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
ECON-NL-ELITE-362.q: Adult population is 300 million. Labor force participation is 62%. The unemployment rate is 5%. How many people are unemployed?

ECON-NL-ELITE-363.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
ECON-NL-ELITE-363.q: The unemployment rate falls from 6% to 5%, but employment also falls. What likely happened?
options: Some unemployed workers left the labor force
Every discouraged worker found a job
ECON-NL-ELITE-363.feedback: The unemployment rate can fall even when employment falls if enough jobless workers stop searching.

ECON-NL-ELITE-364.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
ECON-NL-ELITE-364.q: An economy has 200 adults. 130 are employed and 10 are unemployed. If 10 employed workers retire and stop looking for work, what happens to labor force participation?
ECON-NL-ELITE-364.feedback: Initial labor force = 140, participation = 70%. New labor force = 130, participation = 65%.

ECON-NL-ELITE-365.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-ELITE-365.q: A person works 5 hours per week for pay but wants 40 hours. How is this person treated in the headline unemployment rate?
options: Counted as employed, even though underemployment is present
Counted as unemployed because they want more hours
Counted as not in the labor force
ECON-NL-ELITE-365.feedback: The official unemployment rate counts part-time workers as employed, even if they want full-time work.

ECON-NL-ELITE-366.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-ELITE-366.q: A survey has 84 adults working for pay, including 14 seeking more hours; 6 available jobless adults applied last week; 30 jobless adults are not searching. Which official count and limitation are correct?
options: Labor force 90 and unemployment about 6.7%; underemployment among paid workers is not in that rate
Labor force 104 and unemployment about 19.2%; add those seeking more hours to unemployment
Labor force 120 and unemployment 5%; use every adult in the denominator
Labor force 76 and unemployment about 7.9%; exclude part-time paid workers
ECON-NL-ELITE-366.feedback: All 84 paid workers are employed, including those wanting more hours. Add the 6 active, available seekers for LF = 90; 6/90 ≈ 6.7%. The rate does not measure all of the part-time workers’ unmet demand for hours.

ECON-NL-ELITE-367.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-ELITE-367.q: Which change would reduce the unemployment rate without improving the number of people employed?
options: Unemployed workers become discouraged and stop searching
Discouraged workers begin looking for jobs
ECON-NL-ELITE-367.feedback: When unemployed workers stop searching, they leave the labor force and measured unemployment can fall.

ECON-NL-ELITE-368.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
ECON-NL-ELITE-368.q: A recession causes job loss, and some unemployed workers become discouraged. Why might the unemployment rate understate the recession's damage?
options: Discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed once they stop searching
All discouraged workers are counted as employed
The unemployment rate includes only retired people
ECON-NL-ELITE-368.feedback: Discouraged workers leave the labor force, which can hide labor market weakness.

ECON-NL-ELITE-369.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-ELITE-369.q: A survey classifies people as employed, unemployed, or not in the labor force. Which person is most likely misread by the headline unemployment rate as doing better than they are?
options: A part-time worker who wants full-time work
A full-time worker satisfied with their job
A retiree who does not want work
ECON-NL-ELITE-369.feedback: Involuntary part-time workers are counted as employed, even though their labor situation is weak.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9067.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9067.q: A labor survey starts with 132 employed, 12 unemployed and 56 other adults. Then 4 unemployed find jobs, 3 stop searching, 5 outsiders start searching without finding work, and 2 employed retire. All job seekers are available. What are the new unemployment and participation rates?
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9067.feedback: Employment becomes 132 + 4 - 2 = 134 and unemployment 12 - 4 - 3 + 5 = 10. The labor force is 144 of 200 adults, so participation is 72% and unemployment is 10/144 ≈ 6.9%. The entering and leaving flows happen to offset in total participation.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9068.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9068.q: There are 200 adults, labor-force participation is 75%, and unemployment is 8%. Next month 6 unemployed stop searching, 6 employed retire, and 4 outsiders start searching without finding work. With everyone otherwise unchanged and seekers available, which final account is correct?
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9068.feedback: Initially LF = 150, U = 12 and E = 138. After the flows E = 132, U = 12 - 6 + 4 = 10 and LF = 142. Thus U/LF ≈ 7.0% and LF/adults = 71%. A lower unemployment rate coexists with fewer people employed.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9069.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9069.q: An economy has 90 employed, 10 unemployed, and 50 not in the labor force. Five employed workers lose jobs and search; five unemployed workers stop searching. What happens to unemployment rate?
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9069.feedback: Employed falls to 85. Five newly unemployed workers replace five workers who stop searching, so unemployed remains 10 and the labor force falls to 95. The rate is 10/95 = 10.53%.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9070.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9070.q: A population of 200 adults is unchanged. The unemployment rate stays at 6%, while participation falls from 75% to 70%. Which employment change and interpretation follow?
options: Employment falls by 9.4; a stable unemployment rate does not imply a stable number of jobs
Employment stays at 141; a stable rate fixes employment
Employment falls by 10; every labor-force exit must be an employed worker
Employment rises by 9.4; lower participation indicates more jobs
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9070.feedback: The labor force falls from 150 to 140. Employment is 94% of each total: 141 initially and 131.6 afterward, a decline of 9.4. The unchanged unemployment rate is a ratio, not an unchanged employment count.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9071.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9071.q: A jobless worker applied to three jobs last week. Another jobless worker wants work but last searched two months ago. A third works 3 hours per week but wants full-time work. How are they classified?
options: Unemployed; not in labor force; employed
Employed; unemployed; not in labor force
Not in labor force; unemployed; employed
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9071.feedback: Recent active search means unemployed; no recent search means not in labor force; any paid work means employed.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9072.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9072.q: Which case makes the headline unemployment rate look better than the actual labor market experience?
options: A rise in discouraged workers and involuntary part-time workers
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9072.feedback: Discouraged and involuntary part-time workers are not fully captured by the headline unemployment rate.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9081.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9081.q: A report says unemployment fell from 20 to 12 while employment rose from 180 to 184. Adult population is fixed at 250, and the only flows were unemployed people finding jobs or stopping search. Which decomposition and participation change are implied?
options: 4 found jobs and 4 left search; participation fell from 80% to 78.4%
4 found jobs and 8 left search; participation fell to 76.8%
4 left search and none found jobs; the employment rise is unrelated
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9081.feedback: The employment rise identifies 4 job findings. Of the 8-person unemployment decline, the remaining 4 are exits. LF falls from 200 to 196, so participation falls from 80% to 78.4%. Both hiring and withdrawal contributed to the lower headline rate.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9084.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9084.q: Two districts have the same unemployment rate and population. One has lower participation and a larger share of employed people working part time because full-time work is unavailable. Which additional comparison is best before calling their labor markets equally strong?
options: Compare employment per adult and desired versus actual hours; the headline rate omits both differences
Compare only total unemployment; equal unemployment rates guarantee equal counts
Count all involuntary part-time workers as unemployed before applying the official definition
Exclude discouraged workers from every indicator because they are outside the labor force
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9084.feedback: Unemployment divides job seekers by the labor force. Lower participation can lower employment per adult even at the same rate, while involuntary part-time workers remain employed. Additional participation and hours evidence is needed for the broader assessment.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9089.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9089.q: If measured unemployment falls because 1M unemployed workers become discouraged, while employment is unchanged, what happens to labor force participation?
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9089.feedback: Discouraged workers leave the labor force, so labor force participation falls.

ECON-NL-EASY-64.commonError: Forgetting that the labor force includes employed plus unemployed workers.
ECON-NL-EASY-64.q: If 90 people are employed and 10 are unemployed, what is the labor force?

ECON-NL-EASY-65.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
ECON-NL-EASY-65.q: If 10 people are unemployed and the labor force is 100, what is the unemployment rate?

ECON-NL-EASY-66.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
ECON-NL-EASY-66.q: If the labor force is 160 million and the adult population is 250 million, what is the labor force participation rate?

ECON-NL-HARD-264.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
ECON-NL-HARD-264.q: Adult population is 250 million, labor force participation is 64%, and unemployment is 8 million. How many people are employed?
ECON-NL-HARD-264.feedback: Labor force = 0.64 x 250 = 160 million. Employed = 160 - 8 = 152 million.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-160.commonError: Forgetting that the labor force includes employed plus unemployed workers.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-160.q: An economy has 140 million employed people, 10 million unemployed people, and 50 million people not in the labor force. What is the labor force?

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-161.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-161.q: Using 140 million employed and 10 million unemployed, what is the unemployment rate?

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-162.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-162.q: If the labor force is 150 million and the adult population is 200 million, what is the labor force participation rate?

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-164.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-164.q: An economy has 90 employed, 10 unemployed, and 50 not in the labor force. If 5 unemployed workers stop looking, what is the new unemployment rate?
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-164.feedback: New unemployed = 5 and new labor force = 95, so unemployment = 5/95 = 5.3%.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4000.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4000.q: An economist asks: an adult has no job, wants work, and applied for jobs last week. How is this person classified?
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4000.feedback: A jobless person who is actively searching is counted as unemployed.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4001.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4001.q: A jobless worker wants work but stopped searching because they think no jobs are available. What happens to official unemployment statistics?
options: The worker is not counted as unemployed
The worker is counted as employed
The worker raises employment and unemployment
The worker is counted as unemployed forever
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4001.feedback: Discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed once they stop actively searching.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4002.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4002.q: An economy has 100 employed, 10 unemployed, and 40 not in the labor force. If 5 unemployed workers become discouraged, what is the new unemployment rate?
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4002.feedback: Unemployed falls to 5 and labor force falls to 105, so unemployment is 5/105 = 4.76%.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4003.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4003.q: A survey records 126 employed adults, 14 available jobless adults actively searching, and 60 adults outside the labor force. Which participation calculation is correct, and how does it differ from unemployment?
options: 7% participation; unemployment and participation are the same ratio
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4003.feedback: Participation is (126 + 14)/(126 + 14 + 60) = 70%. Unemployment instead divides the 14 unemployed by the labor force of 140, yielding 10%. The denominators answer different questions.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4004.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4004.q: The unemployment rate falls, but labor force participation also falls sharply. What is the best interpretation?
options: Some workers may have stopped searching
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4004.feedback: A falling unemployment rate can be misleading if workers leave the labor force.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4005.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4005.q: Adult population is 250 million. Employed workers are 150 million and unemployed workers are 10 million. What is the labor force participation rate?

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4006.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4006.q: A jobless adult who had stopped searching accepts a paid part-time job but still wants full-time work. With other adults unchanged, which immediate changes follow?
options: Employment and the labor force rise; involuntary part-time work can remain
Unemployment rises because the worker still wants a full-time job
Employment rises but the labor force stays fixed because the job is part time
Participation falls because part-time employment is outside the labor force
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4006.feedback: The worker moves from outside the labor force to employed. Both employment and the labor force rise, while wanting more hours does not change the official employed classification. The hours shortfall remains relevant to labor-market well-being.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4007.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4007.q: Why can involuntary part-time work make the unemployment rate look better than the labor market feels?
options: Part-time workers are counted as employed even if they want more hours
Part-time workers are counted as unemployed twice
Part-time work is excluded from the labor force
Part-time workers are counted as discouraged
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4007.feedback: The headline unemployment rate does not fully capture underemployment.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4008.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4008.q: An economy has 120 employed, 12 unemployed, and 68 not in the labor force. Four unemployed workers find jobs, and four employed workers move to part-time work but keep paid jobs. What is the new unemployment rate?
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4008.feedback: New employed = 124, unemployed = 8, labor force = 132. Unemployment = 8/132 = 6.1%. Part-time workers remain employed.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4038.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4038.q: An economy has 200 adults, 120 employed, 10 unemployed, and 70 not in the labor force. Then 10 unemployed workers become discouraged. What are the new unemployment rate and participation rate?
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4038.feedback: Unemployed becomes 0 and labor force becomes 120. Unemployment = 0%; participation = 120/200 = 60%.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4039.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4039.q: An economist synthesizes this evidence: a worker is counted as employed even though they want full-time work, another worker is not counted as unemployed because they stopped searching, and actual unemployment is above the natural rate. What is the combined lesson?
options: The headline rate misses underemployment and discouraged workers; excess unemployment signals cyclical weakness
The headline unemployment rate captures all labor pain perfectly
Actual unemployment above natural unemployment means no recessionary pressure
Discouraged workers raise the unemployment rate
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4039.feedback: This pulls together underemployment, discouraged workers, and cyclical unemployment.

P52B-S4-UNEM-B1-001.q: A worker has a part-time job but is actively searching for full-time work. How is the worker classified in official labor statistics?
options: Unemployed, because the worker wants more hours.
Employed, because the worker has a paid job.
Outside the labor force, because the job is part time.
Discouraged, because the worker is searching for another job.
P52B-S4-UNEM-B1-001.commonError: Classifying an underemployed worker as unemployed.
P52B-S4-UNEM-B1-001.feedback: Official employment status is based on having work, not on whether the worker wants additional hours.

P52B-S4-UNEM-B1-002.q: A jobless adult is available to work but has not searched during the past four weeks. How is this person usually classified?
P52B-S4-UNEM-B1-002.commonError: Ignoring the active-search requirement for official unemployment.
P52B-S4-UNEM-B1-002.feedback: A jobless person generally must be available and actively searching to be counted as unemployed.

P52B-S4-UNEM-B1-003.q: Which equation defines the labor force?
options: Labor force = employed people - discouraged workers.
Labor force = working-age population - employed people.
Labor force = employed people + unemployed people.
P52B-S4-UNEM-B1-003.commonError: Including everyone in the population or excluding officially unemployed workers.
P52B-S4-UNEM-B1-003.feedback: The labor force contains people who are employed plus people who are jobless and actively seeking work.

P52B-S4-UNEM-B2-001.q: A discouraged worker stops searching for a job while no one finds employment. What can happen to the official unemployment rate?
options: It can fall because the worker leaves unemployment and the labor force.
It must rise because employment did not increase.
It stays unchanged because discouraged workers remain unemployed.
It becomes zero because the labor force shrinks.
P52B-S4-UNEM-B2-001.commonError: Assuming the unemployment rate can fall only when employment rises.
P52B-S4-UNEM-B2-001.feedback: When a discouraged worker exits the labor force, both the number unemployed and the denominator fall, which can lower the rate.

P52B-S4-UNEM-B2-002.q: An economy has 900 employed people, 100 unemployed people, and 200 adults outside the labor force. What are the unemployment and labor-force participation rates?
options: The unemployment rate is 8.3 percent and participation is 75 percent.
The unemployment rate is 10 percent and participation is about 83.3 percent.
The unemployment rate is 10 percent and participation is 100 percent.
The unemployment rate is 12 percent and participation is about 66.7 percent.
P52B-S4-UNEM-B2-002.commonError: Using the adult population as the unemployment-rate denominator or omitting unemployed workers from participation.
P52B-S4-UNEM-B2-002.feedback: The labor force is 1,000, so unemployment is 100/1,000 = 10 percent; participation is 1,000/1,200 = 83.3 percent.

P52B-S4-UNEM-B2-003.q: An employed worker loses a job and immediately begins an active search. What happens initially?
options: Employment and labor force both rise as the search begins.
Unemployment falls because active search counts as employment.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9078.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9079.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
