It cannot change because the natural rate is fixed.
P52B-S1-NRU-E-003.commonError: Assuming better matching affects only cyclical unemployment.
P52B-S1-NRU-E-003.feedback: Faster matching shortens normal job search and can lower the natural rate.

PM2B4-NRU-E-001.q: If actual unemployment equals the natural rate, which unemployment component is approximately zero?
PM2B4-NRU-E-001.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
PM2B4-NRU-E-001.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

PM2B4-NRU-E-002.q: Which change is most likely to raise the natural rate rather than merely raise cyclical unemployment?
options: A temporary recession that reduces aggregate demand
A one-quarter fall in consumer spending
A short-lived decline in business confidence
A lasting increase in worker-skill mismatch
PM2B4-NRU-E-002.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
PM2B4-NRU-E-002.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-179.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-179.q: Why does the natural rate of unemployment remain positive in the long run?
options: Normal job search and structural mismatches persist
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-179.feedback: The natural rate includes frictional and structural unemployment that persist in normal times.

P52B-S1-NRU-M-001.q: A rapid shift away from coal production leaves many workers without the skills demanded by expanding industries. What is the most likely effect?
options: Cyclical unemployment must fall to zero.
The natural rate must fall because jobs changed.
Structural unemployment and the natural rate may rise.
P52B-S1-NRU-M-001.commonError: Classifying a persistent skill mismatch as only cyclical unemployment.
P52B-S1-NRU-M-001.feedback: Sectoral change can raise structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

P52B-S1-NRU-M-002.q: Actual unemployment is below the estimated natural rate. Which interpretation is strongest?
options: The labor market is unusually tight, with possible inflation pressure.
The economy has eliminated every form of unemployment.
Structural unemployment must have fallen permanently to zero.
The economy must be operating with a recessionary output gap.
P52B-S1-NRU-M-002.commonError: Equating below-natural unemployment with zero unemployment or recession.
P52B-S1-NRU-M-002.feedback: Unemployment below the natural rate indicates a tight labor market, not the disappearance of frictional and structural unemployment.

P52B-S1-NRU-M-003.q: A temporary collapse in aggregate demand ends, and spending returns to normal. What should happen to unemployment if the natural rate itself did not change?
options: The natural rate rises permanently by the recession increase.
Cyclical unemployment fades, moving actual unemployment toward the natural rate.
Frictional unemployment falls permanently to zero after spending recovers.
Actual unemployment remains at its recession peak even after demand returns.
P52B-S1-NRU-M-003.commonError: Treating a temporary demand-driven unemployment increase as a permanent natural-rate shift.
P52B-S1-NRU-M-003.feedback: When the demand shortfall closes, cyclical unemployment recedes and the unemployment rate moves toward its natural benchmark.

PM2B4-NRU-M-001.q: A strong expansion lowers actual unemployment, but worker matching, skills, and labor-market institutions are unchanged. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: Cyclical unemployment may have fallen without changing the natural rate
The natural rate must have fallen by the same amount as actual unemployment
Structural unemployment must have disappeared permanently
The natural rate becomes zero whenever aggregate demand is strong
PM2B4-NRU-M-001.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
PM2B4-NRU-M-001.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

PM2B4-NRU-M-002.q: A retraining program successfully moves displaced workers into growing occupations. If other conditions are unchanged, what is the most likely effect on the natural rate?
options: It must rise because more workers have changed occupations
It changes only if cyclical unemployment rises
It cannot change because the natural rate is fixed forever
It may fall because structural unemployment is reduced
PM2B4-NRU-M-002.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
PM2B4-NRU-M-002.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

ECON-NL-HARD-279.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-HARD-279.q: In a healthy economy, unemployment is still 4.5%. Which explanation best fits the natural rate?
options: Job search and skill mismatches persist
The economy must be in recession
The unemployment data must be impossible
ECON-NL-HARD-279.feedback: The natural rate remains positive because frictional and structural unemployment persist even in normal times.

PM2B4-NRU-H-001.q: Two economies both have 6% actual unemployment. Economy A has a 4% natural rate and Economy B has a 6% natural rate. Which comparison is strongest?
options: Economy A has more positive cyclical unemployment than Economy B
Both economies have the same cyclical unemployment because actual unemployment is equal
Economy B must be in a deeper recession because its natural rate is higher
Neither economy can have frictional or structural unemployment
PM2B4-NRU-H-001.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
PM2B4-NRU-H-001.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

PM2B4-NRU-H-002.q: A new nationwide matching system shortens the average time between jobs without changing aggregate demand. Which effect is most plausible?
options: Structural unemployment must rise by the same amount
The natural rate cannot respond to matching efficiency
Frictional unemployment and the natural rate may decline
PM2B4-NRU-H-002.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
PM2B4-NRU-H-002.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

PM2B4-NRU-H-003.q: A long-lasting geographic mismatch develops: job openings expand in regions that displaced workers cannot easily move to. What is the most likely natural-rate effect?
options: The natural rate falls automatically because jobs exist somewhere
The natural rate is unchanged whenever total vacancies are positive
Structural unemployment can rise, pushing the natural rate upward
Only cyclical unemployment rises because location never affects structural mismatch
PM2B4-NRU-H-003.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
PM2B4-NRU-H-003.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

PM2B4-NRU-H-004.q: Expansionary demand policy lowers actual unemployment from 7% to 5%, while the estimated natural rate remains 5%. Which interpretation fits the change?
options: A positive cyclical unemployment gap was eliminated
The natural rate fell from 7% to 5% because demand increased
PM2B4-NRU-H-004.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
PM2B4-NRU-H-004.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

PM2B4-NRU-H-005.q: A policy improves occupational retraining but also makes job search somewhat longer by allowing workers to search for better matches. What is the best conclusion about the natural rate?
options: The net effect is ambiguous because structural unemployment may fall while frictional search may rise
The natural rate must fall because every labor-market policy lowers unemployment
The natural rate must rise because longer search is the only relevant channel
Only cyclical unemployment can be affected by either policy
PM2B4-NRU-H-005.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
PM2B4-NRU-H-005.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

ECON-NL-ELITE-379.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-ELITE-379.q: Two economies each have 5% natural unemployment. One combines 1% frictional and 4% structural unemployment; the other combines 3% frictional and 2% structural. Which policy comparison fits these equal totals?
options: The first has more mismatch to address; the second has more scope for faster matching, holding effectiveness comparable
The same natural rate proves their underlying labor-market problems are identical
Only the second has natural unemployment because frictional unemployment is the sole component
Both can reach zero unemployment simply by ending a recession
ECON-NL-ELITE-379.feedback: Both totals equal 5%, but the components differ. A common aggregate benchmark does not establish identical barriers or identical policy priorities. Relevant retraining and matching interventions target different components.

P52B-S1-NRU-EL-001.q: A long recession causes workers to lose skills and attachment to the labor force. Why might unemployment remain elevated after aggregate demand recovers?
options: The natural rate must remain unchanged after every recession.
Cyclical unemployment automatically becomes permanent inflation.
Hysteresis may have raised the natural rate through lasting labor-market damage.
Frictional unemployment can exist only while the economy is expanding.
P52B-S1-NRU-EL-001.commonError: Assuming all recession unemployment disappears without lasting effects.
P52B-S1-NRU-EL-001.feedback: A prolonged downturn can create persistent skill loss or detachment that raises structural unemployment and the natural rate.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9075.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9075.q: An economy has 2% frictional, 3% structural and 2% cyclical unemployment. A recovery eliminates the cyclical component. At the same time, better matching lowers frictional unemployment to 1.5%, with structural unemployment unchanged. What actual and natural rates remain?
options: Both are 4.5%; recovery removed the cyclical component and matching lowered the natural rate
Both are 5%; recovery cannot change any observed unemployment rate
Actual is 2.5% and natural is 4.5%; subtract the cyclical decline again
Both are zero because the recession has ended
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9075.feedback: After recovery, cyclical unemployment is zero. The remaining natural rate is 1.5 + 3 = 4.5%, also the actual rate. Ending the downturn and improving normal matching are distinct channels.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9085.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9085.q: Actual unemployment falls from 9% to 7%. Over the same interval, an estimate of the natural rate falls from 6% to 4%. What happens to the cyclical gap, and what claim would overstate the evidence?
options: The gap stays at 3 points; the lower actual rate alone does not show cyclical weakness diminished
The gap falls 2 points; actual unemployment determines the gap by itself
The gap rises 2 points; a lower natural rate always raises the gap by that amount
The gap becomes zero because both rates fell equally
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9085.feedback: Initially the gap is 9 - 6 = 3 points; finally it is 7 - 4 = 3. Actual unemployment fell with the estimated natural benchmark, so these numbers do not show a smaller cyclical component.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9086.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9086.q: Suppose actual unemployment is 4%, natural unemployment is 5%, and inflationary pressure is rising. What is the likely labor-market interpretation?
options: Unemployment below the natural rate signals a tight labor market
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9086.feedback: Actual unemployment below the natural rate suggests tight labor markets and possible inflationary pressure.

PM2B4-NRU-L-001.q: An economy recovers fully from a recession, yet unemployment settles at a higher level than before because displaced workers lost skills during the long downturn. Which explanation best fits?
options: Lasting labor-market damage may have raised the natural rate
Cyclical unemployment must still equal the entire unemployment rate
The natural rate cannot change after any recession
A higher natural rate means all remaining unemployment is frictional
PM2B4-NRU-L-001.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
PM2B4-NRU-L-001.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

PM2B4-NRU-L-002.q: A retraining reform is expected to lower structural unemployment by 1 percentage point, but longer voluntary search raises frictional unemployment by 0.4 point. Cyclical unemployment is unchanged. Which natural-rate prediction follows, conditional on both estimates?
options: It falls 1.4 points; both changes reduce unemployment
It rises 0.4 point; structural mismatch is outside the natural rate
It stays unchanged; only recessions can move the natural rate
It falls 0.6 point; the policy effects partly offset
PM2B4-NRU-L-002.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
PM2B4-NRU-L-002.feedback: The natural rate includes both structural and frictional unemployment. Its predicted change is -1 + 0.4 = -0.6 percentage point. The net estimate is conditional on the two stated mechanisms, not a guarantee about every retraining policy.

PM2B4-NRU-L-003.q: Actual unemployment falls below the estimated natural rate during a strong expansion. Later it returns to the natural rate with no change in worker skills or matching. What is the best interpretation?
options: Structural unemployment must have been negative during the expansion
The return to the natural rate proves frictional unemployment disappeared temporarily
The temporary gap reflected cyclical conditions rather than a permanent change in the natural rate
The natural rate permanently fell and then rose because actual unemployment moved
PM2B4-NRU-L-003.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
PM2B4-NRU-L-003.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4017.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4017.q: Actual unemployment is 8% and the natural rate is 5%. What is cyclical unemployment?
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4017.feedback: Cyclical unemployment = actual unemployment - natural unemployment = 8 - 5 = 3 percentage points.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4033.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4033.q: An economist asks for the normal baseline: the natural rate of unemployment includes mainly:
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4033.feedback: The natural rate includes unemployment from normal search and structural mismatch.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4034.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4034.q: Why does unemployment remain positive even in a healthy economy?
options: Job search and skill or location mismatches remain
Every economy is always in recession
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4034.feedback: Frictional and structural unemployment remain even when the economy is healthy.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4035.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4035.q: Actual unemployment is 4.2% and the natural rate is 5.0%. What does this suggest?
options: The labor market may be unusually tight
The economy must be in a deep recession
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4035.feedback: Actual unemployment below the natural rate can indicate unusually tight labor markets.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4037.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4037.q: Suppose actual unemployment is 7%, natural unemployment is 4.5%, and labor force participation is falling. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: Cyclical unemployment exists, and falling participation may hide more weakness
The labor market is definitely fully healthy
Participation falling proves structural unemployment is zero
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4037.feedback: Actual unemployment exceeds natural unemployment by 2.5 points, and falling participation can hide additional weakness.

PM2B4-NRU-EB-001.q: Which unemployment is included in the natural rate?
PM2B4-NRU-EB-001.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
PM2B4-NRU-EB-001.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

PM2B4-NRU-EB-002.q: Why can a healthy economy have positive unemployment at the natural rate?
options: Every healthy economy must retain recession-driven cyclical unemployment at all times
The natural rate is a policy target chosen to match the current inflation rate
All workers between paychecks are automatically classified as unemployed
Workers still search for jobs and some skills do not match openings
PM2B4-NRU-EB-002.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
PM2B4-NRU-EB-002.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

PM2B4-NRU-EB-003.q: Which change can lower the natural rate?
options: A short recession that increases cyclical unemployment for several months
A one-month decline in consumer confidence with no lasting matching change
Faster job matching that reduces normal search time
A temporary fall in aggregate demand that raises recession-related layoffs
PM2B4-NRU-EB-003.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
PM2B4-NRU-EB-003.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

PM2B4-NRU-MB-004.q: Actual unemployment falls after aggregate demand recovers, while the natural rate estimate is unchanged. What most likely fell?
PM2B4-NRU-MB-004.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
PM2B4-NRU-MB-004.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

PM2B4-NRU-MB-005.q: A permanent occupational shift leaves displaced workers without skills needed in expanding industries. What is the likely effect?
options: Structural unemployment and the natural rate may rise
The natural rate must fall because some industries expanded
PM2B4-NRU-MB-005.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
PM2B4-NRU-MB-005.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

PM2B4-NRU-MB-006.q: A policy improves retraining and job matching at the same time. What is the strongest natural-rate prediction?
options: The natural rate must rise because more workers change jobs
The natural rate remains fixed by definition
The natural rate may fall as structural mismatch and search time decline
PM2B4-NRU-MB-006.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
PM2B4-NRU-MB-006.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9130.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9130.q: Actual unemployment is 7.8%, natural unemployment is 4.6%. What is cyclical unemployment?
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9130.feedback: Cyclical unemployment = actual unemployment - natural unemployment = 7.8 - 4.6 = 3.2 percentage points.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9131.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9131.q: The economy is expanding, but unemployment remains because workers are switching jobs and some skills no longer match available openings. What explains this?
options: The unemployment rate must be zero in expansions
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9131.feedback: Even in expansions, search and mismatch keep the natural rate positive.

PM2B4-NRU-LB-001.q: A country improves worker retraining and job matching for several years, reducing both persistent mismatch and average search time. What is the strongest long-run labor-market conclusion?
options: The natural rate can fall because structural and frictional unemployment are lower
Only cyclical unemployment can fall because training and matching cannot affect the long-run benchmark
The natural rate must remain fixed even when persistent mismatch and search time both decline
The natural rate becomes exactly zero once matching improves enough to shorten normal job searches
PM2B4-NRU-LB-001.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
PM2B4-NRU-LB-001.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

ECON-NL-NATURAL-RATE-5056.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-NATURAL-RATE-5056.q: The natural rate of unemployment includes:
ECON-NL-NATURAL-RATE-5056.feedback: The natural rate includes frictional and structural unemployment.

P52B-S1-NRU-R-001.q: Which statement corrects the claim that the natural rate is always zero and never changes?
options: It always equals cyclical unemployment in the current year.
It is permanently fixed by the central bank’s inflation target.
It includes only people who have completely stopped seeking work.
It is normally positive and can change with labor-market conditions.
P52B-S1-NRU-R-001.commonError: Treating the natural rate as zero and immutable.
P52B-S1-NRU-R-001.feedback: The natural rate reflects normal search and mismatch, and its level can change over time.

PM2B4-NRU-R-001.q: Actual unemployment is above the natural rate during a recession. Which part of the gap is not itself part of the natural rate?
PM2B4-NRU-R-001.commonError: Adding recession-driven cyclical unemployment into the natural-rate benchmark.
PM2B4-NRU-R-001.feedback: The natural rate reflects frictional and structural unemployment. Cyclical unemployment is the business-cycle deviation of actual unemployment from that benchmark.

ECON-NL-NATURAL-RATE-6036.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
ECON-NL-NATURAL-RATE-6036.q: Actual unemployment is 7% and the natural rate is 5%. What is cyclical unemployment?
ECON-NL-NATURAL-RATE-6036.feedback: Cyclical unemployment = actual unemployment - natural unemployment = 2 percentage points.

gdp-measurement.title: GDP Measurement
gdp-measurement.description: Apply the income–expenditure identity and GDP inclusion and exclusion rules.

easy.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
easy.q: In the circular flow of income and expenditure, why does total income equal total expenditure?
options: Every dollar spent by a buyer becomes income for a seller
Government sets income equal to spending
easy.feedback: Income equals expenditure because one person's spending becomes another person's income.

easy.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
easy.q: If households spend $500 billion buying goods and services, what happens to sellers' income in the basic income-expenditure logic?
options: It only rises if taxes fall
easy.feedback: Spending by buyers becomes income for sellers, so seller income rises by the same amount.

easy.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
easy.q: GDP measures which two sides of economic activity?
easy.feedback: GDP can be measured as total income or total expenditure because those two sides are linked.

easy.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
easy.q: Which statement best defines GDP?
options: The value of final goods and services produced domestically during a period
The total value of all used goods sold in a year
The total income earned only by government workers
The total amount of money printed by the central bank
easy.feedback: GDP is the market value of final goods and services produced within a country during a period.

easy.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
easy.q: A newly produced car sold to a household is counted in GDP because it is:
options: A final good produced in the current period
A used good resold in the current period
easy.feedback: Newly produced final goods are counted in GDP.

easy.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
easy.q: Why are intermediate goods usually not counted separately in GDP?
options: Their value is included in the final good.
They are not produced by firms
easy.feedback: Counting intermediate goods separately would double count their value.

easy.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
easy.q: Which purchase is not counted in current GDP?
options: Buying a used textbook from another student
Buying a new laptop made domestically
easy.feedback: Used goods were counted when first produced, so resale does not count in current GDP.

medium.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
medium.q: A student says GDP can be measured by adding up either total income or total expenditure. Why is that true?
options: Each buyer’s spending becomes a seller’s income
GDP only counts income earned by households, not spending
The government adjusts income until it equals spending
Exports and imports must always be equal
medium.feedback: The income and expenditure approaches match because each dollar spent becomes income to someone else.

medium.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
medium.q: Which example best shows the income-expenditure identity in action?
options: A firm sells a $40 meal and the restaurant receives $40 in revenue
A used car is resold and counted twice in GDP
A government transfer payment raises GDP directly
A household saves money under a mattress
medium.feedback: The restaurant sale shows spending by the buyer becoming income to the seller.

medium.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
medium.q: Which transaction is counted in U.S. GDP?
options: A U.S. company buys shares of another company
A U.S. household buys a used refrigerator
A German tourist pays for a hotel room in Florida
A U.S. citizen buys a used car from a neighbor
medium.feedback: The hotel service is produced in the United States, so it counts in U.S. GDP.

medium.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
medium.q: A laptop produced last year is sold used this year for $700. How does this affect this year's GDP?
options: GDP rises only if the laptop was imported
GDP does not rise from the used-good sale
GDP rises by the original price
medium.feedback: Used goods are not counted in current GDP because they were counted when first produced.

medium.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
medium.q: A homeowner pays a contractor $12,000 to renovate a kitchen. Why is this counted in GDP?
options: It is a market service produced during the current period
It is counted only if paid in cash
medium.feedback: Paid renovation work is current market production and is counted in GDP.

medium.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
medium.q: Which item would be excluded from GDP because it is non-market production?
options: A person mowing their own lawn
medium.feedback: Unpaid work performed for yourself is generally not counted in GDP.

medium.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
medium.q: A U.S. firm earns profits from a factory located in Vietnam. Why is this not part of U.S. GDP?
options: GDP counts production within U.S. borders, not income earned abroad by U.S. residents
Profits are excluded from GDP because GDP measures wage income rather than business income earned by firms
Foreign production enters U.S. GDP when the resulting goods or services are eventually sold to U.S. consumers
GDP assigns production to the owner's home country rather than to the country where the production occurs
medium.feedback: GDP is domestic production. Income earned abroad relates more to national income measures, not U.S. GDP.

hard.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
hard.q: A firm produces $600,000 of final output. It pays $350,000 in wages, $100,000 in rent, $50,000 in interest, and keeps $100,000 in profit. What does this example show about GDP measurement?
options: Expenditure on output and income earned from production both equal $600,000
Only wages count in GDP, so GDP is $350,000
Profit is excluded from GDP, so GDP is $500,000
GDP cannot be measured from income
hard.feedback: The value of final output equals the income generated in producing it: wages, rent, interest, and profit all add to $600,000.

hard.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
hard.q: Suppose expenditure GDP is $22 trillion. Income data show $13 trillion in wages, $3 trillion in rent and interest, $4 trillion in profit, and $2 trillion in other production income. What do these figures show?
options: The income and expenditure approaches both measure GDP at $22 trillion.
The income approach measures $20 trillion because other production income is excluded.
The expenditure approach measures $24 trillion because other production income is added again.
The figures cannot be compared because wages are excluded from the income approach.
hard.feedback: The income categories sum to $22 trillion, matching expenditure GDP. The two approaches measure the same current domestic production from different sides.

hard.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
hard.q: Why would counting both the sale of flour to a bakery and the sale of bread to consumers overstate GDP?
options: It counts the flour twice—alone and inside the bread price
It would exclude the baker's labor income
It would treat bread as an import
It would make income less than expenditure by definition
hard.feedback: Intermediate goods are already embodied in the final good, so counting both creates double counting.

hard.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
hard.q: A U.S. company produces $2 million of software in Ireland and sells it to customers in Europe. How does this affect U.S. GDP?
options: It does not count in U.S. GDP
It counts in U.S. GDP because the firm is U.S.-owned
It counts as U.S. government purchases
It counts only if the software is downloaded in the U.S.
hard.feedback: GDP is based on production within a country's borders, not ownership of the firm.

hard.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
hard.q: A Canadian company produces cars in Tennessee and sells them to U.S. households. How are those cars treated in U.S. GDP?
options: They count because they were produced inside the United States
They do not count because the company is foreign-owned
They count only as transfer payments
hard.feedback: GDP counts production within national borders, regardless of whether the producer is domestically or foreign owned.

hard.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
hard.q: A household pays $2,000 for illegal services and $2,000 for legal market services. Which statement best explains the GDP issue?
options: Legal services count; hidden or illegal production is often missed
Both are always fully counted because all services are visible
Neither counts because services are excluded from GDP
Only illegal activity counts because it is current production
hard.feedback: GDP aims to count market production, but illegal or hidden activity is often excluded or poorly measured.

hard.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
hard.q: A restaurant buys $300 of ingredients and receives $900 from customers for meals, including $100 in tips. Ignoring other complications, how much final restaurant service enters GDP?
hard.feedback: The $300 of ingredients are intermediate inputs. The full $900 customer payment, including the $100 in tips, is final expenditure on restaurant service.

elite.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
elite.q: A country reports $18T in consumption, $5T in investment, $6T in government purchases, $4T in exports, and $5T in imports. Separately, income data show $20T in wages, $4T in rents and interest, and $4T in profits plus other production income. What is the best conclusion?
options: The expenditure and income approaches both imply GDP of $28T
The expenditure approach implies $38T while income implies $28T
Imports should be added, so GDP is $38T
Income cannot be used to measure GDP
elite.feedback: Expenditure GDP = 18 + 5 + 6 + (4 - 5) = 28. Income also totals 20 + 4 + 4 = 28.

elite.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
elite.q: A student argues that total spending must exceed total income because consumers sometimes borrow to spend. What is the best correction?
options: Borrowed spending still becomes sellers’ income
Borrowed spending is excluded from GDP
Income only counts wages, so the student is correct
elite.feedback: Borrowing can finance spending, but the expenditure still becomes income for producers.

elite.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
elite.q: A firm produces $1M of output, sells $800,000 to customers, and adds $200,000 to inventory. It pays $600,000 in wages, $100,000 in rent, $100,000 in interest, and has $200,000 in profit. Which statement is correct?
options: GDP rises by $1M and income generated also totals $1M
GDP rises only by $800,000 because inventories are unsold
GDP rises by $1.2M because inventory is added to sales
elite.feedback: Unsold output is inventory investment, so all $1M counts; income payments also total $1M.

elite.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
elite.q: A mill sells $180 of flour made from $70 of current domestic grain. A baker uses all the flour in $310 of bread sold to households. What are the baker’s value added and GDP across the full domestic chain?
options: $130 at the bakery; $310 across the chain
$240 at the bakery; $560 across the chain
$310 at the bakery; $310 across the chain
$130 at the bakery; $490 across the chain
elite.feedback: The baker adds 310 - 180 = 130. Summing domestic value added gives 70 + (180 - 70) + 130 = 310, equal to the final sale. Intermediate sales cannot be added again.

elite.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
elite.q: A U.S. household buys a new $30,000 car built in Mexico, while a Mexican household buys a new $40,000 car built in Michigan. What is the net effect on U.S. GDP from these two transactions?
elite.feedback: Only the car produced in Michigan counts in U.S. GDP. The imported car affects consumption and imports but not domestic production.

elite.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
elite.q: Which transaction is most likely counted in current GDP?
options: A homeowner pays a licensed contractor to build a new deck
A homeowner builds a deck alone using leftover materials already owned
A household buys shares in a construction company
A collector resells an antique table
elite.feedback: Paid current market production counts. Financial transactions, used-good sales, and unpaid household production generally do not.

elite.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
elite.q: A firm imports $500,000 of parts, adds $300,000 of domestic labor and capital services, and sells the final good domestically for $800,000. What is the contribution to domestic GDP?
elite.feedback: Only domestic value added counts in domestic GDP. Imported inputs are not domestic production.

elite.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
elite.q: A country produces only two goods. In 2025 it produces 100 meals at $20 and 50 laptops at $1,000. It imports 10 additional laptops at $900 each for households. What domestic production value is counted in GDP?
elite.feedback: GDP counts domestic production: 100($20) + 50($1,000) = $52,000. Imported laptops are not domestic production.

legendary.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
legendary.q: A domestic assembler sells $420,000 of new equipment, using $150,000 of imported parts and $90,000 of current domestic components. A clerk adds all three values as domestic GDP. What correction reconciles final spending with domestic value added?
options: $270,000 total domestic GDP, including $180,000 at assembly
$420,000 total domestic GDP, including $330,000 at assembly
$510,000 total domestic GDP, including $420,000 at assembly
$180,000 total domestic GDP, excluding the domestic component makers
legendary.feedback: Final spending of 420,000 less imported inputs of 150,000 yields 270,000 domestic value added. Assembly contributes 420,000 - 150,000 - 90,000 = 180,000; domestic component makers contribute the remaining 90,000. Do not count their output twice.

legendary.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
legendary.q: A firm imports $200,000 of components, adds $150,000 of domestic labor and capital services, and sells the final product domestically for $350,000. How much does this production add to domestic GDP?
legendary.feedback: Only domestic value added counts in domestic GDP. Imported components are not domestic production.

legendary.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
legendary.q: A workshop sells $560 of new furniture after buying $140 of domestic lumber. Its wage bill is $250 and rent plus interest is $90. With no other costs or taxes, which value-added and profit account is consistent?
legendary.feedback: Value added is final output less intermediate lumber: 560 - 140 = 420. Of that, wages and rent/interest absorb 340, leaving profit of 80. Subtracting wages when computing value added would remove income generated by production.

legendary.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
legendary.q: A renovation business bills households $96,000, including $24,000 of imported fixtures. It also brokers an old building for a $6,000 fee; the building sells for $310,000. Ignoring other inputs, what current domestic production and counting rule follow?
options: $78,000; count domestic renovation value and the new brokerage service
$388,000; the old building becomes current output when sold
$102,000; imported fixtures count because households bought them
$72,000; services attached to used assets must also be excluded
legendary.feedback: Domestic renovation value is 96,000 - 24,000 = 72,000. The current brokerage service adds 6,000, while the old building itself is not new output. Total current domestic production is 78,000.

legendary.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
legendary.q: A production audit reports $74 million of final sales and $6 million of new inventories. Domestic production income is $51 million in wages, $9 million in rent and interest, and unreported profit. With no imports, taxes or depreciation adjustments, which result closes both accounts?
legendary.feedback: Current production includes the unsold 6 million, giving expenditure GDP of 80 million. Wages and rent/interest total 60 million, so residual profit is 20 million. Sales alone omit inventory investment.

legendary.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
legendary.q: A used machine changes hands for $40,000 through a broker charging $2,000. A new domestic machine worth $28,000 is produced but remains unsold. An analyst counts only the $40,000 resale as this year’s GDP. What is the corrected contribution?
options: $2,000: unsold output cannot count until purchased
legendary.feedback: The resale transfers an existing asset; the newly produced brokerage service counts. The unsold new machine is inventory investment when produced. Thus current GDP includes 2,000 + 28,000 = 30,000.

legendary.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
legendary.q: A household pays $30 for a restaurant meal, including $5 of sales tax. How should this be interpreted for GDP?
options: Count the final service; the tax is not government purchases
Only the pre-tax $25 counts because taxes are never linked to GDP
Only the $5 tax counts as government purchases
Nothing counts because meals are services
legendary.feedback: GDP counts the market value of final goods and services; taxes do not turn the meal into government purchases.

calculation.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
calculation.q: If total expenditure in an economy is $20 trillion, what is total income in the basic GDP accounting identity?
calculation.feedback: In the basic circular-flow logic, total expenditure equals total income.

calculation.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
calculation.q: A bakery buys flour for $20 and sells bread for $50. What value is counted in GDP from the final bread sale?
calculation.feedback: GDP counts the final good, so the bread sale counts as $50.

calculation.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
calculation.q: A firm buys steel for $80, adds labor and capital services, and sells a machine for $230 to another firm. If the machine is newly produced and used in production, how much does GDP increase?
calculation.feedback: The newly produced machine is a final capital good, so its full market value of $230 is counted.

calculation.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
calculation.q: Suppose firms sell $900 billion of final goods and households, firms, government, and foreigners buy all of it. What should total income from producing those goods equal?
calculation.feedback: Total expenditure on final output becomes total income earned from producing that output.

calculation.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
calculation.q: If total income generated by current production is $18 trillion, what is total expenditure on that production?
calculation.feedback: In GDP accounting, total income and total expenditure are two ways of measuring the same economic activity.

calculation.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
calculation.q: A farmer sells wheat to a miller for $100. The miller sells flour to a baker for $160. The baker sells bread to consumers for $250. How much is added to GDP?
calculation.feedback: GDP counts the final bread sale of $250, not each intermediate transaction separately.

boss.q: Which transaction would be counted in U.S. GDP?
options: A new car produced and sold in the United States this year
A used car resold from one household to another
A parent cooking dinner at home
A stock purchase through a brokerage account
boss.commonError: counts_used_goods_or_financial_transactions_in_gdp
boss.feedback: GDP counts newly produced final goods and services within a country during a period.

boss.q: Which of these items is included in current GDP: a new laptop, a used bike, a homemade dinner, or a stock purchase?
boss.commonError: counts_nonmarket_or_resale_activity
boss.feedback: The new laptop is newly produced and sold in a market. Used goods, home production, and stock trades are not counted the same way.

boss.q: GDP is best defined as:
options: Final domestic production during a period
The total value of all used goods sold this year
The total value of all financial transactions
The amount of money held by households
boss.commonError: counts_financial_transactions_or_used_goods_as_gdp
boss.feedback: GDP measures the market value of final goods and services produced within a country during a period.

boss.q: Why is a tire sold to a car manufacturer usually not counted separately in GDP when the final car is sold?
options: Counting tire and car double counts production
The tire was not produced in a market
boss.commonError: double_counts_intermediate_goods
boss.feedback: GDP counts final goods to avoid double counting intermediate goods already included in the final product's value.

boss.q: Why does total income equal total expenditure for the economy as a whole?
boss.commonError: misses_two_sides_of_each_transaction
boss.feedback: For the economy as a whole, spending by buyers becomes income for sellers.

boss.q: If one person’s spending is another person’s income, does every transaction increase GDP?
options: No; GDP counts current final production
Yes, every financial transaction raises GDP
Yes, all used goods sales raise GDP again
boss.commonError: thinks_all_transactions_count_in_gdp
boss.feedback: Income and expenditure are two sides of transactions, but GDP only counts current production of final goods and services.

boss.q: Why is GDP usually studied in macroeconomics rather than microeconomics?
options: It measures total production for the economy as a whole
It measures one firm's output only
It measures only one household's choices
It tracks only one product's demand curve
boss.commonError: treats_gdp_as_single_firm_measure
boss.feedback: GDP measures aggregate production for the whole economy, which makes it a macroeconomic measure.

boss.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
boss.q: Why can GDP be measured as both total income and total expenditure?
options: Because every dollar spent by a buyer becomes income for a seller
Because income is always higher than spending
Because prices do not affect GDP
boss.feedback: GDP can be measured either way because one person's spending becomes another person's income.

boss.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
boss.q: A household spends $500 at a local repair shop. In the income-expenditure flow, what happens to the repair shop?
boss.feedback: The household's expenditure becomes income for the repair shop.

boss.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
boss.q: If total expenditure on final goods and services is $18 trillion, what should total income equal in the basic GDP identity?
boss.feedback: Total income equals total expenditure, so both are $18 trillion.

boss.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
boss.q: An economist asks which item belongs in GDP. Which one counts?
options: A newly produced washing machine sold to a household
A used washing machine resold online
A gift from one household to another
boss.feedback: GDP counts newly produced final goods and services.

boss.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
boss.q: Why is a used car sale usually not counted in current GDP?
options: The car was counted when it was first produced
Cars are never counted in GDP
boss.feedback: Used goods are not current production, so they are not counted again.

boss.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
boss.q: A bakery buys flour for $40 and sells bread to consumers for $100. How much is counted in GDP from the final bread sale?
boss.feedback: GDP counts the value of the final good, which is the $100 bread sale.

boss.q: Which transaction is included in current-year GDP?
options: A used refrigerator resold by its owner.
A household purchase of corporate stock.
An unpaid repair performed by the homeowner.
A newly produced refrigerator purchased by a household.
boss.commonError: Counting asset transfers, used goods, or unpaid household work as current production.
boss.feedback: GDP includes newly produced final goods and services, not transfers of existing assets or unpaid household production.

boss.q: A bakery buys flour for $2 and sells bread to a household for $5. How much does the bread transaction add to GDP if the flour was produced this year?
options: $5, because the final sale already includes the flour’s value.
$7, because both the flour and bread sales are added.
$3, because only the bakery’s value added counts and the flour is excluded everywhere.
$2, because intermediate goods are the only production counted.
boss.commonError: Double counting an intermediate input and the final product.
boss.feedback: Counting the $5 final bread sale captures the value of the flour and the bakery’s value added without double counting.

boss.q: Why does total income equal total expenditure in the national accounts?
options: Government legally requires national income to equal national expenditure each year.
Each transaction is spending for a buyer and income for a seller.
Households always spend every dollar of income and never save financial assets.
Imports are recorded as both domestic production income and domestic expenditure.
boss.commonError: Treating the accounting identity as a behavioral claim that everyone spends all income.
boss.feedback: The same transaction is recorded from two sides: one party’s expenditure is another party’s income.

boss.q: A domestic firm produces a machine this year but does not sell it until next year. How is the machine treated this year?
options: It is excluded until a customer buys it next year.
It is counted as household consumption this year.
It is counted as inventory investment in this year’s GDP.
It is counted only if the firm imports the parts.
boss.commonError: Assuming unsold output is not counted until the final sale.
boss.feedback: Newly produced unsold goods enter inventories, which are counted as investment in the year of production.

boss.q: A U.S.-owned factory located in Mexico produces a car. Which statement is correct for U.S. GDP?
options: The car is included because the factory has a U.S. owner.
The car is included only if sold to a U.S. resident.
The car is counted as U.S. government production.
The car is excluded because it was produced outside the United States.
boss.commonError: Using ownership instead of location to define domestic product.
boss.feedback: GDP is based on production within a country’s borders, regardless of the producer’s nationality.

boss.q: A homeowner buys paint for $200 and paints the house without pay. What enters GDP?
options: The $200 market purchase of paint, but not the unpaid painting service.
Both the paint and an imputed value for the homeowner’s labor.
Only the homeowner’s labor because it creates the final service.
Neither the paint nor the labor because the house already existed.
boss.commonError: Excluding a purchased input because the final service is unpaid, or imputing all household labor.
boss.feedback: The market purchase of paint is counted, while unpaid household labor generally is not recorded in GDP.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
legendaryBoss.q: A firm produces $400 million of output, sells $340 million, and adds $60 million to inventory. Income paid to workers, lenders, landlords, and owners totals $400 million. What is GDP under the expenditure and income approaches?
options: GDP is $400M by both expenditure and income logic
GDP is $340M because only sold goods count
GDP is $460M because inventory adds to sales twice
GDP is $60M because only unsold goods are investment
legendaryBoss.feedback: Inventory investment counts, so expenditure GDP is $400M. Income generated is also $400M.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
legendaryBoss.q: A U.S. company produces $700 million of output abroad, while a foreign company produces $600 million of output inside the United States. How much is counted in U.S. GDP?
legendaryBoss.feedback: U.S. GDP counts production inside U.S. borders, regardless of ownership.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
legendaryBoss.q: A final good sells for $500 after using $180 of imported inputs. All remaining production occurs domestically, including $120 of domestic intermediate production. How much does the good add to domestic GDP across all domestic stages?
options: $500 because the final sale includes imported input value.
$180 because only the imported input is counted.
$440 because the domestic intermediate value is added again.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Domestic value added across all domestic stages is $500 − $180 = $320. The $120 of domestic intermediate production is included once within that total rather than counted again.

repairQuestions.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
repairQuestions.q: GDP counts goods and services that are:
options: Final, newly produced, and produced within the country
Used, resold, and produced long ago

options: It was counted when first produced

options: Because one person's spending becomes another person's income

repairQuestions.q: If a customer spends $100 at a business, what happens to the business in the income-expenditure flow?
repairQuestions.feedback: The customer's spending is the business's income.

repairQuestions.q: Why are intermediate goods not counted separately in GDP?
options: Their value is included in the final good.
repairQuestions.feedback: Counting intermediate goods separately would double count their value.

repairQuestions.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
repairQuestions.q: Flour sold to a bakery is usually considered what kind of good?
repairQuestions.feedback: The flour is used to produce bread, so it is an intermediate good.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.

options: A newly built apartment rented to tenants
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Newly produced housing services count; used goods and financial transfers do not add current production.

bridgeQuestions.q: If total expenditure on final goods is $21 trillion, what should total income from producing those goods be?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Total income and total expenditure are two sides of the same GDP activity.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.

gdp-components.title: GDP Components
gdp-components.description: Calculate consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports.

easy.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
easy.q: Which of the following is one of the four components of GDP expenditure?

easy.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
easy.q: The GDP expenditure identity is:

easy.q: Net exports are calculated as:

easy.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.

easy.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.

hard.q: A domestic software firm exports $4 million of services, imports $1.5 million of servers, and adds $0.5 million of current domestic output to inventory. What is the direct contribution to domestic GDP?

hard.feedback: The $4 million export and $0.5 million of inventory are current domestic production. The imported servers do not add domestic production, so the direct contribution is $4.5 million.

elite.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
elite.q: Consumption is $9T, investment is $3T, government purchases are $4T, exports are $2T, and imports are $3T. Then households buy $1T more imported goods, with no change in domestic production. What happens to measured GDP?
options: It rises by $1T because consumption rises
It falls by $1T because imports rise
It rises by $2T because trade increases
elite.feedback: Imported consumption raises C but lowers NX by the same amount, so domestic GDP is unchanged.

elite.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
elite.q: A government spends $100B hiring workers to build bridges and also sends $100B in Social Security payments. If recipients spend all Social Security payments on current domestic goods, what is the maximum direct GDP increase described?
elite.feedback: Bridge spending is government purchases, and household spending from transfers can count as consumption. The transfer itself is not counted separately.

elite.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
elite.q: If C = $15T, I = $4T, G = $6T, imports = $5T, and GDP = $23T, what are exports?

elite.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
elite.q: A household buys a newly built condo for $250,000 and pays $3,000 in property taxes. Which is the best GDP treatment?
options: The condo is investment; the property tax is not current output
The condo is consumption and the tax is government purchases
elite.feedback: New residential construction is investment. A tax payment is not itself government purchase of a final good or service.

legendary.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
legendary.q: An economy reports C = 46, G = 13, exports = 9, imports = 11, and GDP = 72, all in billions. A separate inventory report records 4 billion of new unsold output. What investment total reconciles the accounts, and how should the inventory figure be treated?
options: I = 15; the 4 of inventories is included within that total
I = 19; add inventories after solving the identity
I = 7; subtract inventories twice to avoid unsold output
I = 37; imports should be added when solving for investment
legendary.feedback: The expenditure identity gives I = 72 - 46 - 13 - 9 + 11 = 15. Inventory investment is one part of I, leaving 11 in other investment; it is not an extra addition after reconciliation.

legendary.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
legendary.q: A government purchases $18 million of new domestic flood barriers and pays $12 million in household benefits. Recipients spend $7 million on new domestic services and $3 million on imported goods, saving the rest. What GDP contribution and expenditure classification follow?
options: $37 million; benefits and recipient purchases both count
$28 million; imported purchases count only in C
$18 million; spending financed by benefits is excluded
legendary.feedback: The benefit payment itself is a transfer. Recipient purchases enter C = 7 + 3 = 10; M = 3 removes the imported goods. G = 18, so domestic GDP rises 18 + 10 - 3 = 25 million, without counting the transfer again.

legendary.commonError: Excluding unsold current production instead of counting it as inventory investment.
legendary.q: At the start of a year, a producer has $8 million of goods made last year. It produces $30 million this year and sells $34 million, leaving $4 million in inventory. With unchanged prices, no imports and all sales to final users, which GDP account is correct?
options: $30 million: final sales 34 plus inventory investment of -4
$34 million: sales determine the production year
$38 million: add beginning inventories to new output
$42 million: add beginning inventories to final sales
legendary.feedback: Inventory investment is the change in stock: 4 - 8 = -4. Sales of 34 plus inventory investment of -4 equal current production of 30. Selling previously produced goods does not create output again.

legendary.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
legendary.q: A revision adds $6 billion of imported household appliances to consumption and records $2 billion of previously omitted current domestic installation services. The same imported appliances were missing from M. How should measured GDP change after all corrections?
options: Rise $2 billion; imported spending cancels while domestic installation remains
Rise $8 billion; all added consumption is domestic output
Fall $4 billion; imports are subtracted without adding their spending
Remain unchanged; every correction associated with imports cancels
legendary.feedback: C rises by 8 billion and M by 6 billion. The net 2-billion increase is the newly measured domestic service. Subtracting imports removes foreign production, not the associated domestic activity.

calculation.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
calculation.q: If C = 10, I = 3, G = 4, and NX = -1, what is GDP?

calculation.feedback: The new house and groceries count. The used car resale does not add to current GDP, so GDP rises by $305,000.

calculation.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
calculation.q: Suppose C = $14T, I = $4T, G = $5T, exports = $3T, and imports = $4.5T. What is GDP?

$70 million because only sold goods count
calculation.feedback: Current production counts whether sold or added to inventories, so all $100 million counts.

calculation.feedback: Unsold output is counted as inventory investment, so all $10 million is counted.

boss.q: A household buys groceries, a firm buys machinery, and the government pays workers to repair roads. Which GDP components are involved?
boss.commonError: puts_all_spending_into_consumption
boss.feedback: Household groceries are consumption, machinery is investment, and road repair workers are government purchases.

boss.q: A family buys a new refrigerator for its home. Which GDP component does this most directly enter?
boss.commonError: puts_household_durable_goods_into_investment
boss.feedback: Household purchases of goods and services are consumption, even when the good is durable.

boss.q: A firm buys a new machine to produce more output next year. Which GDP component does this enter?
boss.commonError: confuses_business_investment_with_financial_investment
boss.feedback: Business purchases of capital equipment count as investment in GDP accounting.

boss.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
boss.q: Which formula correctly gives GDP using the expenditure approach?

boss.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
boss.q: A firm buys a new machine to produce more goods. Which GDP component does this enter?
boss.feedback: Business purchases of new capital goods are investment.

boss.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
boss.q: If C = 8, I = 2, G = 3, and NX = -1, what is GDP?

boss.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
boss.q: An economist asks how net exports are calculated:
boss.feedback: Net exports equal exports minus imports.

boss.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
boss.q: A U.S. household buys an imported phone. What happens inside the GDP formula?
options: Consumption rises and net exports fall
GDP automatically rises by the phone price
boss.feedback: Imported consumer goods raise consumption but lower net exports, so domestic GDP does not rise from foreign production.

boss.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
boss.q: If exports are $600 billion and imports are $750 billion, what are net exports?
boss.feedback: Net exports = 600 - 750 = -150 billion.

boss.q: C includes $8 million of spending, including $2 million on imports. I is $3 million, G is $4 million, and exports are $1 million. What is GDP?
boss.commonError: Adds financial transfers, used goods, or imported production to domestic GDP.
boss.feedback: GDP is $8 million of consumption + $3 million of investment + $4 million of government purchases + $1 million of exports − $2 million of imports = $14 million.

boss.q: A factory produces $10 million of goods, sells $7 million domestically and $1 million abroad, and stores the rest. How much enters current GDP?
boss.commonError: Treats only machines as investment and misses new homes or inventory changes.
boss.feedback: All $10 million of current production enters GDP: $8 million is sold domestically or exported, and the remaining $2 million is inventory investment.

options: $11 million: government purchases plus domestic services
$6 million: road repair plus recipients’ domestic services

boss.feedback: The imported equipment adds nothing to domestic production. Domestic road repair adds $4 million of government purchases, the transfer itself is excluded, and recipients

boss.q: A county buys new snowplows and sends households heating-assistance checks. Which classification is correct?
options: The snowplows enter G; the checks are transfers
Both enter G because the county pays
boss.commonError: Counts a government transfer as government purchases before any recipient buys output.
boss.feedback: Transfers redistribute income and are excluded from G; a later purchase can enter the appropriate spending component.

boss.q: A household buys an imported television. Why do C and M both change?
options: C excludes the television, while M adds its retail value
Both entries reduce GDP because the good is imported
M records a transfer from government to the household
C records the purchase, while subtracting M removes foreign production
boss.commonError: Treats the subtraction of imports as a claim that imported goods are inherently harmful or absent from spending.
boss.feedback: Imports are subtracted because imported final spending may already appear in C, I, or G and foreign production must not enter domestic GDP.

boss.q: Which pair is classified as investment in GDP accounting?
options: A pension payment plus a household appliance purchase
An imported restaurant meal plus a tax refund
A new home plus added business inventories
A used home plus a corporate bond purchase
boss.commonError: Treats only machines as investment and misses new homes or inventory changes.
boss.feedback: GDP investment includes business fixed investment, residential construction, and changes in inventories.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
legendaryBoss.q: C = $12 trillion, I = $3 trillion, G = $4 trillion, exports = $2 trillion, and imports = $3 trillion. Households then buy $1 trillion more of imported goods, with no change in domestic production. What is final GDP?
legendaryBoss.feedback: Initial GDP = 12 + 3 + 4 + (2 - 3) = 18. Imported consumption raises C and lowers NX equally, so GDP stays 18.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
legendaryBoss.q: A household buys a new domestically built house for $300,000, a used car for $20,000, and $10,000 of imported furniture. What directly adds to domestic GDP?
legendaryBoss.feedback: The new domestic house counts as residential investment. Used car resale and imported furniture do not add to domestic GDP.

What is GDP from these transactions?
legendaryBoss.commonError: Adds financial transfers, used goods, or imported production to domestic GDP.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Domestic services add $3 million, domestic machinery adds $4 million, bridges add $5 million, and exports add $2 million. Imports, stock purchases, and transfers add no domestic production directly, so GDP is $14 million.

repairQuestions.q: Which equation correctly states the expenditure approach to GDP?
repairQuestions.feedback: GDP equals consumption plus investment plus government purchases plus net exports.

repairQuestions.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
repairQuestions.q: A household buying groceries is counted under which GDP component?
repairQuestions.feedback: Household spending on goods and services is consumption.

repairQuestions.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
repairQuestions.q: Net exports equal:
repairQuestions.feedback: Net exports are exports minus imports.

repairQuestions.q: Why are imports subtracted after imported spending may appear in C, I, or G?
options: To remove foreign production from domestic GDP
To erase the buyer’s spending from every account
Because exports must always exceed imports
repairQuestions.feedback: Imports are subtracted because imported final spending may already appear in C, I, or G and foreign production must not enter domestic GDP.

repairQuestions.commonError: Excluding unsold current production instead of counting it as inventory investment.
repairQuestions.q: Unsold goods produced this year are counted as:
repairQuestions.feedback: Goods produced but not sold are counted as inventory investment.

repairQuestions.commonError: Counts a government transfer as government purchases before any recipient buys output.
repairQuestions.q: Does a government benefit payment enter G when it is sent?
options: Yes; every government payment enters G
Yes; but only if the household saves it
No; it is a transfer, not a purchase of current output
repairQuestions.feedback: Transfers redistribute income and are excluded from G; a later purchase can enter the appropriate spending component.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Classifies by the buyer label instead of the economic transaction.
bridgeQuestions.q: A firm buys a newly produced domestic machine. How is this expenditure classified in the GDP identity?
options: Classify the machine as business investment
Treat the final machine as an intermediate input and omit it
Classify the domestic machine purchase as a government transfer
Subtract the machine as an import even though it is domestic
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Classify final spending by household consumption, business/residential investment, government purchases, or net exports.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Infers output growth directly from nominal GDP growth.

bridgeQuestions.feedback: Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production.

options: Inventory is treated as a transfer from the firm
Foreign production is added before subtracting every import
Current final production is counted when produced
