bridgeQuestions.feedback: Because the goods were produced this period, they count in current GDP; the unsold amount is recorded as inventory investment.

real-versus-nominal-gdp.title: Real versus Nominal GDP
real-versus-nominal-gdp.description: Distinguish nominal and real GDP and calculate the GDP deflator.

easy.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
easy.q: Nominal GDP values output using:
easy.feedback: Nominal GDP uses current prices.

easy.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
easy.q: Real GDP values output using:
easy.feedback: Real GDP uses constant base-year prices to remove the effect of price changes.

easy.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
easy.q: If nominal GDP rises but real GDP does not, what likely happened?
options: Prices rose but actual output did not
Actual output rose but prices fell
easy.feedback: Nominal GDP can rise because prices rise, even if real output does not.

easy.q: Why is real GDP generally preferred to nominal GDP when comparing production across years?
options: It includes only goods and services purchased by the government.
It values every year’s output using that year’s current market prices.
It guarantees that measured production rises from one year to the next.
It holds prices constant so the comparison focuses on changes in output.
easy.commonError: Assuming nominal values isolate changes in physical production.
easy.feedback: Real GDP uses constant prices to separate changes in quantities from changes in the price level.

easy.q: Quantity is unchanged, but the current price of the only final good falls. With the same base year, what happens?
options: Nominal GDP falls while real GDP is unchanged
Both nominal and real GDP fall
Nominal GDP is unchanged while real GDP falls
easy.commonError: Infers output growth directly from nominal GDP growth.
easy.feedback: Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production.

easy.q: The base-year price is $10 and current production is 8 units. What is current real GDP?
easy.commonError: Mixes current and base-year prices while valuing current output.
easy.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

medium.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
medium.q: Suppose an economy produces only 10 bikes. In year 1, each bike sells for $100. In year 2, the economy still produces 10 bikes but each sells for $120. What happens?
options: Nominal GDP rises, but real GDP is unchanged if year 1 is the base year
Real GDP rises, but nominal GDP is unchanged
Both nominal and real GDP must fall
medium.feedback: Nominal GDP rises because prices rise, while real GDP is unchanged because output did not change.

medium.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
medium.q: Which situation would cause real GDP to rise?
options: Prices rise while output stays the same
Output rises while base-year prices are used
The CPI rises while production is unchanged
Used goods are resold more often
medium.feedback: Real GDP rises when actual production rises, not merely when prices rise.

medium.q: An economy produces exactly the same quantities of every final good in two years, but current prices change. Using fixed base-year prices, which statement must be true?
options: The GDP deflator must equal 100 in both years.
Real GDP must rise because some current prices changed.
medium.commonError: Treating current-price changes as changes in real output.
medium.feedback: With quantities unchanged, valuing both years at the same base-year prices leaves real GDP unchanged.

medium.q: Two years have the same nominal GDP, but the second year has a higher GDP deflator. Which year has higher real GDP?
options: They must have equal real GDP.
The answer depends only on population.
medium.commonError: Assuming equal nominal GDP implies equal real output despite different price levels.
medium.feedback: Real GDP equals nominal GDP divided by the price index. With equal nominal GDP, the year with the lower deflator has higher real GDP.

medium.q: Current output is 20 units, the current price is $9, and the base-year price is $6. What are nominal and real GDP?
medium.commonError: Mixes current and base-year prices while valuing current output.
medium.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

medium.q: Real GDP rises from $100 billion to $110 billion. What is the percentage growth rate?
medium.commonError: Uses the new level rather than the initial real-GDP level as the percentage-growth denominator.
medium.feedback: Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.

hard.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
hard.q: Nominal GDP rises from $20T to $22T while real GDP rises from $18T to $18.9T. What is the best interpretation?
options: Both prices and real output likely rose
hard.feedback: Real GDP rose 5%, while nominal GDP rose 10%, so both output and prices likely increased.

hard.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
hard.q: An economy produces only apples. Quantity rises from 1,000 to 1,100 and price rises from $2 to $3. What happens to nominal and real GDP using the first year as base?
options: Nominal GDP rises by more than real GDP
Real GDP rises by more than nominal GDP
Nominal GDP falls while real GDP rises
hard.feedback: Nominal GDP reflects both higher quantity and higher price, while real GDP only reflects higher quantity.

hard.q: Nominal GDP falls 2 percent while the GDP deflator falls 5 percent. What is the best approximate conclusion?
hard.commonError: Adding nominal and price changes instead of separating them.
hard.feedback: Approximate real GDP growth equals nominal GDP growth minus inflation in the deflator: −2% − (−5%) = about 3%.

hard.q: Base-year prices are $4 for books and $10 for meals. This year the economy produces 120 books and 30 meals. What is this year’s real GDP?
hard.commonError: Using current prices or adding quantities without base-year valuation.
hard.feedback: Real GDP uses base-year prices: (120 × $4) + (30 × $10) = $780.

hard.q: Nominal GDP grows 18% while the GDP deflator grows 10%. To one decimal place, what is the exact real-GDP growth implied by the ratio of the indexes?
hard.commonError: Uses the new level rather than the initial real-GDP level as the percentage-growth denominator.
hard.feedback: Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.
hard.roundingRule: Round real-GDP growth to one decimal place.

hard.q: An accountant divides current nominal GDP of $864 billion by a deflator of 120 and reports real GDP of $7.2 billion. Last year real GDP was $640 billion. Which correction and growth rate are right?
hard.commonError: Uses the new level rather than the initial real-GDP level as the percentage-growth denominator.
hard.feedback: An index with base 100 requires dividing by 120/100, not 120: 864/1.2 = 720. Real growth is (720 - 640)/640 = 12.5%. The deflator’s level is not the output growth rate.
hard.roundingRule: Round real-GDP growth to one decimal place.

elite.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
elite.q: Nominal GDP rises from $25T to $30T. The GDP deflator rises from 100 to 120. What happens to real GDP?
elite.feedback: Initial real GDP = 25. New real GDP = 30 / 1.20 = 25. Real GDP is unchanged.

elite.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
elite.q: An economy produces 20 units at $5 in the base year. This year it produces 25 units at $8. What are nominal GDP and real GDP this year?
elite.feedback: Nominal GDP uses current price: 25 x 8 = 200. Real GDP uses base price: 25 x 5 = 125.

elite.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
elite.q: Real GDP rises 5% while nominal GDP rises 15.5%. A report calls the full nominal increase output growth. What price change and correction follow?
options: Deflator is unchanged; the two growth rates use different units
elite.feedback: The price-index ratio is 1.155/1.05 = 1.10. Thus the deflator rises 10%, while the stated real production increase remains 5%. Price and quantity growth combine multiplicatively.

elite.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
elite.q: If nominal GDP is $36T and real GDP is $30T, then the GDP deflator indicates:
options: The price level is 20% above the base-year level
The price level is 20% below the base-year level
Real output is 120% higher than nominal output
elite.feedback: GDP deflator = 36/30 x 100 = 120, meaning prices are 20% above the base-year level.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
legendary.q: A country’s nominal GDP is $468 billion and its deflator is 130. Next year real GDP rises 10%, but nominal GDP is $475.2 billion. Which new deflator and interpretation reconcile these facts?
options: 120; real output rises while the domestic price level falls
132; nominal and real growth must move together
145.2; add real growth to the old deflator
120; the lower deflator proves real production fell
legendary.feedback: Initial real GDP is 468/1.30 = 360. It grows to 396; the new deflator is 475.2/396 × 100 = 120. Output grew despite a decline in the price index from 130 to 120.

legendary.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
legendary.q: A workshop economy makes pumps and repair visits. Base prices are $40 and $20. Current quantities are 60 pumps and an unreported number of visits; current prices are $50 and $30. Current nominal GDP is $6,000. What real GDP and deflator follow?
legendary.feedback: Pumps account for 60 × 50 = 3,000 nominal dollars, leaving 3,000/30 = 100 visits. At base prices real GDP is 60 × 40 + 100 × 20 = 4,400. The deflator is 6,000/4,400 × 100 ≈ 136.4.

legendary.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
legendary.q: Two new domestic goods have current prices of $12 and $30 and base prices of $10 and $20. Output of the first is 80 units; total real GDP is $2,400. A report calls $2,400 current nominal GDP. What is the correct nominal total and source of the difference?
options: $3,360; recover 80 units of the second good and value both at current prices
$2,880; raise all real output by the first good’s price increase
$2,400; real and nominal GDP use the same quantities, so they are equal
$4,320; current prices must be applied to the dollar value of real GDP
legendary.feedback: Base-price output of the first good is 800, leaving 1,600/20 = 80 units of the second. Nominal GDP is 80 × 12 + 80 × 30 = 3,360. The same quantities have different values at different price vectors.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
legendary.q: Nominal GDP grows 8% and the GDP deflator grows 12.5%. Population is unchanged. Which conclusion best evaluates the claim that average real production rose?
options: Real GDP per person falls 4%; nominal growth does not establish output growth
Real GDP per person falls 4.5%; subtracting rates gives an exact result
Real GDP per person rises 8%; population did not change
Real GDP per person rises 20.5%; combine both positive rates
legendary.feedback: The real-output ratio is 1.08/1.125 = 0.96, a 4% fall. With population fixed, real GDP per person falls by the same proportion. Nominal output rose only because the price increase exceeded the real contraction.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
legendary.q: An economy produces 50 units at $10 in year 1 and 60 units at $12 in year 2. Using year 1 as base, what are year 2 nominal GDP, real GDP, and the GDP deflator?
legendary.feedback: Nominal GDP = 60 x 12 = 720. Real GDP = 60 x 10 = 600. Deflator = 720/600 x 100 = 120.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
legendary.q: Nominal GDP rises 32% over two years. Real GDP rises 10% in the first year and is unchanged in the second. The deflator started at 125. Which final deflator and cumulative price change follow?
options: 152.5; subtracting growth rates gives an exact 22% price rise
150; the domestic price level rose 50% during these two years
legendary.feedback: Real GDP’s cumulative factor is 1.10. The price factor is 1.32/1.10 = 1.20, giving deflator 125 × 1.20 = 150. A level of 150 is 50% above the base year, but only 20% above the initial 125.

calculation.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
calculation.q: If nominal GDP is $30T and real GDP is $25T, what is the GDP deflator?
calculation.feedback: GDP deflator = nominal GDP / real GDP x 100 = 30/25 x 100 = 120.

calculation.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
calculation.q: An economy produces 100 units at $5 in year 1 and 110 units at $6 in year 2. Using year 1 as the base year, what is year 2 real GDP?
calculation.feedback: Real GDP uses base-year prices, so year 2 real GDP = 110 x $5 = $550.

boss.feedback: Nominal GDP values output using current-year prices.

boss.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
boss.q: Real GDP is useful because it:
options: Uses current prices to preserve every change in inflation
Uses base-year quantities instead of current output quantities

Uses base-year prices to remove inflation

boss.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
boss.q: An economy produces 10 units. The base-year price is $5 and the current price is $8. What is real GDP using base-year prices?
boss.feedback: Real GDP = 10 x $5 = $50.

boss.q: An analyst values base-year quantities at current prices and labels the result current real GDP. What correction is required?
options: Subtract the inflation rate from the nominal dollar total
Use current quantities valued at base-year prices
Use base-year quantities valued at current prices again
Use current quantities valued at current prices for real GDP
boss.commonError: Mixes current and base-year prices while valuing current output.
boss.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

options: It rises from $700 billion to $750 billion
It rises from $840 billion to $990 billion
It falls from $700 billion to $660 billion
boss.commonError: Infers output growth directly from nominal GDP growth.
boss.feedback: Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production.

boss.q: A country produces more units while their prices fall enough to leave nominal GDP unchanged. What can real GDP do?
options: Real GDP must remain unchanged with nominal GDP
Real GDP must fall because current prices fell
Real GDP equals nominal GDP minus the price decline
Real GDP can rise because fixed-price output increased
boss.commonError: Infers output growth directly from nominal GDP growth.
boss.feedback: Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production.

boss.q: Current quantity is 30 units, current price is $8, and base-year price is $5. Which pair is correct?
boss.commonError: Mixes current and base-year prices while valuing current output.
boss.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

boss.q: Nominal GDP grows 10% while real GDP grows 2%. What is the best interpretation?
options: Production rose 10% with no price change
Production rose, and prices also rose
boss.commonError: Infers output growth directly from nominal GDP growth.
boss.feedback: Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production.

boss.q: Real GDP rises from $500 billion to $525 billion. Which growth calculation uses the correct denominator?
boss.commonError: Uses the new level rather than the initial real-GDP level as the percentage-growth denominator.
boss.feedback: Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
legendaryBoss.q: A statistical office reports nominal GDP of $715 billion with a deflator of 130, followed by $756 billion with a deflator of 140. Which real-output comparison is consistent, to one decimal place?
options: Real GDP falls from $550 billion to $540 billion, about 1.8%
Real GDP rises from $550 billion to $756 billion, about 37.5%
Real GDP rises from $715 billion to $756 billion, about 5.7%
Real GDP is unchanged because nominal GDP and prices both rise
legendaryBoss.feedback: Deflate each observation: 715/1.30 = 550 and 756/1.40 = 540. The change is -10/550 × 100 ≈ -1.8%. Higher nominal GDP does not prevent real output from falling.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
legendaryBoss.q: In year 1, an economy produces 10 units at $50 each. In year 2, it produces 12 units at $70 each. Using year 1 as the base year, what are year 2 nominal GDP, real GDP, and the GDP deflator?

Base-year prices are $4 for books and $10 for meals. Base quantities are 100 books and 20 meals. Current quantities are 120 books and 24 meals, at current prices of $5 and $12. What are current nominal GDP, current real GDP, and real-GDP growth?
legendaryBoss.commonError: Mixes current and base-year prices while valuing current output.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

repairQuestions.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
repairQuestions.q: The GDP deflator compares:
options: Real-GDP growth to nominal interest-rate growth
Current output quantities to base-year output quantities
The GDP price index to the consumer price index
repairQuestions.feedback: The GDP deflator is based on nominal GDP divided by real GDP.

repairQuestions.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
repairQuestions.q: If nominal GDP is higher than real GDP, the GDP deflator is usually:
repairQuestions.feedback: A deflator above 100 means current prices are above base-year prices.

repairQuestions.commonError: Infers output growth directly from nominal GDP growth.
repairQuestions.q: Nominal GDP rises while quantities are unchanged. Does that prove production increased?
options: No; higher current prices can raise nominal GDP
Yes; nominal GDP measures only changes in physical quantities
Yes; every nominal increase establishes the same real growth
No; nominal GDP deliberately excludes every change in prices
repairQuestions.feedback: Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production.

repairQuestions.commonError: Mixes current and base-year prices while valuing current output.
repairQuestions.q: Is real GDP calculated by simply subtracting the inflation rate from nominal GDP?
options: Yes; subtract the inflation percentage directly from the nominal dollar level
Yes; but only when the measured inflation rate remains positive
No; value current quantities at current prices in both measures
No; value current quantities at consistent base-year prices
repairQuestions.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Mixes current and base-year prices while valuing current output.
bridgeQuestions.q: GDP measurement identifies current final output. Which added step makes output comparable across years with changing prices?
options: Value current quantities at consistent base-year prices
Subtract all imports from every year twice
Add transfer payments to nominal GDP
Replace quantities with current interest rates
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
bridgeQuestions.q: Real GDP per person rises, but leisure and environmental quality worsen. Which family destination evaluates the remaining question?
options: GDP components and the expenditure identity alone
Inventory investment and unsold production accounting
Nominal GDP measured only with current market prices
Limits of GDP and welfare measurement
bridgeQuestions.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

limits-of-gdp.title: Limits of GDP
limits-of-gdp.description: Evaluate GDP as a measure of well-being.

easy.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
easy.q: GDP is an imperfect measure of well-being because it excludes:
easy.feedback: GDP misses some things that matter for well-being, such as leisure and environmental quality.

easy.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
easy.q: Which statement about GDP and well-being is most accurate?
options: GDP helps but is an incomplete welfare measure
easy.feedback: GDP is useful, but it does not capture every part of economic well-being.

easy.q: A parent provides full-time unpaid child care at home. How is this usually treated in GDP?
options: The valuable nonmarket service is generally omitted
It is counted as government purchases
It is counted as business investment
easy.commonError: Assumes valuable activity must appear in GDP even without a recorded market transaction.
easy.feedback: Unpaid household production and unreported underground activity can be omitted from measured GDP.

easy.q: Two economies have equal GDP per person, but workers in one have much more leisure. What can GDP alone establish?
options: Their total well-being must be equal
The economy with less leisure is necessarily better off
Leisure is already fully priced in GDP
Their measured output is equal, not their total well-being
easy.commonError: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
easy.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

easy.q: Average GDP per person rises while nearly all gains go to a small group. Which limitation matters?
options: The higher average establishes that every household received an equal gain
Income distribution is already deducted when real GDP is calculated
The average does not show how income is distributed
GDP cannot measure the value of any recorded market production
easy.commonError: Uses an average output measure to infer distribution or every quality improvement.
easy.feedback: GDP per person does not show distribution and may incompletely capture product-quality change.

easy.q: A business produces market services but hides the sales from official records. What is the likely measurement issue?
options: Only nonmarket household work can be omitted
Underground activity can make measured GDP understate production
The hidden sales automatically enter government purchases
GDP must overstate output by the same amount
easy.commonError: Assumes valuable activity must appear in GDP even without a recorded market transaction.
easy.feedback: Unpaid household production and unreported underground activity can be omitted from measured GDP.

medium.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
medium.q: Why can GDP rise while well-being does not clearly improve?
options: GDP fails to record any final goods sold in legal markets
Every production increase automatically reduces leisure and environmental quality
Higher GDP guarantees equal gains for households across the income distribution
GDP may ignore pollution, leisure loss, and unequal distribution
medium.feedback: GDP is useful, but it misses important quality-of-life factors.

medium.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
medium.q: Which statement is the strongest evaluation of GDP as a welfare measure?
options: GDP is complete whenever nominal prices remain unchanged
GDP measures only leisure, safety, and environmental quality
GDP is useful but misses nonmarket quality-of-life factors
GDP is useless because it excludes all current market production
medium.feedback: GDP is useful but incomplete as a measure of well-being.

medium.q: A software update greatly improves usefulness while its market price is unchanged. What difficulty can arise?
options: GDP may not fully capture the quality improvement
Real GDP must fall because price is unchanged
The update counts only as a transfer
GDP already measures every consumer benefit exactly
medium.commonError: Uses an average output measure to infer distribution or every quality improvement.
medium.feedback: GDP per person does not show distribution and may incompletely capture product-quality change.

medium.q: A factory expands output while causing more pollution. What is the careful conclusion?
options: GDP and welfare must rise by the same percentage
Welfare must fall because production increased
Pollution is subtracted automatically from nominal GDP
GDP rises, while the net welfare effect remains uncertain
medium.commonError: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
medium.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

medium.q: A family replaces unpaid home cooking with otherwise similar restaurant meals. What can happen?
options: GDP is unchanged because meals are identical
GDP rises because more activity is purchased in markets
GDP falls because restaurant work is intermediate
medium.commonError: Equates a change in market spending with the same change in total useful services.
medium.feedback: Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently.

medium.q: Production is unchanged, but workplace injuries fall after a safety improvement. What does GDP alone miss?
options: A transfer counted in government purchases
A welfare gain from greater safety
A decline in all final output
medium.commonError: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
medium.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

hard.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
hard.q: A country cuts pollution regulations, output rises, but air quality worsens and illness increases. What does this show about GDP?
options: GDP must fall whenever pollution or illness increases after production
GDP automatically subtracts every environmental and health cost from output
Higher measured production proves that every resident became better off
GDP may rise even when broader well-being does not clearly improve
hard.feedback: GDP counts production but does not fully capture environmental damage or health costs.

hard.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
hard.q: Which scenario best shows why GDP per person is more useful than total GDP for comparing living standards?
options: A country’s total GDP rises while its population remains unchanged
A country’s real GDP per person rises while total GDP remains fixed
A country’s GDP doubles while its population triples
A country’s GDP and population both double over the same period
hard.feedback: If population grows faster than GDP, average income may fall even though total GDP rises.

hard.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
hard.q: Two countries have equal GDP per person, but one has more leisure, cleaner air, and lower crime. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: GDP per person misses some important parts of well-being
The cleaner country must have lower real GDP
Crime and leisure are already fully included in GDP
hard.feedback: GDP per person is useful but incomplete because it misses non-market quality-of-life factors.

hard.q: Two countries have the same real GDP per person, but one has longer life expectancy, safer streets, and cleaner water. What follows?
options: Equal measured output does not imply equal well-being
Both countries must have equal welfare
The safer country must have lower real GDP
Health and safety are fully included in the GDP average
hard.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
hard.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

hard.q: Pollution causes more medical and cleanup spending, raising measured output. Why can the welfare conclusion differ from the GDP change?
options: Medical and cleanup services are excluded whenever pollution caused the demand
GDP subtracts the environmental damage and then subtracts cleanup spending again
Any increase in measured cleanup output proves the original damage improved welfare
GDP counts the services produced but not the full damage that made them necessary
hard.commonError: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
hard.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

hard.q: Workers choose shorter workweeks, measured output falls, and leisure rises. Which inference is justified?
options: GDP stays unchanged because added leisure replaces every lost unit of production
The leisure gain is automatically valued and added to business investment
GDP falls, but well-being could rise or fall
Both measured GDP and total well-being must decline by the same amount
hard.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
hard.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

elite.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
elite.q: Country A has higher GDP per person than Country B, but Country B has cleaner air, more leisure, and longer life expectancy. What should an economist conclude?
options: GDP per person is useful but incomplete for comparing well-being
Country A must have higher well-being in every respect
Country B must have higher GDP once adjusted correctly
elite.feedback: GDP per person helps compare material output but misses some important well-being measures.

elite.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
elite.q: A hurricane destroys homes, and rebuilding activity raises GDP. Why is this not necessarily an improvement in well-being?
options: GDP excludes all construction completed after a natural disaster
Destroyed homes are recorded as current business investment spending
Rebuilding makes the original household losses irrelevant to welfare
GDP counts rebuilding, not the destruction’s welfare loss
elite.feedback: GDP can rise from rebuilding even though society is replacing destroyed assets.

elite.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
elite.q: A country increases GDP by requiring longer work hours and reducing vacation time. What GDP limitation does this expose?
elite.feedback: GDP measures production but does not fully value leisure.

legendary.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
legendary.q: Two regions report real GDP per person of $44,000 and $40,000. In the first, output per hour is $40 and annual hours per resident are 1,100; in the second they are $50 and 800. Which comparison is supported without assigning a value to leisure?
options: The first has higher output per person; the second has higher hourly productivity, so welfare is not ranked
The first is more productive per hour because its GDP per person is higher
The second has higher GDP per person because it is more productive per hour
The first has higher overall welfare by exactly 10%
legendary.feedback: The products 40 × 1,100 = 44,000 and 50 × 800 = 40,000 reconcile the figures. More hours explain the first region’s higher average output despite lower hourly productivity. Neither GDP nor these hours alone values all welfare differences.

legendary.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
legendary.q: After a storm, rebuilding adds $12 million of current production while lost business activity reduces other current production by $5 million. Destroyed existing buildings were worth $30 million. Which GDP and welfare statement is defensible?
options: GDP is $7 million higher than otherwise; this does not establish a welfare improvement
GDP is $23 million lower because destroyed wealth is subtracted from current production
GDP is $12 million higher; lost current production is irrelevant
GDP is $37 million higher because rebuilding replaces the destroyed stock
legendary.feedback: The change in current production is 12 - 5 = 7 million. Destruction of existing wealth is a separate loss, not a negative item of current production. Higher measured GDP therefore does not establish higher well-being.

legendary.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
legendary.q: A country has GDP of $2T and population of 20M. Another has GDP of $4T and population of 80M. Which has higher GDP per person?
options: The first country, with $100,000 per person versus $50,000
The second country, because total GDP is larger
They are equal because both are measured in trillions
It cannot be determined without imports
legendary.feedback: GDP per person is $2T/20M = $100,000 and $4T/80M = $50,000.

legendary.q: Country A has higher market output but more pollution and inequality; Country B has more leisure and unpaid household production. Which comparison is defensible?
options: Country A must have higher well-being because its recorded market GDP is higher
Country B must have higher measured GDP after valuing every hour of leisure
GDP is useless because it measures neither legal market goods nor services
GDP compares market production, but these facts do not settle overall well-being
legendary.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
legendary.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

legendary.q: A free translation tool replaces $9 million of paid translation services. Users report more completed translations and less effort; domestic firms produce $2 million of new paid implementation services. No other output changes. Which claim is supported?
options: Measured GDP falls $9 million; the implementation services do not count
Measured GDP rises because the number of translations rose
Measured GDP falls $7 million; the value of users’ net welfare gain is not determined
Measured GDP falls $7 million, proving welfare fell by $7 million
legendary.commonError: Equates a change in market spending with the same change in total useful services.
legendary.feedback: The measured output change is -9 + 2 = -7 million. Greater use and convenience can improve welfare despite reduced market spending, but the stated information does not price the total welfare change.

legendary.q: A storm destroys productive assets, followed by a surge in rebuilding services. What distinction is essential?
options: Higher rebuilding output proves the storm created a net gain for every household
Current production can rise while lost wealth and hardship leave welfare lower
Rebuilding services cannot enter GDP because the storm destroyed assets first
The destroyed productive assets are added to current household consumption spending
legendary.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
legendary.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

boss.q: A country produces more goods this year, but some of that production replaces worn-out equipment. What does this example show about GDP?
options: GDP measures every environmental and leisure dimension of welfare
GDP excludes all replacement investment from measured current production
GDP directly reports how national income is distributed across households
GDP measures production, not all well-being
boss.commonError: treats_gdp_as_perfect_wellbeing_measure
boss.feedback: GDP measures market production, but it is not a perfect measure of well-being.

boss.q: A country has higher GDP, but also more pollution and longer work hours. What should the student conclude?
options: Pollution and longer work hours are fully deducted from real GDP already
GDP is useless because it measures no current market production at all
GDP is useful, but it does not capture every part of well-being
Higher GDP proves every household receives exactly the same welfare gain
boss.commonError: treats_gdp_as_complete_measure_of_living_standards
boss.feedback: GDP is useful because income matters, but it leaves out things like leisure, environmental quality, and some nonmarket activity.

boss.q: GDP rises after a natural disaster because rebuilding spending increases. What is the best interpretation?
options: GDP automatically subtracts every hardship caused by the original disaster
GDP can rise without well-being rising
Rebuilding activity is excluded whenever a natural disaster occurred first
Higher construction spending guarantees that destroyed household wealth is restored
boss.commonError: assumes_higher_gdp_always_means_higher_wellbeing
boss.feedback: GDP can rise when rebuilding activity increases, but that does not automatically mean well-being improved.

boss.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
boss.q: GDP is useful as a measure of well-being mainly because:
options: Higher production guarantees equal gains for each household
GDP measures only transfers rather than market output
People generally prefer more income and output
GDP records every environmental and leisure benefit
boss.feedback: GDP is useful because income and production matter, but it is not perfect.

boss.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
boss.q: Why might GDP rise while well-being does not clearly improve?
options: GDP excludes every final good produced in a legal market
GDP measures only the distribution of current household income
GDP includes complete adjustments for leisure and environmental quality
boss.feedback: GDP misses some important parts of well-being.

boss.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
boss.q: A country produces more output by making people work longer hours with less leisure. What limitation of GDP does this show?
boss.feedback: GDP counts the extra production but does not fully subtract the loss of leisure.

boss.q: Two policies produce the same real GDP. One also yields cleaner air and more leisure. What is the best assessment?
options: Additional leisure is already recorded as government purchases
Equal output does not erase the second policy’s other benefits
Equal real GDP establishes identical well-being under both policies
Cleaner air necessarily makes measured real GDP lower
boss.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
boss.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

boss.q: A flood destroys homes, and rebuilding later raises current GDP. What must a welfare analysis also consider?
options: The destruction of wealth and household hardship
Only the construction wages in nominal GDP
A required subtraction of all rebuilding services
The fact that every household received a transfer
boss.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
boss.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

boss.q: Real GDP per person grows while preventable illness and workplace injuries rise. Which conclusion is sound?
options: The health evidence proves that measured real GDP actually fell
Real-GDP growth already contains a complete health and safety adjustment
Broader well-being must rise at exactly the measured output rate
Output rose, while the broader welfare change remains uncertain
boss.commonError: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
boss.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

boss.q: Unpaid elder care becomes an otherwise similar paid service. What is most likely?
options: GDP rises although useful care changes little
GDP falls because all paid care becomes intermediate production
GDP stays fixed whenever the underlying service appears similar
Business investment rises by the full wage paid for care
boss.commonError: Equates a change in market spending with the same change in total useful services.
boss.feedback: Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently.

boss.q: Output rises while leisure and air quality decline. What can GDP alone determine?
options: The environmental loss is already netted from GDP
Market production rose; the welfare change is ambiguous
boss.commonError: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
boss.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

boss.q: GDP per person rises, but the median household’s income is unchanged. What limitation is relevant?
options: The median household must always equal the national average
Income distribution determines only the nominal price level
The average conceals how gains are distributed
GDP fails to measure any current market production
boss.commonError: Uses an average output measure to infer distribution or every quality improvement.
boss.feedback: GDP per person does not show distribution and may incompletely capture product-quality change.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
legendaryBoss.q: A flood destroys homes, then rebuilding raises measured GDP. Which judgment is most defensible?
options: GDP falls because every rebuilding service is excluded after a disaster
Welfare fully recovers whenever current construction spending increases
Destroyed homes are added to current GDP as household consumption
GDP rises, but welfare may remain below its pre-flood level
legendaryBoss.feedback: GDP counts current production but misses much of the welfare loss from destruction.

legendaryBoss.q: Country A’s real GDP per person rises 4% as leisure falls and pollution increases. Country B’s rises 2% while leisure and environmental quality improve. What can the data establish?
options: A grew faster, but GDP alone cannot rank welfare changes
A necessarily experienced the larger overall gain in well-being
B necessarily produced more recorded market output per person
Both countries experienced identical welfare changes because both grew
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
legendaryBoss.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

legendaryBoss.q: A free technology replaces paid translation services, measured GDP falls, and users translate more text with less effort. Which diagnosis is complete?
options: Real GDP must rise by the value users assign to time saved
The technology is counted as government purchases
The GDP decline proves total welfare fell
Measured market output falls, while an unpriced consumer benefit can rise
legendaryBoss.commonError: Equates a change in market spending with the same change in total useful services.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently.

repairQuestions.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
repairQuestions.q: GDP misses which part of well-being?
options: Recorded production of final market goods
Government purchases of current public services
Business investment in newly produced capital
repairQuestions.feedback: GDP misses some quality-of-life factors like leisure and environmental quality.

repairQuestions.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
repairQuestions.q: GDP is best described as:
options: Useless for measuring current market production
A direct measure of leisure and environmental quality
Useful for production, but incomplete for well-being
A complete index of every household’s welfare
repairQuestions.feedback: GDP is useful, but it is not a complete measure of well-being.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
bridgeQuestions.q: GDP rises after a natural disaster because rebuilding increases construction. Why might well-being still be lower?
options: Rebuilding services are excluded because the disaster happened first
Destroyed homes are added to GDP as current household consumption
GDP automatically subtracts every loss of wealth and personal hardship
GDP counts rebuilding but not the original welfare loss
bridgeQuestions.feedback: GDP can rise from replacement activity even if people are worse off.

cpi-and-inflation-measurement.title: CPI and Inflation Measurement
cpi-and-inflation-measurement.description: Calculate CPI and inflation using a market basket.

easy.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
easy.q: The consumer price index measures:
options: The cost of a fixed basket of goods and services over time
The number of workers in the labor force
easy.feedback: The CPI tracks the cost of a fixed basket of consumer goods and services.

easy.commonError: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.
easy.q: The inflation rate is usually calculated as:
options: The percentage change in the price index
The level of GDP divided by population
The number of unemployed divided by population
easy.feedback: Inflation is the percentage change in a price index such as the CPI.

easy.q: In the CPI, the base-year index is usually set equal to:
easy.commonError: Forgetting the index convention for the base year.
easy.feedback: The base-year basket cost is indexed to 100.

easy.q: If the CPI is 125, the fixed consumer basket costs:
options: 75 percent less than in the base year.
25 percent more than in the base year.
125 percent more than in the base year.
easy.commonError: Reading the index level as a percentage increase of the same size.
easy.feedback: A CPI of 125 means the basket cost is 1.25 times its base-year cost.

easy.q: The inflation rate from one year to the next uses:
options: The percentage change in real GDP.
The percentage change in the CPI.
The dollar change in the CPI basket only.
The CPI level divided by 100 with no comparison.
easy.commonError: Using an index-point change instead of a percentage change.
easy.feedback: Inflation is the percentage change in the CPI across periods.

easy.q: A fixed market basket costs $240 in the base year and $240 this year. The CPI is:
easy.commonError: Treating no price change as a zero index.

medium.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
medium.q: If the CPI is 140, what does that mean relative to the base year?
options: The basket costs 40% more than in the base year
The basket costs 140% less than in the base year
medium.feedback: A CPI of 140 means the basket costs 40% more than in the base year.

medium.q: A basket costs $500 in the base year and $575 today. Today’s CPI is:
medium.commonError: Using the dollar increase rather than the basket-cost ratio.

medium.q: An index moves from 175 to 189. A report calls the 14-point rise “14 percent inflation.” Which correction uses the proper comparison?
options: 7.4%, because the 14-point rise is divided by 189
14%, because one index point is one percent
8%, because the 14-point rise is divided by 175
89%, because every comparison must begin at 100
medium.commonError: Using the 9-point index change as the inflation rate.
medium.feedback: Inflation is the change relative to the previous index: (189 - 175)/175 × 100 = 8%. Index points and percentage changes are different.

medium.q: A basket cost $360 in the base year. If the CPI is 140, the current basket cost is:
medium.commonError: Multiplying or dividing the index incorrectly.
medium.feedback: Current cost = 1.40 × $360 = $504.

medium.q: The CPI falls from 200 to 190. The inflation rate is:
medium.commonError: Using the point change or ignoring the sign.
medium.feedback: The percentage change is (190 − 200)/200 = -5 percent.

medium.q: A fixed basket has two meals at a base price of $4 each and one fare at $12. Meal prices rise 10%; the fare is unchanged. What CPI results, with the base set to 100?
options: 106.7; meals were two-thirds of the units
110; use the price change of the only item that rose
140; the meal expenditure weight is the inflation rate
104; meals had 40% of base basket spending
medium.commonError: Ignoring basket quantities when combining price changes.
medium.feedback: Base cost is 2 × 4 + 12 = 20. Current cost is 2 × 4.40 + 12 = 20.80, giving CPI 104. The relevant weight is the 8/20 spending share, not the two-of-three item count.

hard.q: The base-year basket cost is $640, last year’s CPI was 125, and the basket costs $856 now. Which pair gives the current CPI and inflation since last year?
hard.commonError: Using the base-year cost in the inflation denominator.
hard.feedback: Current CPI is 100 × 856/640 = 133.75; inflation is (133.75 − 125)/125 = 7 percent.

hard.q: The CPI is 132 and the current basket costs $924. What was the base-year basket cost?
hard.commonError: Multiplying by the index instead of dividing by 1.32.

The new current index is 116; the benefit lost purchasing power
The new current index is 110; the benefit gained 6% in real terms
The new current index is 100; rebasing removes inflation
