cpi-bias.title: CPI Bias
cpi-bias.description: Analyze substitution, quality, and new-goods bias.

easy.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
easy.q: One reason the CPI can overstate inflation is:
options: Consumers substitute toward relatively cheaper goods
Consumers never change what they buy
easy.feedback: The CPI uses a fixed basket, so it can miss substitution toward cheaper goods.

easy.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
easy.q: Substitution bias occurs when:
options: A fixed basket misses switches to cheaper goods
easy.feedback: Substitution bias happens because the CPI fixed basket may not reflect how consumers adjust.

easy.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
easy.q: The introduction of new goods can make the CPI imperfect because:
options: New goods add choice and buying power the CPI may miss
New goods are always intermediate goods
easy.feedback: New goods can improve well-being, but the CPI may not fully capture that gain.

easy.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
easy.q: Unmeasured quality improvement causes CPI problems because:
options: A higher price may partly reflect a better product
easy.feedback: If goods improve in quality, price increases may overstate the rise in the cost of living.

easy.q: A new low-cost streaming platform gives households an option that did not exist in the base period. Which CPI challenge is this?
options: A change in nominal interest rates
easy.commonError: Treats a newly available product as if it creates no gain until it enters an old basket.
easy.feedback: New goods expand choice and can improve purchasing power before a fixed basket fully incorporates them.

easy.q: A refrigerator sells for the same price but uses much less electricity and lasts longer. Which CPI issue matters?
options: Substitution toward a cheaper old good
Introduction of an imported good only
A decline in the nominal price level
easy.commonError: Treats every observed price increase as pure inflation even when product quality changes.
easy.feedback: Separate the value of quality improvement from the pure price change when interpreting cost-of-living inflation.

medium.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
medium.q: A CPI basket keeps 10 pounds of beef even after beef becomes expensive and consumers switch to chicken. Which CPI problem is this?
medium.feedback: A fixed basket can miss consumer substitution toward cheaper goods.

medium.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
medium.q: Why does substitution bias usually cause the CPI to overstate inflation?
options: Consumers switch toward relatively cheaper substitutes
Consumers never change behavior when prices change
The CPI counts used goods twice
medium.feedback: If consumers substitute, their actual cost of living may rise less than the fixed basket suggests.

medium.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
medium.q: A smartphone costs more than an old flip phone but also provides far more services. Which CPI issue does this illustrate?
medium.feedback: Some price increases reflect quality improvements, which the CPI may not fully measure.

medium.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
medium.q: A new product gives consumers a useful option that did not previously exist. Why can that make the CPI imperfect?
options: The CPI may miss gains from new variety and improved purchasing power
The CPI automatically falls to zero
The new product must be an intermediate good
medium.feedback: New goods can make consumers better off in ways not fully captured by the CPI.

medium.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
medium.q: Which example would most likely make the CPI overstate the true rise in the cost of living?
options: Consumers switch from expensive beef to cheaper chicken
All consumers buy exactly the fixed CPI basket forever
Quality falls but prices fall more
medium.feedback: Substitution toward cheaper goods means the fixed basket may exaggerate cost increases.

medium.q: A name-brand medicine becomes expensive and buyers switch to an equivalent store brand. A fixed basket changes slowly. What is the main issue?
medium.commonError: Assumes a fixed basket fully reflects how households respond to changes in relative prices.
medium.feedback: Substitution bias arises when consumers shift toward relatively cheaper alternatives but the fixed basket does not fully reflect that response.

hard.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
hard.q: A fixed CPI basket shows inflation of 12%, but households avoided much of the increase by switching away from the goods with the largest price increases. What is the likely issue?
options: The CPI may overstate the rise in the cost of living
The CPI must understate inflation because substitution is illegal
The GDP deflator must be zero
The nominal interest rate must equal 12%
hard.feedback: Substitution bias means consumers can reduce the actual cost increase by switching purchases, but the fixed basket may miss that.

hard.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
hard.q: A phone price rises 20%, but the new model has twice the storage, better battery life, and better cameras. Why might measured inflation be overstated?
options: Part of the price increase reflects better quality
All quality improvements are counted as unemployment
The phone is an intermediate good
The CPI excludes consumer electronics entirely
hard.feedback: If quality improves, a price increase may exaggerate the true increase in the cost of living.

hard.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
hard.q: Which CPI problem is most directly tied to the fact that consumers gain from products that did not exist in the base year?
hard.feedback: New goods can improve consumer welfare before the fixed CPI basket fully captures them.

hard.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
hard.q: Suppose beef rises from $10 to $20 and chicken rises from $10 to $12. The CPI basket assumes consumers still buy equal amounts of beef and chicken, but consumers buy much more chicken. What is the main measurement problem?
options: The fixed basket misses substitution toward chicken
The CPI ignores all food prices
The GDP deflator cannot measure domestic goods
The real interest rate becomes negative
hard.feedback: Consumers switch toward relatively cheaper chicken, so the fixed basket can overstate inflation.

hard.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
hard.q: Which statement gives the best overall critique of the CPI?
options: Useful, but biased by substitution, new goods, and quality
It is useless because no prices are included
It measures only business investment prices
hard.feedback: The CPI is useful, but it is not a perfect cost-of-living measure.

hard.q: A treatment keeps the same sticker price but cuts side effects and recovery time. Why can CPI miss part of the consumer gain?
options: The measured price may not capture improved quality
Consumers necessarily switch away from every treatment whose quality improves
The treatment becomes an imported capital good
The fixed basket counts the price twice
hard.commonError: Treats every observed price increase as pure inflation even when product quality changes.
hard.feedback: Separate the value of quality improvement from the pure price change when interpreting cost-of-living inflation.

elite.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
elite.q: A fixed CPI basket includes 10 gallons of gasoline and 10 bus rides. Gas prices double, bus fares barely rise, and consumers switch heavily toward buses. What does the CPI likely do?
options: Overstates the rise in cost of living
Perfectly measures welfare because the basket is fixed
elite.feedback: The CPI fixed basket can exaggerate cost-of-living increases when consumers substitute away from goods whose prices rise.

elite.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
elite.q: A medical procedure rises in price from $2,000 to $2,600, but the new version cuts recovery time in half and lowers risk. Why is CPI measurement difficult?
options: Part of the higher price reflects quality improvement, not just inflation
Medical care is never included in CPI
Quality improvements always make inflation negative
GDP deflator and CPI are identical
elite.feedback: Quality change makes it hard to know how much of a price increase is true inflation.

elite.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
elite.q: Which scenario combines two CPI biases at once?
options: A new streaming service draws consumers from expensive cable
A worker becomes unemployed during a recession
elite.feedback: New goods and substitution both complicate CPI measurement.

elite.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
elite.q: If official CPI inflation is 6%, but consumers increasingly substitute toward cheaper goods and product quality improves, the true cost-of-living increase may be:
elite.feedback: Substitution and quality improvements often mean CPI overstates true cost-of-living increases.

elite.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
elite.q: A student's laptop costs 25% more than five years ago, but it is faster, lighter, and has much longer battery life. What should a careful CPI interpretation conclude?
options: The full 25% price increase should not automatically be treated as pure inflation
The CPI must ignore the laptop because quality changed
The GDP deflator counts it as unemployment
The real price definitely rose by 25%
elite.feedback: Quality improvements mean some of the price increase may reflect a better product, not just inflation.

legendary.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
legendary.q: A basket agency sees households replacing a newly expensive rail route with an existing bus route. A trial finds the cheaper travel bundle preserves the same commuting service. Which evidence supports substitution bias, and what does it fail to establish?
options: A fixed bundle overstates the cost of that service; the evidence does not quantify bias for the whole CPI
The bus is a new good; the evidence measures all economy-wide quality gains
The rail price rise is entirely a quality change; no pure inflation occurred
The change proves the whole CPI should fall because one alternative is cheaper
legendary.feedback: The same service can be maintained at lower cost by changing an existing bundle, which is the substitution mechanism. A travel example alone does not measure the full index’s bias or imply that overall prices fell.

legendary.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
legendary.q: A new pump costs 12% more than the old model and lasts 12% longer with identical annual performance and maintenance costs. Ignoring discounting, which conclusion is supported for this product, and which is not?
options: Cost per service-year is unchanged; economy-wide inflation cannot be inferred
Cost per service-year rises 12%; durability is irrelevant to quality
Cost per service-year falls 12%; equal percentage changes must be subtracted from price twice
Economy-wide inflation is zero because this product has no service-cost rise
legendary.feedback: Price per lifetime service-year changes by 1.12/1.12 = 1. The sticker-price rise alone is therefore not pure service-cost inflation for this product. Its example cannot establish the economy-wide price change.

legendary.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
legendary.q: A streaming service did not exist in the base year and later gives consumers a cheaper alternative to cable. Which CPI problems are most directly involved?
options: Introduction of new goods and substitution bias
legendary.feedback: New goods improve choice, and substitution toward them can reduce actual cost-of-living increases.

legendary.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
legendary.q: If CPI inflation is 7% but the fixed basket misses major quality gains and substitution toward cheaper goods, the CPI most likely:
options: Overstates the rise in the cost of living
Understates the rise in the cost of living by definition
legendary.feedback: Substitution and quality improvements usually make CPI overstate true cost-of-living increases.

legendary.q: A fixed basket costs 9% more, while a redesigned bundle costs only 3% more. Before concluding that substitution bias is six percentage points, what must an analyst establish?
options: The redesigned bundle preserves the relevant living standard, with comparable quality and coverage
Households bought fewer total items, regardless of the services they lost
Both bundles contain the same number of product names, regardless of quantities
The redesigned bundle is cheaper, even if it provides less value
legendary.commonError: Assumes a fixed basket fully reflects how households respond to changes in relative prices.
legendary.feedback: A cheaper bundle can reflect reduced consumption or quality rather than cost-saving substitution at the same living standard. The comparison must hold the relevant standard of living constant before interpreting the gap as bias.

legendary.q: Statisticians update baskets and adjust for quality, yet CPI still requires judgment. What is the sound conclusion?
options: CPI becomes useless once any adjustment is required
Every quality adjustment eliminates substitution bias permanently
Updated baskets make CPI identical to the GDP deflator
Measurement improvements reduce bias, but index-number challenges remain
legendary.commonError: Concludes that known index limitations make CPI useless.
legendary.feedback: CPI remains useful, while substitution, new-good, and quality challenges can make measured inflation differ from true cost-of-living growth.

boss.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
boss.q: One reason CPI can overstate the cost of living is:
options: It may miss substitution toward cheaper goods
It measures unemployment instead of prices
boss.feedback: The fixed basket can miss how consumers substitute toward relatively cheaper goods.

boss.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
boss.q: Beef becomes expensive, so households buy more chicken instead. Which CPI problem does this illustrate?
boss.feedback: Substitution bias occurs when consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.

boss.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
boss.q: A product becomes more expensive but also much higher quality. Why can that make CPI inflation misleading?
options: Part of the price increase reflects better quality
Quality changes are always counted perfectly
The product becomes an import automatically
boss.feedback: If quality improves, a higher price may overstate the true rise in cost of living.

boss.q: A new generic drug enters below the brand price and patients switch rapidly. Which diagnosis is strongest?
options: The case concerns only the GDP deflator
New-goods gains and substitution can both reduce true living-cost growth
Only quality deterioration can explain why patients switch to the lower-priced generic
CPI must understate inflation whenever a generic appears
boss.commonError: Concludes that known index limitations make CPI useless.
boss.feedback: CPI remains useful, while substitution, new-good, and quality challenges can make measured inflation differ from true cost-of-living growth.

boss.q: A pension is fully indexed to CPI, but CPI overstates true living-cost growth. What can happen over time?
options: The pension can rise in real purchasing-power terms
The pension must lose nominal dollars
The CPI and true cost of living become identical
Indexation automatically removes every measurement issue
boss.commonError: Concludes that known index limitations make CPI useless.
boss.feedback: CPI remains useful, while substitution, new-good, and quality challenges can make measured inflation differ from true cost-of-living growth.

boss.q: Known CPI biases are found in a report. Which conclusion is defensible?
options: CPI contains no useful information about consumer prices or their changes over time
Every measured price change is quality improvement
The GDP deflator is always the correct household index
CPI remains useful, but measured inflation may differ from true living-cost growth
boss.commonError: Concludes that known index limitations make CPI useless.
boss.feedback: CPI remains useful, while substitution, new-good, and quality challenges can make measured inflation differ from true cost-of-living growth.

boss.q: Substitution bias means consumers respond to a relative-price increase by doing what?
options: Buying relatively more of available cheaper alternatives
Stopping all purchases of every good whose price rose
Treating every new good as lower quality
Replacing the CPI with the GDP deflator
boss.commonError: Assumes a fixed basket fully reflects how households respond to changes in relative prices.
boss.feedback: Substitution bias arises when consumers shift toward relatively cheaper alternatives but the fixed basket does not fully reflect that response.

boss.q: Why can a genuinely new product make an old fixed basket overstate the cost of maintaining well-being?
options: Every new product must have a lower sticker price
New products are automatically excluded from consumer spending
The GDP deflator fixes the CPI basket immediately
The new option can expand choice and purchasing power
boss.commonError: Treats a newly available product as if it creates no gain until it enters an old basket.
boss.feedback: New goods expand choice and can improve purchasing power before a fixed basket fully incorporates them.

boss.q: A laptop price rises while speed and battery life improve. What should a careful CPI interpretation separate?
options: Quality improvement from pure price inflation
Domestic production from imported production only
boss.commonError: Treats every observed price increase as pure inflation even when product quality changes.
boss.feedback: Separate the value of quality improvement from the pure price change when interpreting cost-of-living inflation.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
legendaryBoss.q: Beef doubles in price, chicken rises 10%, and consumers switch heavily from beef to chicken. What likely happens to CPI-measured inflation?
options: It likely overstates inflation by missing substitution
It understates inflation because beef doubled
legendaryBoss.feedback: The fixed basket does not fully capture substitution toward relatively cheaper goods.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
legendaryBoss.q: A product rises from $800 to $1,000, but quality improves enough that consumers get twice the useful service. What is the CPI problem?
options: Measured inflation may overstate true cost-of-living growth
Measured inflation must be exactly 25% in welfare terms
The product must be removed from GDP
The real interest rate rises automatically
legendaryBoss.feedback: Quality improvements mean the price increase is not pure inflation.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
legendaryBoss.q: CPI inflation is high, but the CPI misses substitution toward cheaper goods and quality improvements. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: True living-cost growth may be below CPI inflation
The true cost-of-living increase must be higher
The GDP deflator must equal CPI
Real interest rates cannot be calculated
legendaryBoss.feedback: Substitution and quality improvements can make CPI overstate cost-of-living increases.

repairQuestions.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
repairQuestions.q: A higher price can overstate inflation when the product also has:
repairQuestions.feedback: Some price increases reflect quality improvement.

repairQuestions.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
repairQuestions.q: New goods create CPI problems because they can:
options: Expand choice before the fixed basket catches up
repairQuestions.feedback: New goods can improve consumer welfare in ways the CPI may miss.

repairQuestions.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
repairQuestions.q: Substitution bias happens because consumers:
repairQuestions.feedback: Consumers substitute toward goods that become relatively cheaper.

repairQuestions.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
repairQuestions.q: If beef gets expensive and consumers buy more chicken, the CPI may:
options: Overstate the rise in cost of living
repairQuestions.feedback: The fixed CPI basket may miss substitution toward cheaper chicken.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Concludes that known index limitations make CPI useless.
bridgeQuestions.q: If CPI overstates living-cost growth because quality gains are missed, what can happen to a benefit indexed fully to CPI?
options: Its true purchasing power can rise
Its real value must fall by the CPI rate
It becomes indexed to the GDP deflator
bridgeQuestions.feedback: CPI remains useful, while substitution, new-good, and quality challenges can make measured inflation differ from true cost-of-living growth.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assumes a fixed basket fully reflects how households respond to changes in relative prices.
bridgeQuestions.q: A fixed CPI basket misses consumers’ shift toward cheaper substitutes. Which measurement design creates this bias?
options: Subtracting imports from the expenditure identity
Using actual inflation in an ex post real rate
Holding the consumer basket fixed while buying patterns change
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Substitution bias arises when consumers shift toward relatively cheaper alternatives but the fixed basket does not fully reflect that response.

cpi-versus-gdp-deflator.title: CPI versus GDP Deflator
cpi-versus-gdp-deflator.description: Compare the construction and uses of CPI and the GDP deflator.

easy.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
easy.q: Which price index uses a fixed basket of consumer goods?
easy.feedback: The CPI uses a fixed basket of consumer goods and services.

easy.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
easy.q: The GDP deflator is based on:
easy.feedback: The GDP deflator reflects prices of domestically produced goods and services.

easy.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
easy.q: An imported television bought by consumers affects which index more directly?
easy.feedback: Imported consumer goods are included in the CPI but not the GDP deflator.

easy.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
easy.q: Which statement correctly compares the CPI and GDP deflator?
options: CPI uses a fixed basket; the GDP deflator uses current output
They are exactly the same index
The CPI includes only investment goods
The GDP deflator includes only imports
easy.feedback: The CPI and GDP deflator both measure prices, but they use different baskets.

easy.q: The price of a domestically produced aircraft sold to a foreign airline rises. Which index directly includes that domestic export price?
easy.commonError: Treats CPI and the GDP deflator as interchangeable measures of the same set of prices.
easy.feedback: CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.

easy.q: Which index is designed for tracking the prices paid for a representative consumer basket?
easy.commonError: Chooses an index by familiarity rather than by the purpose of the comparison.
easy.feedback: Use CPI for consumer purchasing-power questions and the GDP deflator for the price level of current domestic GDP.

medium.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
medium.q: Which price change affects the CPI but not the GDP deflator directly?
options: A price increase for imported coffee bought by households
A price increase for domestically produced tractors
A price increase for government services
A price increase for domestically produced bread
medium.feedback: Imported consumer goods are included in the CPI but excluded from the GDP deflator.

medium.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
medium.q: Which price index better captures prices of all currently produced domestic final goods and services?
medium.feedback: The GDP deflator reflects the prices of domestically produced final goods and services.

medium.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
medium.q: Why can the GDP deflator change differently from the CPI?
options: GDP deflator uses current output; CPI uses a fixed basket
They measure exactly the same basket
The GDP deflator only counts imports
medium.feedback: The CPI and GDP deflator use different baskets and coverage.

medium.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
medium.q: A domestically produced machine purchased by a business becomes more expensive. Which index is more likely to capture this directly?
medium.feedback: Capital goods produced domestically are included in GDP and affect the GDP deflator.

medium.q: A domestic firm buys newly produced business software whose price rises. Which index directly covers that final domestic product?
options: The CPI because every business purchase is consumer spending
Neither index because software is intangible
The CPI only when the firm imports the software
medium.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
medium.feedback: The GDP deflator covers newly produced final goods and services made domestically, including business software. The CPI is limited to the consumer basket.

medium.q: Imported prescription-drug prices rise while prices of domestic hospital services are unchanged. Which outcome is plausible?
options: GDP-deflator inflation must exceed CPI inflation
Both indexes must change by the same amount
Neither index can reflect a medical price change
medium.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
medium.feedback: Imported prescription drugs can raise the CPI because they are consumer purchases. They are not domestic production, so they do not directly raise the GDP deflator; unchanged domestic hospital prices add no offsetting price increase.

hard.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
hard.q: Oil imported from abroad becomes more expensive and is heavily used by consumers. What happens to CPI and the GDP deflator, all else equal?
options: CPI includes imported consumer goods; the GDP deflator excludes imports
The GDP deflator rises directly, but CPI cannot
hard.feedback: Imported consumer goods affect the CPI but are not part of domestic production measured by the GDP deflator.

hard.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
hard.q: A domestically produced factory robot rises in price and is purchased by firms. Which index is more directly affected?
hard.feedback: Domestically produced capital goods are included in GDP and affect the GDP deflator.

hard.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
hard.q: Why does the GDP deflator not rely on a fixed basket in the same way as the CPI?
options: Its basket changes with current domestic production
hard.feedback: The GDP deflator changes with the composition of current domestic production.

hard.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
hard.q: If consumers buy more imported goods and fewer domestically produced goods, why might CPI and GDP deflator diverge?
options: CPI includes imported consumer goods; the GDP deflator covers domestic output
Both indexes are based only on labor force statistics
The GDP deflator includes imports twice
The CPI excludes all consumer purchases
hard.feedback: Different coverage of imports can cause CPI and GDP deflator movements to differ.

hard.q: Prices of domestically produced aircraft exports rise while imported smartphones bought by households become cheaper. Which combination is plausible?
options: The GDP deflator rises while the CPI falls
The CPI rises while the GDP deflator falls
Both indexes must rise because one price increased
Both indexes must fall because consumers buy smartphones
hard.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
hard.feedback: The aircraft exports are domestic production and enter the GDP deflator, so their higher prices push it up. Imported smartphones enter the CPI but not the GDP deflator; their lower price can pull CPI inflation down.

hard.q: Between two years, individual prices do not change, but domestic production shifts toward goods whose current prices are higher relative to their base-year prices. Why can a fixed-base GDP deflator rise?
options: The deflator must be unchanged whenever current-year prices are unchanged
The deflator begins including imported consumer goods as domestic output
A shift toward goods with higher dollar prices raises every index regardless of base prices
Current quantities put more weight on goods with larger price increases since the base year
hard.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
hard.feedback: The deflator compares current-price and base-price values of current quantities. Changing the output mix toward larger current-to-base price relatives can raise the ratio even with no new individual price changes. High dollar prices alone do not establish that result.

elite.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
elite.q: Imported coffee prices rise sharply, while prices of domestically produced machinery fall. Which index is likely pushed up more directly by the coffee price increase?
elite.feedback: Imported consumer goods affect the CPI more directly than the GDP deflator.

elite.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
elite.q: Domestic firms produce fewer computers and more health care services. Computer prices fall while health care prices rise. Why might the GDP deflator respond differently from the CPI?
options: GDP deflator basket changes with output; the CPI basket is fixed
The CPI never includes health care
The GDP deflator includes imports only
elite.feedback: The GDP deflator reflects the changing composition of current production.

elite.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
elite.q: A government must update a household allowance and also convert nominal GDP to real GDP. Imported household energy gets dearer while domestic investment equipment gets cheaper. Which pairing and interpretation fit?
options: Use CPI for the allowance and the GDP deflator for GDP; the indexes can move differently
Use the GDP deflator for both because energy purchases reduce net exports
Use CPI for both because every domestic output price is in its basket
Use either index for either task because all price changes have equal weights
elite.feedback: The household payment needs a consumer-price measure, which includes imported consumer energy. Deflating GDP requires prices of domestic production, including investment goods. Their differing coverage permits divergent movements.

elite.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
elite.q: A country produces only domestic wheat and imports all oil. Oil prices rise while wheat prices are unchanged. What is most likely?
options: CPI rises more than the GDP deflator if consumers buy oil
GDP deflator rises more because oil is imported
elite.feedback: Imported oil affects consumer prices but is not domestic production, so it is not directly in the GDP deflator.

legendary.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
legendary.q: An economy’s consumer basket has base spending of $40 on imported tea and $60 on domestic services. Tea prices rise 25%; services prices stay fixed. The only other domestic output is exported machinery, whose price falls 10%. With quantities fixed, which conclusion is justified?
options: CPI rises 10%; the GDP deflator falls, but its size needs domestic-output weights
Both indexes rise 25% because imports are in consumer spending
CPI rises 25%; the GDP deflator falls exactly 10%
CPI is unchanged; imported consumer prices are excluded
legendary.feedback: The consumer basket rises from 100 to 40 × 1.25 + 60 = 110, a 10% increase. The domestic deflator includes unchanged service prices and lower machinery prices, so it falls; their output weights are needed to measure the decline.

legendary.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
legendary.q: Domestic output consists of 10 machines and 100 services. Base prices are $100 and $10; current prices are $120 and $10. Consumers buy the services and imported clothing; the clothing price is unchanged. Which price-index account is supported?
options: GDP deflator 110; CPI unchanged if its fixed basket contains only those consumer purchases
GDP deflator 120; CPI rises 20% because domestic machines got dearer
GDP deflator 110; CPI must rise by the same 10%
GDP deflator 100; business equipment is not final domestic output
legendary.feedback: Base-price domestic output is 10 × 100 + 100 × 10 = 2,000; current-price output is 2,200, giving deflator 110. The stated consumer prices did not change, so their fixed basket’s CPI is unchanged.

legendary.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
legendary.q: Why can the CPI overstate inflation while the GDP deflator still moves differently for valid reasons?
options: CPI uses a fixed basket; the GDP deflator uses current output
Both measure the exact same goods but use different names
legendary.feedback: These indexes differ both because of CPI bias issues and because they cover different baskets.

legendary.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
legendary.q: A country imports most consumer goods but produces mostly capital equipment. Imported consumer prices rise while domestic capital prices fall. Which statement is most accurate?
options: CPI and GDP deflator can move in opposite directions
CPI and GDP deflator must move together
GDP deflator must include imported consumer goods
CPI must include capital equipment bought by firms
legendary.feedback: Different baskets mean the CPI and GDP deflator can diverge sharply.

legendary.q: Imported home solar panels become cheaper while domestically produced industrial turbines become more expensive. Why can CPI and the GDP deflator move in opposite directions?
options: The indexes cover different goods and use different weighting frameworks
Both indexes measure only domestic consumer purchases
The CPI excludes imports while the deflator includes them
The GDP deflator fixes a household basket while CPI tracks current output
legendary.commonError: Treats CPI and the GDP deflator as interchangeable measures of the same set of prices.
legendary.feedback: CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.

legendary.q: A household grant rises from $2,000 to $2,160 as CPI moves from 125 to 135. Nominal GDP rises 8% while the GDP deflator rises 4%. Which combined assessment uses the appropriate indexes?
options: The grant gains 8% purchasing power; real GDP rises 8%
The grant loses purchasing power; real GDP is unchanged
Both real changes are zero because each nominal value rose 8%
The grant preserves purchasing power; real GDP rises about 3.8%
legendary.commonError: Chooses an index by familiarity rather than by the purpose of the comparison.
legendary.feedback: The grant and consumer-price factors are both 1.08, preserving purchasing power. GDP requires its own price factor: 1.08/1.04 - 1 ≈ 3.8%. Matching nominal rates do not imply matching real changes with different deflators.

boss.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
boss.q: Which price index uses a fixed basket of consumer goods and services?
boss.feedback: The CPI uses a fixed basket of consumer goods and services.

boss.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
boss.q: An imported coffee price rises. Which index is affected more directly?
boss.feedback: Imported consumer goods affect the CPI but are excluded from the GDP deflator.

boss.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
boss.q: Which statement correctly compares CPI and the GDP deflator?
options: CPI uses a fixed basket; the GDP deflator uses current output
CPI tracks only exports; the GDP deflator tracks only imports
boss.feedback: The CPI and GDP deflator both measure prices, but they use different baskets.

boss.q: Imported consumer electronics rise 20%, domestic investment equipment falls 10%, and other prices are stable. Which conclusion is best?
options: CPI must exclude the consumer electronics
CPI can rise while the GDP deflator falls
The GDP deflator must include the imported electronics
boss.commonError: Treats CPI and the GDP deflator as interchangeable measures of the same set of prices.
boss.feedback: CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.

boss.q: An analyst deflates nominal GDP with CPI. What is the central scope problem?
options: CPI tracks consumer purchases, not all current domestic output
CPI measures only exported capital goods
The GDP deflator excludes domestic services
Nominal GDP contains only household consumption
boss.commonError: Chooses an index by familiarity rather than by the purpose of the comparison.
boss.feedback: Use CPI for consumer purchasing-power questions and the GDP deflator for the price level of current domestic GDP.

boss.q: Consumer import prices fall, domestic export prices rise, and output shifts toward exports. Why might the GDP deflator rise as CPI falls?
options: Both indexes use the same fixed imported-goods basket
CPI assigns all weight to domestic exports
The deflator measures consumer purchasing power only
Coverage and current-output weights reinforce the divergence
boss.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
boss.feedback: Falling consumer-import prices can lower CPI, while rising prices for domestic exports raise the GDP deflator. A shift in output toward exports gives those higher domestic-export prices more weight in the deflator.

boss.q: A city buys domestic transit vehicles while households buy imported fuel. Which mapping is correct?
options: Vehicle prices enter the GDP deflator; imported fuel can enter CPI
Both prices enter only the GDP deflator
Imported fuel enters the GDP deflator but not CPI
boss.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
boss.feedback: Domestic transit vehicles are newly produced domestic output, so their prices enter the GDP deflator. Imported fuel bought by households is in the consumer basket and can enter CPI, but it is not domestic production.

boss.q: Domestic food-export prices rise and imported-clothing prices fall. What can happen?
options: CPI rises and the GDP deflator falls by definition
Both indexes must move together because trade is involved
The GDP deflator rises while CPI falls
boss.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
boss.feedback: Domestic food exports are part of current domestic production and can raise the GDP deflator. Imported clothing is in the consumer basket and can lower CPI, so the two indexes can move in opposite directions.

boss.q: Why can a changing mix of domestic output affect the GDP deflator more directly than CPI?
options: The deflator uses a permanently fixed consumer basket
CPI includes only domestic investment goods
boss.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
boss.feedback: The GDP deflator uses weights based on current domestic output, so a changing production mix changes its basket. CPI uses a fixed consumer basket and is not reweighted by the current mix of domestic production.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
legendaryBoss.q: Imported consumer goods rise sharply in price while domestically produced capital goods fall sharply. Which result is plausible?
options: CPI rises while GDP deflator falls
GDP deflator rises while CPI cannot change
Neither can change because quantities are fixed
legendaryBoss.feedback: Imported consumer goods are included in CPI, so their higher prices can raise CPI. Domestically produced capital goods enter the GDP deflator, so their lower prices can pull the deflator down.

legendaryBoss.q: A household buys an imported tablet, a firm buys a domestic robot, and each price rises. Which index covers each price directly?
options: CPI covers the tablet; the GDP deflator covers the robot
The GDP deflator covers both the imported tablet and the domestic business robot
Neither index covers a business purchase
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats CPI and the GDP deflator as interchangeable measures of the same set of prices.
legendaryBoss.feedback: CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.

legendaryBoss.q: Imported consumer prices fall, domestic capital and export prices rise, and production shifts toward capital goods. Which explanation best supports a rising deflator alongside falling CPI?
options: A shared fixed basket forces the indexes apart
CPI includes only exports while the deflator includes only imports
Nominal interest rates determine both price indexes
Different coverage plus current domestic-output weights
legendaryBoss.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Falling imported consumer prices can lower CPI, while rising prices for domestically produced capital goods and exports raise the GDP deflator. The shift toward capital goods gives those higher domestic prices greater weight in the deflator.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
repairQuestions.q: The CPI focuses on:
options: A fixed basket of consumer goods and services
repairQuestions.feedback: CPI uses a fixed consumer basket.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
repairQuestions.q: The GDP deflator focuses on prices of:
repairQuestions.feedback: The GDP deflator reflects prices of current domestic production.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
bridgeQuestions.q: Imported coffee rises in price. Which index is affected more directly?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Imported consumer goods affect CPI but not the GDP deflator directly.

indexing-and-real-values.title: Indexing and Real Values
indexing-and-real-values.description: Convert nominal values across time and apply indexation.

easy.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
easy.q: To convert a dollar amount from the past into today's dollars, you should use:
easy.feedback: Dollar figures across time should be adjusted with a price index.

easy.q: A worker receives a nominal raise equal to the inflation rate. What happens approximately to purchasing power?
options: It rises by the full nominal raise
easy.commonError: Equates a higher nominal payment with a higher real payment.
easy.feedback: Compare the nominal change with the relevant price-index change to determine purchasing-power change.

easy.q: What is the purpose of a cost-of-living adjustment in a pension?
options: To convert the pension into a new category of private business investment
To guarantee a real gain every year
To replace CPI with nominal GDP
To help preserve the payment’s purchasing power
easy.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
easy.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

easy.q: Why might a tax threshold be indexed to a price index?
options: To set the real interest rate on loans
To keep inflation alone from lowering the threshold’s real value
To make every taxpayer’s nominal income fall even when purchasing power is unchanged
easy.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
easy.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

easy.q: An indexed benefit rises in dollars at the same pace as prices. Which statement is best?
options: Its real purchasing power is approximately unchanged
Its real value rises by the full nominal increase
easy.commonError: Equates a higher nominal payment with a higher real payment.
easy.feedback: Compare the nominal change with the relevant price-index change to determine purchasing-power change.

easy.q: To compare a scholarship from two different years, what should be done first?
options: Express both amounts at a common price level
Compare only the printed dollar amounts
easy.commonError: Compares dollar amounts from different periods without a common price level.
easy.feedback: Put nominal amounts in common purchasing-power units before making the real comparison.

medium.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
medium.q: Why is it misleading to compare a $5 wage in 1970 directly to a $15 wage today?
options: The purchasing power of money changes over time
Inflation only affects GDP, not wages
Nominal values are always real values
medium.feedback: Dollar amounts from different years need to be adjusted for changes in the price level.

medium.q: A pension has a full cost-of-living adjustment tied to the CPI. If measured inflation is 4 percent, what is the intended effect?
options: Raise the nominal payment about 4% to protect purchasing power.
Reduce the nominal payment about 4% to offset inflation.
Hold the nominal payment fixed so its real value automatically rises.
Convert the pension payment into a market interest rate.
medium.commonError: Confusing nominal indexation with a reduction in benefits.
medium.feedback: A CPI-linked adjustment raises the nominal amount to offset measured price growth.

medium.q: A salary rises 6% while the relevant price index rises 4%. What happens to real purchasing power?
medium.commonError: Equates a higher nominal payment with a higher real payment.
medium.feedback: Compare the nominal change with the relevant price-index change to determine purchasing-power change.

medium.q: A rent payment is indexed upward 3% when the relevant price index rises 3%. What is the intended real effect?
options: Convert rent into a real interest rate
Keep the payment’s purchasing power roughly constant
medium.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
medium.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

medium.q: A benefit rises 2% while consumer prices rise 5%. What happens to its purchasing power?
medium.commonError: Equates a higher nominal payment with a higher real payment.
medium.feedback: Compare the nominal change with the relevant price-index change to determine purchasing-power change.

medium.q: A nominal salary is unchanged while the consumer price level falls. What happens to its purchasing power?
options: It becomes an indexed tax threshold
It remains unchanged in real terms
medium.commonError: Compares dollar amounts from different periods without a common price level.
medium.feedback: Put nominal amounts in common purchasing-power units before making the real comparison.

hard.q: Suppose the CPI systematically overstates the rise in the true cost of living. What can happen to a benefit that is fully indexed to the CPI?
options: The nominal benefit must decline every year.
The benefit can become too generous in real terms.
The real value remains exactly constant by definition.
Indexing removes every possible measurement problem.
hard.commonError: Assuming an index-linked adjustment is exact even when the index is biased.
hard.feedback: If the CPI overstates cost-of-living growth, full CPI indexation can overcompensate recipients in real terms.

hard.q: A nominal wage rises 8% while CPI rises 5%. Using the exact ratio and rounding to one decimal place, how much does the real wage rise?
hard.commonError: Compares dollar amounts from different periods without a common price level.
hard.feedback: Put nominal amounts in common purchasing-power units before making the real comparison.
hard.roundingRule: Use (1.08 ÷ 1.05) − 1 and round to one decimal place.

hard.q: A tax threshold is adjusted by only half of CPI inflation. What happens to its real value?
options: It becomes a nominal interest rate
hard.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.

real-versus-nominal-interest-rates.title: Real versus Nominal Interest Rates
real-versus-nominal-interest-rates.description: Calculate and interpret real and nominal interest rates.

easy.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
easy.q: The nominal interest rate is:
options: The interest rate usually reported before correcting for inflation
The interest rate after subtracting inflation
The same as the unemployment rate
easy.feedback: The nominal interest rate is the stated or reported interest rate before adjusting for inflation.

easy.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
easy.q: The real interest rate is approximately:
options: Nominal interest rate minus inflation rate
Nominal interest rate plus inflation rate
easy.feedback: The real interest rate adjusts the nominal rate for inflation.

easy.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
easy.q: If inflation rises while the nominal interest rate stays the same, the real interest rate:
easy.feedback: Higher inflation reduces the real interest rate when the nominal rate is unchanged.

easy.q: Inflation is higher than the nominal interest earned on an account. What is true of the approximate real return?
options: It is greater than the nominal rate
It is unrelated to purchasing power
easy.commonError: Uses the nominal rate alone to infer the purchasing-power return.
easy.feedback: For introductory approximation, real interest is nominal interest minus inflation.

easy.q: What does a real interest rate describe that a nominal rate does not?
easy.commonError: Uses the nominal rate alone to infer the purchasing-power return.
easy.feedback: For introductory approximation, real interest is nominal interest minus inflation.

easy.q: Unexpected inflation is higher than lenders and borrowers expected on a fixed-rate loan. Who generally benefits?
options: Both gain the same purchasing power
easy.commonError: Misses how unexpected inflation changes the real burden of a fixed nominal loan.
easy.feedback: Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real repayment burden and shifts purchasing power from lender to borrower.

medium.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
medium.q: A bank pays 6% interest and inflation is 2%. What happened to purchasing power in the account?
medium.feedback: The real interest rate is about 4%, so purchasing power rises by about 4%.

medium.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
medium.q: Which borrower benefits most from unexpectedly high inflation?
options: A borrower with a fixed nominal interest rate
A lender with a fixed nominal interest rate
A saver earning a low fixed rate
A worker paid only in real wages
medium.feedback: Unexpected inflation reduces the real burden of fixed nominal debt.

medium.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes ex ante and ex post real interest rates?
options: Both measures subtract actual inflation from the nominal rate.
Ex ante adds expected inflation to the nominal interest rate.
Ex post is known with certainty when the loan contract is signed.
Ex ante uses expected inflation; ex post uses actual inflation.
medium.commonError: Using actual inflation for both the expected and realized real return.
medium.feedback: The expected real return is based on expected inflation, while the realized real return uses actual inflation.

medium.q: Actual inflation exceeds expected inflation while a loan’s nominal rate is fixed. What happens to the lender’s realized real return?
medium.commonError: Uses actual inflation to describe an expected return or expected inflation to describe the realized return.
medium.feedback: Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.

medium.q: Actual inflation is lower than expected on a fixed nominal loan. Who bears a higher real repayment burden than anticipated?
medium.commonError: Misses how unexpected inflation changes the real burden of a fixed nominal loan.
medium.feedback: Because actual inflation is lower than expected, the repayment dollars retain more purchasing power than anticipated, increasing the borrower’s real burden.

medium.q: Which inflation rate belongs in an ex post real-interest calculation?
medium.commonError: Uses actual inflation to describe an expected return or expected inflation to describe the realized return.
medium.feedback: Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.

hard.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
hard.q: A borrower agrees to repay a loan at 6% nominal interest. Inflation unexpectedly rises from 2% to 8%. Who is helped, other things equal?
options: The borrower, because the real repayment burden falls
The lender, because the real return rises
Neither side, because inflation does not affect real payments
Only the government, because GDP falls
hard.feedback: Unexpected inflation lowers the real value of fixed nominal repayments, helping borrowers.

hard.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
hard.q: If nominal interest is 4% and inflation is 7%, what does the real interest rate imply?
hard.feedback: Real interest = 4% - 7% = -3%, so purchasing power falls.

hard.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
hard.q: Which statement best explains why inflation matters for interest rates?
options: Nominal rate shows dollar growth; real rate shows buying-power growth
The nominal rate is always lower than inflation
Inflation only affects unemployment, not borrowing
hard.feedback: The real rate adjusts nominal interest for inflation to show changes in purchasing power.

hard.q: A savings account earns 5% nominal interest while inflation is 7%. What happens?
options: The balance rises in dollars but loses purchasing power
Both the dollar balance and purchasing power fall 2%
The real return equals the nominal return
hard.commonError: Uses the nominal rate alone to infer the purchasing-power return.
hard.feedback: For introductory approximation, real interest is nominal interest minus inflation.

hard.q: A fixed loan carries 8% nominal interest. Expected inflation is 3%, but actual inflation is 6%. What are the approximate ex ante and ex post real rates?
hard.commonError: Uses actual inflation to describe an expected return or expected inflation to describe the realized return.
hard.feedback: Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.

hard.q: A loan’s fixed nominal rate is 9%. During its year, CPI rises from 200 to 212. Which conclusion is supported by these observations without a theory of how future loan rates are set?
options: Next year’s nominal rate must rise to 15%
Expected inflation at signing must have been 6%
The realized real return is approximately 3%
The realized real return is approximately 15%
hard.commonError: Turns a measurement question into a claim about long-run nominal-rate adjustment.
hard.feedback: Observed inflation is (212 - 200)/200 = 6%, so the approximate realized real return is 9 - 6 = 3%. These observations do not reveal prior expectations or determine future nominal rates.

elite.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
elite.q: A lender expects 3% inflation and wants a 4% real return. What nominal interest rate should the lender charge approximately?
elite.feedback: Nominal interest rate ≈ real interest rate + expected inflation = 4% + 3% = 7%.

elite.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
elite.q: A loan has a fixed nominal rate of 5%. Expected inflation was 2%, but actual inflation is 6%. What happened to the real interest rate relative to what was expected?
options: It was 4 percentage points lower than expected
It was 4 percentage points higher than expected
elite.feedback: Expected real rate was 3%; actual real rate was -1%, so it was 4 points lower.

elite.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
elite.q: A lender expected a 2% real return on a fixed 7% nominal loan. Actual inflation was 2 percentage points higher than expected. Which inflation and realized real rate follow using the approximation?
options: 7% actual inflation and 0% realized real return
5% actual inflation and 2% realized real return
9% actual inflation and -2% realized real return
7% actual inflation and 4% realized real return
elite.feedback: Expected inflation was 7 - 2 = 5%. Actual inflation was 7%, leaving realized real return 7 - 7 = 0%. The two-point surprise lowers the realized real rate by two points.

The saver has fewer dollars and less purchasing power
The saver has more purchasing power because nominal interest is positive
elite.feedback: A positive nominal return can still be a negative real return when inflation is higher.

legendary.q: A lender charged a fixed 8% nominal rate to target a 3% expected real return. CPI subsequently moved from 160 to 172.8. What realized real rate and forecast error follow using approximate real interest?

3% realized real return; the target guarantees the outcome

5% realized real return; actual inflation was below expected
legendary.feedback: The target implies expected inflation of 8 - 3 = 5%. Observed inflation is (172.8 - 160)/160 = 8%, so realized real interest is 0%. Inflation exceeded the expectation by 3 percentage points.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
legendary.q: Two one-year accounts each credit 6% nominal interest. Account A’s year has basket costs moving from $400 to $420; B’s year moves from $500 to $540. Which real-return comparison is valid using the approximation?
options: A gains about 1%; B loses about 2%, despite equal nominal rates
Both gain 6%, since account balances rise at the same rate
A loses 14%; B loses 34%, using basket-dollar increases as inflation
A gains about 11%; B gains about 14%, adding inflation to interest
legendary.feedback: Inflation is 20/400 = 5% for A and 40/500 = 8% for B. Subtracting from 6% gives +1% and -2%. The appropriate price growth, not the nominal rate alone, determines the purchasing-power return.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.

legendary.feedback: Expected inflation is 5/125 = 4%, so the target nominal rate is 2 + 4 = 6%. Actual inflation is 10/125 = 8%, giving approximate realized return 6 - 8 = -2%. Use the stated approximation, not the exact Fisher ratio.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.

legendary.feedback: Actual real = 12 - 8 = 4. Expected real = 12 - 5 = 7.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.

The nominal rate automatically adjusted to 13%

easy.commonError: Using total output without adjusting for population size.
easy.feedback: Real GDP per person relates inflation-adjusted output to the number of people sharing that output.

easy.q: Over long periods, the most important source of rising average living standards is usually growth in:
options: Productivity, meaning more output produced from each unit of labor input.
The current price level, meaning higher prices for the same output.
The money supply, even when physical production remains unchanged.
One month’s unemployment rate, regardless of long-run output per worker.
easy.commonError: Treating nominal variables as the main source of sustained real living-standard growth.
easy.feedback: Higher productivity lets an economy produce more goods and services from its available labor and resources.

easy.q: If real GDP grows 2 percent and population grows 3 percent, real GDP per person will approximately:
easy.commonError: Adding population growth to output growth.
easy.feedback: Approximate per-person growth is 2% − 3% = −1%.

medium.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
medium.q: Country A grows at 1% per year and Country B grows at 4% per year. What is the most likely long-run result?
options: The income gap can become much larger over time
Both countries must end with the same income
Country A must always become richer
Growth rates do not affect living standards
medium.feedback: Small growth-rate differences compound into large long-run income differences.

medium.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
medium.q: Why can a country that is poor today become much richer over several decades?
options: Sustained productivity growth can raise real GDP per person
medium.feedback: Long-run growth in productivity can dramatically raise living standards.

medium.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
medium.q: Which comparison best captures differences in living standards across countries?
medium.feedback: Real GDP per person is commonly used to compare living standards.

medium.q: A country’s real GDP grows 4 percent and population grows 1 percent. Approximate growth in real GDP per person is:
medium.commonError: Using total GDP growth without adjusting for population.
medium.feedback: Approximate real GDP per person growth is 4% − 1% = 3%.

medium.q: A country raises output mainly by requiring much longer workweeks, while output per hour is unchanged. What is the most careful interpretation?
options: Productivity must rise because total output increased after workers supplied more hours.
Living standards must fall because any increase in work hours necessarily reduces output.
Real GDP per person cannot change when total hours worked change but output per hour does not.
Real GDP may rise, but productivity is unchanged and lost leisure can limit the welfare gain.
medium.commonError: Equating more total labor input with higher productivity and complete welfare improvement.
medium.feedback: More hours can raise output without raising output per hour, and GDP does not fully value lost leisure.

medium.q: Why can a country with lower initial income eventually catch a richer country?
options: A persistently higher growth rate can compound enough to close the initial income gap.
Lower initial income automatically guarantees convergence even without faster growth.
Nominal GDP always grows faster in poorer countries because their prices are lower.
Population growth alone raises real output per person without any productivity change.
medium.commonError: Assuming starting income permanently fixes a country’s relative position.
medium.feedback: Sustained differences in growth rates compound over time and can outweigh an initial income gap.

hard.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
hard.q: A country with lower current income grows rapidly for several decades and catches up to richer countries. Which concept best explains this possibility?
options: Sustained growth and the catch-up effect
hard.feedback: Growth compounds over time, and poorer countries may grow faster when capital is scarce.

hard.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
hard.q: Which country likely has the higher living standard, holding other quality-of-life factors aside?
options: Country A with real GDP of $1T and population of 10M
Country B with real GDP of $2T and population of 80M
Country C with nominal GDP of $3T but unknown prices
hard.feedback: Country A has real GDP per person of $100,000; Country B has $25,000.

hard.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
hard.q: Why can rankings of countries by income change dramatically over time?
options: Different growth rates compound over many years
The Rule of 70 prevents poor countries from growing
hard.feedback: Long-run differences in growth rates can greatly change relative income levels.

hard.q: Real GDP rises from $1.20 trillion to $1.32 trillion while population rises from 40 million to 42 million. Approximately how does real GDP per person change?
options: It rises from $30,000 to $33,000, a gain of exactly 10 percent.
It rises from $30,000 to about $31,429, a gain of roughly 4.8 percent.
It falls from $30,000 to about $28,571 as population increases.
It stays at $30,000 because both real GDP and population rose.
hard.commonError: Comparing total GDP growth without recomputing output per person.

hard.q: A country’s real GDP per person rises 3 percent, but most of the gain goes to a small share of households. What can be concluded?
options: Every household’s real income must have risen by exactly 3 percent.
Real GDP per person must have fallen because the distribution changed.
Average output per person rose, but the typical household may have gained less.
The price level must have increased by the same 3 percent.
hard.commonError: Treating an average as a description of every household’s experience.
hard.feedback: Real GDP per person is an average and does not reveal how income or output gains are distributed.

hard.q: A country’s real GDP grows 3 percent while its population grows 4 percent. Approximately what happens to real GDP per person?
hard.commonError: Adding population growth to output growth instead of subtracting it.
hard.feedback: Approximate per-person growth equals real GDP growth minus population growth: 3% − 4% = −1%.

elite.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
elite.q: Country A has real GDP per person of $20,000 and grows at 2%. Country B has real GDP per person of $10,000 and grows at 6%. Using the Rule of 70, what is the strongest long-run implication?
options: B can catch up because it doubles much faster than A
A must always remain richer because it starts ahead
B cannot grow because it is poorer
elite.feedback: A doubles in about 35 years; B doubles in about 11.7 years, so B can catch up if growth persists.

elite.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
elite.q: A country grows real GDP by 6% while population grows by 2%. Approximately what happens to real GDP per person?
elite.feedback: Real GDP per person grows roughly by real GDP growth minus population growth, or about 4%.

elite.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
elite.q: A country with rapid population growth sees total real GDP rise but real GDP per person stay flat. What is the best interpretation?
options: Output is rising, but not faster than population
Living standards must be rising quickly
elite.feedback: Living standards are better captured by output per person, not total output alone.

elite.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
elite.q: Using the Rule of 70, Country X growing at 3.5% doubles in about how many years, and Country Y growing at 1.75% doubles in about how many years?

elite.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
elite.q: Two economies have equally scarce capital and similar access to technology. One has reliable electricity and trained operators; the other has frequent outages and little training. Which evidence best limits a claim that both must catch up equally fast?
options: The complementary inputs differ, so equal capital scarcity does not imply equal realized gains
Scarce capital has a low marginal product in both, regardless of complementary inputs
Technology access proves training and infrastructure no longer matter
A country’s current income ranking fixes its future growth ranking
elite.feedback: Capital scarcity can create high-return opportunities, but skilled workers and usable infrastructure help realize them. Catch-up is conditional; equal starting capital alone does not establish equal productivity growth.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
legendary.q: At the start, real GDP per person is $32,000 in Alder and $8,000 in Birch. Their persistent growth rates are 1.75% and 7%. Using the Rule of 70, which comparison follows after 40 years?
options: Alder is near $64,000 and Birch near $128,000; matching Alder’s initial level earlier was not yet catching its moving level
Both are near $64,000 because Birch began at one-quarter of Alder’s level
Alder is near $64,000 and Birch near $32,000; count only one doubling for Birch
Birch stays poorer because a lower starting level cannot be overcome
legendary.feedback: Approximate doubling times are 40 years for Alder and 10 for Birch. Over 40 years Alder doubles once to 64,000, while Birch doubles four times to 128,000. Reaching a rival’s initial level is distinct from catching a rival that also grows.

legendary.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
legendary.q: Over a decade, real GDP rises 12%, population rises 5%, and total labor hours rise 20%. Which pair best evaluates average material output and hourly productivity, to one decimal place?
options: Real GDP per person rises 6.7%; output per hour falls 6.7%
Both rise 12% because total real GDP rose
Real GDP per person rises 7%; output per hour falls exactly 8%
Real GDP per person falls 6.7%; output per hour rises 6.7%
legendary.feedback: Per-person output changes by 1.12/1.05 - 1 ≈ 6.7%; hourly output changes by 1.12/1.20 - 1 ≈ -6.7%. More total hours can raise average output even while productivity per hour falls.

legendary.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
legendary.q: Cedar reports nominal GDP of $960 billion, a deflator of 120, and 32 million residents. Delta reports $1,320 billion, a deflator of 150, and 44 million residents. Which current real-GDP-per-person comparison is supported using comparable base prices?
options: Cedar $25,000; Delta $20,000, so higher nominal total does not imply higher average real output
Cedar $30,000; Delta $30,000, so average real output is equal
Cedar $25,000; Delta $30,000, because only Cedar needs deflation
Cedar $20,000; Delta $25,000, because the larger deflator raises real output
legendary.feedback: Real GDP is 960/1.20 = 800 billion for Cedar and 1,320/1.50 = 880 billion for Delta. Divide by populations: 25,000 and 20,000 per person. The larger nominal aggregate does not settle the living-standard comparison.

legendary.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
legendary.q: A poor country grows quickly after gaining stable property rights, schools, and foreign investment. Which explanation is strongest?
options: Growth must be caused only by inflation
Poor countries grow automatically regardless of policy
legendary.feedback: Catch-up growth is more likely when institutions support investment, human capital, and technology adoption.

legendary.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
legendary.q: Real output per hour rises 10%, annual hours per employed person fall 5%, and the employed share of the population falls from 60% to 58%. Which conclusion about real GDP per person follows, assuming these cover all production?
options: It rises about 1.0%; the other two factors offset much of the productivity gain
It rises 10%; hourly productivity alone determines the exact change
It falls 7%; add the percentage and percentage-point declines
It rises 5%; the employed share does not enter output per person
legendary.feedback: Output per person equals output/hour × hours/worker × workers/person. Its factor is 1.10 × 0.95 × (58/60) ≈ 1.01017. Average output rises about 1.0%, much less than the hourly-productivity increase.

legendary.q: Real GDP per person rises, but average leisure falls sharply and pollution worsens. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: Market output per person rose, but overall well-being may have changed differently.
Living standards rose by exactly the same rate because GDP per person captures all welfare changes.
GDP per person becomes unusable whenever leisure or environmental quality changes.
Pollution and lost leisure are already fully subtracted from measured real GDP.
legendary.commonError: Treating real GDP per person as a complete measure of welfare.
legendary.feedback: Real GDP per person is useful for material output, but it does not fully capture leisure, environmental quality, distribution, or nonmarket activity.

calculation.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.

calculation.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
calculation.q: Country A grows at 2% and Country B grows at 5%. Using the Rule of 70, how much sooner does Country B double its income?
calculation.feedback: Country A doubles in about 35 years; Country B doubles in about 14 years, so B doubles about 21 years sooner.

calculation.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
calculation.q: If real GDP per person rises from $20,000 to $26,000, what is the percentage increase?

calculation.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
