boss.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
boss.q: An economist asks: why do small differences in annual growth rates matter so much over long periods?
boss.feedback: Small growth differences compound and can create large income gaps over decades.

boss.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
boss.q: Country A grows at 2% while Country B grows at 5%. What should you expect over several decades?
options: Country B's income will rise much faster if the growth rates persist
Both countries will end with the same income
Country A must grow faster because it starts slower
Growth rates do not affect living standards
boss.feedback: Higher sustained growth leads to much larger long-run income gains.

boss.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
boss.q: Using the Rule of 70, how long does it take income to double at a 5% annual growth rate?
boss.feedback: The Rule of 70 gives 70 / 5 = 14 years.

boss.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
boss.q: An economist points to two countries. Which measure is usually better for comparing average living standards?
boss.feedback: Real GDP per person is usually better for comparing average material living standards.

boss.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
boss.q: Country A has higher total GDP than Country B, but also has a much larger population. What should you check before comparing living standards?
boss.feedback: Total GDP can be misleading when countries have different population sizes.

boss.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
boss.q: Country A has real GDP of $2 trillion and a population of 50 million. What is real GDP per person?
boss.feedback: Real GDP per person = $2 trillion / 50 million = $40,000.

boss.q: A country reports $750 billion in inflation-adjusted output and 25 million residents. Which real-GDP-per-person figure is correct?
boss.commonError: Dividing by the wrong population scale.
boss.feedback: $750 billion ÷ 25 million residents = $30,000 per person.

boss.q: Using the Rule of 70, income growing at 3.5 percent per year doubles in about:
boss.commonError: Multiplying 70 by the growth rate instead of dividing.

boss.q: If population grows faster than real GDP, real GDP per person will generally:
boss.commonError: Ignoring population growth when evaluating average output.
boss.feedback: Per-person output falls when the population denominator grows faster than total real output.

boss.q: Country A grows 2 percent annually and Country B grows 4 percent. Using the Rule of 70, their approximate doubling times are:
options: 35 years for A and 17.5 years for B.
14 years for A and 28 years for B.
17.5 years for A and 35 years for B.
boss.commonError: Reversing the relationship between growth rates and doubling times.
boss.feedback: Doubling time is 70 divided by the growth rate: 70/2 = 35 and 70/4 = 17.5.

boss.q: Country A has real GDP of $2 trillion and 100 million people. Country B has real GDP of $1.5 trillion and 50 million people. Which has higher real GDP per person?
options: Country A because its total real GDP is larger.
They are equal because both figures are measured in real terms.
boss.commonError: Ranking living standards by total GDP rather than GDP per person.
boss.feedback: A has $20,000 per person; B has $30,000 per person, so B has the higher average output per person.

boss.q: Real GDP grows 5 percent and population grows 2 percent. Approximate real GDP per person growth is:
boss.commonError: Adding population growth to output growth.
boss.feedback: Approximate per-person growth is 5% − 2% = 3%.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
legendaryBoss.q: Boss Audit: Country A starts at $60,000 per person and grows at 2%. Country B starts at $30,000 and grows at 7%. Using Rule of 70, what is the best implication?
options: B reaches $60,000 in about 10 years; A doubles in about 35
B cannot catch up because it starts lower
legendaryBoss.feedback: B doubles in about 10 years; A doubles in about 35 years.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
legendaryBoss.q: Boss Audit: Real GDP rises 4%, population rises 1.5%, and output per worker rises 2%. What is approximate real GDP per person growth?
legendaryBoss.feedback: Real GDP per person growth is roughly real GDP growth minus population growth: 4 - 1.5 = 2.5%.

legendaryBoss.q: Country A starts at $48,000 real GDP per person and grows 2 percent annually. Country B starts at $24,000 and grows 4 percent. Using the Rule of 70, what is the strongest implication after about 35 years?
options: A remains twice as rich because starting income determines the permanent ranking.
B reaches only $48,000 because a 4 percent rate doubles once in 35 years.
A reaches $192,000 while B remains at $24,000.
Both are near $96,000 per person because A doubles once and B doubles twice.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Ignoring compounding and different doubling times when comparing convergence.
legendaryBoss.feedback: At 2 percent A doubles in about 35 years. At 4 percent B doubles in about 17.5 years, so it doubles twice in roughly 35 years.

repairQuestions.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
repairQuestions.q: Real GDP per person is calculated as:
repairQuestions.feedback: Real GDP per person is real GDP divided by population.

repairQuestions.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
repairQuestions.q: If real GDP is $1 trillion and population is 50 million, real GDP per person is:
repairQuestions.feedback: $1 trillion / 50 million = $20,000.

repairQuestions.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
repairQuestions.q: Which doubling-time question can be answered with the Rule of 70?
options: How long it takes income to double
repairQuestions.feedback: The Rule of 70 estimates doubling time.

repairQuestions.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
repairQuestions.q: At 2% growth, income doubles in about:

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
bridgeQuestions.q: Real GDP is $3 trillion and population is 100 million. What is real GDP per person?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: $3 trillion / 100 million = $30,000.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.

productivity-measurement.title: Productivity Measurement
productivity-measurement.description: Calculate output per worker and interpret productivity changes.

easy.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
easy.q: Productivity is best defined as:
options: Output produced per unit of labor input
easy.feedback: Productivity measures output per unit of labor input.

easy.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
easy.q: Why is productivity important for living standards?
options: Higher productivity allows workers to produce more goods and services
Higher productivity always means higher inflation
easy.feedback: A country can consume more when its workers produce more output per worker.

easy.q: In GROWTH-01, point A is located at capital per worker of 20. What output per worker is shown at A?
easy.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
easy.feedback: Point A shows output per worker of 28.53, so that is the productivity value read from the graph.

easy.q: Two factories produce 1,000 units. Factory A uses 100 labor hours and Factory B uses 125. Which factory has higher labor productivity?
options: They have equal productivity because output is equal
Productivity cannot be compared without the product price
easy.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
easy.feedback: Factory A produces 10 units per labor hour (1,000/100), versus 8 for Factory B (1,000/125), so A is more productive.

easy.q: A plant produces 10 percent more output with the same labor hours. What happens to output per labor hour?
options: It rises only if the number of workers also rises
easy.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
easy.feedback: With labor hours unchanged, a 10% increase in output raises output per labor hour by 10%.

easy.q: A business uses more labor hours but produces the same amount of output. What happens to labor productivity?
options: It becomes equal to total output
easy.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
easy.feedback: With output fixed, adding labor hours increases the denominator, so output per labor hour falls.

medium.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
medium.q: A country wants to raise living standards. Why is raising productivity more important than simply working more hours forever?
options: Higher worker output supports higher income per person
Working hours are the same as net exports
medium.feedback: Sustained living-standard gains come from producing more output per worker.

medium.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
medium.q: If two countries have the same number of workers but one produces twice as much output, the key difference is likely:
medium.feedback: More output with the same labor means higher productivity.

medium.q: Using GROWTH-01, moving from point A to point B raises output per worker by approximately how much?
medium.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
medium.feedback: Output per worker rises from 28.53 at A to 36.37 at B: 36.37−28.53=7.84.

medium.q: A firm produces 1,200 units in 100 hours, then 1,320 units in the same 100 hours. What is the productivity increase?
medium.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
medium.feedback: Productivity rises from 12 units/hour (1,200/100) to 13.2 (1,320/100), a 10% increase.

medium.q: Two economies have the same output per person, but workers in Economy X work fewer hours per person. What is the strongest inference?
options: The economies must have identical technology
Economy X necessarily has more natural resources
Economy X has higher output per hour worked
Economy X must have lower output per worker
medium.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
medium.feedback: The same output per person produced in fewer hours means more output per hour worked.

medium.q: Output grows 12 percent while total labor hours grow 4 percent. What happens to labor productivity?
options: It cannot change unless population changes
medium.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
medium.feedback: Productivity is output divided by labor hours; output grew faster than labor hours, so it rises.

hard.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
hard.q: Output rises from 10,000 units to 12,000 units while labor rises from 100 workers to 150 workers. What happens to productivity?
options: It falls from 100 units per worker to 80 units per worker
It rises from 100 units per worker to 120 units per worker
It stays at 100 units per worker
hard.feedback: Initial productivity is 100; new productivity is 12000/150 = 80, so productivity falls.

hard.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
hard.q: A country raises total output by adding more workers, but output per worker does not rise. What is the best conclusion?
options: GDP may rise without much gain in productivity or living standards
Real GDP per person must double
Productivity must rise because output rose
hard.feedback: More workers can raise total output without raising output per worker.

hard.q: GROWTH-01 becomes flatter as capital per worker rises. After moving from A to B, what should be expected from another equal increase in capital per worker, holding other factors constant?
options: A smaller additional gain in output per worker than the A-to-B gain
A larger gain because the economy is richer
No further output gain is possible
hard.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
hard.feedback: The curve is flatter to the right, so an equal additional amount of capital produces a smaller marginal output gain than A-to-B.

hard.q: Output rises 30 percent while labor hours rise 20 percent. To one decimal place, what is the exact increase in output per labor hour?
hard.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
hard.feedback: Productivity changes by (1.30/1.20)−1 = 8.3% when output rises 30% and labor hours rise 20%.
hard.roundingRule: Compute 1.30 ÷ 1.20 − 1 and round to one decimal place.

hard.q: Output per worker rises, but output per labor hour is unchanged. Which explanation is consistent with both facts?
options: The labor force must have shrunk to zero
Average hours worked per worker increased
Every worker became more productive per hour
hard.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
hard.feedback: If output per worker rises while output per hour is unchanged, each worker must be working more hours on average.

hard.q: Total output falls 2 percent while labor hours fall 5 percent. To one decimal place, what happens to labor productivity?
hard.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
hard.feedback: Productivity changes by (0.98/0.95)−1 ≈ 3.2%, so it rises.
hard.roundingRule: Compute 0.98 ÷ 0.95 − 1 and round to one decimal place.

elite.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
elite.q: Output rises from 50,000 to 60,000 while labor hours rise from 10,000 to 12,500. What happens to productivity?
options: It falls from 5 to 4.8 units per hour
It rises from 5 to 6 units per hour
It stays at 5 units per hour
It rises from 4.8 to 5 units per hour
elite.feedback: Initial productivity = 50,000/10,000 = 5. New productivity = 60,000/12,500 = 4.8.

elite.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
elite.q: A country's output per worker rises from $80,000 to $92,000. What is the percentage increase in productivity?
elite.feedback: Increase = 12,000 on a base of 80,000, so productivity rises by 15%.

elite.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
elite.q: Two countries have the same real GDP, but Country A has half as many workers as Country B. What must be true?
options: Country A has higher output per worker
Country A has lower real GDP per worker by definition
elite.feedback: Producing the same output with fewer workers means higher productivity.

elite.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
elite.q: A country raises output by increasing labor force participation, but output per worker falls. What is the most precise conclusion?
options: Total production rose, but productivity declined
Real GDP cannot rise when productivity falls
elite.feedback: More workers can raise total output even while output per worker falls.

legendary.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.q: A plant initially produces 24,000 units using 20 workers who each work 100 hours. Next period, 24 workers each work 80 hours and produce 25,344 units. Which comparison is correct?
options: Output per worker falls 12%; output per hour rises 10%
Both productivity measures rise 5.6%, matching total output
Output per worker rises 10%; output per hour falls 12%
Output per hour is unchanged because the plant hired more workers
legendary.feedback: Per-worker output falls from 1,200 to 1,056, or 12%. Total hours fall from 2,000 to 1,920; hourly output rises from 12 to 13.2, or 10%. Changes in hours per worker make the productivity measures diverge.

legendary.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.q: An economy initially produces $90 billion using 3 billion labor hours. A plan targets $108 billion while limiting total hours to 3.2 billion. What hourly productivity and increase over the initial level are required?
options: $30 per hour, with no productivity gain
legendary.feedback: Initial productivity is 90/3 = 30 dollars per hour. The target requires 108/3.2 = 33.75, or 12.5% more. Output growth alone overstates the needed productivity increase because hours also expand.

legendary.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.q: Two countries have equal real GDP per person, but one works far fewer hours per person. What can be inferred?
options: The country with fewer hours likely has higher output per hour
They must have identical productivity per hour
The country with more hours must be richer
Real GDP per person cannot be compared
legendary.feedback: Equal output per person with fewer hours implies greater output per hour.

legendary.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.q: A country’s real GDP rises 6% while employment rises 10%. Population is unchanged. Which assessment separates average material output from output per worker?
options: Output per person rises 6%; output per worker falls about 3.6%
Both fall about 3.6% because productivity declined
Output per person falls 4%; subtract employment growth from GDP growth
legendary.feedback: With population fixed, GDP per person rises 6%. Output per worker changes by 1.06/1.10 - 1 ≈ -3.6%. A productivity decline does not imply that average output per resident also declined.

legendary.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.q: Output per worker rises from $50,000 to $55,000, but real GDP per resident stays at $30,000. What must happen to the employed share of residents, assuming the measures cover the same output?
options: It falls from 60% to about 54.5%, offsetting the productivity rise
It rises from 60% to 66%, reinforcing the productivity rise
It stays at 60% because output per resident is unchanged
It falls from 50% to 45%, because wages determine employment shares
legendary.feedback: Workers/residents equals output/resident divided by output/worker. The share changes from 30,000/50,000 = 60% to 30,000/55,000 ≈ 54.5%. This accounting result does not identify why the employment share fell.

legendary.q: In GROWTH-01, two otherwise similar economies begin at A and B. Each receives the same small addition to capital per worker. Which conclusion is best supported by the graph?
options: Point A has the larger marginal output gain; convergence is not guaranteed
Point B must gain more because its current output per worker is already higher
Both economies must receive exactly the same output gain whenever capital increases by the same amount
Point A is guaranteed to overtake point B even if institutions and technology differ
legendary.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.feedback: The graph is steeper at A, so the same small capital addition yields a larger marginal output gain there; this alone does not guarantee convergence.

legendary.q: A plant automates part of production. Output rises 18 percent while labor hours fall 5 percent. To one decimal place, what happens to output per labor hour?
legendary.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.feedback: Productivity changes by (1.18/0.95)−1 ≈ 24.2%, because output rises while labor hours fall.
legendary.roundingRule: Compute 1.18 ÷ 0.95 − 1 and round to one decimal place.

calculation.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
calculation.q: If an economy produces 1,000 units with 100 workers, productivity is:

calculation.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
calculation.q: If output is 500 and labor hours are 50, productivity is:

calculation.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
calculation.q: A factory produces $900,000 of output using 30 workers. What is output per worker?

calculation.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
calculation.q: Workers produce 500 units in 1,000 hours before training and 650 units in 1,000 hours after training. What happened?
options: Productivity rose from 0.5 to 0.65 units per hour
Productivity fell from 2 to 1.54 units per hour
Output rose but productivity cannot change
calculation.feedback: Productivity is output per hour: 500/1000 = 0.5 and 650/1000 = 0.65.

calculation.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
calculation.q: If a firm produces 2,400 units with 300 labor hours, productivity is:
calculation.feedback: Productivity = output/labor hours = 2400/300 = 8 units per hour.

calculation.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
calculation.q: If productivity rises from 20 units per worker to 25 units per worker, what is the percentage increase?
calculation.feedback: The increase is 5 on a base of 20, so productivity rises by 25%.

boss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.q: An economist asks for the core driver of long-run living standards. What is the best answer?
boss.feedback: Long-run living standards depend heavily on productivity.

boss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.q: Why does higher productivity raise living standards?
options: Workers can produce more goods and services per unit of labor
Workers automatically work fewer hours with no tradeoff
boss.feedback: Higher productivity means more output can be produced from the same labor input.

boss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.q: A factory produces 4,800 units using 600 labor hours. What is productivity?
boss.feedback: Productivity = output / labor hours = 4,800 / 600 = 8 units per hour.

boss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.q: Productivity is calculated as:
boss.feedback: Productivity is output per unit of labor input.

boss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.q: Output rises, but labor input rises even faster. What happens to productivity?
options: Productivity is unchanged by labor input
boss.feedback: If labor rises faster than output, output per unit of labor falls.

boss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.q: Output rises from 1,000 to 1,200 while labor hours rise from 100 to 150. What happens to productivity?
options: It falls from 10 to 8 units per hour
It rises from 10 to 12 units per hour
It stays at 10 units per hour
It rises from 8 to 10 units per hour
boss.feedback: Initial productivity is 1,000/100 = 10. New productivity is 1,200/150 = 8.

boss.q: A factory produces 900 units in 90 labor hours. What is labor productivity?
boss.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.feedback: Labor productivity is output divided by labor hours: 900/90 = 10 units per labor hour.

boss.q: In GROWTH-01, which point has both lower capital per worker and lower output per worker?
options: Both points have the same capital per worker
Neither point lies on the production curve
boss.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.feedback: Point A is lower on both axes, so it has lower capital per worker and lower output per worker.

boss.q: A company hires more workers and total output rises, but output per labor hour does not change. What happened to labor productivity?
options: It became equal to output per worker automatically
It rose because total output rose
boss.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.feedback: Output and labor hours increased in the same proportion, leaving output per labor hour unchanged.

boss.q: Use the displayed GROWTH-01 coordinates. Moving from A to B doubles capital per worker. Approximately how much does output per worker rise, and what is consistent with the curve’s shape?
options: 7.84%; the numerical output increase is already a percentage
27.5%; the same further capital increase would add less output
27.5%; each further equal capital increase must add more output
boss.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.feedback: The graph gives output 28.53 at A and 36.37 at B. The increase is 7.84/28.53 × 100 ≈ 27.5%. The flattening curve shows diminishing marginal gains from equal additional capital, holding other inputs fixed.

boss.q: A factory targets 300,000 units of output and productivity of 12.5 units per labor hour. How many labor hours can it use and still meet that productivity target?
boss.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.feedback: Required labor hours equal output divided by target productivity: 300,000/12.5 = 24,000 hours.

boss.q: Economy A produces 480 billion units with 24 billion labor hours; Economy B produces 420 billion units with 20 billion labor hours. Which has higher labor productivity?
options: Economy A, because its total output is larger
They have equal productivity because both use billions of hours
Economy B, because it uses more labor hours
Economy B, at 21 units per hour versus 20 for Economy A
boss.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.feedback: Economy A produces 20 units/hour (480/24), while B produces 21 (420/20), so B is higher.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendaryBoss.q: Boss Audit: Output rises from 200,000 to 260,000 while labor hours rise from 20,000 to 25,000. What happens to productivity?
options: It rises from 10 to 10.4 units per hour
legendaryBoss.feedback: Initial productivity = 10. New productivity = 260,000/25,000 = 10.4.

legendaryBoss.q: Output grows 25 percent while labor hours grow 20 percent. To one decimal place, what is the exact productivity growth rate?
legendaryBoss.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Productivity changes by (1.25/1.20)−1 ≈ 4.2%, not by the simple difference in growth rates.
legendaryBoss.roundingRule: Compute 1.25 ÷ 1.20 − 1 and round to one decimal place.

legendaryBoss.q: GROWTH-01 shows A at lower capital per worker on the steeper portion of the curve and B farther to the right where the curve is flatter. What is the strongest productivity interpretation?
options: Equal capital additions must create identical output gains at every point on the curve
Output per worker is higher at A than at B even though A has less capital
The graph proves that every low-capital economy must eventually converge regardless of its other conditions
Equal new capital likely adds more output near A than near B
legendaryBoss.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Because the curve is steeper near A, an equal new capital addition is expected to add more output per worker near A.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
repairQuestions.q: Productivity is:
options: Output per unit of labor input
repairQuestions.feedback: Productivity measures output per unit of labor.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
repairQuestions.q: If output is 500 and labor hours are 100, productivity is:
repairQuestions.feedback: 500 / 100 = 5 units per hour.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
bridgeQuestions.q: Output is 2,400 units and labor input is 300 hours. What is productivity?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: 2,400 / 300 = 8 units per hour.

sources-of-productivity.title: Sources of Productivity
sources-of-productivity.description: Analyze physical capital, human capital, natural resources, and technology.

easy.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
easy.q: Physical capital refers to:
easy.feedback: Physical capital includes tools, machines, buildings, and equipment used in production.

easy.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
easy.q: Human capital refers to:
easy.feedback: Human capital is the knowledge and skill workers bring to production.

easy.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
easy.q: Natural resources are:
easy.feedback: Natural resources are inputs into production supplied by nature.

easy.commonError: Confusing better production methods with more labor or more machines.
easy.q: Technological knowledge means:
options: The market basket used for CPI
easy.feedback: Technological knowledge is know-how about production methods.

easy.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
easy.q: If workers receive better training, which productivity factor has increased?
easy.feedback: Training raises human capital.

easy.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
easy.q: If a firm gives workers better machines, which productivity factor has increased?
easy.feedback: Better machines increase physical capital per worker.

easy.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
easy.q: Diminishing returns to capital means:
options: Each added unit of capital contributes less extra output
easy.feedback: Diminishing returns means extra capital still helps, but by smaller amounts as capital accumulates.

easy.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
easy.q: The catch-up effect suggests that poorer countries may grow faster because:
options: They can get larger gains from additional capital
easy.feedback: Poorer countries may have less capital, so new capital can produce larger gains.

medium.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
medium.q: A new irrigation machine allows farmers to grow more crops with the same labor. Which productivity factor improved most directly?
medium.feedback: Better production methods and equipment raise productivity.

medium.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
medium.q: A nation invests heavily in worker training and apprenticeship programs. Which factor of productivity is most directly increased?
medium.feedback: Training and education increase human capital.

medium.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
medium.q: A country discovers large deposits of rare minerals used in manufacturing. Which productivity factor increased?
medium.feedback: Mineral deposits are natural resources.

medium.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
medium.q: A factory adds more machines for each worker. What should happen to output per worker, other things equal?
medium.feedback: More physical capital per worker generally raises productivity.

medium.commonError: Confusing better production methods with more labor or more machines.
medium.q: Which example best illustrates technological knowledge?
options: A new production process that uses fewer inputs per unit of output
A higher CPI for imported goods
medium.feedback: Technological knowledge means knowing better ways to produce.

medium.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
medium.q: Diminishing returns imply that if a country keeps adding capital while labor stays fixed:
options: Each additional unit of capital eventually adds smaller increases in output
Each additional unit of capital adds larger increases forever
Capital stops being counted in GDP
medium.feedback: Diminishing returns means extra capital becomes less productive as more of it is added.

medium.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
medium.q: Why might poorer countries experience faster growth than richer countries, other things equal?
options: Scarce capital can earn higher returns in poorer countries
Inflation forces poor countries to grow
medium.feedback: The catch-up effect occurs because capital may be especially productive where it is scarce.

hard.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
hard.q: A country buys more machines, improves schools, and adopts better production software. Which productivity factors are increasing?
hard.feedback: Machines raise physical capital, schools raise human capital, and software/process improvements reflect technological knowledge.

hard.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
hard.q: Two countries have similar workers and technology, but one has far more equipment per worker. Which difference most directly explains higher productivity?
hard.feedback: More equipment per worker generally raises output per worker.

hard.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
hard.q: A country with strong education but weak roads, ports, and electricity may still struggle with productivity because it lacks:
hard.feedback: Infrastructure is part of the physical capital that helps workers produce efficiently.

hard.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
hard.q: A new farming method raises output per acre without increasing land, labor, or machinery. Which factor is most directly responsible?
hard.feedback: A better method of production is technological knowledge.

hard.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
hard.q: Which example best illustrates human capital rather than technological knowledge?
options: Workers complete advanced training in machine repair
A firm invents a new production algorithm
hard.feedback: Training workers increases human capital; an invention or method itself is technological knowledge.

hard.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
hard.q: Why does capital deepening eventually face limits if technology and human capital do not improve?
options: Each extra machine adds less output as capital accumulates
Output per worker must become zero
hard.feedback: Diminishing returns limit the gains from adding more capital alone.

hard.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
hard.q: A poor country has little capital per worker. A new investment project adds basic equipment to farms and factories. Why might returns be high?
options: Because capital is scarce, the marginal product of additional capital can be large
Because diminishing returns never exist in poor countries
Because inflation makes machines cheaper in real terms
hard.feedback: The catch-up effect comes from high returns to capital where capital is scarce.

elite.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
elite.q: A government gives firms tax incentives to buy machines, funds technical colleges, and expands broadband infrastructure. Which productivity factors are targeted?
elite.feedback: Machines are physical capital, technical colleges build human capital, and broadband supports technological/infrastructure capacity.

elite.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
elite.q: Which change most clearly increases human capital rather than physical capital?
options: Workers complete coding and equipment-maintenance training
elite.feedback: Training raises worker knowledge and skills, which is human capital.

elite.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
elite.q: A country has abundant natural resources but weak education, poor infrastructure, and unstable property rights. What is the best growth interpretation?
options: Resources need skills, capital, technology, and institutions
Natural resources guarantee high living standards
Education is irrelevant if resources are abundant
GDP must equal natural resource value
elite.feedback: Natural resources help, but productivity also depends on skills, capital, technology, and institutions.

elite.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
elite.q: A new algorithm lets firms produce the same output with fewer machines and workers. Which factor best explains the improvement?
elite.feedback: A better production method is technological knowledge.

elite.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
elite.q: A country doubles its capital stock, but output rises by less than double. Which concept is most directly illustrated?
elite.feedback: Diminishing returns means additional capital raises output, but by less and less as capital accumulates.

elite.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
elite.q: A poor country receives basic tractors for farms that previously used hand tools. A rich country adds another advanced tractor to farms already full of equipment. Which investment likely has the higher marginal return?
options: The poor country's investment, because capital is scarcer
The rich country's investment, because diminishing returns never apply
elite.feedback: Capital tends to have higher marginal returns when it is scarce.

elite.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
elite.q: Which statement best connects diminishing returns and the catch-up effect?
options: Scarce capital has high returns, which fall as capital accumulates
Poor countries grow slower because every new unit of capital has zero return
Rich countries grow faster because diminishing returns help them
Catch-up occurs because inflation is lower in rich countries
elite.feedback: The catch-up effect relies on high returns to scarce capital, but diminishing returns eventually reduce those gains.

legendary.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
legendary.q: A factory adds machinery but productivity barely changes. After operator training, output rises with the same machines and labor hours. A manager concludes that machines have no productive value. Which interpretation best fits both stages?
options: Training helped realize the value of complementary capital; the first stage did not show that machines were useless
Training proves all earlier spending on machines should be subtracted from GDP
The later gain must be more physical capital because worker skills are unchanged by training
The data prove training raises output equally in every factory, regardless of equipment
legendary.feedback: The second stage changes human capital while holding physical inputs fixed. Its effect can reflect complementarity between skills and machinery. A weak result before training does not identify a zero contribution from capital.

legendary.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
legendary.q: A country discovers oil but has weak courts, low education, and poor infrastructure. Why might productivity remain low?
options: Resources alone do not guarantee high productivity
Oil is not a natural resource
Education matters only in service economies
legendary.feedback: Natural resources can help, but productivity depends on several complementary factors.

legendary.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
legendary.q: Two plants initially use the same machines and hours. Plant A adopts a freely available scheduling method and raises output 8%. Plant B trains operators without changing its method and raises output 8%. What can be inferred about productivity sources?
options: A changed technological knowledge and B human capital; equal output gains do not make the mechanisms identical
Both added physical capital because output rose without more labor hours
Both changed natural resources because the gain has the same size
A’s gain is human capital and B’s is technology solely because both involve information
legendary.feedback: A new production method is technological knowledge; skills acquired by workers are human capital. Equal measured gains do not identify a common mechanism or prove the two interventions would have equal effects elsewhere.

legendary.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
legendary.q: A country builds ports, roads, and power grids while also expanding vocational education. Which factors are increased?
legendary.feedback: Infrastructure is physical capital; vocational education builds human capital.

legendary.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.q: With labor, skills and technology fixed, output at 10, 20 and 30 identical machines is 100, 160 and 200 units. A planner predicts that 40 machines must yield 260. Which assessment follows from the observed pattern?
options: The successive gains are 60 and 40; continued diminishing marginal returns would put the next gain below 40
The observed average gain is 50, so 40 machines must yield exactly 250
The capital stock doubled once, proving output must double at 40 machines
The last gain was 40, so every later ten machines must add exactly 40
legendary.feedback: Equal capital increments add 60 then 40 units while other inputs are fixed. If the diminishing-returns pattern continues, the next increment adds less than 40; the table alone does not supply an exact future output level.

legendary.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
legendary.q: A low-capital economy gets basic tools and output jumps sharply. Later, additional tools add smaller gains. Which pattern is this?
options: Catch-up effect followed by diminishing returns
CPI substitution bias followed by inflation
Frictional unemployment followed by cyclical unemployment
legendary.feedback: Capital is highly productive when scarce, but additional capital eventually yields smaller gains.

legendary.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.q: A poor country and a rich country both add $1,000 of capital per worker. Why might the poor country gain more output per worker?
options: Poor countries do not face diminishing returns
The CPI is lower in poor countries
legendary.feedback: The catch-up effect depends on higher marginal returns to capital where capital is scarce.

boss.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
boss.q: Physical capital includes:
boss.feedback: Physical capital is the equipment and structures used to produce goods and services.

boss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.q: If workers receive better machinery, what should happen to productivity, other things equal?
options: It no longer depends on output
boss.feedback: Better machinery usually allows workers to produce more output per hour.

boss.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
boss.q: A business has 10 workers and 20 machines. It adds 10 more machines while employment stays the same. What has increased?
boss.feedback: More machines with the same number of workers means more physical capital per worker.

boss.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
boss.q: Two countries use similar machines, but one invests heavily in worker education and training. Which productivity factor differs most?
boss.feedback: Education and training build human capital—the knowledge and skills workers bring to production.

boss.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
boss.q: A country expands technical training and apprenticeship programs. Which productivity factor increases most directly?
boss.feedback: Training programs increase worker skills, which raises human capital.

boss.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
boss.q: Two factories use the same machines, but one has better-trained workers. Why might that factory produce more?
options: Its workers have more human capital
It has more natural resources by definition
boss.feedback: Better-trained workers can use tools and processes more effectively.

boss.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
boss.q: Which item is a natural resource used in production?
boss.feedback: Natural resources are inputs supplied by nature, such as land, water, minerals, and oil.

boss.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
boss.q: A new drilling method allows firms to extract more oil with the same workers and equipment. Which factor changed most directly?
boss.feedback: A better method of production is technological knowledge.

boss.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
boss.q: A country discovers large copper deposits but lacks skilled workers and roads. What is the best interpretation?
options: Resources help, but skills and capital also matter
Natural resources alone guarantee high living standards
boss.feedback: Natural resources are useful, but they work best alongside skills, infrastructure, and technology.

boss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.q: A factory keeps the workforce fixed and adds identical machines. Each new machine raises output by less than the previous one. What principle is shown?
boss.feedback: With other inputs fixed, each additional unit of capital eventually adds less output.

boss.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
boss.q: A worker with no tools gains a hammer and becomes much more productive. A worker with ten hammers gains an eleventh and barely improves. What does this show?
boss.feedback: The extra hammer matters more when capital is scarce.

boss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.q: Capital per worker doubles, but output per worker rises by only 25%. What does that suggest?
boss.feedback: Output rose less than proportionally to capital, which is consistent with diminishing returns.

boss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.q: The catch-up effect says:
options: Scarce capital can produce faster catch-up growth
Growth rates are unrelated to capital
boss.feedback: The catch-up effect occurs when capital-scarce economies can gain more from new investment.

boss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.q: Why might a poor country gain more from one additional machine than a rich country?
options: Scarcer capital can have a higher marginal return
The rich country cannot use machines
The poor country has no workers
Machines count only in poor countries
boss.feedback: Capital tends to have a higher marginal product when it is scarce.

boss.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
boss.q: Country A has very little capital per worker and Country B has abundant capital per worker. If each receives the same new equipment, which country may grow faster from that addition?
boss.feedback: Country A may gain more because capital is scarcer there.

boss.q: A worker receives a new machine that raises output with the same labor time. Which productivity input increased most directly?
boss.commonError: Treats every increase in capital as producing the same output gain.
boss.feedback: Providing a new machine increases physical capital per worker; with labor time unchanged, that can raise output per worker.

boss.q: In GROWTH-01, why does an equal small addition to capital have greater output potential near point A than near point B?
options: Point A has more output per worker than B
The curve is vertical near B
Capital has no relationship to output near A
The curve is steeper near A
boss.commonError: Treats every increase in capital as producing the same output gain.
boss.feedback: The curve is steeper near A, so an equal small capital addition produces a larger additional output per worker there.

boss.q: A new production method lets the same workers and machines produce more output. Which source of productivity improved?
boss.commonError: Confuses technological knowledge with merely owning more machines.
boss.feedback: Technology raises the efficiency with which available inputs are transformed into output.

boss.q: GROWTH-01 is upward sloping but becomes flatter as capital per worker rises. Which concept is represented by that shape?
options: A fixed level of productivity at all capital levels
boss.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
boss.feedback: An upward-sloping curve that becomes flatter means capital still raises output per worker, but each additional unit adds less: diminishing returns to capital.

boss.q: A low-capital country buys machinery, but workers lack training and firms cannot reliably obtain electricity. Why might catch-up remain limited?
options: Physical capital works with human capital, infrastructure, and other complementary inputs
Catch-up requires natural resources and nothing else
More machines always guarantee convergence regardless of other conditions
Human capital matters only after a country becomes rich
boss.commonError: Treats every increase in capital as producing the same output gain.
boss.feedback: Catch-up is limited because capital works with skills, reliable infrastructure, and institutions; machinery alone cannot overcome missing complements.

boss.q: Two countries add the same number of machines. One also improves worker training and production methods. Why can its productivity gain be larger?
options: Machines reduce productivity whenever training also rises
Human capital and technology affect only total population
Natural resources must fall when technology improves
Capital can complement human capital and technological knowledge
boss.commonError: Treats worker knowledge and skills as physical equipment.
boss.feedback: Training and better production methods complement machines, so the same equipment can generate a larger productivity gain.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
legendaryBoss.q: Boss Audit: A country improves schools but has no reliable electricity, roads, or legal protection for investors. What limits growth?
options: Skills need capital, infrastructure, and reliable institutions
Legal institutions matter only for unemployment
legendaryBoss.feedback: Productivity depends on complementary factors, not education alone.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendaryBoss.q: Two equal additions to capital per worker produce output gains of 9 and 6 with skills and technology fixed. A later 9-unit gain occurs after a new production method is introduced. Does that last observation refute diminishing returns to capital?
options: No; the first two gains compare capital with other inputs fixed, while technology changed in the third
Yes; any later larger gain refutes diminishing returns regardless of other changes
No; diminishing returns means total output must fall after adding capital
Yes; introducing technology changes physical capital into a natural resource
legendaryBoss.feedback: Diminishing marginal returns concerns additional capital with other determinants held fixed. The first two gains fit that pattern. A technology improvement changes the production relationship, so the larger third gain is not a comparable capital-only experiment.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendaryBoss.q: Boss Audit: A poor country with little capital receives basic machinery and output rises sharply. A rich country adds similar machinery and output barely changes. Why?
options: Scarce capital has a higher marginal product
Poor countries do not need human capital
legendaryBoss.feedback: The catch-up effect reflects high returns to capital where capital is scarce.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
repairQuestions.q: The catch-up effect says poorer countries may grow faster because:
options: Capital is scarce and may have high returns
repairQuestions.feedback: Capital may have high marginal returns when it is scarce.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
repairQuestions.q: Diminishing returns means extra capital eventually adds:
repairQuestions.feedback: Additional capital still helps, but by smaller amounts as capital becomes abundant.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
repairQuestions.q: Human capital means:
repairQuestions.feedback: Human capital is worker knowledge and skills.

repairQuestions.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
repairQuestions.q: Which description defines natural resources as a productivity input?
repairQuestions.feedback: Natural resources include land, water, minerals, oil, and other natural inputs.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
repairQuestions.q: Which option consists entirely of physical capital?
repairQuestions.feedback: Physical capital is equipment and structures used in production.

repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing better production methods with more labor or more machines.
repairQuestions.q: Which description defines technological knowledge as a productivity input?
options: Knowing better ways to produce goods and services
repairQuestions.feedback: Technological knowledge is production know-how.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
bridgeQuestions.q: A poor country gains basic tools and output jumps sharply. What concept does this fit?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Capital can have high returns where it is scarce.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
bridgeQuestions.q: A factory adds more and more machines, but each extra machine adds less output than the previous one. What is this?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Diminishing returns means each extra unit adds less additional output.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
bridgeQuestions.q: A firm trains workers to use advanced equipment. Which productivity factor rises?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Training increases worker skills.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
bridgeQuestions.q: A country discovers rare minerals used in manufacturing. Which productivity factor increased?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Minerals are natural resources.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
bridgeQuestions.q: Workers receive better machines but no extra labor is added. What should happen to productivity, other things equal?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: More or better capital helps workers produce more.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Confusing better production methods with more labor or more machines.
bridgeQuestions.q: A new production method lets firms make more output with the same inputs. What improved?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Better production methods are technological knowledge.
