economic-growth-policy.title: Economic Growth Policy
economic-growth-policy.description: Evaluate policies affecting long-run productivity and growth.

easy.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
easy.q: Which policy is most likely to support long-run productivity growth?
easy.feedback: Saving and investment help build capital and support growth.

easy.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
easy.q: Why can education policy raise economic growth?
easy.feedback: Education builds human capital, which can raise productivity.

easy.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
easy.q: Which policy environment is best for investment and growth?
options: Stable property rights and political stability
easy.feedback: Investment is more likely when property rights are stable and political institutions are reliable.

easy.q: Why can improved public health support long-run economic growth?
options: It guarantees faster money growth and permanently lower real interest rates.
Healthier workers can be more productive and miss fewer workdays.
It removes scarcity by preventing workers from ever becoming ill.
It raises real output only by increasing the economy’s current price level.
easy.commonError: Treating public health as unrelated to human capital and productivity.
easy.feedback: Health investments can strengthen human capital by improving worker productivity, attendance, and productive lifespans.

easy.q: Which policy most directly supports technological progress over the long run?
options: Protecting incentives for research, innovation, and technology adoption
Restricting firms from adopting or developing new production methods
Discouraging education and training that would help workers use new technologies
Making long-term investment and innovation rules less predictable for firms
easy.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
easy.feedback: Research, innovation incentives, and technology diffusion directly support new and adopted production methods, raising long-run productivity.

easy.q: Why can reliable courts and secure property rights support economic growth?
options: They guarantee that every investment succeeds
They eliminate diminishing returns to capital
They raise real GDP by redefining the price level
They make productive investment less risky
easy.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
easy.feedback: Reliable courts and secure property rights lower the risk that investors lose returns, encouraging productive long-term investment.

medium.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
medium.q: Which policy would most likely reduce long-run growth?
options: Weakening property rights so investors fear losing assets
medium.feedback: Weak property rights discourage investment and reduce growth potential.

medium.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
medium.q: Why can free trade support productivity growth?
options: Specialization, larger markets, and better inputs or technology
It guarantees no workers will lose jobs
medium.feedback: Trade can raise productivity by improving specialization, competition, and access to inputs or ideas.

medium.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
medium.q: A government wants to raise productivity over time. Which policy bundle makes the most sense?
options: Education, stable property rights, investment incentives, and research support
Higher uncertainty, weaker courts, and lower investment
medium.feedback: Growth-friendly policies support human capital, capital formation, innovation, and stable institutions.

medium.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
medium.q: Why can encouraging saving increase future productivity?
options: Saving can finance investment in capital goods
Saving directly lowers the unemployment rate to zero
Saving makes the CPI fixed basket disappear
medium.feedback: Saving helps provide funds for investment, which can increase capital and productivity.

medium.q: A low-income country has little capital per worker but weak courts and frequent asset seizure. What is the best catch-up diagnosis?
options: Catch-up is possible, but weak institutions can block productive investment
Low income guarantees rapid convergence even when investment incentives and institutions remain weak
Weak institutions automatically increase capital productivity enough to overcome poor investment incentives
Catch-up depends only on population growth rather than capital formation or productivity
medium.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
medium.feedback: Scarce capital creates catch-up potential, but insecure property rights and asset seizure can prevent the investment needed to realize it.

medium.q: Households save more, but firms cannot obtain financing for productive projects. What is missing from the growth channel?
options: A higher inflation rate that reduces the real value of accumulated household saving
A larger government transfer program that does not finance productive investment projects
A lower level of worker education that prevents any saving from reaching firms
Financial and institutional channels that turn saving into productive investment
medium.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
medium.feedback: Saving supports growth only when financial and institutional channels connect it to firms’ productive investment projects.

hard.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
hard.q: Which policy mix is most likely to support sustained productivity growth rather than only a temporary boost?
options: Education, investment, property rights, trade, and research support
Price ceilings on all capital goods
hard.feedback: Sustained growth comes from policies that improve capital, skills, innovation, and institutions.

hard.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
hard.q: Why might political instability reduce long-run growth?
hard.feedback: Investment is less likely when property rights and future rules are uncertain.

hard.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
hard.q: A government restricts foreign direct investment to protect domestic firms. What is a possible long-run cost?
options: Less capital, technology, and productivity growth
hard.feedback: Foreign investment can bring capital and technology, so restricting it may slow productivity growth.

hard.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
hard.q: Why can research and development policies raise living standards even if they do not immediately raise output?
options: They expand technology and future productivity
They directly count as discouraged workers
They only change the CPI basket
hard.feedback: R&D can improve production methods and technologies that raise future output per worker.

hard.q: GROWTH-01 shows that capital deepening can move an economy from A toward B, but the curve becomes flatter. Which policy implication is strongest?
options: Capital raises output, while sustained growth also needs broader productivity gains
Capital accumulation becomes completely useless as soon as the economy reaches point B on the graph
The graph implies that low-capital economies should stop investment before they approach point B
Long-run growth can rely on repeated physical-capital accumulation forever without complementary productivity improvements
hard.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
hard.feedback: Capital deepening raises output but faces diminishing returns; sustained growth also requires skills, technology, and sound institutions.

hard.q: A government uses a temporary spending surge that raises current output but does not change capital, worker skills, technology, or institutions. What is the main long-run limitation?
options: It permanently doubles output per worker even though productive capacity is unchanged
It guarantees a permanently lower natural unemployment rate without changing labor-market institutions
It eliminates diminishing returns to capital even though the capital stock is unchanged
It does not directly strengthen long-run productivity fundamentals
hard.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
hard.feedback: A temporary spending surge can raise current demand/output, but without stronger fundamentals it does not directly raise long-run productivity.

elite.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
elite.q: A government wants growth but repeatedly changes tax rules, seizes assets, and restricts courts. Which policy failure matters most?
elite.feedback: Unstable property rights reduce incentives to invest and innovate.

elite.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
elite.q: Why might openness to foreign investment raise productivity?
options: Capital, technology, management, and market links
It guarantees no domestic firms fail
It only changes the CPI basket
elite.feedback: Foreign investment can increase capital and transmit technology or business practices.

elite.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
elite.q: A country funds education but blocks firms from adopting new technologies and discourages investment. What is the likely issue?
options: Skills need complementary capital and technology
Investment is unrelated to output per worker
elite.feedback: Productivity growth usually requires complementary gains in skills, capital, and technology.

elite.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
elite.q: A country wants continuing productivity growth after a one-time equipment grant has raised capital per worker. Which package best addresses the limitation imposed by diminishing returns?
options: Maintain useful investment while improving skills, research and adoption of better methods
Repeat equal equipment grants and assume each creates a larger marginal output gain
Increase working hours and treat all additional output as higher hourly productivity
Replace training with equipment because physical and human capital cannot complement each other
elite.feedback: Additional capital can still raise output, but its marginal contribution may diminish with other inputs fixed. Skills and technological progress complement capital and support productivity growth beyond a single level increase.

legendary.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
legendary.q: A country raises saving incentives, yet surveyed firms postpone equipment purchases because contracts are often unenforceable. A proposed response doubles the saving subsidy without changing courts. Which recommendation is best supported?
options: Address enforcement risk alongside finance; more saving alone may not make productive investment attractive
Double the subsidy because every extra saved dollar necessarily becomes domestic machinery
Reduce worker training because courts and skills are substitute measures of the same input
Infer that physical capital has zero marginal product because investment is currently weak
legendary.feedback: The evidence identifies insecure returns as a barrier between available funds and investment. Predictable enforcement can complement financing. The survey does not establish an optimal subsidy or prove capital has no productive value.

legendary.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
legendary.q: A government blocks foreign investment to protect domestic firms. What long-run growth cost is most plausible?
options: Less capital inflow, less technology transfer, and weaker productivity growth
Higher productivity from isolation by definition
legendary.feedback: Foreign investment can bring capital, technology, and management know-how.

legendary.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
legendary.q: A region has trained engineers and funds for new equipment, but a rule prevents firms from using improved production methods. A review proposes more of the same training while keeping that rule. Which response best addresses the stated constraint?
options: Permit useful method adoption while maintaining skills and investment; training alone may not release the constraint
Purchase equipment alone because methods cannot affect output with machines fixed
Keep the rule because a stock of trained workers guarantees continuing productivity growth
Stop all training because technological knowledge makes human capital unproductive
legendary.feedback: The constrained margin is adopting better methods. Technology, skills and equipment can complement one another; repeating one input policy while blocking another can limit the gain. This is a conditional recommendation from the stated evidence.

legendary.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
legendary.q: A policy package improves contract enforcement, funds technical training, and supports research trials. After two years, capital and skill measures rise but output growth remains modest. Which assessment best separates a coherent strategy from a guaranteed result?
options: The package targets productivity determinants; implementation, diffusion and time still matter for realized growth
The package failed in principle because research must raise output immediately
The capital increase proves the research trials caused all future growth
The modest output change proves institutions cannot affect investment incentives
legendary.feedback: The instruments address institutions, human capital and technological knowledge. These are plausible growth channels, but observed short-run output alone neither guarantees eventual success nor disproves the channels. Implementation and technology diffusion must be evaluated.

legendary.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
legendary.q: Why can population growth reduce GDP per person even while raising total GDP?
options: Total GDP may rise while output per person falls
Capital per worker automatically rises with population
legendary.feedback: Population growth can dilute capital per worker unless investment keeps pace.

legendary.q: A country saves heavily and imports machinery, yet productivity barely rises because schools are weak, power is unreliable, and contracts are insecure. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Capital alone may not deliver catch-up when complementary conditions are weak
High saving guarantees convergence even when schools, infrastructure, and institutions remain persistently weak
The country should restrict technological adoption so scarce capital continues to have a high marginal product
The catch-up effect requires poorer economies to have lower productivity growth than richer economies
legendary.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
legendary.feedback: Investment needs complementary human capital, infrastructure, technology, and secure institutions; capital alone may not deliver catch-up.

legendary.q: A government subsidizes investment for five years, raising capital per worker, but it makes no lasting change to research, education, or institutions. Which long-run caution is most appropriate?
options: The temporary subsidy guarantees a permanently higher growth rate even after capital deepening slows
Research and education matter only for short-run aggregate demand
Institutions become irrelevant once the capital stock has increased
The capital increase can raise the output level, but sustained productivity growth needs broader continuing sources
legendary.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
legendary.feedback: More capital can raise the output level, but continuing productivity growth requires ongoing gains in skills, technology, and institutions.

boss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
boss.q: One policy that can support long-run productivity growth is:
boss.feedback: Saving and investment can build capital and raise productivity.

boss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
boss.q: Why can higher saving support future growth?
options: It can finance investment in capital goods
boss.feedback: Saving can provide funds for investment, which builds productive capital.

boss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
boss.q: A country saves more, and firms use those funds to buy machines and build factories. Which growth channel is operating?
boss.feedback: Saving can finance investment, and investment builds physical capital.

boss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
boss.q: Property rights matter for growth because they:
boss.feedback: Secure property rights encourage people and firms to invest.

boss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
boss.q: A country has skilled workers and natural resources, but businesses fear the government may seize assets. What is likely to happen to investment?
options: Investment is likely to be weaker
boss.feedback: Weak property rights and political instability discourage investment.

boss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
boss.q: Which policy environment is most growth-friendly?
options: Secure property rights and predictable rules
Frequent asset seizure and unclear laws
boss.feedback: Growth is more likely when institutions support investment and long-run planning.

boss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
boss.q: Education supports growth mainly by increasing:
boss.feedback: Education increases human capital, which can raise productivity.

boss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
boss.q: Why can openness to trade support productivity growth?
options: Specialization plus better inputs, ideas, and markets
boss.feedback: Trade can improve productivity through specialization, competition, and access to inputs and ideas.

boss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
boss.q: A government funds universities, public health, infrastructure, and research. What is it mainly trying to improve?
options: The resale value of old goods
boss.feedback: Education, health, infrastructure, and research can all support long-run productivity growth.

boss.q: Which policy most directly strengthens incentives for private long-term investment?
options: Secure property rights with predictable contract enforcement
Frequent asset seizure that makes long-term investment returns highly uncertain
Unpredictable contract enforcement that raises risk for firms making long-term investments
Bans on productive capital formation that prevent firms from expanding productive capacity
boss.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
boss.feedback: Secure property rights and predictable contract enforcement protect investment returns, strengthening incentives for private long-term investment.

boss.q: Which policy most directly builds human capital?
options: Reducing access to schooling and limiting opportunities for workers to acquire new skills
Making private research illegal and restricting firms from adopting outside technologies
Replacing productive investment with longer workweeks while worker skills remain unchanged
Improving education, job training, and basic health
boss.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
boss.feedback: Education, job training, and basic health build workers’ human capital and can raise productivity.

boss.q: Which policy most directly supports technological knowledge?
options: Increasing transfer payments without changing productive capacity
Research, innovation, and diffusion of better production methods
boss.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
boss.feedback: Research and innovation create technological knowledge, while diffusion spreads more productive methods to firms.

boss.q: A policy raises current consumer spending but leaves physical capital, human capital, technology, and institutions unchanged. Why is it not a complete long-run growth strategy?
options: It does not directly raise productivity fundamentals
Consumer spending can never affect measured GDP
Long-run growth is determined only by population
boss.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
boss.feedback: Higher current spending can raise demand, but leaving capital, skills, technology, and institutions unchanged does not raise the core productivity fundamentals.

boss.q: A poor economy has little capital but weak schools, unreliable infrastructure, and insecure property rights. Which policy package best supports conditional catch-up?
options: Improve institutions and human capital while enabling productive investment and technology adoption
Rely only on its low starting income to guarantee convergence
Block new technology so existing capital remains scarce
Raise population growth without expanding capital or skills
boss.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
boss.feedback: Conditional catch-up requires institutions and skills that let investment and technology adoption work productively, not just more capital.

boss.q: In GROWTH-01, moving from A toward B through capital accumulation raises output per worker, but the curve flattens. Which policy best complements continued capital deepening?
options: A policy that prevents workers from learning new methods
A policy that makes investment returns less secure
Policies that improve skills, innovation, and productive institutions
boss.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
boss.feedback: Once capital deepening faces diminishing returns, better skills, innovation, and productive institutions provide complementary sources of productivity growth.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
legendaryBoss.q: Boss Audit: A government wants sustained growth. Which combination is strongest?
options: Property rights, investment, education, trade, infrastructure, and R&D
Price controls, weak courts, and blocked technology
Transfers only, with no investment or training
Higher population growth with no capital deepening
legendaryBoss.feedback: Sustained productivity growth requires institutions, capital, human capital, technology, and openness.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
legendaryBoss.q: Boss Audit: A country saves more, but political instability causes investors to hold funds abroad instead of building domestic capital. What went wrong?
options: Saving did not translate into domestic investment
Saving always guarantees domestic capital accumulation
Capital flight increases GDP by definition
legendaryBoss.feedback: Saving supports growth only when institutions allow savings to become productive investment.

legendaryBoss.q: GROWTH-01 shows a low-capital economy at A with catch-up potential. Its government wants that potential to become sustained growth rather than remain a possibility. Which strategy is strongest?
options: Support productive investment while strengthening human capital, technology adoption, infrastructure, and institutions
Assume low initial capital alone guarantees convergence
Rely only on repeated additions of physical capital with no complementary improvements
Discourage investment so the marginal product of capital stays high
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Turning catch-up potential into sustained growth requires productive investment plus human capital, technology adoption, infrastructure, and secure institutions.

repairQuestions.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
repairQuestions.q: Which policy supports long-run productivity growth?
repairQuestions.feedback: Saving and investment can build capital and support productivity.

repairQuestions.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
repairQuestions.q: Secure property rights support growth because they:
repairQuestions.feedback: People invest more when they can keep the returns.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
bridgeQuestions.q: A government improves courts, property rights, schools, and infrastructure. What is it trying to support?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Those policies support investment, skills, and productivity.

unemployment-measurement.title: Unemployment Measurement
unemployment-measurement.description: Classify labor-force status and calculate unemployment and participation rates.

easy.commonError: Forgetting that the labor force includes employed plus unemployed workers.
easy.q: The labor force equals:
options: Unemployed plus not in labor force
easy.feedback: The labor force includes people who are employed and unemployed.

easy.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
easy.q: The unemployment rate is calculated as:
options: Unemployed divided by labor force times 100
Unemployed divided by adult population times 100
Not in labor force divided by employed times 100
easy.feedback: The unemployment rate is unemployed workers divided by the labor force.

easy.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
easy.q: The labor force participation rate is calculated as:
options: Labor force divided by adult population times 100
Unemployed divided by labor force times 100
easy.feedback: Labor force participation measures the share of adults in the labor force.

easy.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
easy.q: A person with a paid job is classified as:
easy.feedback: A person with a paid job is employed.

easy.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
easy.q: A person without a job who has actively looked for work in the last four weeks is classified as:
easy.feedback: Someone without a job who is actively looking is unemployed.

easy.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
easy.q: A retired person who is not looking for work is classified as:
easy.feedback: People not working and not looking for work are not in the labor force.

easy.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
easy.q: A discouraged worker is usually counted as:
easy.feedback: Discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed because they are not actively looking for work.

medium.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
medium.q: If 2 million unemployed workers become discouraged and stop looking for work, what happens immediately to the measured unemployment rate?
options: It rises because discouraged workers become unemployed
It falls because they leave the labor force
It is unchanged because employment rises
medium.feedback: Discouraged workers leave the labor force, which can lower the measured unemployment rate.

medium.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
medium.q: A parent who stays home full-time and is not seeking paid work is classified as:
medium.feedback: Someone not working and not looking for paid work is not in the labor force.

medium.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
medium.q: A person works one hour for pay during the survey week while looking for full-time work. How is the person classified?
medium.feedback: A person who does any paid work during the survey period is counted as employed.

medium.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
medium.q: A worker without a job sends out applications during the last four weeks. How is the worker classified?
medium.feedback: Actively looking for work while jobless means the person is unemployed.

medium.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
medium.q: A discouraged worker wants a job but stopped searching because they believe no jobs are available. How is this worker classified in official unemployment statistics?
medium.feedback: Discouraged workers are not in the labor force because they are not actively searching.

medium.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
medium.q: Which classification is most likely to make the unemployment rate understate labor market weakness?
options: Counting discouraged workers as not in the labor force
Counting active job seekers as unemployed
Counting unemployed workers in the labor force
medium.feedback: Discouraged workers are excluded from unemployment, which can hide labor market weakness.

hard.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
hard.q: An economy has 180 million employed, 12 million unemployed, and 68 million not in the labor force. What are the unemployment rate and labor force participation rate?
hard.feedback: Labor force = 192M; unemployment = 12/192 = 6.25%; adult population = 260M; participation = 192/260 = 73.85%.

hard.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
hard.q: An economy has 95 employed, 5 unemployed, and 50 not in the labor force. Ten people who were not in the labor force begin looking for work but do not find jobs. What is the new unemployment rate?
hard.feedback: Unemployed rises to 15 and labor force rises to 110, so unemployment = 15/110 = 13.6%.

hard.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
hard.q: An economy has 100 employed and 20 unemployed. Five unemployed workers find jobs, while five others stop looking. What happens to the unemployment rate?
options: It falls because unemployment decreases and the labor force shrinks
It stays unchanged because ten workers changed status
hard.feedback: Unemployed falls to 10 and labor force falls to 115, so the unemployment rate falls from 16.7% to about 8.7%.

hard.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
hard.q: If the unemployment rate falls because many jobless workers stop searching, what is the best interpretation?
options: Measured unemployment fell, but the labor market may not have improved
hard.feedback: A falling unemployment rate can be misleading if discouraged workers leave the labor force.

hard.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
hard.q: A person has no job, wants work, is available, but has not searched in six weeks because they think no jobs exist. How is this person classified and why does it matter?
options: Outside the labor force; this can understate labor-market weakness
Unemployed; all jobless people are counted
Structurally employed; skills do not matter
hard.feedback: Without active search, discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed, which can understate weakness.

hard.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
hard.q: A worker has a part-time job but wants full-time work. How is the worker officially classified?
options: Employed, even though the situation may show underemployment
Unemployed because the worker wants more hours
Not in the labor force because the job is part time
Discouraged because the worker is dissatisfied
hard.feedback: Part-time workers are counted as employed, even when they would prefer full-time work.

hard.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
hard.q: Which case creates the biggest problem for interpreting the official unemployment rate?
options: A large increase in discouraged workers
A worker voluntarily switches jobs and searches for one week
A student works part time by choice
hard.feedback: Discouraged workers are excluded from measured unemployment, hiding some labor market distress.

hard.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
hard.q: A laid-off engineer searches actively for work in the same field. A retired teacher does not want work. A discouraged factory worker wants work but stopped searching. Who is counted as unemployed?
options: The engineer and discouraged factory worker
hard.feedback: Only jobless people actively searching are counted as unemployed.

hard.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
hard.q: Why does the official unemployment rate miss some labor market pain?
options: It misses discouraged workers and involuntary part-time work
It counts all adults as unemployed
hard.feedback: The unemployment rate is useful but misses discouraged workers and underemployment.

elite.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
elite.q: An economy has 155 million employed, 9 million unemployed, and 96 million not in the labor force. What are the unemployment rate and labor force participation rate?
elite.feedback: Labor force = 164M; unemployment = 9/164 = 5.49%; adult population = 260M; participation = 164/260 = 63.08%.

elite.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
elite.q: An economy has 120 employed, 8 unemployed, and 72 not in the labor force. Four unemployed workers find jobs, and six people outside the labor force begin searching but do not find work. What is the new unemployment rate?
elite.feedback: New employed = 124, unemployed = 10, labor force = 134. Unemployment = 10/134 = 7.46%.

elite.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
elite.q: Adult population is 300 million. Labor force participation is 62%. The unemployment rate is 5%. How many people are unemployed?
elite.feedback: Labor force = 0.62 x 300 = 186M. Unemployed = 0.05 x 186 = 9.3M.

elite.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
elite.q: The unemployment rate falls from 6% to 5%, but employment also falls. What likely happened?
options: Some unemployed workers left the labor force
Every discouraged worker found a job
elite.feedback: The unemployment rate can fall even when employment falls if enough jobless workers stop searching.

elite.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
elite.q: An economy has 200 adults. 130 are employed and 10 are unemployed. If 10 employed workers retire and stop looking for work, what happens to labor force participation?
elite.feedback: Initial labor force = 140, participation = 70%. New labor force = 130, participation = 65%.

elite.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
elite.q: A person works 5 hours per week for pay but wants 40 hours. How is this person treated in the headline unemployment rate?
options: Counted as employed, even though underemployment is present
Counted as unemployed because they want more hours
Counted as not in the labor force
elite.feedback: The official unemployment rate counts part-time workers as employed, even if they want full-time work.

elite.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
elite.q: A survey has 84 adults working for pay, including 14 seeking more hours; 6 available jobless adults applied last week; 30 jobless adults are not searching. Which official count and limitation are correct?
options: Labor force 90 and unemployment about 6.7%; underemployment among paid workers is not in that rate
Labor force 104 and unemployment about 19.2%; add those seeking more hours to unemployment
Labor force 120 and unemployment 5%; use every adult in the denominator
Labor force 76 and unemployment about 7.9%; exclude part-time paid workers
elite.feedback: All 84 paid workers are employed, including those wanting more hours. Add the 6 active, available seekers for LF = 90; 6/90 ≈ 6.7%. The rate does not measure all of the part-time workers’ unmet demand for hours.

elite.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
elite.q: Which change would reduce the unemployment rate without improving the number of people employed?
options: Unemployed workers become discouraged and stop searching
Discouraged workers begin looking for jobs
elite.feedback: When unemployed workers stop searching, they leave the labor force and measured unemployment can fall.

elite.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
elite.q: A recession causes job loss, and some unemployed workers become discouraged. Why might the unemployment rate understate the recession's damage?
options: Discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed once they stop searching
All discouraged workers are counted as employed
The unemployment rate includes only retired people
elite.feedback: Discouraged workers leave the labor force, which can hide labor market weakness.

elite.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
elite.q: A survey classifies people as employed, unemployed, or not in the labor force. Which person is most likely misread by the headline unemployment rate as doing better than they are?
options: A part-time worker who wants full-time work
A full-time worker satisfied with their job
A retiree who does not want work
elite.feedback: Involuntary part-time workers are counted as employed, even though their labor situation is weak.

legendary.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
legendary.q: A labor survey starts with 132 employed, 12 unemployed and 56 other adults. Then 4 unemployed find jobs, 3 stop searching, 5 outsiders start searching without finding work, and 2 employed retire. All job seekers are available. What are the new unemployment and participation rates?
legendary.feedback: Employment becomes 132 + 4 - 2 = 134 and unemployment 12 - 4 - 3 + 5 = 10. The labor force is 144 of 200 adults, so participation is 72% and unemployment is 10/144 ≈ 6.9%. The entering and leaving flows happen to offset in total participation.

legendary.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
legendary.q: There are 200 adults, labor-force participation is 75%, and unemployment is 8%. Next month 6 unemployed stop searching, 6 employed retire, and 4 outsiders start searching without finding work. With everyone otherwise unchanged and seekers available, which final account is correct?
legendary.feedback: Initially LF = 150, U = 12 and E = 138. After the flows E = 132, U = 12 - 6 + 4 = 10 and LF = 142. Thus U/LF ≈ 7.0% and LF/adults = 71%. A lower unemployment rate coexists with fewer people employed.

legendary.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
legendary.q: An economy has 90 employed, 10 unemployed, and 50 not in the labor force. Five employed workers lose jobs and search; five unemployed workers stop searching. What happens to unemployment rate?
legendary.feedback: Employed falls to 85. Five newly unemployed workers replace five workers who stop searching, so unemployed remains 10 and the labor force falls to 95. The rate is 10/95 = 10.53%.

legendary.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
legendary.q: A population of 200 adults is unchanged. The unemployment rate stays at 6%, while participation falls from 75% to 70%. Which employment change and interpretation follow?
options: Employment falls by 9.4; a stable unemployment rate does not imply a stable number of jobs
Employment stays at 141; a stable rate fixes employment
Employment falls by 10; every labor-force exit must be an employed worker
Employment rises by 9.4; lower participation indicates more jobs
legendary.feedback: The labor force falls from 150 to 140. Employment is 94% of each total: 141 initially and 131.6 afterward, a decline of 9.4. The unchanged unemployment rate is a ratio, not an unchanged employment count.

legendary.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
legendary.q: A jobless worker applied to three jobs last week. Another jobless worker wants work but last searched two months ago. A third works 3 hours per week but wants full-time work. How are they classified?
options: Unemployed; not in labor force; employed
Employed; unemployed; not in labor force
Not in labor force; unemployed; employed
legendary.feedback: Recent active search means unemployed; no recent search means not in labor force; any paid work means employed.

legendary.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
legendary.q: Which case makes the headline unemployment rate look better than the actual labor market experience?
options: A rise in discouraged workers and involuntary part-time workers
legendary.feedback: Discouraged and involuntary part-time workers are not fully captured by the headline unemployment rate.

legendary.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
legendary.q: A report says unemployment fell from 20 to 12 while employment rose from 180 to 184. Adult population is fixed at 250, and the only flows were unemployed people finding jobs or stopping search. Which decomposition and participation change are implied?
options: 4 found jobs and 4 left search; participation fell from 80% to 78.4%
4 found jobs and 8 left search; participation fell to 76.8%
4 left search and none found jobs; the employment rise is unrelated
legendary.feedback: The employment rise identifies 4 job findings. Of the 8-person unemployment decline, the remaining 4 are exits. LF falls from 200 to 196, so participation falls from 80% to 78.4%. Both hiring and withdrawal contributed to the lower headline rate.

legendary.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
legendary.q: Two districts have the same unemployment rate and population. One has lower participation and a larger share of employed people working part time because full-time work is unavailable. Which additional comparison is best before calling their labor markets equally strong?
options: Compare employment per adult and desired versus actual hours; the headline rate omits both differences
Compare only total unemployment; equal unemployment rates guarantee equal counts
Count all involuntary part-time workers as unemployed before applying the official definition
Exclude discouraged workers from every indicator because they are outside the labor force
legendary.feedback: Unemployment divides job seekers by the labor force. Lower participation can lower employment per adult even at the same rate, while involuntary part-time workers remain employed. Additional participation and hours evidence is needed for the broader assessment.

legendary.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
legendary.q: If measured unemployment falls because 1M unemployed workers become discouraged, while employment is unchanged, what happens to labor force participation?
legendary.feedback: Discouraged workers leave the labor force, so labor force participation falls.

calculation.commonError: Forgetting that the labor force includes employed plus unemployed workers.
calculation.q: If 90 people are employed and 10 are unemployed, what is the labor force?

calculation.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
calculation.q: If 10 people are unemployed and the labor force is 100, what is the unemployment rate?

calculation.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
calculation.q: If the labor force is 160 million and the adult population is 250 million, what is the labor force participation rate?

calculation.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
calculation.q: Adult population is 250 million, labor force participation is 64%, and unemployment is 8 million. How many people are employed?
calculation.feedback: Labor force = 0.64 x 250 = 160 million. Employed = 160 - 8 = 152 million.

calculation.commonError: Forgetting that the labor force includes employed plus unemployed workers.
calculation.q: An economy has 140 million employed people, 10 million unemployed people, and 50 million people not in the labor force. What is the labor force?

calculation.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
calculation.q: Using 140 million employed and 10 million unemployed, what is the unemployment rate?

calculation.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
calculation.q: If the labor force is 150 million and the adult population is 200 million, what is the labor force participation rate?

calculation.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
calculation.q: An economy has 90 employed, 10 unemployed, and 50 not in the labor force. If 5 unemployed workers stop looking, what is the new unemployment rate?
calculation.feedback: New unemployed = 5 and new labor force = 95, so unemployment = 5/95 = 5.3%.

boss.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
boss.q: An economist asks: an adult has no job, wants work, and applied for jobs last week. How is this person classified?
boss.feedback: A jobless person who is actively searching is counted as unemployed.

boss.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
boss.q: A jobless worker wants work but stopped searching because they think no jobs are available. What happens to official unemployment statistics?
options: The worker is not counted as unemployed
The worker is counted as employed
The worker raises employment and unemployment
The worker is counted as unemployed forever
boss.feedback: Discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed once they stop actively searching.

boss.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
boss.q: An economy has 100 employed, 10 unemployed, and 40 not in the labor force. If 5 unemployed workers become discouraged, what is the new unemployment rate?
boss.feedback: Unemployed falls to 5 and labor force falls to 105, so unemployment is 5/105 = 4.76%.

boss.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
boss.q: A survey records 126 employed adults, 14 available jobless adults actively searching, and 60 adults outside the labor force. Which participation calculation is correct, and how does it differ from unemployment?
options: 7% participation; unemployment and participation are the same ratio
boss.feedback: Participation is (126 + 14)/(126 + 14 + 60) = 70%. Unemployment instead divides the 14 unemployed by the labor force of 140, yielding 10%. The denominators answer different questions.

boss.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
boss.q: The unemployment rate falls, but labor force participation also falls sharply. What is the best interpretation?
options: Some workers may have stopped searching
boss.feedback: A falling unemployment rate can be misleading if workers leave the labor force.

boss.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
boss.q: Adult population is 250 million. Employed workers are 150 million and unemployed workers are 10 million. What is the labor force participation rate?
boss.feedback: Labor force = 150 + 10 = 160 million. Participation = 160/250 x 100 = 64%.

boss.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
boss.q: A jobless adult who had stopped searching accepts a paid part-time job but still wants full-time work. With other adults unchanged, which immediate changes follow?
options: Employment and the labor force rise; involuntary part-time work can remain
Unemployment rises because the worker still wants a full-time job
Employment rises but the labor force stays fixed because the job is part time
Participation falls because part-time employment is outside the labor force
boss.feedback: The worker moves from outside the labor force to employed. Both employment and the labor force rise, while wanting more hours does not change the official employed classification. The hours shortfall remains relevant to labor-market well-being.

boss.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
boss.q: Why can involuntary part-time work make the unemployment rate look better than the labor market feels?
options: Part-time workers are counted as employed even if they want more hours
Part-time workers are counted as unemployed twice
Part-time work is excluded from the labor force
Part-time workers are counted as discouraged
boss.feedback: The headline unemployment rate does not fully capture underemployment.

boss.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
boss.q: An economy has 120 employed, 12 unemployed, and 68 not in the labor force. Four unemployed workers find jobs, and four employed workers move to part-time work but keep paid jobs. What is the new unemployment rate?
boss.feedback: New employed = 124, unemployed = 8, labor force = 132. Unemployment = 8/132 = 6.1%. Part-time workers remain employed.

boss.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
boss.q: An economy has 200 adults, 120 employed, 10 unemployed, and 70 not in the labor force. Then 10 unemployed workers become discouraged. What are the new unemployment rate and participation rate?
boss.feedback: Unemployed becomes 0 and labor force becomes 120. Unemployment = 0%; participation = 120/200 = 60%.

boss.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
boss.q: An economist synthesizes this evidence: a worker is counted as employed even though they want full-time work, another worker is not counted as unemployed because they stopped searching, and actual unemployment is above the natural rate. What is the combined lesson?
options: The headline rate misses underemployment and discouraged workers; excess unemployment signals cyclical weakness
The headline unemployment rate captures all labor pain perfectly
Actual unemployment above natural unemployment means no recessionary pressure
Discouraged workers raise the unemployment rate
boss.feedback: This pulls together underemployment, discouraged workers, and cyclical unemployment.

boss.q: A worker has a part-time job but is actively searching for full-time work. How is the worker classified in official labor statistics?
options: Unemployed, because the worker wants more hours.
Employed, because the worker has a paid job.
Outside the labor force, because the job is part time.
Discouraged, because the worker is searching for another job.
boss.commonError: Classifying an underemployed worker as unemployed.
boss.feedback: Official employment status is based on having work, not on whether the worker wants additional hours.

boss.q: A jobless adult is available to work but has not searched during the past four weeks. How is this person usually classified?
boss.commonError: Ignoring the active-search requirement for official unemployment.
boss.feedback: A jobless person generally must be available and actively searching to be counted as unemployed.

boss.q: Which equation defines the labor force?
options: Labor force = employed people - discouraged workers.
Labor force = working-age population - employed people.
Labor force = employed people + unemployed people.
boss.commonError: Including everyone in the population or excluding officially unemployed workers.
boss.feedback: The labor force contains people who are employed plus people who are jobless and actively seeking work.

boss.q: A discouraged worker stops searching for a job while no one finds employment. What can happen to the official unemployment rate?
options: It can fall because the worker leaves unemployment and the labor force.
It must rise because employment did not increase.
It stays unchanged because discouraged workers remain unemployed.
It becomes zero because the labor force shrinks.
boss.commonError: Assuming the unemployment rate can fall only when employment rises.
boss.feedback: When a discouraged worker exits the labor force, both the number unemployed and the denominator fall, which can lower the rate.

boss.q: An economy has 900 employed people, 100 unemployed people, and 200 adults outside the labor force. What are the unemployment and labor-force participation rates?
options: The unemployment rate is 8.3 percent and participation is 75 percent.
The unemployment rate is 10 percent and participation is about 83.3 percent.
The unemployment rate is 10 percent and participation is 100 percent.
The unemployment rate is 12 percent and participation is about 66.7 percent.
boss.commonError: Using the adult population as the unemployment-rate denominator or omitting unemployed workers from participation.
boss.feedback: The labor force is 1,000, so unemployment is 100/1,000 = 10 percent; participation is 1,000/1,200 = 83.3 percent.

boss.q: An employed worker loses a job and immediately begins an active search. What happens initially?
options: Employment and labor force both rise as the search begins.
Unemployment falls because active search counts as employment.
Employment falls, unemployment rises, and the labor force is unchanged.
The worker exits the labor force despite beginning a search.
boss.commonError: Treating job loss with active search as labor-force exit.
boss.feedback: The person moves from employed to unemployed but remains in the labor force, raising the unemployment rate.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
legendaryBoss.q: Employed = 150M, unemployed = 12M, not in labor force = 88M. Then 4M unemployed find jobs, and 6M leave the labor force. What is the new unemployment rate?
legendaryBoss.feedback: New employed = 154M, unemployed = 2M, and the labor force = 156M. Unemployment = 2/156 = 1.28%.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
legendaryBoss.q: Adult population is 320M, participation is 62.5%, and unemployment is 5%. How many are employed?
legendaryBoss.feedback: Labor force = 0.625 x 320 = 200M. Unemployed = 10M. Employed = 190M.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
legendaryBoss.q: Boss Audit: A discouraged worker starts searching again but does not find work. What happens immediately?
options: Labor force and measured unemployment both rise
legendaryBoss.feedback: A discouraged worker who resumes active search is counted as unemployed and reenters the labor force.

repairQuestions.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
repairQuestions.q: A discouraged worker is usually classified as:
repairQuestions.feedback: Discouraged workers are not actively searching, so they are not in the labor force.

repairQuestions.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
repairQuestions.q: In official labor statistics, how is a person with a paid job classified?
repairQuestions.feedback: A paid job means the person is employed.

repairQuestions.commonError: Forgetting that the labor force includes employed plus unemployed workers.
repairQuestions.q: Which two groups are added to calculate the labor force?
repairQuestions.feedback: The labor force is employed plus unemployed.

repairQuestions.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
repairQuestions.q: Labor force participation rate is:
options: Labor force divided by adult population times 100
repairQuestions.feedback: Labor force participation measures the share of adults in the labor force.

repairQuestions.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
repairQuestions.q: The unemployment rate is:
options: Unemployed divided by labor force times 100
repairQuestions.feedback: Unemployment rate = unemployed / labor force x 100.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
bridgeQuestions.q: A discouraged worker starts applying for jobs again but does not find one. What happens?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Active job search moves the worker into the labor force as unemployed.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
bridgeQuestions.q: A person works one paid hour but wants full-time work. How are they counted?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Paid work means employed, even if underemployed.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Forgetting that the labor force includes employed plus unemployed workers.
bridgeQuestions.q: Use the labor-force identity: with 90 employed and 10 unemployed, what is the labor force?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Labor force = employed + unemployed = 100.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
bridgeQuestions.q: If the labor force is 150 and adult population is 250, what is labor force participation?

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
bridgeQuestions.q: If 8 people are unemployed and the labor force is 160, what is the unemployment rate?

unemployment-types.title: Types of Unemployment
unemployment-types.description: Distinguish frictional, structural, and cyclical unemployment.

easy.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
easy.q: Frictional unemployment is caused by:
options: The time it takes workers to search for suitable jobs
A long-term mismatch between skills and jobs
easy.feedback: Frictional unemployment comes from job search and matching.

easy.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
easy.q: Structural unemployment is caused by:
options: A mismatch between worker skills and available jobs
easy.feedback: Structural unemployment occurs when workers' skills or locations do not match available jobs.

easy.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
easy.q: Cyclical unemployment is associated with:
easy.feedback: Cyclical unemployment rises during recessions or weak economic conditions.

easy.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
easy.q: A worker quits one job and spends two weeks looking for a better one. This is:
easy.feedback: Short-term job search is frictional unemployment.

easy.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
easy.q: A factory worker loses a job because the industry permanently shifts to automation and the worker lacks new skills. This is:
easy.feedback: A lasting skills mismatch is structural unemployment.

easy.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
easy.q: A worker loses a job because a recession causes customers to spend less. This is:
easy.feedback: Job loss from weak demand during a recession is cyclical unemployment.

medium.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
medium.q: A college graduate takes two months to find a first job that matches their skills. This is most likely:
medium.feedback: Job search while matching workers and firms is frictional unemployment.

medium.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
medium.q: A coal miner loses work because the economy shifts permanently toward other energy sources and the miner lacks transferable skills. This is:
medium.feedback: A long-term mismatch between skills and available jobs is structural unemployment.

medium.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
medium.q: A hotel lays off workers because a recession reduces travel demand. This is:
medium.feedback: Layoffs from weak demand during a recession are cyclical unemployment.

medium.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
medium.q: Which type of unemployment would still exist even when the economy is healthy?
medium.feedback: Frictional unemployment exists because workers and firms take time to match.

medium.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
medium.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes structural from frictional unemployment?
options: Structural means mismatch; frictional means normal job search
Frictional unemployment is always permanent, while structural unemployment lasts one day
Structural unemployment is caused only by inflation
medium.feedback: Structural unemployment is about mismatch; frictional unemployment is about normal search.

medium.q: A worker leaves a job to move to another city and spends six weeks searching for a similar position while local demand remains strong. Which type of unemployment best fits the case?
options: The worker is outside the labor force
medium.commonError: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
medium.feedback: Frictional unemployment comes from normal search and matching as workers move between jobs or enter the labor market.

hard.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
hard.q: A recession causes restaurants to lay off workers. At the same time, some workers quit jobs to search for better matches. Which types of unemployment are present?
hard.feedback: Recession layoffs are cyclical; voluntary job search is frictional.

hard.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
hard.q: A city loses manufacturing jobs permanently, but health care jobs expand and require different credentials. Which unemployment type dominates?
hard.feedback: A mismatch between worker skills and available jobs is structural unemployment.

hard.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
hard.q: Which example is most clearly frictional rather than structural unemployment?
options: A worker leaves one accounting job and searches for another accounting job in the same city
A miner cannot find work after mines permanently close
A worker is laid off because recession reduces demand
A cashier loses work because all stores automate checkout permanently
hard.feedback: Short-term search between similar jobs is frictional unemployment.

hard.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
hard.q: Cyclical unemployment differs from the natural rate because cyclical unemployment:
options: Rises during downturns when aggregate demand is weak
Exists only because workers search for better jobs
Is caused by long-run skill mismatch only
Is always zero when inflation rises
hard.feedback: Cyclical unemployment is tied to business-cycle downturns.

hard.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
hard.q: A software worker is unemployed for three weeks while comparing offers. A former textile worker is unemployed for two years because local factories closed. What is the best classification?
options: Software worker: frictional; textile worker: structural
The software worker is not in the labor force
hard.feedback: Short job search is frictional; long-term mismatch after industry decline is structural.

hard.q: A worker is laid off when a recession cuts sales. By the time demand recovers, the firm has automated the old job and the worker lacks the new required skills. What best describes the worker’s unemployment now?
options: It began as cyclical but is now primarily structural
It remains purely cyclical because the original layoff occurred in a recession
It is frictional because every unemployed worker is searching
It is no longer unemployment once the original recession ends
hard.commonError: Confuses persistent skill or location mismatch with temporary search or weak aggregate demand.
hard.feedback: Structural unemployment reflects a durable mismatch between workers and available jobs, skills, or locations.

elite.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
elite.q: A recession closes restaurants temporarily, while automation permanently reduces demand for cashiers. Which unemployment types are present?
elite.feedback: Recession-related layoffs are cyclical; permanent automation mismatch is structural.

elite.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
elite.q: A worker leaves a job voluntarily to search for a better match during a strong economy. A different worker loses a job because their industry permanently shrinks. Which pairing is correct?
elite.feedback: Voluntary job search is frictional; long-term industry decline creates structural unemployment.

elite.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
elite.q: Why is cyclical unemployment not part of the natural rate?
options: It reflects short-run downturns rather than normal job search or structural mismatch
It is always caused by unions
It exists only because workers quit to find better jobs
It is another name for frictional unemployment
elite.feedback: The natural rate includes frictional and structural unemployment, not recession-driven cyclical unemployment.

elite.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
elite.q: Which worker is most clearly structurally unemployed?
options: A typist whose skills are outdated after firms switch to new software systems
A nurse moving between hospitals in the same city
A waiter laid off during a short recession
A teacher taking summer vacation but returning in August
elite.feedback: Structural unemployment involves a mismatch between worker skills and available jobs.

elite.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
elite.q: A worker has the right skills but needs time to find the right employer. Another has obsolete skills and needs retraining. What separates the two cases?
elite.feedback: Frictional unemployment is search time; structural unemployment is mismatch.

legendary.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
legendary.q: A worker is laid off because a recession reduces sales. Six months later, the worker's old industry adopts technology that permanently eliminates the job type. How should the unemployment diagnosis change?
options: Cyclical at first; structural if the job type disappears
It must be natural unemployment only
legendary.feedback: Weak demand causes cyclical unemployment, but permanent skill/job mismatch is structural.

legendary.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
legendary.q: After a regional downturn ends, one group has suitable job offers but needs time to choose; another cannot meet credentials for expanding occupations. A third group has already accepted paid part-time work while seeking full-time jobs. Which diagnosis respects both cause and official status?
options: The first group is frictionally unemployed, the second structurally unemployed, and the third employed
All three are structurally unemployed because each wants a different job
The first is cyclical, the second frictional, and the third outside the labor force
All three are unemployed until they obtain their preferred full-time jobs
legendary.feedback: Normal matching among suitable jobs is frictional; a persistent credential mismatch is structural. A paid part-time job makes the third group employed under the official measure, even though underemployment may remain.

legendary.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
legendary.q: Spending and total vacancies recover after a downturn, but vacancies concentrate in licensed occupations while displaced workers lack the credentials. Which evidence would most directly strengthen a structural diagnosis over a purely cyclical one?
options: Credential training is followed by placements into the unfilled occupations while overall spending changes little
All vacancies disappear when spending weakens again
Workers have suitable offers and are briefly choosing among them
Unemployment falls only when economy-wide spending rises sharply, with no change in skills
legendary.feedback: The mismatch between expanding occupations and worker credentials points to a structural barrier. Placements after relevant training, with demand broadly unchanged, strengthen that mechanism rather than a claim based only on weak spending or ordinary search.

legendary.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
legendary.q: A worker is unemployed because moving to available jobs is too costly, even though jobs exist elsewhere. Which type is most likely?
legendary.feedback: Geographic mismatch is a form of structural unemployment.

legendary.q: A regional downturn eliminates jobs at several firms. One year later overall demand has recovered, but many displaced workers remain unemployed because growing industries require different credentials. Which diagnosis is most accurate?
options: Cyclical unemployment fell, while structural unemployment remains
The remaining unemployment must still be entirely cyclical
The recovery eliminates both structural and frictional unemployment
The remaining unemployment is frictional simply because workers are looking for jobs
legendary.commonError: Confuses persistent skill or location mismatch with temporary search or weak aggregate demand.
legendary.feedback: Structural unemployment reflects a durable mismatch between workers and available jobs, skills, or locations.

legendary.q: A city’s jobless population includes skilled movers choosing among local openings and workers whose occupation disappeared. A single faster job-listing service is proposed for both. Which prediction is best supported?
options: It must eliminate both groups’ unemployment because each can read the same vacancies
It affects only cyclical unemployment because information is part of total spending
It turns structurally unemployed workers into employed people as soon as listings are viewed
It can shorten matching for the first group; the second may also need retraining or mobility support
legendary.commonError: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
legendary.feedback: The first group faces search frictions among suitable jobs. The second faces a durable mismatch that information alone may not remove. Diagnosis should guide the intervention without assuming guaranteed placement.

boss.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
boss.q: An economist asks about job search: frictional unemployment is mainly caused by:
options: The time required for workers and firms to find good matches
A permanent mismatch between skills and jobs
boss.feedback: Frictional unemployment comes from normal job search and matching.

boss.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
boss.q: A software developer quits one job and spends three weeks comparing offers from similar firms. What type of unemployment is this?

boss.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.

options: Structural unemployment from a persistent skill mismatch
Cyclical unemployment caused by a recession
Outside the labor force because the worker is not searching
