labor-market-institutions.title: Labor-Market Institutions
labor-market-institutions.description: Analyze minimum wages, unions, job search, and efficiency wages.

easy.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
easy.q: Unemployment insurance may increase frictional unemployment because it can:
options: Reduce the urgency of job search
Remove workers from the adult population
easy.feedback: Unemployment insurance can reduce the cost of continued job search, which may lengthen unemployment spells.

easy.commonError: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
easy.q: A binding minimum wage can create unemployment because it:
options: Raises the wage above equilibrium and creates a surplus of labor
Increases labor demand above labor supply
easy.feedback: A binding minimum wage can create a surplus of labor, meaning more workers want jobs than firms want to hire.

easy.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
easy.q: Unions can contribute to unemployment when they:
options: Push wages above equilibrium in unionized labor markets
Remove all bargaining power from workers
easy.feedback: Union wage bargaining can raise wages above equilibrium and reduce the quantity of labor demanded.

easy.q: A job-placement service that quickly matches workers with suitable openings is most likely to reduce:
options: Frictional unemployment caused by normal job search.
Cyclical unemployment caused by weak aggregate demand.
Structural unemployment caused by a lasting skill mismatch.
Seasonal unemployment caused by predictable calendar changes.
easy.commonError: Confusing job matching with policies that address cyclical demand shortfalls.
easy.feedback: Better matching shortens normal job-search spells and therefore reduces frictional unemployment.

easy.q: A firm deliberately pays above the market-clearing wage to reduce turnover and encourage effort. Which idea best describes the policy?
easy.commonError: Treats union wage setting and efficiency wages as identical mechanisms or ignores their tradeoffs.
easy.feedback: Unions bargain over wages, while firms may voluntarily pay efficiency wages; both can keep wages above market-clearing levels under some conditions.

easy.q: Workers bargain collectively with an employer over wages and working conditions. Which institution is most directly involved?
easy.commonError: Treats union wage setting and efficiency wages as identical mechanisms or ignores their tradeoffs.
easy.feedback: Unions bargain over wages, while firms may voluntarily pay efficiency wages; both can keep wages above market-clearing levels under some conditions.

medium.commonError: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
medium.q: A binding minimum wage above equilibrium creates unemployment because:
options: Quantity of labor supplied exceeds quantity of labor demanded
Quantity of labor demanded exceeds quantity supplied
All workers leave the labor force
medium.feedback: A wage floor above equilibrium creates a surplus of labor.

medium.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
medium.q: How can unemployment insurance improve worker outcomes even if it lengthens unemployment spells?
options: It gives workers income support and time to find better job matches
It forces all firms to hire
It lowers the labor force to zero
medium.feedback: Unemployment insurance can support job seekers, but may also reduce urgency to accept a job quickly.

medium.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
medium.q: A union negotiates wages above the competitive equilibrium. What is the likely effect in that labor market?
options: More workers want jobs than firms want to hire
Firms hire every worker who wants a job
The unemployment rate is impossible to calculate
medium.feedback: Above-equilibrium wages can create a surplus of labor in that market.

medium.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
medium.q: Efficiency wage theory says firms may pay above-equilibrium wages because higher wages can:
options: Improve effort, retention, or worker quality
medium.feedback: Efficiency wages can make workers more productive or reduce costly turnover.

medium.q: How do a union wage and an efficiency wage differ most directly?
options: A union wage is bargained collectively; an efficiency wage is voluntarily chosen by the firm
A union wage is always below equilibrium; an efficiency wage is always legally mandated
A union wage affects only prices; an efficiency wage affects only GDP accounting
They are identical policies imposed by government in every labor market
medium.commonError: Treats union wage setting and efficiency wages as identical mechanisms or ignores their tradeoffs.
medium.feedback: Unions bargain over wages, while firms may voluntarily pay efficiency wages; both can keep wages above market-clearing levels under some conditions.

medium.q: A state improves job-search assistance while leaving unemployment benefits unchanged. Which outcome is most directly targeted?
options: Higher cyclical unemployment through weaker aggregate demand
A larger labor surplus from a binding minimum wage
A permanent increase in structural mismatch
Shorter frictional unemployment spells through faster matching
medium.commonError: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
medium.feedback: Job-search assistance improves worker-firm matching, so it can shorten normal search spells and reduce frictional unemployment.

hard.commonError: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
hard.q: A binding minimum wage raises hourly pay for workers who keep jobs but reduces low-skill employment. What is the strongest economic interpretation?
options: Higher wages for some, fewer opportunities for others
The policy must help every worker equally
The policy has no effect if firms dislike it
hard.feedback: A binding wage floor can raise wages for some workers while creating a labor surplus.

hard.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
hard.q: Unemployment insurance increases from 12 weeks to 40 weeks. What is the likely tradeoff?
options: Better income protection, but longer searches and more frictional unemployment
Lower income protection and shorter unemployment spells only
A guaranteed fall in labor force participation to zero
hard.feedback: Unemployment insurance helps workers smooth income but can reduce urgency to accept work quickly.

hard.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
hard.q: A union contract raises wages above the competitive equilibrium. Which workers are most likely hurt?
options: Workers no longer hired at the higher union wage
All union workers who keep their jobs
hard.feedback: Above-equilibrium wages can reduce labor demanded, hurting workers who cannot get hired.

hard.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
hard.q: Why might a firm voluntarily pay an efficiency wage above equilibrium?
options: To reduce turnover, attract better applicants, and encourage effort
To guarantee all unemployed workers get jobs
To make nominal GDP equal real GDP
hard.feedback: Efficiency wages can be profitable if they improve worker quality, effort, morale, or retention.

hard.q: Unemployment benefits become more generous while a new matching platform sharply improves the quality and speed of job referrals. What is the best prediction for frictional unemployment?
options: The net effect is ambiguous because the two changes work in opposite directions
It must rise because matching services cannot offset the weaker search incentives created by benefits
It must fall because unemployment benefits never change search incentives when matching technology improves
Only structural unemployment can change because neither policy affects normal search and matching
hard.commonError: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
hard.feedback: Frictional unemployment comes from normal search and matching as workers move between jobs or enter the labor market.

hard.q: A firm raises wages above equilibrium and worker effort rises enough to improve productivity, but fewer workers are hired at the higher wage. Which interpretation is most complete?
options: Higher productivity guarantees every worker seeking a job will be hired despite the higher wage
The wage increase must be a legally binding minimum wage rather than a voluntary firm decision
The policy can raise worker effort only when cyclical unemployment has already fallen to zero
Efficiency-wage benefits can coexist with a labor surplus and fewer job opportunities
hard.commonError: Treats union wage setting and efficiency wages as identical mechanisms or ignores their tradeoffs.
hard.feedback: An efficiency wage can raise effort and productivity, but if it is above equilibrium, firms may hire fewer workers, creating a labor surplus.

elite.commonError: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
elite.q: A wage floor is $16. At that wage, 112 workers seek jobs and firms hire 88. A demand increase raises desired hiring to 100 while the wage and labor supply stay fixed. What happens to the labor surplus?
options: It falls from 24 to 12; higher labor demand reduces the excess supply
It stays at 24 because the statutory wage did not change
It rises from 24 to 36 because firms want more labor
It disappears because any increase in demand makes a floor nonbinding
elite.feedback: Initially the surplus is 112 - 88 = 24. With hiring demand of 100, it is 112 - 100 = 12. The wage floor can remain binding even as the size of the labor surplus changes.

elite.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
elite.q: Unemployment insurance gives workers time to search, but also reduces urgency. Which unemployment type is most directly affected?
elite.feedback: Unemployment insurance most directly affects job search behavior, which relates to frictional unemployment.

elite.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
elite.q: A union wage raises pay for employed members but reduces hiring by firms. Which statement best captures the tradeoff?
options: Insiders gain while some outsiders lose job opportunities
The unemployment rate must fall to zero
elite.feedback: Union wage gains can help employed members but reduce opportunities for workers not hired.

elite.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
elite.q: A firm pays above-equilibrium wages and finds quits fall, applicant quality improves, and effort rises. Which theory explains this?
elite.feedback: Efficiency wage theory explains why above-equilibrium wages may raise productivity or reduce turnover.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
legendary.q: In a competitive labor market, employment is 100 at the clearing wage. A binding wage floor produces labor supply of 140 and demand of 95. Assuming everyone seeking work is available and active, which comparison is correct?
options: Employment falls by 5, while the labor surplus is 45; these are different quantities
Employment falls by 45 because every person in the surplus previously had a job
Employment falls by 40, matching the increase in labor supply
There is no surplus because 95 people remain employed
legendary.feedback: Employment changes from 100 to 95, a loss of 5. The new excess of labor supplied over labor demanded is 140 - 95 = 45, including the effect of increased job seeking as well as reduced hiring. The surplus is not the number of pre-existing jobs lost.

legendary.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
legendary.q: A benefit extension lowers the cost of continued search. A simultaneous placement program improves matching. Average unemployment duration then falls. Which conclusion is warranted from these facts alone?
options: The combined outcome improved duration; it does not show that the benefit extension by itself shortened search
The fall proves benefit extensions always shorten search
The extension must have been ineffective at protecting income because duration fell
The placement program cannot matter because benefits determine every search decision
legendary.feedback: Income support can reduce search urgency while better matching shortens search. Their combined result does not isolate either effect; a credible separate comparison would be needed. The duration result also does not measure the value of income protection.

legendary.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
legendary.q: A negotiated wage rises from $20 to $24 while employment falls from 100 to 90, with hours per worker fixed. What happens to the total wage bill, and what distributional claim is justified?
options: The wage bill rises 8%; retained workers gain hourly pay while some workers lose jobs
The wage bill falls 10%; no workers gain from the contract
The wage bill rises 20%; the employment change is irrelevant
The wage bill rises 8%; this proves every original worker is better off
legendary.feedback: The wage bill changes from 20 × 100 = 2,000 to 24 × 90 = 2,160 per common unit of hours, an 8% rise. The aggregate increase does not erase the job losses; gains to retained workers and losses to displaced workers differ.

legendary.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
legendary.q: A firm considers raising wages from $18 to $21 per hour. Output per hour is expected to rise from 6 to 7 units through better retention and effort, with other unit costs unchanged. Which cost calculation and caution are correct?
options: Wage cost stays $3 per unit if the productivity forecast holds; the forecast still needs evidence
$3.50 per unit is certain because productivity cannot respond to wages
$2.57 per unit is certain because the old wage applies to the new output
$3 per unit proves the wage policy eliminates unemployment throughout the economy
legendary.feedback: The old wage cost is 18/6 = 3 per unit; the proposed cost is 21/7 = 3 if the effort/retention forecast occurs. This makes an efficiency-wage rationale possible, but does not prove the forecast or settle economy-wide unemployment.

legendary.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
legendary.q: Which policy most directly targets structural unemployment?
options: More generous unemployment insurance with no training
Changing GDP from nominal to real
legendary.feedback: Structural unemployment comes from mismatch, so retraining can help.

legendary.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
legendary.q: Which policy most directly affects frictional unemployment?
options: Job-search assistance that improves matching speed
A new GDP deflator base year
legendary.feedback: Frictional unemployment is about search and matching, so better matching can reduce it.

legendary.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
legendary.q: A recession increases layoffs, while unemployment insurance helps workers avoid immediate hardship but lengthens some searches. Which pair of concepts is involved?
options: Cyclical unemployment and frictional unemployment incentives
legendary.feedback: The recession creates cyclical unemployment; unemployment insurance affects job-search incentives.

boss.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
boss.q: Which policy best targets structural unemployment?
boss.feedback: Retraining can reduce mismatch between worker skills and available jobs.

boss.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
boss.q: An economist asks about worker protection: unemployment insurance is designed mainly to:

boss.feedback: Unemployment insurance gives income support to workers who lose jobs.

boss.q: Why can unemployment insurance increase frictional unemployment?

boss.feedback: Benefits can make longer job search less costly, increasing frictional unemployment.

boss.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
boss.q: A state increases unemployment benefits but also improves job-placement services. What is the most careful prediction?

boss.feedback: Two forces move in opposite directions, so the net effect is not automatic.

boss.feedback: A binding minimum wage is above equilibrium and prevents the wage from falling to market-clearing level.

boss.feedback: Labor surplus = quantity supplied - quantity demanded = 140 - 100 = 40 workers.

boss.commonError: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.

options: Higher wages for some, fewer job opportunities for others

boss.q: An economist examines bargaining power: unions can contribute to unemployment when they:
options: Push wages above equilibrium in unionized labor markets
Make all labor markets perfectly competitive
boss.feedback: Union wage bargaining can raise wages above equilibrium and reduce labor demanded.

boss.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.

boss.feedback: The labor surplus is 500 - 420 = 80 workers.

boss.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.

boss.feedback: Efficiency wages can be profitable if they improve worker productivity or reduce costly turnover.

boss.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.

They reduce labor supply to zero

A shortage of workers because labor demand exceeds labor supply

repairQuestions.q: Unions and efficiency wages can both create unemployment when they:
repairQuestions.feedback: Above-equilibrium wages can create a surplus of labor.

repairQuestions.q: Why can more generous unemployment insurance lengthen some unemployment spells even while protecting workers?
options: It can reduce search urgency while providing income support
It permanently destroys worker skills by definition
It makes every unemployed worker leave the labor force
It raises labor demand above labor supply automatically
repairQuestions.commonError: Treating unemployment insurance as either purely harmful or guaranteed to reduce unemployment.
repairQuestions.feedback: Unemployment insurance protects income and may improve match quality, but more generous benefits can also reduce search urgency and lengthen some frictional unemployment spells.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
bridgeQuestions.q: At a minimum wage, 120 workers want jobs and firms hire 90. What is the labor surplus?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Surplus = 120 - 90 = 30 workers.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
bridgeQuestions.q: A firm pays above-equilibrium wages to reduce quits and increase effort. What theory explains this?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Efficiency wages can improve effort and reduce turnover.

bridgeQuestions.q: A new job-matching service reduces the average time workers spend between jobs. What family-level implication follows?
options: Lower frictional unemployment can reduce the natural rate
Lower frictional unemployment must raise cyclical unemployment
The natural rate is fixed and cannot respond to matching
Only the measured CPI can change from better matching
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Failing to connect institutions that change search efficiency with the frictional component of the natural rate.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Faster matching reduces frictional unemployment; because frictional unemployment is part of the natural rate, the natural rate can fall.

natural-rate-of-unemployment.title: Natural Rate of Unemployment
natural-rate-of-unemployment.description: Interpret the natural rate and deviations caused by business cycles.

easy.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
easy.q: The natural rate of unemployment exists because:
options: Even in the long run, frictional and structural unemployment remain
Cyclical unemployment is always zero in recessions
easy.feedback: The natural rate reflects unemployment that remains from normal job search and structural mismatches.

easy.q: Which unemployment is excluded from the natural rate?
options: Cyclical unemployment caused by a recessionary gap.
Unemployment caused by normal worker turnover.
easy.commonError: Including cyclical unemployment in the natural-rate baseline.
easy.feedback: The natural rate includes frictional and structural unemployment, not recession-driven cyclical unemployment.

easy.q: The natural rate of unemployment is best described as:
options: A fixed constant that must be identical in every decade.
A normal benchmark that can change as labor-market conditions change.
The unemployment rate observed only during recessions.
easy.commonError: Treating the natural rate as zero or permanently fixed.
easy.feedback: Demographics, institutions, matching efficiency, and structural change can alter the natural rate.

easy.q: A more effective job-search platform helps workers find suitable jobs faster. What is the most likely effect on the natural rate?
options: It rises because cyclical unemployment increases.
It becomes equal to the inflation rate.
It falls because frictional unemployment is reduced.
It cannot change because the natural rate is fixed.
easy.commonError: Assuming better matching affects only cyclical unemployment.
easy.feedback: Faster matching shortens normal job search and can lower the natural rate.

easy.q: If actual unemployment equals the natural rate, which unemployment component is approximately zero?
easy.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
easy.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

easy.q: Which change is most likely to raise the natural rate rather than merely raise cyclical unemployment?
options: A temporary recession that reduces aggregate demand
A one-quarter fall in consumer spending
A short-lived decline in business confidence
A lasting increase in worker-skill mismatch
easy.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
easy.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

medium.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
medium.q: Why does the natural rate of unemployment remain positive in the long run?
options: Normal job search and structural mismatches persist
medium.feedback: The natural rate includes frictional and structural unemployment that persist in normal times.

medium.q: A rapid shift away from coal production leaves many workers without the skills demanded by expanding industries. What is the most likely effect?
options: Cyclical unemployment must fall to zero.
The natural rate must fall because jobs changed.
Structural unemployment and the natural rate may rise.
medium.commonError: Classifying a persistent skill mismatch as only cyclical unemployment.
medium.feedback: Sectoral change can raise structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

medium.q: Actual unemployment is below the estimated natural rate. Which interpretation is strongest?
options: The labor market is unusually tight, with possible inflation pressure.
The economy has eliminated every form of unemployment.
Structural unemployment must have fallen permanently to zero.
The economy must be operating with a recessionary output gap.
medium.commonError: Equating below-natural unemployment with zero unemployment or recession.
medium.feedback: Unemployment below the natural rate indicates a tight labor market, not the disappearance of frictional and structural unemployment.

medium.q: A temporary collapse in aggregate demand ends, and spending returns to normal. What should happen to unemployment if the natural rate itself did not change?
options: The natural rate rises permanently by the recession increase.
Cyclical unemployment fades, moving actual unemployment toward the natural rate.
Frictional unemployment falls permanently to zero after spending recovers.
Actual unemployment remains at its recession peak even after demand returns.
medium.commonError: Treating a temporary demand-driven unemployment increase as a permanent natural-rate shift.
medium.feedback: When the demand shortfall closes, cyclical unemployment recedes and the unemployment rate moves toward its natural benchmark.

medium.q: A strong expansion lowers actual unemployment, but worker matching, skills, and labor-market institutions are unchanged. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: Cyclical unemployment may have fallen without changing the natural rate
The natural rate must have fallen by the same amount as actual unemployment
Structural unemployment must have disappeared permanently
The natural rate becomes zero whenever aggregate demand is strong
medium.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
medium.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

medium.q: A retraining program successfully moves displaced workers into growing occupations. If other conditions are unchanged, what is the most likely effect on the natural rate?
options: It must rise because more workers have changed occupations
It changes only if cyclical unemployment rises
It cannot change because the natural rate is fixed forever
It may fall because structural unemployment is reduced
medium.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
medium.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

hard.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
hard.q: In a healthy economy, unemployment is still 4.5%. Which explanation best fits the natural rate?
options: Job search and skill mismatches persist
The economy must be in recession
The unemployment data must be impossible
hard.feedback: The natural rate remains positive because frictional and structural unemployment persist even in normal times.

hard.q: Two economies both have 6% actual unemployment. Economy A has a 4% natural rate and Economy B has a 6% natural rate. Which comparison is strongest?
options: Economy A has more positive cyclical unemployment than Economy B
Both economies have the same cyclical unemployment because actual unemployment is equal
Economy B must be in a deeper recession because its natural rate is higher
Neither economy can have frictional or structural unemployment
hard.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
hard.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

hard.q: A new nationwide matching system shortens the average time between jobs without changing aggregate demand. Which effect is most plausible?
options: Structural unemployment must rise by the same amount
The natural rate cannot respond to matching efficiency
Frictional unemployment and the natural rate may decline
hard.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
hard.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

hard.q: A long-lasting geographic mismatch develops: job openings expand in regions that displaced workers cannot easily move to. What is the most likely natural-rate effect?
options: The natural rate falls automatically because jobs exist somewhere
The natural rate is unchanged whenever total vacancies are positive
Structural unemployment can rise, pushing the natural rate upward
Only cyclical unemployment rises because location never affects structural mismatch
hard.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
hard.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

hard.q: Expansionary demand policy lowers actual unemployment from 7% to 5%, while the estimated natural rate remains 5%. Which interpretation fits the change?
options: A positive cyclical unemployment gap was eliminated
The natural rate fell from 7% to 5% because demand increased
hard.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
hard.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

hard.q: A policy improves occupational retraining but also makes job search somewhat longer by allowing workers to search for better matches. What is the best conclusion about the natural rate?
options: The net effect is ambiguous because structural unemployment may fall while frictional search may rise
The natural rate must fall because every labor-market policy lowers unemployment
The natural rate must rise because longer search is the only relevant channel
Only cyclical unemployment can be affected by either policy
hard.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
hard.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

elite.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
elite.q: Two economies each have 5% natural unemployment. One combines 1% frictional and 4% structural unemployment; the other combines 3% frictional and 2% structural. Which policy comparison fits these equal totals?
options: The first has more mismatch to address; the second has more scope for faster matching, holding effectiveness comparable
The same natural rate proves their underlying labor-market problems are identical
Only the second has natural unemployment because frictional unemployment is the sole component
Both can reach zero unemployment simply by ending a recession
elite.feedback: Both totals equal 5%, but the components differ. A common aggregate benchmark does not establish identical barriers or identical policy priorities. Relevant retraining and matching interventions target different components.

elite.q: A long recession causes workers to lose skills and attachment to the labor force. Why might unemployment remain elevated after aggregate demand recovers?
options: The natural rate must remain unchanged after every recession.
Cyclical unemployment automatically becomes permanent inflation.
Hysteresis may have raised the natural rate through lasting labor-market damage.
Frictional unemployment can exist only while the economy is expanding.
elite.commonError: Assuming all recession unemployment disappears without lasting effects.
elite.feedback: A prolonged downturn can create persistent skill loss or detachment that raises structural unemployment and the natural rate.

legendary.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
legendary.q: An economy has 2% frictional, 3% structural and 2% cyclical unemployment. A recovery eliminates the cyclical component. At the same time, better matching lowers frictional unemployment to 1.5%, with structural unemployment unchanged. What actual and natural rates remain?
options: Both are 4.5%; recovery removed the cyclical component and matching lowered the natural rate
Both are 5%; recovery cannot change any observed unemployment rate
Actual is 2.5% and natural is 4.5%; subtract the cyclical decline again
Both are zero because the recession has ended
legendary.feedback: After recovery, cyclical unemployment is zero. The remaining natural rate is 1.5 + 3 = 4.5%, also the actual rate. Ending the downturn and improving normal matching are distinct channels.

legendary.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
legendary.q: Actual unemployment falls from 9% to 7%. Over the same interval, an estimate of the natural rate falls from 6% to 4%. What happens to the cyclical gap, and what claim would overstate the evidence?
options: The gap stays at 3 points; the lower actual rate alone does not show cyclical weakness diminished
The gap falls 2 points; actual unemployment determines the gap by itself
The gap rises 2 points; a lower natural rate always raises the gap by that amount
The gap becomes zero because both rates fell equally
legendary.feedback: Initially the gap is 9 - 6 = 3 points; finally it is 7 - 4 = 3. Actual unemployment fell with the estimated natural benchmark, so these numbers do not show a smaller cyclical component.

legendary.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
legendary.q: Suppose actual unemployment is 4%, natural unemployment is 5%, and inflationary pressure is rising. What is the likely labor-market interpretation?
options: Unemployment below the natural rate signals a tight labor market
legendary.feedback: Actual unemployment below the natural rate suggests tight labor markets and possible inflationary pressure.

legendary.q: An economy recovers fully from a recession, yet unemployment settles at a higher level than before because displaced workers lost skills during the long downturn. Which explanation best fits?
options: Lasting labor-market damage may have raised the natural rate
Cyclical unemployment must still equal the entire unemployment rate
The natural rate cannot change after any recession
A higher natural rate means all remaining unemployment is frictional
legendary.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
legendary.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

legendary.q: A retraining reform is expected to lower structural unemployment by 1 percentage point, but longer voluntary search raises frictional unemployment by 0.4 point. Cyclical unemployment is unchanged. Which natural-rate prediction follows, conditional on both estimates?
options: It falls 1.4 points; both changes reduce unemployment
It rises 0.4 point; structural mismatch is outside the natural rate
It stays unchanged; only recessions can move the natural rate
It falls 0.6 point; the policy effects partly offset
legendary.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
legendary.feedback: The natural rate includes both structural and frictional unemployment. Its predicted change is -1 + 0.4 = -0.6 percentage point. The net estimate is conditional on the two stated mechanisms, not a guarantee about every retraining policy.

legendary.q: Actual unemployment falls below the estimated natural rate during a strong expansion. Later it returns to the natural rate with no change in worker skills or matching. What is the best interpretation?
options: Structural unemployment must have been negative during the expansion
The return to the natural rate proves frictional unemployment disappeared temporarily
The temporary gap reflected cyclical conditions rather than a permanent change in the natural rate
The natural rate permanently fell and then rose because actual unemployment moved
legendary.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
legendary.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

boss.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
boss.q: Actual unemployment is 8% and the natural rate is 5%. What is cyclical unemployment?
boss.feedback: Cyclical unemployment = actual unemployment - natural unemployment = 8 - 5 = 3 percentage points.

boss.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
boss.q: An economist asks for the normal baseline: the natural rate of unemployment includes mainly:
boss.feedback: The natural rate includes unemployment from normal search and structural mismatch.

boss.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
boss.q: Why does unemployment remain positive even in a healthy economy?
options: Job search and skill or location mismatches remain
Every economy is always in recession
boss.feedback: Frictional and structural unemployment remain even when the economy is healthy.

boss.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
boss.q: Actual unemployment is 4.2% and the natural rate is 5.0%. What does this suggest?
options: The labor market may be unusually tight
The economy must be in a deep recession
boss.feedback: Actual unemployment below the natural rate can indicate unusually tight labor markets.

boss.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
boss.q: Suppose actual unemployment is 7%, natural unemployment is 4.5%, and labor force participation is falling. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: Cyclical unemployment exists, and falling participation may hide more weakness
The labor market is definitely fully healthy
Participation falling proves structural unemployment is zero
boss.feedback: Actual unemployment exceeds natural unemployment by 2.5 points, and falling participation can hide additional weakness.

boss.q: Which unemployment is included in the natural rate?
boss.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
boss.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

boss.q: Why can a healthy economy have positive unemployment at the natural rate?
options: Every healthy economy must retain recession-driven cyclical unemployment at all times
The natural rate is a policy target chosen to match the current inflation rate
All workers between paychecks are automatically classified as unemployed
Workers still search for jobs and some skills do not match openings
boss.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
boss.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

boss.q: Which change can lower the natural rate?
options: A short recession that increases cyclical unemployment for several months
A one-month decline in consumer confidence with no lasting matching change
Faster job matching that reduces normal search time
A temporary fall in aggregate demand that raises recession-related layoffs
boss.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
boss.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

boss.q: Actual unemployment falls after aggregate demand recovers, while the natural rate estimate is unchanged. What most likely fell?
boss.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
boss.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

boss.q: A permanent occupational shift leaves displaced workers without skills needed in expanding industries. What is the likely effect?
options: Structural unemployment and the natural rate may rise
The natural rate must fall because some industries expanded
boss.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
boss.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

boss.q: A policy improves retraining and job matching at the same time. What is the strongest natural-rate prediction?
options: The natural rate must rise because more workers change jobs
The natural rate remains fixed by definition
The natural rate may fall as structural mismatch and search time decline
boss.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
boss.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
legendaryBoss.q: Actual unemployment is 7.8%, natural unemployment is 4.6%. What is cyclical unemployment?
legendaryBoss.feedback: Cyclical unemployment = actual unemployment - natural unemployment = 7.8 - 4.6 = 3.2 percentage points.

legendaryBoss.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
legendaryBoss.q: The economy is expanding, but unemployment remains because workers are switching jobs and some skills no longer match available openings. What explains this?
options: The unemployment rate must be zero in expansions
legendaryBoss.feedback: Even in expansions, search and mismatch keep the natural rate positive.

legendaryBoss.q: A country improves worker retraining and job matching for several years, reducing both persistent mismatch and average search time. What is the strongest long-run labor-market conclusion?
options: The natural rate can fall because structural and frictional unemployment are lower
Only cyclical unemployment can fall because training and matching cannot affect the long-run benchmark
The natural rate must remain fixed even when persistent mismatch and search time both decline
The natural rate becomes exactly zero once matching improves enough to shorten normal job searches
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

repairQuestions.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
repairQuestions.q: The natural rate of unemployment includes:
repairQuestions.feedback: The natural rate includes frictional and structural unemployment.

repairQuestions.q: Which statement corrects the claim that the natural rate is always zero and never changes?
options: It always equals cyclical unemployment in the current year.
It is permanently fixed by the central bank’s inflation target.
It includes only people who have completely stopped seeking work.
It is normally positive and can change with labor-market conditions.
repairQuestions.commonError: Treating the natural rate as zero and immutable.
repairQuestions.feedback: The natural rate reflects normal search and mismatch, and its level can change over time.

repairQuestions.q: Actual unemployment is above the natural rate during a recession. Which part of the gap is not itself part of the natural rate?
repairQuestions.commonError: Adding recession-driven cyclical unemployment into the natural-rate benchmark.
repairQuestions.feedback: The natural rate reflects frictional and structural unemployment. Cyclical unemployment is the business-cycle deviation of actual unemployment from that benchmark.

bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
bridgeQuestions.q: Actual unemployment is 7% and the natural rate is 5%. What is cyclical unemployment?
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Cyclical unemployment = actual unemployment - natural unemployment = 2 percentage points.

easy.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
easy.q: In the circular flow of income and expenditure, why does total income equal total expenditure?
options: Every dollar spent by a buyer becomes income for a seller
Government sets income equal to spending
easy.feedback: Income equals expenditure because one person's spending becomes another person's income.

easy.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
easy.q: If households spend $500 billion buying goods and services, what happens to sellers' income in the basic income-expenditure logic?
options: It only rises if taxes fall
easy.feedback: Spending by buyers becomes income for sellers, so seller income rises by the same amount.

easy.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
easy.q: GDP measures which two sides of economic activity?
easy.feedback: GDP can be measured as total income or total expenditure because those two sides are linked.

easy.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
easy.q: Which statement best defines GDP?
options: The value of final goods and services produced domestically during a period
The total value of all used goods sold in a year
The total income earned only by government workers
The total amount of money printed by the central bank
easy.feedback: GDP is the market value of final goods and services produced within a country during a period.

easy.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
easy.q: A newly produced car sold to a household is counted in GDP because it is:
options: A final good produced in the current period
A used good resold in the current period
easy.feedback: Newly produced final goods are counted in GDP.

easy.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
easy.q: Why are intermediate goods usually not counted separately in GDP?
options: Their value is included in the final good.
They are not produced by firms
easy.feedback: Counting intermediate goods separately would double count their value.

easy.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
easy.q: Which purchase is not counted in current GDP?
options: Buying a used textbook from another student
Buying a new laptop made domestically
easy.feedback: Used goods were counted when first produced, so resale does not count in current GDP.

easy.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
easy.q: If total expenditure in an economy is $20 trillion, what is total income in the basic GDP accounting identity?
easy.feedback: In the basic circular-flow logic, total expenditure equals total income.

easy.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
easy.q: A bakery buys flour for $20 and sells bread for $50. What value is counted in GDP from the final bread sale?
easy.feedback: GDP counts the final good, so the bread sale counts as $50.

easy.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
easy.q: Which of the following is one of the four components of GDP expenditure?
easy.feedback: Consumption is one of the four expenditure components of GDP.

easy.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
easy.q: The GDP expenditure identity is:
easy.feedback: GDP expenditure is consumption plus investment plus government purchases plus net exports.

easy.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
easy.q: Net exports are calculated as:
easy.feedback: Net exports equal exports minus imports.

easy.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
easy.q: A household buys groceries. Which GDP component does this most directly enter?
easy.feedback: Household spending on goods and services is consumption.

easy.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
easy.q: A firm buys new machinery to produce more output. Which GDP component does this enter?
easy.feedback: Business spending on capital goods is investment.

easy.q: A domestic winery ships newly produced wine to customers in Canada. Which expenditure entry records the sale?
easy.commonError: Classifies by the buyer label instead of the economic transaction.
easy.feedback: Because the wine is produced domestically and purchased by foreign customers, the sale is an export and increases net exports.

easy.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
easy.q: If C = 10, I = 3, G = 4, and NX = -1, what is GDP?

easy.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
easy.q: Nominal GDP values output using:
easy.feedback: Nominal GDP uses current prices.

easy.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
easy.q: Real GDP values output using:
easy.feedback: Real GDP uses constant base-year prices to remove the effect of price changes.

easy.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
easy.q: If nominal GDP rises but real GDP does not, what likely happened?
options: Prices rose but actual output did not
Actual output rose but prices fell
easy.feedback: Nominal GDP can rise because prices rise, even if real output does not.

easy.q: Why is real GDP generally preferred to nominal GDP when comparing production across years?
options: It includes only goods and services purchased by the government.
It values every year’s output using that year’s current market prices.
It guarantees that measured production rises from one year to the next.
It holds prices constant so the comparison focuses on changes in output.
easy.commonError: Assuming nominal values isolate changes in physical production.
easy.feedback: Real GDP uses constant prices to separate changes in quantities from changes in the price level.

easy.q: Quantity is unchanged, but the current price of the only final good falls. With the same base year, what happens?
options: Nominal GDP falls while real GDP is unchanged
Both nominal and real GDP fall
Nominal GDP is unchanged while real GDP falls
easy.commonError: Infers output growth directly from nominal GDP growth.
easy.feedback: Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production.

easy.q: The base-year price is $10 and current production is 8 units. What is current real GDP?
easy.commonError: Mixes current and base-year prices while valuing current output.
easy.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

easy.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
easy.q: GDP is an imperfect measure of well-being because it excludes:
easy.feedback: GDP misses some things that matter for well-being, such as leisure and environmental quality.

easy.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
easy.q: Which statement about GDP and well-being is most accurate?
options: GDP helps but is an incomplete welfare measure
easy.feedback: GDP is useful, but it does not capture every part of economic well-being.

easy.q: A parent provides full-time unpaid child care at home. How is this usually treated in GDP?
options: The valuable nonmarket service is generally omitted
It is counted as government purchases
It is counted as business investment
easy.commonError: Assumes valuable activity must appear in GDP even without a recorded market transaction.
easy.feedback: Unpaid household production and unreported underground activity can be omitted from measured GDP.

easy.q: Two economies have equal GDP per person, but workers in one have much more leisure. What can GDP alone establish?
options: Their total well-being must be equal
The economy with less leisure is necessarily better off
Leisure is already fully priced in GDP
Their measured output is equal, not their total well-being
easy.commonError: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
easy.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

easy.q: Average GDP per person rises while nearly all gains go to a small group. Which limitation matters?
options: The higher average establishes that every household received an equal gain
Income distribution is already deducted when real GDP is calculated
The average does not show how income is distributed
GDP cannot measure the value of any recorded market production
easy.commonError: Uses an average output measure to infer distribution or every quality improvement.
easy.feedback: GDP per person does not show distribution and may incompletely capture product-quality change.

easy.q: A business produces market services but hides the sales from official records. What is the likely measurement issue?
options: Only nonmarket household work can be omitted
Underground activity can make measured GDP understate production
The hidden sales automatically enter government purchases
GDP must overstate output by the same amount
easy.commonError: Assumes valuable activity must appear in GDP even without a recorded market transaction.
easy.feedback: Unpaid household production and unreported underground activity can be omitted from measured GDP.

easy.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
easy.q: The consumer price index measures:
options: The cost of a fixed basket of goods and services over time
The number of workers in the labor force
easy.feedback: The CPI tracks the cost of a fixed basket of consumer goods and services.

easy.commonError: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.
easy.q: The inflation rate is usually calculated as:
options: The percentage change in the price index
The level of GDP divided by population
The number of unemployed divided by population
easy.feedback: Inflation is the percentage change in a price index such as the CPI.

easy.q: In the CPI, the base-year index is usually set equal to:
easy.commonError: Forgetting the index convention for the base year.
easy.feedback: The base-year basket cost is indexed to 100.

easy.q: If the CPI is 125, the fixed consumer basket costs:
options: 75 percent less than in the base year.
25 percent more than in the base year.
125 percent more than in the base year.
easy.commonError: Reading the index level as a percentage increase of the same size.
easy.feedback: A CPI of 125 means the basket cost is 1.25 times its base-year cost.

easy.q: The inflation rate from one year to the next uses:
options: The percentage change in real GDP.
The percentage change in the CPI.
The dollar change in the CPI basket only.

options: Because every import directly reduces household consumption spending
To force exports and imports to carry opposite accounting signs
To remove foreign production already embedded in domestic spending
Because imported goods provide no value to domestic buyers
medium.commonError: Treats the subtraction of imports as a claim that imported goods are inherently harmful or absent from spending.
medium.feedback: Imports are subtracted because imported final spending may already appear in C, I, or G and foreign production must not enter domestic GDP.

medium.commonError: Excluding unsold current production instead of counting it as inventory investment.
medium.q: A firm produces $500M in goods, sells $450M, and unintentionally accumulates $50M in inventories. Which GDP component includes the unsold goods?
medium.feedback: Inventory accumulation is counted as investment, even when unplanned.

medium.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
medium.q: A firm produces $10M of goods in December but sells $7M in December and $3M in January. How should the $3M be treated for December GDP?
options: It counts as inventory investment in December
It counts as consumption in December
It is subtracted from December GDP
medium.feedback: Goods produced but not sold are counted as inventory investment in the period produced.

medium.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
medium.q: A firm buys a new domestically produced machine for $1M and a share of stock in another company for $1M. What is the direct effect on GDP?
options: GDP rises $1M; the stock purchase is financial
GDP rises by $2M because both are investments
GDP does not change because firms made both purchases
GDP rises only from the stock purchase
medium.feedback: Economic investment in GDP means new capital goods, not financial asset purchases.

medium.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
medium.q: If consumption is $12 trillion, investment is $4 trillion, government purchases are $5 trillion, exports are $3 trillion, and imports are $4 trillion, what is GDP?

medium.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
medium.q: If exports are $800 billion and imports are $1.1 trillion, net exports equal:

medium.commonError: Excluding unsold current production instead of counting it as inventory investment.
medium.q: A U.S. firm produces $10 million in goods but sells only $7 million this year. The remaining $3 million is added to inventories. How much is counted in GDP?
medium.feedback: Unsold output is counted as inventory investment, so all $10 million is counted.

medium.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
medium.q: Suppose an economy produces only 10 bikes. In year 1, each bike sells for $100. In year 2, the economy still produces 10 bikes but each sells for $120. What happens?
options: Nominal GDP rises, but real GDP is unchanged if year 1 is the base year
Real GDP rises, but nominal GDP is unchanged
Both nominal and real GDP must fall
medium.feedback: Nominal GDP rises because prices rise, while real GDP is unchanged because output did not change.

medium.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
medium.q: Which situation would cause real GDP to rise?
options: Prices rise while output stays the same
Output rises while base-year prices are used
The CPI rises while production is unchanged
Used goods are resold more often
medium.feedback: Real GDP rises when actual production rises, not merely when prices rise.

medium.q: An economy produces exactly the same quantities of every final good in two years, but current prices change. Using fixed base-year prices, which statement must be true?
options: The GDP deflator must equal 100 in both years.
Real GDP must rise because some current prices changed.
medium.commonError: Treating current-price changes as changes in real output.
medium.feedback: With quantities unchanged, valuing both years at the same base-year prices leaves real GDP unchanged.

medium.q: Two years have the same nominal GDP, but the second year has a higher GDP deflator. Which year has higher real GDP?
options: They must have equal real GDP.
The answer depends only on population.
medium.commonError: Assuming equal nominal GDP implies equal real output despite different price levels.
medium.feedback: Real GDP equals nominal GDP divided by the price index. With equal nominal GDP, the year with the lower deflator has higher real GDP.

medium.q: Current output is 20 units, the current price is $9, and the base-year price is $6. What are nominal and real GDP?
medium.commonError: Mixes current and base-year prices while valuing current output.
medium.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

medium.q: Real GDP rises from $100 billion to $110 billion. What is the percentage growth rate?
medium.commonError: Uses the new level rather than the initial real-GDP level as the percentage-growth denominator.
medium.feedback: Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.

medium.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
medium.q: If nominal GDP is $24 trillion and the GDP deflator is 120, real GDP is:
medium.feedback: Real GDP = nominal GDP / (deflator/100) = 24 / 1.20 = 20 trillion.

medium.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
medium.q: Why can GDP rise while well-being does not clearly improve?
options: GDP fails to record any final goods sold in legal markets
Every production increase automatically reduces leisure and environmental quality
Higher GDP guarantees equal gains for households across the income distribution
GDP may ignore pollution, leisure loss, and unequal distribution
medium.feedback: GDP is useful, but it misses important quality-of-life factors.

medium.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
medium.q: Which statement is the strongest evaluation of GDP as a welfare measure?
options: GDP is complete whenever nominal prices remain unchanged
GDP measures only leisure, safety, and environmental quality
GDP is useful but misses nonmarket quality-of-life factors
GDP is useless because it excludes all current market production
medium.feedback: GDP is useful but incomplete as a measure of well-being.

medium.q: A software update greatly improves usefulness while its market price is unchanged. What difficulty can arise?
options: GDP may not fully capture the quality improvement
Real GDP must fall because price is unchanged
The update counts only as a transfer
GDP already measures every consumer benefit exactly
medium.commonError: Uses an average output measure to infer distribution or every quality improvement.
medium.feedback: GDP per person does not show distribution and may incompletely capture product-quality change.

medium.q: A factory expands output while causing more pollution. What is the careful conclusion?
options: GDP and welfare must rise by the same percentage
Welfare must fall because production increased
Pollution is subtracted automatically from nominal GDP
GDP rises, while the net welfare effect remains uncertain
medium.commonError: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
medium.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

medium.q: A family replaces unpaid home cooking with otherwise similar restaurant meals. What can happen?
options: GDP is unchanged because meals are identical
GDP rises because more activity is purchased in markets
GDP falls because restaurant work is intermediate
medium.commonError: Equates a change in market spending with the same change in total useful services.
medium.feedback: Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently.

medium.q: Production is unchanged, but workplace injuries fall after a safety improvement. What does GDP alone miss?
options: A transfer counted in government purchases
A welfare gain from greater safety
A decline in all final output
medium.commonError: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
medium.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

medium.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
medium.q: If the CPI is 140, what does that mean relative to the base year?
options: The basket costs 40% more than in the base year
The basket costs 140% less than in the base year
medium.feedback: A CPI of 140 means the basket costs 40% more than in the base year.

medium.q: A basket costs $500 in the base year and $575 today. Today’s CPI is:
medium.commonError: Using the dollar increase rather than the basket-cost ratio.

medium.q: An index moves from 175 to 189. A report calls the 14-point rise “14 percent inflation.” Which correction uses the proper comparison?
options: 7.4%, because the 14-point rise is divided by 189
14%, because one index point is one percent
8%, because the 14-point rise is divided by 175
89%, because every comparison must begin at 100

medium.feedback: Inflation is the change relative to the previous index: (189 - 175)/175 × 100 = 8%. Index points and percentage changes are different.

medium.q: A basket cost $360 in the base year. If the CPI is 140, the current basket cost is:
medium.commonError: Multiplying or dividing the index incorrectly.
medium.feedback: Current cost = 1.40 × $360 = $504.

medium.q: The CPI falls from 200 to 190. The inflation rate is:

medium.feedback: The percentage change is (190 − 200)/200 = -5 percent.

medium.q: A fixed basket has two meals at a base price of $4 each and one fare at $12. Meal prices rise 10%; the fare is unchanged. What CPI results, with the base set to 100?
options: 106.7; meals were two-thirds of the units
110; use the price change of the only item that rose
140; the meal expenditure weight is the inflation rate

medium.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
medium.q: A CPI basket costs $400 in the base year and $460 this year. What is the CPI this year?

medium.commonError: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.
medium.q: If the CPI falls from 200 to 190, what happened?
options: The real interest rate must be zero
medium.feedback: The CPI fell by 10 from 200, so the inflation rate is -5%, meaning deflation.

medium.q: A basket has 4 pizzas and 2 haircuts. In the base year, pizzas cost $10 and haircuts cost $20. This year, pizzas cost $12 and haircuts cost $25. What is this year's CPI?
medium.feedback: Base basket cost = 4(10)+2(20)=80. Current cost = 4(12)+2(25)=98. CPI = 122.5.

medium.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
medium.q: A CPI basket keeps 10 pounds of beef even after beef becomes expensive and consumers switch to chicken. Which CPI problem is this?
medium.feedback: A fixed basket can miss consumer substitution toward cheaper goods.

medium.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
medium.q: Why does substitution bias usually cause the CPI to overstate inflation?
options: Consumers switch toward relatively cheaper substitutes
Consumers never change behavior when prices change
The CPI counts used goods twice
medium.feedback: If consumers substitute, their actual cost of living may rise less than the fixed basket suggests.

medium.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
medium.q: A smartphone costs more than an old flip phone but also provides far more services. Which CPI issue does this illustrate?
medium.feedback: Some price increases reflect quality improvements, which the CPI may not fully measure.

medium.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
medium.q: A new product gives consumers a useful option that did not previously exist. Why can that make the CPI imperfect?
options: The CPI may miss gains from new variety and improved purchasing power
The CPI automatically falls to zero
The new product must be an intermediate good
medium.feedback: New goods can make consumers better off in ways not fully captured by the CPI.

medium.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
medium.q: Which example would most likely make the CPI overstate the true rise in the cost of living?
options: Consumers switch from expensive beef to cheaper chicken
All consumers buy exactly the fixed CPI basket forever
Quality falls but prices fall more
medium.feedback: Substitution toward cheaper goods means the fixed basket may exaggerate cost increases.

medium.q: A name-brand medicine becomes expensive and buyers switch to an equivalent store brand. A fixed basket changes slowly. What is the main issue?
medium.commonError: Assumes a fixed basket fully reflects how households respond to changes in relative prices.
medium.feedback: Substitution bias arises when consumers shift toward relatively cheaper alternatives but the fixed basket does not fully reflect that response.

medium.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.

options: A price increase for imported coffee bought by households
A price increase for domestically produced tractors
A price increase for government services
A price increase for domestically produced bread
medium.feedback: Imported consumer goods are included in the CPI but excluded from the GDP deflator.

medium.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
medium.q: Which price index better captures prices of all currently produced domestic final goods and services?
medium.feedback: The GDP deflator reflects the prices of domestically produced final goods and services.

medium.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
medium.q: Why can the GDP deflator change differently from the CPI?
options: GDP deflator uses current output; CPI uses a fixed basket
They measure exactly the same basket
The GDP deflator only counts imports
medium.feedback: The CPI and GDP deflator use different baskets and coverage.

medium.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
medium.q: A domestically produced machine purchased by a business becomes more expensive. Which index is more likely to capture this directly?
medium.feedback: Capital goods produced domestically are included in GDP and affect the GDP deflator.

medium.q: A domestic firm buys newly produced business software whose price rises. Which index directly covers that final domestic product?
options: The CPI because every business purchase is consumer spending
Neither index because software is intangible
The CPI only when the firm imports the software
medium.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
medium.feedback: The GDP deflator covers newly produced final goods and services made domestically, including business software. The CPI is limited to the consumer basket.

medium.q: Imported prescription-drug prices rise while prices of domestic hospital services are unchanged. Which outcome is plausible?
options: GDP-deflator inflation must exceed CPI inflation
Both indexes must change by the same amount
Neither index can reflect a medical price change
medium.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
medium.feedback: Imported prescription drugs can raise the CPI because they are consumer purchases. They are not domestic production, so they do not directly raise the GDP deflator; unchanged domestic hospital prices add no offsetting price increase.

medium.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
medium.q: Why is it misleading to compare a $5 wage in 1970 directly to a $15 wage today?
options: The purchasing power of money changes over time
Inflation only affects GDP, not wages
Nominal values are always real values
medium.feedback: Dollar amounts from different years need to be adjusted for changes in the price level.

medium.q: A pension has a full cost-of-living adjustment tied to the CPI. If measured inflation is 4 percent, what is the intended effect?
options: Raise the nominal payment about 4% to protect purchasing power.
Reduce the nominal payment about 4% to offset inflation.
Hold the nominal payment fixed so its real value automatically rises.
Convert the pension payment into a market interest rate.
medium.commonError: Confusing nominal indexation with a reduction in benefits.
medium.feedback: A CPI-linked adjustment raises the nominal amount to offset measured price growth.

medium.q: A salary rises 6% while the relevant price index rises 4%. What happens to real purchasing power?
medium.commonError: Equates a higher nominal payment with a higher real payment.
medium.feedback: Compare the nominal change with the relevant price-index change to determine purchasing-power change.

medium.q: A rent payment is indexed upward 3% when the relevant price index rises 3%. What is the intended real effect?
options: Convert rent into a real interest rate
Keep the payment’s purchasing power roughly constant
medium.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
medium.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

medium.q: A benefit rises 2% while consumer prices rise 5%. What happens to its purchasing power?
medium.commonError: Equates a higher nominal payment with a higher real payment.
medium.feedback: Compare the nominal change with the relevant price-index change to determine purchasing-power change.

medium.q: A nominal salary is unchanged while the consumer price level falls. What happens to its purchasing power?
options: It becomes an indexed tax threshold
It remains unchanged in real terms
medium.commonError: Compares dollar amounts from different periods without a common price level.
medium.feedback: Put nominal amounts in common purchasing-power units before making the real comparison.

medium.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
medium.q: A salary was $30,000 when the CPI was 150. The CPI is now 225. What is that salary in today's dollars?

medium.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.

medium.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
medium.q: A bank pays 6% interest and inflation is 2%. What happened to purchasing power in the account?
medium.feedback: The real interest rate is about 4%, so purchasing power rises by about 4%.

medium.q: Which borrower benefits most from unexpectedly high inflation?
options: A borrower with a fixed nominal interest rate
A lender with a fixed nominal interest rate
A saver earning a low fixed rate
A worker paid only in real wages
medium.feedback: Unexpected inflation reduces the real burden of fixed nominal debt.

medium.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes ex ante and ex post real interest rates?

Ex ante adds expected inflation to the nominal interest rate.
Ex post is known with certainty when the loan contract is signed.
Ex ante uses expected inflation; ex post uses actual inflation.
medium.commonError: Using actual inflation for both the expected and realized real return.
medium.feedback: The expected real return is based on expected inflation, while the realized real return uses actual inflation.

medium.q: Actual inflation exceeds expected inflation while a loan’s nominal rate is fixed. What happens to the lender’s realized real return?
medium.commonError: Uses actual inflation to describe an expected return or expected inflation to describe the realized return.
medium.feedback: Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.

medium.q: Actual inflation is lower than expected on a fixed nominal loan. Who bears a higher real repayment burden than anticipated?
medium.commonError: Misses how unexpected inflation changes the real burden of a fixed nominal loan.
medium.feedback: Because actual inflation is lower than expected, the repayment dollars retain more purchasing power than anticipated, increasing the borrower’s real burden.

medium.q: Which inflation rate belongs in an ex post real-interest calculation?
medium.commonError: Uses actual inflation to describe an expected return or expected inflation to describe the realized return.
medium.feedback: Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.

medium.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
medium.q: If the nominal interest rate is 7% and the inflation rate is 9%, the real interest rate is approximately:

medium.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
medium.q: Country A grows at 1% per year and Country B grows at 4% per year. What is the most likely long-run result?
options: The income gap can become much larger over time
Both countries must end with the same income
Country A must always become richer

medium.feedback: Small growth-rate differences compound into large long-run income differences.

medium.feedback: Long-run growth in productivity can dramatically raise living standards.

medium.commonError: Using total GDP growth without adjusting for population.

medium.q: A country raises output mainly by requiring much longer workweeks, while output per hour is unchanged. What is the most careful interpretation?

Working hours are the same as net exports

medium.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.

medium.q: A discouraged worker wants a job but stopped searching because they believe no jobs are available. How is this worker classified in official unemployment statistics?
medium.feedback: Discouraged workers are not in the labor force because they are not actively searching.

medium.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
medium.q: Which classification is most likely to make the unemployment rate understate labor market weakness?
options: Counting discouraged workers as not in the labor force
Counting active job seekers as unemployed
Counting unemployed workers in the labor force
medium.feedback: Discouraged workers are excluded from unemployment, which can hide labor market weakness.

medium.commonError: Forgetting that the labor force includes employed plus unemployed workers.
medium.q: An economy has 140 million employed people, 10 million unemployed people, and 50 million people not in the labor force. What is the labor force?
medium.feedback: Labor force = employed + unemployed = 140 + 10 = 150 million.

medium.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
medium.q: Using 140 million employed and 10 million unemployed, what is the unemployment rate?
medium.feedback: Unemployment rate = 10 / 150 x 100 = 6.7%.

medium.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
medium.q: If the labor force is 150 million and the adult population is 200 million, what is the labor force participation rate?
medium.feedback: Labor force participation = 150 / 200 x 100 = 75%.

medium.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
medium.q: An economy has 90 employed, 10 unemployed, and 50 not in the labor force. If 5 unemployed workers stop looking, what is the new unemployment rate?
