medium.feedback: New unemployed = 5 and new labor force = 95, so unemployment = 5/95 = 5.3%.

medium.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
medium.q: A college graduate takes two months to find a first job that matches their skills. This is most likely:
medium.feedback: Job search while matching workers and firms is frictional unemployment.

medium.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
medium.q: A coal miner loses work because the economy shifts permanently toward other energy sources and the miner lacks transferable skills. This is:
medium.feedback: A long-term mismatch between skills and available jobs is structural unemployment.

medium.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
medium.q: A hotel lays off workers because a recession reduces travel demand. This is:
medium.feedback: Layoffs from weak demand during a recession are cyclical unemployment.

medium.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
medium.q: Which type of unemployment would still exist even when the economy is healthy?
medium.feedback: Frictional unemployment exists because workers and firms take time to match.

medium.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
medium.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes structural from frictional unemployment?
options: Structural means mismatch; frictional means normal job search
Frictional unemployment is always permanent, while structural unemployment lasts one day
Structural unemployment is caused only by inflation
medium.feedback: Structural unemployment is about mismatch; frictional unemployment is about normal search.

medium.q: A worker leaves a job to move to another city and spends six weeks searching for a similar position while local demand remains strong. Which type of unemployment best fits the case?
options: The worker is outside the labor force
medium.commonError: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
medium.feedback: Frictional unemployment comes from normal search and matching as workers move between jobs or enter the labor market.

medium.commonError: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
medium.q: A binding minimum wage above equilibrium creates unemployment because:
options: Quantity of labor supplied exceeds quantity of labor demanded
Quantity of labor demanded exceeds quantity supplied
All workers leave the labor force
medium.feedback: A wage floor above equilibrium creates a surplus of labor.

medium.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
medium.q: How can unemployment insurance improve worker outcomes even if it lengthens unemployment spells?
options: It gives workers income support and time to find better job matches
It forces all firms to hire
It lowers the labor force to zero
medium.feedback: Unemployment insurance can support job seekers, but may also reduce urgency to accept a job quickly.

medium.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
medium.q: A union negotiates wages above the competitive equilibrium. What is the likely effect in that labor market?
options: More workers want jobs than firms want to hire
Firms hire every worker who wants a job
The unemployment rate is impossible to calculate
medium.feedback: Above-equilibrium wages can create a surplus of labor in that market.

medium.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
medium.q: Efficiency wage theory says firms may pay above-equilibrium wages because higher wages can:
options: Improve effort, retention, or worker quality
medium.feedback: Efficiency wages can make workers more productive or reduce costly turnover.

medium.q: How do a union wage and an efficiency wage differ most directly?
options: A union wage is bargained collectively; an efficiency wage is voluntarily chosen by the firm
A union wage is always below equilibrium; an efficiency wage is always legally mandated
A union wage affects only prices; an efficiency wage affects only GDP accounting
They are identical policies imposed by government in every labor market
medium.commonError: Treats union wage setting and efficiency wages as identical mechanisms or ignores their tradeoffs.
medium.feedback: Unions bargain over wages, while firms may voluntarily pay efficiency wages; both can keep wages above market-clearing levels under some conditions.

medium.q: A state improves job-search assistance while leaving unemployment benefits unchanged. Which outcome is most directly targeted?
options: Higher cyclical unemployment through weaker aggregate demand
A larger labor surplus from a binding minimum wage
A permanent increase in structural mismatch
Shorter frictional unemployment spells through faster matching
medium.commonError: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
medium.feedback: Job-search assistance improves worker-firm matching, so it can shorten normal search spells and reduce frictional unemployment.

medium.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
medium.q: Why does the natural rate of unemployment remain positive in the long run?
options: Normal job search and structural mismatches persist
medium.feedback: The natural rate includes frictional and structural unemployment that persist in normal times.

medium.q: A rapid shift away from coal production leaves many workers without the skills demanded by expanding industries. What is the most likely effect?
options: Cyclical unemployment must fall to zero.
The natural rate must fall because jobs changed.
Structural unemployment and the natural rate may rise.
medium.commonError: Classifying a persistent skill mismatch as only cyclical unemployment.
medium.feedback: Sectoral change can raise structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

medium.q: Actual unemployment is below the estimated natural rate. Which interpretation is strongest?
options: The labor market is unusually tight, with possible inflation pressure.
The economy has eliminated every form of unemployment.
Structural unemployment must have fallen permanently to zero.
The economy must be operating with a recessionary output gap.
medium.commonError: Equating below-natural unemployment with zero unemployment or recession.
medium.feedback: Unemployment below the natural rate indicates a tight labor market, not the disappearance of frictional and structural unemployment.

medium.q: A temporary collapse in aggregate demand ends, and spending returns to normal. What should happen to unemployment if the natural rate itself did not change?
options: The natural rate rises permanently by the recession increase.
Cyclical unemployment fades, moving actual unemployment toward the natural rate.
Frictional unemployment falls permanently to zero after spending recovers.
Actual unemployment remains at its recession peak even after demand returns.
medium.commonError: Treating a temporary demand-driven unemployment increase as a permanent natural-rate shift.
medium.feedback: When the demand shortfall closes, cyclical unemployment recedes and the unemployment rate moves toward its natural benchmark.

medium.q: A strong expansion lowers actual unemployment, but worker matching, skills, and labor-market institutions are unchanged. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: Cyclical unemployment may have fallen without changing the natural rate
The natural rate must have fallen by the same amount as actual unemployment
Structural unemployment must have disappeared permanently
The natural rate becomes zero whenever aggregate demand is strong
medium.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
medium.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

medium.q: A retraining program successfully moves displaced workers into growing occupations. If other conditions are unchanged, what is the most likely effect on the natural rate?
options: It must rise because more workers have changed occupations
It changes only if cyclical unemployment rises
It cannot change because the natural rate is fixed forever
It may fall because structural unemployment is reduced
medium.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
medium.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

hard.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
hard.q: A firm produces $600,000 of final output. It pays $350,000 in wages, $100,000 in rent, $50,000 in interest, and keeps $100,000 in profit. What does this example show about GDP measurement?
options: Expenditure on output and income earned from production both equal $600,000
Only wages count in GDP, so GDP is $350,000
Profit is excluded from GDP, so GDP is $500,000
GDP cannot be measured from income
hard.feedback: The value of final output equals the income generated in producing it: wages, rent, interest, and profit all add to $600,000.

hard.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
hard.q: Suppose expenditure GDP is $22 trillion. Income data show $13 trillion in wages, $3 trillion in rent and interest, $4 trillion in profit, and $2 trillion in other production income. What do these figures show?
options: The income and expenditure approaches both measure GDP at $22 trillion.
The income approach measures $20 trillion because other production income is excluded.
The expenditure approach measures $24 trillion because other production income is added again.
The figures cannot be compared because wages are excluded from the income approach.
hard.feedback: The income categories sum to $22 trillion, matching expenditure GDP. The two approaches measure the same current domestic production from different sides.

hard.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
hard.q: Why would counting both the sale of flour to a bakery and the sale of bread to consumers overstate GDP?
options: It counts the flour twice—alone and inside the bread price
It would exclude the baker's labor income
It would treat bread as an import
It would make income less than expenditure by definition
hard.feedback: Intermediate goods are already embodied in the final good, so counting both creates double counting.

hard.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
hard.q: A U.S. company produces $2 million of software in Ireland and sells it to customers in Europe. How does this affect U.S. GDP?
options: It does not count in U.S. GDP
It counts in U.S. GDP because the firm is U.S.-owned
It counts as U.S. government purchases
It counts only if the software is downloaded in the U.S.
hard.feedback: GDP is based on production within a country's borders, not ownership of the firm.

hard.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
hard.q: A Canadian company produces cars in Tennessee and sells them to U.S. households. How are those cars treated in U.S. GDP?
options: They count because they were produced inside the United States
They do not count because the company is foreign-owned
They count only as transfer payments
hard.feedback: GDP counts production within national borders, regardless of whether the producer is domestically or foreign owned.

hard.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
hard.q: A household pays $2,000 for illegal services and $2,000 for legal market services. Which statement best explains the GDP issue?
options: Legal services count; hidden or illegal production is often missed
Both are always fully counted because all services are visible
Neither counts because services are excluded from GDP
Only illegal activity counts because it is current production
hard.feedback: GDP aims to count market production, but illegal or hidden activity is often excluded or poorly measured.

hard.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
hard.q: A restaurant buys $300 of ingredients and receives $900 from customers for meals, including $100 in tips. Ignoring other complications, how much final restaurant service enters GDP?
hard.feedback: The $300 of ingredients are intermediate inputs. The full $900 customer payment, including the $100 in tips, is final expenditure on restaurant service.

hard.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
hard.q: A firm buys steel for $80, adds labor and capital services, and sells a machine for $230 to another firm. If the machine is newly produced and used in production, how much does GDP increase?
hard.feedback: The newly produced machine is a final capital good, so its full market value of $230 is counted.

hard.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
hard.q: A government sends $1,000 unemployment checks to households, and households spend the full amount on groceries. What is the GDP effect?
options: The transfer is excluded; grocery purchases count as consumption
Both the transfer and groceries count, so GDP rises by $2,000
Neither counts because government is involved
Only the transfer counts as government purchases
hard.feedback: Transfer payments are not purchases of current goods and services, but later household spending can count as consumption.

hard.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
hard.q: A U.S. household buys a $40,000 car produced in Germany. In U.S. GDP accounting, what happens?
options: Consumption rises $40,000 and net exports fall $40,000; GDP is unchanged
Consumption rises and GDP rises by $40,000
Investment rises and imports are ignored
Government purchases rise and GDP is unchanged
hard.feedback: Imported consumer goods enter consumption but are subtracted through imports in net exports, so domestic GDP does not rise.

hard.q: A household buys a $2,000 imported laptop, a firm buys a $5,000 domestic machine, and the government sends a $1,000 benefit check. What directly adds to domestic GDP?
hard.commonError: Adds financial transfers, used goods, or imported production to domestic GDP.
hard.feedback: The domestic machine adds $5,000 of business investment. The imported laptop is offset by imports, and the benefit check is a transfer rather than a purchase of current output.

hard.q: A retailer sells $4 million of goods produced last year and produces $6 million of new goods this year. What production enters this year’s GDP?
hard.commonError: Treats only machines as investment and misses new homes or inventory changes.
hard.feedback: GDP records the $6 million of goods produced this year. Selling $4 million of goods produced last year changes inventories but does not add new current production.

hard.q: A city buys $3 million of domestic buses and sends $2 million in transfers. Recipients spend $1.5 million on imported services. What is the direct increase in domestic GDP?
hard.commonError: Adds financial transfers, used goods, or imported production to domestic GDP.
hard.feedback: The $3 million of domestic buses is government purchases. Transfers do not enter GDP directly, and the recipients

hard.q: A domestic software firm exports $4 million of services, imports $1.5 million of servers, and adds $0.5 million of current domestic output to inventory. What is the direct contribution to domestic GDP?
hard.commonError: Treats the subtraction of imports as a claim that imported goods are inherently harmful or absent from spending.
hard.feedback: The $4 million export and $0.5 million of inventory are current domestic production. The imported servers do not add domestic production, so the direct contribution is $4.5 million.

hard.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
hard.q: A household buys a newly built house for $300,000, a used car for $15,000, and $5,000 of groceries. What amount is added to GDP from these purchases?
hard.feedback: The new house and groceries count. The used car resale does not add to current GDP, so GDP rises by $305,000.

hard.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
hard.q: Suppose C = $14T, I = $4T, G = $5T, exports = $3T, and imports = $4.5T. What is GDP?

hard.commonError: Excluding unsold current production instead of counting it as inventory investment.
hard.q: A U.S. firm builds $100 million of equipment domestically and sells $70 million of it this year, keeping $30 million in inventory. What is counted in GDP?
options: $100 million because unsold output is inventory investment
$70 million because only sold goods count
hard.feedback: Current production counts whether sold or added to inventories, so all $100 million counts.

hard.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
hard.q: Nominal GDP rises from $20T to $22T while real GDP rises from $18T to $18.9T. What is the best interpretation?
options: Both prices and real output likely rose
hard.feedback: Real GDP rose 5%, while nominal GDP rose 10%, so both output and prices likely increased.

hard.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
hard.q: An economy produces only apples. Quantity rises from 1,000 to 1,100 and price rises from $2 to $3. What happens to nominal and real GDP using the first year as base?
options: Nominal GDP rises by more than real GDP
Real GDP rises by more than nominal GDP
Nominal GDP falls while real GDP rises
hard.feedback: Nominal GDP reflects both higher quantity and higher price, while real GDP only reflects higher quantity.

hard.q: Nominal GDP falls 2 percent while the GDP deflator falls 5 percent. What is the best approximate conclusion?
hard.commonError: Adding nominal and price changes instead of separating them.
hard.feedback: Approximate real GDP growth equals nominal GDP growth minus inflation in the deflator: −2% − (−5%) = about 3%.

hard.q: Base-year prices are $4 for books and $10 for meals. This year the economy produces 120 books and 30 meals. What is this year’s real GDP?
hard.commonError: Using current prices or adding quantities without base-year valuation.
hard.feedback: Real GDP uses base-year prices: (120 × $4) + (30 × $10) = $780.

hard.q: Nominal GDP grows 18% while the GDP deflator grows 10%. To one decimal place, what is the exact real-GDP growth implied by the ratio of the indexes?
hard.commonError: Uses the new level rather than the initial real-GDP level as the percentage-growth denominator.
hard.feedback: Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.
hard.roundingRule: Round real-GDP growth to one decimal place.

hard.q: An accountant divides current nominal GDP of $864 billion by a deflator of 120 and reports real GDP of $7.2 billion. Last year real GDP was $640 billion. Which correction and growth rate are right?
hard.commonError: Uses the new level rather than the initial real-GDP level as the percentage-growth denominator.
hard.feedback: An index with base 100 requires dividing by 120/100, not 120: 864/1.2 = 720. Real growth is (720 - 640)/640 = 12.5%. The deflator’s level is not the output growth rate.
hard.roundingRule: Round real-GDP growth to one decimal place.

hard.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
hard.q: If nominal GDP is $30T and real GDP is $25T, what is the GDP deflator?
hard.feedback: GDP deflator = nominal GDP / real GDP x 100 = 30/25 x 100 = 120.

hard.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
hard.q: An economy produces 100 units at $5 in year 1 and 110 units at $6 in year 2. Using year 1 as the base year, what is year 2 real GDP?
hard.feedback: Real GDP uses base-year prices, so year 2 real GDP = 110 x $5 = $550.

hard.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
hard.q: A country cuts pollution regulations, output rises, but air quality worsens and illness increases. What does this show about GDP?
options: GDP must fall whenever pollution or illness increases after production
GDP automatically subtracts every environmental and health cost from output
Higher measured production proves that every resident became better off
GDP may rise even when broader well-being does not clearly improve
hard.feedback: GDP counts production but does not fully capture environmental damage or health costs.

hard.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
hard.q: Which scenario best shows why GDP per person is more useful than total GDP for comparing living standards?
options: A country’s total GDP rises while its population remains unchanged
A country’s real GDP per person rises while total GDP remains fixed
A country’s GDP doubles while its population triples
A country’s GDP and population both double over the same period
hard.feedback: If population grows faster than GDP, average income may fall even though total GDP rises.

hard.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
hard.q: Two countries have equal GDP per person, but one has more leisure, cleaner air, and lower crime. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: GDP per person misses some important parts of well-being
The cleaner country must have lower real GDP
Crime and leisure are already fully included in GDP
hard.feedback: GDP per person is useful but incomplete because it misses non-market quality-of-life factors.

hard.q: Two countries have the same real GDP per person, but one has longer life expectancy, safer streets, and cleaner water. What follows?
options: Equal measured output does not imply equal well-being
Both countries must have equal welfare
The safer country must have lower real GDP
Health and safety are fully included in the GDP average
hard.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
hard.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

hard.q: Pollution causes more medical and cleanup spending, raising measured output. Why can the welfare conclusion differ from the GDP change?
options: Medical and cleanup services are excluded whenever pollution caused the demand
GDP subtracts the environmental damage and then subtracts cleanup spending again
Any increase in measured cleanup output proves the original damage improved welfare
GDP counts the services produced but not the full damage that made them necessary
hard.commonError: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
hard.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

hard.q: Workers choose shorter workweeks, measured output falls, and leisure rises. Which inference is justified?
options: GDP stays unchanged because added leisure replaces every lost unit of production
The leisure gain is automatically valued and added to business investment
GDP falls, but well-being could rise or fall
Both measured GDP and total well-being must decline by the same amount
hard.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
hard.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

hard.q: The base-year basket cost is $640, last year’s CPI was 125, and the basket costs $856 now. Which pair gives the current CPI and inflation since last year?
hard.commonError: Using the base-year cost in the inflation denominator.
hard.feedback: Current CPI is 100 × 856/640 = 133.75; inflation is (133.75 − 125)/125 = 7 percent.

hard.q: The CPI is 132 and the current basket costs $924. What was the base-year basket cost?
hard.commonError: Multiplying by the index instead of dividing by 1.32.

hard.q: A basket contains 4 units of A and 6 units of B. Base prices are $5 and $10; current prices are $8 and $12. What is the CPI?
hard.commonError: Averaging price changes without using basket quantities.
hard.feedback: Base cost is $80; current cost is $104; CPI = 130.

hard.q: The CPI rises from 180 to 189 and then to 198.45. Which statement is correct?
options: Inflation is 5 percent in each period.
Inflation is 9 percent and then 9.45 percent.
Inflation is 10.25 percent in both periods.
hard.commonError: Comparing index-point changes rather than percentage changes.
hard.feedback: Each increase is 5 percent of the previous CPI level.

hard.q: A base-year basket costs $1,000. Current prices make it cost $1,275. If next year the same basket costs $1,326, next year’s inflation rate is:
hard.commonError: Using the base-year basket cost rather than the current-year cost as the denominator.
hard.feedback: The CPI moves from 127.5 to 132.6, a 4 percent increase.

hard.q: A basket has 10 units of food and 1 unit of electronics. Food prices rise 4 percent and the electronics price rises 40 percent. Which conclusion is justified without more information?
options: ‘Food must dominate because there are more units.’
The CPI change depends on the dollar expenditure weights, not just the percentage changes.
‘The two percentage changes should be averaged equally.’
hard.commonError: Using quantities or percentage changes alone without dollar weights.
hard.feedback: The contribution of each item depends on quantity times price in the basket.

hard.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
hard.q: A CPI basket has 3 books and 2 meals. Base-year prices are $20 per book and $10 per meal. Current prices are $25 per book and $15 per meal. What is the current CPI?

hard.commonError: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.
hard.q: If the CPI rises from 125 to 155, what is the inflation rate?

hard.commonError: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.
hard.q: A basket costs $900 in the base year, $1,080 last year, and $1,188 this year. What is this year's inflation rate?
hard.feedback: Last year's CPI is 120 and this year's CPI is 132, so inflation is 10%.

hard.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
hard.q: If the CPI is 250 today and was 200 five years ago, what is the total inflation over the period?

hard.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
hard.q: A fixed CPI basket shows inflation of 12%, but households avoided much of the increase by switching away from the goods with the largest price increases. What is the likely issue?
options: The CPI may overstate the rise in the cost of living
The CPI must understate inflation because substitution is illegal
The GDP deflator must be zero
The nominal interest rate must equal 12%
hard.feedback: Substitution bias means consumers can reduce the actual cost increase by switching purchases, but the fixed basket may miss that.

hard.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
hard.q: A phone price rises 20%, but the new model has twice the storage, better battery life, and better cameras. Why might measured inflation be overstated?
options: Part of the price increase reflects better quality
All quality improvements are counted as unemployment
The phone is an intermediate good
The CPI excludes consumer electronics entirely
hard.feedback: If quality improves, a price increase may exaggerate the true increase in the cost of living.

hard.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
hard.q: Which CPI problem is most directly tied to the fact that consumers gain from products that did not exist in the base year?
hard.feedback: New goods can improve consumer welfare before the fixed CPI basket fully captures them.

hard.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
hard.q: Suppose beef rises from $10 to $20 and chicken rises from $10 to $12. The CPI basket assumes consumers still buy equal amounts of beef and chicken, but consumers buy much more chicken. What is the main measurement problem?
options: The fixed basket misses substitution toward chicken
The CPI ignores all food prices
The GDP deflator cannot measure domestic goods
The real interest rate becomes negative
hard.feedback: Consumers switch toward relatively cheaper chicken, so the fixed basket can overstate inflation.

hard.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
hard.q: Which statement gives the best overall critique of the CPI?
options: Useful, but biased by substitution, new goods, and quality
It is useless because no prices are included
It measures only business investment prices
hard.feedback: The CPI is useful, but it is not a perfect cost-of-living measure.

hard.q: A treatment keeps the same sticker price but cuts side effects and recovery time. Why can CPI miss part of the consumer gain?
options: The measured price may not capture improved quality
Consumers necessarily switch away from every treatment whose quality improves
The treatment becomes an imported capital good
The fixed basket counts the price twice
hard.commonError: Treats every observed price increase as pure inflation even when product quality changes.
hard.feedback: Separate the value of quality improvement from the pure price change when interpreting cost-of-living inflation.

hard.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
hard.q: Oil imported from abroad becomes more expensive and is heavily used by consumers. What happens to CPI and the GDP deflator, all else equal?
options: CPI includes imported consumer goods; the GDP deflator excludes imports
The GDP deflator rises directly, but CPI cannot
hard.feedback: Imported consumer goods affect the CPI but are not part of domestic production measured by the GDP deflator.

hard.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
hard.q: A domestically produced factory robot rises in price and is purchased by firms. Which index is more directly affected?
hard.feedback: Domestically produced capital goods are included in GDP and affect the GDP deflator.

hard.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
hard.q: Why does the GDP deflator not rely on a fixed basket in the same way as the CPI?
options: Its basket changes with current domestic production
hard.feedback: The GDP deflator changes with the composition of current domestic production.

hard.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
hard.q: If consumers buy more imported goods and fewer domestically produced goods, why might CPI and GDP deflator diverge?
options: CPI includes imported consumer goods; the GDP deflator covers domestic output
Both indexes are based only on labor force statistics
The GDP deflator includes imports twice
The CPI excludes all consumer purchases
hard.feedback: Different coverage of imports can cause CPI and GDP deflator movements to differ.

hard.q: Prices of domestically produced aircraft exports rise while imported smartphones bought by households become cheaper. Which combination is plausible?
options: The GDP deflator rises while the CPI falls
The CPI rises while the GDP deflator falls
Both indexes must rise because one price increased
Both indexes must fall because consumers buy smartphones
hard.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
hard.feedback: The aircraft exports are domestic production and enter the GDP deflator, so their higher prices push it up. Imported smartphones enter the CPI but not the GDP deflator; their lower price can pull CPI inflation down.

hard.q: Between two years, individual prices do not change, but domestic production shifts toward goods whose current prices are higher relative to their base-year prices. Why can a fixed-base GDP deflator rise?
options: The deflator must be unchanged whenever current-year prices are unchanged
The deflator begins including imported consumer goods as domestic output
A shift toward goods with higher dollar prices raises every index regardless of base prices
Current quantities put more weight on goods with larger price increases since the base year
hard.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
hard.feedback: The deflator compares current-price and base-price values of current quantities. Changing the output mix toward larger current-to-base price relatives can raise the ratio even with no new individual price changes. High dollar prices alone do not establish that result.

hard.q: Suppose the CPI systematically overstates the rise in the true cost of living. What can happen to a benefit that is fully indexed to the CPI?
options: The nominal benefit must decline every year.
The benefit can become too generous in real terms.
The real value remains exactly constant by definition.
Indexing removes every possible measurement problem.
hard.commonError: Assuming an index-linked adjustment is exact even when the index is biased.
hard.feedback: If the CPI overstates cost-of-living growth, full CPI indexation can overcompensate recipients in real terms.

hard.q: A nominal wage rises 8% while CPI rises 5%. Using the exact ratio and rounding to one decimal place, how much does the real wage rise?
hard.commonError: Compares dollar amounts from different periods without a common price level.
hard.feedback: Put nominal amounts in common purchasing-power units before making the real comparison.
hard.roundingRule: Use (1.08 ÷ 1.05) − 1 and round to one decimal place.

hard.q: A tax threshold is adjusted by only half of CPI inflation. What happens to its real value?
options: It becomes a nominal interest rate
hard.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
hard.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

hard.q: A retiree benefit is indexed to overall CPI, but retirees buy a systematically different basket. What limitation remains?
options: The benefit should be deflated with the GDP deflator only
CPI cannot measure any consumer prices
The chosen index may not match the retiree’s actual cost changes
Indexation guarantees identical costs for every household
hard.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
hard.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

hard.q: A salary adjustment uses last year’s CPI while inflation accelerates this year. What can happen before the next adjustment?
options: Real value must rise because the contract is indexed
hard.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
hard.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

hard.q: A contract raises its nominal payment 3% each year while inflation is 6%. What happens to the real payment?
options: It remains constant because the payment increased
It equals the nominal interest rate
hard.commonError: Equates a higher nominal payment with a higher real payment.
hard.feedback: Compare the nominal change with the relevant price-index change to determine purchasing-power change.

hard.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
hard.q: A wage was $18,000 when the CPI was 90. The CPI is now 270. What is the wage in today's dollars?
hard.feedback: Today's dollars = 18000 x 270/90 = 54000.

hard.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
hard.q: A tuition bill was $4,000 when the CPI was 125. In today's dollars, it equals $6,400. What is today's CPI?
hard.feedback: 6400 = 4000 x today's CPI/125, so today's CPI = 200.

hard.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
hard.q: A salary is $72,000 today when the CPI is 240. What was its equivalent value in year-T dollars when the CPI was 160?

hard.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
hard.q: A borrower agrees to repay a loan at 6% nominal interest. Inflation unexpectedly rises from 2% to 8%. Who is helped, other things equal?
options: The borrower, because the real repayment burden falls
The lender, because the real return rises
Neither side, because inflation does not affect real payments
Only the government, because GDP falls
hard.feedback: Unexpected inflation lowers the real value of fixed nominal repayments, helping borrowers.

hard.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
hard.q: If nominal interest is 4% and inflation is 7%, what does the real interest rate imply?
hard.feedback: Real interest = 4% - 7% = -3%, so purchasing power falls.

hard.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
hard.q: Which statement best explains why inflation matters for interest rates?
options: Nominal rate shows dollar growth; real rate shows buying-power growth
The nominal rate is always lower than inflation
Inflation only affects unemployment, not borrowing
hard.feedback: The real rate adjusts nominal interest for inflation to show changes in purchasing power.

hard.q: A savings account earns 5% nominal interest while inflation is 7%. What happens?
options: The balance rises in dollars but loses purchasing power
Both the dollar balance and purchasing power fall 2%
The real return equals the nominal return
hard.commonError: Uses the nominal rate alone to infer the purchasing-power return.
hard.feedback: For introductory approximation, real interest is nominal interest minus inflation.

hard.q: A fixed loan carries 8% nominal interest. Expected inflation is 3%, but actual inflation is 6%. What are the approximate ex ante and ex post real rates?
hard.commonError: Uses actual inflation to describe an expected return or expected inflation to describe the realized return.
hard.feedback: Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.

hard.q: A loan’s fixed nominal rate is 9%. During its year, CPI rises from 200 to 212. Which conclusion is supported by these observations without a theory of how future loan rates are set?
options: Next year’s nominal rate must rise to 15%
Expected inflation at signing must have been 6%
The realized real return is approximately 3%
The realized real return is approximately 15%
hard.commonError: Turns a measurement question into a claim about long-run nominal-rate adjustment.
hard.feedback: Observed inflation is (212 - 200)/200 = 6%, so the approximate realized real return is 9 - 6 = 3%. These observations do not reveal prior expectations or determine future nominal rates.

hard.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
hard.q: If a lender charges 9% nominal interest and expected inflation is 4%, what real return does the lender expect?
hard.feedback: Expected real interest rate = nominal rate - expected inflation = 9% - 4% = 5%.

hard.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
hard.q: A country with lower current income grows rapidly for several decades and catches up to richer countries. Which concept best explains this possibility?
options: Sustained growth and the catch-up effect
hard.feedback: Growth compounds over time, and poorer countries may grow faster when capital is scarce.

hard.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
hard.q: Which country likely has the higher living standard, holding other quality-of-life factors aside?
options: Country A with real GDP of $1T and population of 10M
Country B with real GDP of $2T and population of 80M
Country C with nominal GDP of $3T but unknown prices
hard.feedback: Country A has real GDP per person of $100,000; Country B has $25,000.

hard.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
hard.q: Why can rankings of countries by income change dramatically over time?
options: Different growth rates compound over many years
The Rule of 70 prevents poor countries from growing
hard.feedback: Long-run differences in growth rates can greatly change relative income levels.

hard.q: Real GDP rises from $1.20 trillion to $1.32 trillion while population rises from 40 million to 42 million. Approximately how does real GDP per person change?
options: It rises from $30,000 to $33,000, a gain of exactly 10 percent.
It rises from $30,000 to about $31,429, a gain of roughly 4.8 percent.
It falls from $30,000 to about $28,571 as population increases.
It stays at $30,000 because both real GDP and population rose.
hard.commonError: Comparing total GDP growth without recomputing output per person.

hard.q: A country’s real GDP per person rises 3 percent, but most of the gain goes to a small share of households. What can be concluded?
options: Every household’s real income must have risen by exactly 3 percent.
Real GDP per person must have fallen because the distribution changed.
Average output per person rose, but the typical household may have gained less.
The price level must have increased by the same 3 percent.
hard.commonError: Treating an average as a description of every household’s experience.
hard.feedback: Real GDP per person is an average and does not reveal how income or output gains are distributed.

hard.q: A country’s real GDP grows 3 percent while its population grows 4 percent. Approximately what happens to real GDP per person?
hard.commonError: Adding population growth to output growth instead of subtracting it.
hard.feedback: Approximate per-person growth equals real GDP growth minus population growth: 3% − 4% = −1%.

hard.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
hard.q: Country A grows at 2% and Country B grows at 5%. Using the Rule of 70, how much sooner does Country B double its income?
hard.feedback: Country A doubles in about 35 years; Country B doubles in about 14 years, so B doubles about 21 years sooner.

hard.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
hard.q: If real GDP per person rises from $20,000 to $26,000, what is the percentage increase?

hard.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
hard.q: Output rises from 10,000 units to 12,000 units while labor rises from 100 workers to 150 workers. What happens to productivity?
options: It falls from 100 units per worker to 80 units per worker
It rises from 100 units per worker to 120 units per worker
It stays at 100 units per worker
hard.feedback: Initial productivity is 100; new productivity is 12000/150 = 80, so productivity falls.

hard.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
hard.q: A country raises total output by adding more workers, but output per worker does not rise. What is the best conclusion?
options: GDP may rise without much gain in productivity or living standards
Real GDP per person must double
Productivity must rise because output rose
hard.feedback: More workers can raise total output without raising output per worker.

hard.q: GROWTH-01 becomes flatter as capital per worker rises. After moving from A to B, what should be expected from another equal increase in capital per worker, holding other factors constant?
options: A smaller additional gain in output per worker than the A-to-B gain
A larger gain because the economy is richer
No further output gain is possible
hard.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
hard.feedback: The curve is flatter to the right, so an equal additional amount of capital produces a smaller marginal output gain than A-to-B.

hard.q: Output rises 30 percent while labor hours rise 20 percent. To one decimal place, what is the exact increase in output per labor hour?
hard.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
hard.feedback: Productivity changes by (1.30/1.20)−1 = 8.3% when output rises 30% and labor hours rise 20%.
hard.roundingRule: Compute 1.30 ÷ 1.20 − 1 and round to one decimal place.

hard.q: Output per worker rises, but output per labor hour is unchanged. Which explanation is consistent with both facts?
options: The labor force must have shrunk to zero
Average hours worked per worker increased
Every worker became more productive per hour
hard.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
hard.feedback: If output per worker rises while output per hour is unchanged, each worker must be working more hours on average.

hard.q: Total output falls 2 percent while labor hours fall 5 percent. To one decimal place, what happens to labor productivity?
hard.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
hard.feedback: Productivity changes by (0.98/0.95)−1 ≈ 3.2%, so it rises.
hard.roundingRule: Compute 0.98 ÷ 0.95 − 1 and round to one decimal place.

hard.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
hard.q: A factory produces $900,000 of output using 30 workers. What is output per worker?
hard.feedback: Productivity = output/workers = 900000/30 = 30000 per worker.

hard.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
hard.q: Workers produce 500 units in 1,000 hours before training and 650 units in 1,000 hours after training. What happened?
options: Productivity rose from 0.5 to 0.65 units per hour
Productivity fell from 2 to 1.54 units per hour
Output rose but productivity cannot change
hard.feedback: Productivity is output per hour: 500/1000 = 0.5 and 650/1000 = 0.65.

hard.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
hard.q: A country buys more machines, improves schools, and adopts better production software. Which productivity factors are increasing?
hard.feedback: Machines raise physical capital, schools raise human capital, and software/process improvements reflect technological knowledge.

hard.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
hard.q: Two countries have similar workers and technology, but one has far more equipment per worker. Which difference most directly explains higher productivity?
hard.feedback: More equipment per worker generally raises output per worker.

hard.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
hard.q: A country with strong education but weak roads, ports, and electricity may still struggle with productivity because it lacks:
hard.feedback: Infrastructure is part of the physical capital that helps workers produce efficiently.

hard.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
hard.q: A new farming method raises output per acre without increasing land, labor, or machinery. Which factor is most directly responsible?
hard.feedback: A better method of production is technological knowledge.

hard.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
hard.q: Which example best illustrates human capital rather than technological knowledge?
options: Workers complete advanced training in machine repair
A firm invents a new production algorithm
hard.feedback: Training workers increases human capital; an invention or method itself is technological knowledge.

hard.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
hard.q: Why does capital deepening eventually face limits if technology and human capital do not improve?
options: Each extra machine adds less output as capital accumulates
Output per worker must become zero
hard.feedback: Diminishing returns limit the gains from adding more capital alone.

hard.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
hard.q: A poor country has little capital per worker. A new investment project adds basic equipment to farms and factories. Why might returns be high?
options: Because capital is scarce, the marginal product of additional capital can be large
Because diminishing returns never exist in poor countries
Because inflation makes machines cheaper in real terms
hard.feedback: The catch-up effect comes from high returns to capital where capital is scarce.

hard.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
hard.q: Which policy mix is most likely to support sustained productivity growth rather than only a temporary boost?
options: Education, investment, property rights, trade, and research support
Price ceilings on all capital goods
hard.feedback: Sustained growth comes from policies that improve capital, skills, innovation, and institutions.

hard.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
hard.q: Why might political instability reduce long-run growth?
hard.feedback: Investment is less likely when property rights and future rules are uncertain.

hard.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
hard.q: A government restricts foreign direct investment to protect domestic firms. What is a possible long-run cost?
options: Less capital, technology, and productivity growth
hard.feedback: Foreign investment can bring capital and technology, so restricting it may slow productivity growth.

hard.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
hard.q: Why can research and development policies raise living standards even if they do not immediately raise output?
options: They expand technology and future productivity
They directly count as discouraged workers
They only change the CPI basket
hard.feedback: R&D can improve production methods and technologies that raise future output per worker.

hard.q: GROWTH-01 shows that capital deepening can move an economy from A toward B, but the curve becomes flatter. Which policy implication is strongest?
options: Capital raises output, while sustained growth also needs broader productivity gains
Capital accumulation becomes completely useless as soon as the economy reaches point B on the graph
The graph implies that low-capital economies should stop investment before they approach point B
Long-run growth can rely on repeated physical-capital accumulation forever without complementary productivity improvements
hard.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
hard.feedback: Capital deepening raises output but faces diminishing returns; sustained growth also requires skills, technology, and sound institutions.

hard.q: A government uses a temporary spending surge that raises current output but does not change capital, worker skills, technology, or institutions. What is the main long-run limitation?
options: It permanently doubles output per worker even though productive capacity is unchanged
It guarantees a permanently lower natural unemployment rate without changing labor-market institutions
It eliminates diminishing returns to capital even though the capital stock is unchanged
It does not directly strengthen long-run productivity fundamentals
hard.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
hard.feedback: A temporary spending surge can raise current demand/output, but without stronger fundamentals it does not directly raise long-run productivity.

hard.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
hard.q: An economy has 180 million employed, 12 million unemployed, and 68 million not in the labor force. What are the unemployment rate and labor force participation rate?
hard.feedback: Labor force = 192M; unemployment = 12/192 = 6.25%; adult population = 260M; participation = 192/260 = 73.85%.

hard.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
hard.q: An economy has 95 employed, 5 unemployed, and 50 not in the labor force. Ten people who were not in the labor force begin looking for work but do not find jobs. What is the new unemployment rate?
hard.feedback: Unemployed rises to 15 and labor force rises to 110, so unemployment = 15/110 = 13.6%.

hard.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
hard.q: An economy has 100 employed and 20 unemployed. Five unemployed workers find jobs, while five others stop looking. What happens to the unemployment rate?
options: It falls because unemployment decreases and the labor force shrinks
It stays unchanged because ten workers changed status
hard.feedback: Unemployed falls to 10 and labor force falls to 115, so the unemployment rate falls from 16.7% to about 8.7%.

hard.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
hard.q: If the unemployment rate falls because many jobless workers stop searching, what is the best interpretation?
options: Measured unemployment fell, but the labor market may not have improved
hard.feedback: A falling unemployment rate can be misleading if discouraged workers leave the labor force.

hard.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
hard.q: A person has no job, wants work, is available, but has not searched in six weeks because they think no jobs exist. How is this person classified and why does it matter?
options: Outside the labor force; this can understate labor-market weakness
Unemployed; all jobless people are counted
Structurally employed; skills do not matter
hard.feedback: Without active search, discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed, which can understate weakness.

hard.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
hard.q: A worker has a part-time job but wants full-time work. How is the worker officially classified?
options: Employed, even though the situation may show underemployment
Unemployed because the worker wants more hours
Not in the labor force because the job is part time
Discouraged because the worker is dissatisfied
hard.feedback: Part-time workers are counted as employed, even when they would prefer full-time work.

hard.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
hard.q: Which case creates the biggest problem for interpreting the official unemployment rate?
options: A large increase in discouraged workers
A worker voluntarily switches jobs and searches for one week
A student works part time by choice
hard.feedback: Discouraged workers are excluded from measured unemployment, hiding some labor market distress.

hard.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
hard.q: A laid-off engineer searches actively for work in the same field. A retired teacher does not want work. A discouraged factory worker wants work but stopped searching. Who is counted as unemployed?
options: The engineer and discouraged factory worker
hard.feedback: Only jobless people actively searching are counted as unemployed.

hard.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
hard.q: Why does the official unemployment rate miss some labor market pain?
options: It misses discouraged workers and involuntary part-time work
It counts all adults as unemployed
hard.feedback: The unemployment rate is useful but misses discouraged workers and underemployment.

hard.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
hard.q: Adult population is 250 million, labor force participation is 64%, and unemployment is 8 million. How many people are employed?
hard.feedback: Labor force = 0.64 x 250 = 160 million. Employed = 160 - 8 = 152 million.

hard.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
hard.q: A recession causes restaurants to lay off workers. At the same time, some workers quit jobs to search for better matches. Which types of unemployment are present?
hard.feedback: Recession layoffs are cyclical; voluntary job search is frictional.

hard.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
hard.q: A city loses manufacturing jobs permanently, but health care jobs expand and require different credentials. Which unemployment type dominates?
hard.feedback: A mismatch between worker skills and available jobs is structural unemployment.

hard.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
hard.q: Which example is most clearly frictional rather than structural unemployment?
options: A worker leaves one accounting job and searches for another accounting job in the same city
A miner cannot find work after mines permanently close
A worker is laid off because recession reduces demand
A cashier loses work because all stores automate checkout permanently
hard.feedback: Short-term search between similar jobs is frictional unemployment.

hard.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
hard.q: Cyclical unemployment differs from the natural rate because cyclical unemployment:
options: Rises during downturns when aggregate demand is weak
Exists only because workers search for better jobs
Is caused by long-run skill mismatch only
Is always zero when inflation rises
hard.feedback: Cyclical unemployment is tied to business-cycle downturns.

hard.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
hard.q: A software worker is unemployed for three weeks while comparing offers. A former textile worker is unemployed for two years because local factories closed. What is the best classification?
options: Software worker: frictional; textile worker: structural
The software worker is not in the labor force
hard.feedback: Short job search is frictional; long-term mismatch after industry decline is structural.

hard.q: A worker is laid off when a recession cuts sales. By the time demand recovers, the firm has automated the old job and the worker lacks the new required skills. What best describes the worker’s unemployment now?
options: It began as cyclical but is now primarily structural
It remains purely cyclical because the original layoff occurred in a recession
It is frictional because every unemployed worker is searching
It is no longer unemployment once the original recession ends
hard.commonError: Confuses persistent skill or location mismatch with temporary search or weak aggregate demand.
hard.feedback: Structural unemployment reflects a durable mismatch between workers and available jobs, skills, or locations.

hard.commonError: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
hard.q: A binding minimum wage raises hourly pay for workers who keep jobs but reduces low-skill employment. What is the strongest economic interpretation?
options: Higher wages for some, fewer opportunities for others
The policy must help every worker equally
The policy has no effect if firms dislike it
hard.feedback: A binding wage floor can raise wages for some workers while creating a labor surplus.

hard.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
hard.q: Unemployment insurance increases from 12 weeks to 40 weeks. What is the likely tradeoff?
options: Better income protection, but longer searches and more frictional unemployment
Lower income protection and shorter unemployment spells only
A guaranteed fall in labor force participation to zero
hard.feedback: Unemployment insurance helps workers smooth income but can reduce urgency to accept work quickly.

hard.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
hard.q: A union contract raises wages above the competitive equilibrium. Which workers are most likely hurt?
options: Workers no longer hired at the higher union wage
All union workers who keep their jobs
hard.feedback: Above-equilibrium wages can reduce labor demanded, hurting workers who cannot get hired.

hard.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
hard.q: Why might a firm voluntarily pay an efficiency wage above equilibrium?
options: To reduce turnover, attract better applicants, and encourage effort
To guarantee all unemployed workers get jobs
To make nominal GDP equal real GDP
hard.feedback: Efficiency wages can be profitable if they improve worker quality, effort, morale, or retention.

hard.q: Unemployment benefits become more generous while a new matching platform sharply improves the quality and speed of job referrals. What is the best prediction for frictional unemployment?
options: The net effect is ambiguous because the two changes work in opposite directions
It must rise because matching services cannot offset the weaker search incentives created by benefits
It must fall because unemployment benefits never change search incentives when matching technology improves
Only structural unemployment can change because neither policy affects normal search and matching
hard.commonError: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
hard.feedback: Frictional unemployment comes from normal search and matching as workers move between jobs or enter the labor market.

hard.q: A firm raises wages above equilibrium and worker effort rises enough to improve productivity, but fewer workers are hired at the higher wage. Which interpretation is most complete?
options: Higher productivity guarantees every worker seeking a job will be hired despite the higher wage
The wage increase must be a legally binding minimum wage rather than a voluntary firm decision
The policy can raise worker effort only when cyclical unemployment has already fallen to zero
Efficiency-wage benefits can coexist with a labor surplus and fewer job opportunities
hard.commonError: Treats union wage setting and efficiency wages as identical mechanisms or ignores their tradeoffs.
hard.feedback: An efficiency wage can raise effort and productivity, but if it is above equilibrium, firms may hire fewer workers, creating a labor surplus.

hard.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
hard.q: In a healthy economy, unemployment is still 4.5%. Which explanation best fits the natural rate?
options: Job search and skill mismatches persist
The economy must be in recession
The unemployment data must be impossible
hard.feedback: The natural rate remains positive because frictional and structural unemployment persist even in normal times.

hard.q: Two economies both have 6% actual unemployment. Economy A has a 4% natural rate and Economy B has a 6% natural rate. Which comparison is strongest?
options: Economy A has more positive cyclical unemployment than Economy B
Both economies have the same cyclical unemployment because actual unemployment is equal
Economy B must be in a deeper recession because its natural rate is higher
Neither economy can have frictional or structural unemployment
hard.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
hard.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

hard.q: A new nationwide matching system shortens the average time between jobs without changing aggregate demand. Which effect is most plausible?
options: Structural unemployment must rise by the same amount
The natural rate cannot respond to matching efficiency
Frictional unemployment and the natural rate may decline
hard.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
hard.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

hard.q: A long-lasting geographic mismatch develops: job openings expand in regions that displaced workers cannot easily move to. What is the most likely natural-rate effect?
options: The natural rate falls automatically because jobs exist somewhere
The natural rate is unchanged whenever total vacancies are positive
Structural unemployment can rise, pushing the natural rate upward
Only cyclical unemployment rises because location never affects structural mismatch
hard.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
hard.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

hard.q: Expansionary demand policy lowers actual unemployment from 7% to 5%, while the estimated natural rate remains 5%. Which interpretation fits the change?
options: A positive cyclical unemployment gap was eliminated
The natural rate fell from 7% to 5% because demand increased
hard.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
hard.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

hard.q: A policy improves occupational retraining but also makes job search somewhat longer by allowing workers to search for better matches. What is the best conclusion about the natural rate?
options: The net effect is ambiguous because structural unemployment may fall while frictional search may rise
The natural rate must fall because every labor-market policy lowers unemployment
The natural rate must rise because longer search is the only relevant channel
Only cyclical unemployment can be affected by either policy
hard.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
hard.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

elite.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
elite.q: A country reports $18T in consumption, $5T in investment, $6T in government purchases, $4T in exports, and $5T in imports. Separately, income data show $20T in wages, $4T in rents and interest, and $4T in profits plus other production income. What is the best conclusion?
options: The expenditure and income approaches both imply GDP of $28T
The expenditure approach implies $38T while income implies $28T
Imports should be added, so GDP is $38T
Income cannot be used to measure GDP
elite.feedback: Expenditure GDP = 18 + 5 + 6 + (4 - 5) = 28. Income also totals 20 + 4 + 4 = 28.

elite.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
elite.q: A student argues that total spending must exceed total income because consumers sometimes borrow to spend. What is the best correction?
options: Borrowed spending still becomes sellers’ income
Borrowed spending is excluded from GDP
Income only counts wages, so the student is correct
elite.feedback: Borrowing can finance spending, but the expenditure still becomes income for producers.

elite.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
elite.q: A firm produces $1M of output, sells $800,000 to customers, and adds $200,000 to inventory. It pays $600,000 in wages, $100,000 in rent, $100,000 in interest, and has $200,000 in profit. Which statement is correct?
options: GDP rises by $1M and income generated also totals $1M
GDP rises only by $800,000 because inventories are unsold
GDP rises by $1.2M because inventory is added to sales
elite.feedback: Unsold output is inventory investment, so all $1M counts; income payments also total $1M.

elite.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
elite.q: A mill sells $180 of flour made from $70 of current domestic grain. A baker uses all the flour in $310 of bread sold to households. What are the baker’s value added and GDP across the full domestic chain?
options: $130 at the bakery; $310 across the chain
$240 at the bakery; $560 across the chain
$310 at the bakery; $310 across the chain
$130 at the bakery; $490 across the chain
elite.feedback: The baker adds 310 - 180 = 130. Summing domestic value added gives 70 + (180 - 70) + 130 = 310, equal to the final sale. Intermediate sales cannot be added again.

elite.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
elite.q: A U.S. household buys a new $30,000 car built in Mexico, while a Mexican household buys a new $40,000 car built in Michigan. What is the net effect on U.S. GDP from these two transactions?
elite.feedback: Only the car produced in Michigan counts in U.S. GDP. The imported car affects consumption and imports but not domestic production.

elite.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
elite.q: Which transaction is most likely counted in current GDP?
options: A homeowner pays a licensed contractor to build a new deck
A homeowner builds a deck alone using leftover materials already owned
A household buys shares in a construction company
A collector resells an antique table
elite.feedback: Paid current market production counts. Financial transactions, used-good sales, and unpaid household production generally do not.

elite.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
elite.q: A firm imports $500,000 of parts, adds $300,000 of domestic labor and capital services, and sells the final good domestically for $800,000. What is the contribution to domestic GDP?
elite.feedback: Only domestic value added counts in domestic GDP. Imported inputs are not domestic production.

elite.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
elite.q: A country produces only two goods. In 2025 it produces 100 meals at $20 and 50 laptops at $1,000. It imports 10 additional laptops at $900 each for households. What domestic production value is counted in GDP?
elite.feedback: GDP counts domestic production: 100($20) + 50($1,000) = $52,000. Imported laptops are not domestic production.

elite.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
elite.q: Consumption is $9T, investment is $3T, government purchases are $4T, exports are $2T, and imports are $3T. Then households buy $1T more imported goods, with no change in domestic production. What happens to measured GDP?
options: It rises by $1T because consumption rises
It falls by $1T because imports rise
It rises by $2T because trade increases
elite.feedback: Imported consumption raises C but lowers NX by the same amount, so domestic GDP is unchanged.

elite.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
elite.q: A government spends $100B hiring workers to build bridges and also sends $100B in Social Security payments. If recipients spend all Social Security payments on current domestic goods, what is the maximum direct GDP increase described?
elite.feedback: Bridge spending is government purchases, and household spending from transfers can count as consumption. The transfer itself is not counted separately.

elite.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
elite.q: If C = $15T, I = $4T, G = $6T, imports = $5T, and GDP = $23T, what are exports?

elite.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
elite.q: A household buys a newly built condo for $250,000 and pays $3,000 in property taxes. Which is the best GDP treatment?
options: The condo is investment; the property tax is not current output
The condo is consumption and the tax is government purchases
elite.feedback: New residential construction is investment. A tax payment is not itself government purchase of a final good or service.

elite.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
elite.q: Nominal GDP rises from $25T to $30T. The GDP deflator rises from 100 to 120. What happens to real GDP?
elite.feedback: Initial real GDP = 25. New real GDP = 30 / 1.20 = 25. Real GDP is unchanged.

elite.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
elite.q: An economy produces 20 units at $5 in the base year. This year it produces 25 units at $8. What are nominal GDP and real GDP this year?
elite.feedback: Nominal GDP uses current price: 25 x 8 = 200. Real GDP uses base price: 25 x 5 = 125.

elite.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
elite.q: Real GDP rises 5% while nominal GDP rises 15.5%. A report calls the full nominal increase output growth. What price change and correction follow?
options: Deflator is unchanged; the two growth rates use different units
elite.feedback: The price-index ratio is 1.155/1.05 = 1.10. Thus the deflator rises 10%, while the stated real production increase remains 5%. Price and quantity growth combine multiplicatively.

elite.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
elite.q: If nominal GDP is $36T and real GDP is $30T, then the GDP deflator indicates:
options: The price level is 20% above the base-year level
The price level is 20% below the base-year level
Real output is 120% higher than nominal output
elite.feedback: GDP deflator = 36/30 x 100 = 120, meaning prices are 20% above the base-year level.

elite.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
elite.q: Country A has higher GDP per person than Country B, but Country B has cleaner air, more leisure, and longer life expectancy. What should an economist conclude?
options: GDP per person is useful but incomplete for comparing well-being
Country A must have higher well-being in every respect
Country B must have higher GDP once adjusted correctly
elite.feedback: GDP per person helps compare material output but misses some important well-being measures.

elite.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
elite.q: A hurricane destroys homes, and rebuilding activity raises GDP. Why is this not necessarily an improvement in well-being?
options: GDP excludes all construction completed after a natural disaster
Destroyed homes are recorded as current business investment spending
Rebuilding makes the original household losses irrelevant to welfare
GDP counts rebuilding, not the destruction’s welfare loss
elite.feedback: GDP can rise from rebuilding even though society is replacing destroyed assets.

elite.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
elite.q: A country increases GDP by requiring longer work hours and reducing vacation time. What GDP limitation does this expose?
elite.feedback: GDP measures production but does not fully value leisure.

elite.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
elite.q: A CPI basket contains 5 bus tickets and 2 meals. Base-year prices are $2 per bus ticket and $10 per meal. Current prices are $3 per bus ticket and $14 per meal. What is the CPI?

elite.commonError: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.
elite.q: A basket costs $750 when the CPI is 125. One year later the same basket costs $810. Which new index and claim about inflation are correct?
options: CPI 135; inflation is 8%, although the index rose 10 points
CPI 108; inflation is 8%, because the old index resets each year
CPI 135; inflation is 10%, matching the index-point increase
CPI 162; inflation is 35%, measured from the base year
elite.feedback: The unchanged base-basket cost is 750/1.25 = 600. The new index is 810/600 × 100 = 135. The 10-point increase is 10/125 = 8%, not 10%.

elite.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
elite.q: A basket cost $320 in the base year. The CPI is now 175. What does the basket cost now?
elite.feedback: Current cost = 320 x 175/100 = $560.

elite.commonError: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.
elite.q: A CPI basket costs $500 in the base year, $650 last year, and $702 this year. What is this year's inflation rate?
elite.feedback: Last year's CPI = 130 and this year's CPI = 140.4. Inflation = (140.4 - 130)/130 = 8%.

elite.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
elite.q: A fixed CPI basket includes 10 gallons of gasoline and 10 bus rides. Gas prices double, bus fares barely rise, and consumers switch heavily toward buses. What does the CPI likely do?
options: Overstates the rise in cost of living
Perfectly measures welfare because the basket is fixed
elite.feedback: The CPI fixed basket can exaggerate cost-of-living increases when consumers substitute away from goods whose prices rise.

elite.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
elite.q: A medical procedure rises in price from $2,000 to $2,600, but the new version cuts recovery time in half and lowers risk. Why is CPI measurement difficult?
options: Part of the higher price reflects quality improvement, not just inflation
Medical care is never included in CPI
Quality improvements always make inflation negative
GDP deflator and CPI are identical
elite.feedback: Quality change makes it hard to know how much of a price increase is true inflation.

elite.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
elite.q: Which scenario combines two CPI biases at once?
options: A new streaming service draws consumers from expensive cable
A worker becomes unemployed during a recession
elite.feedback: New goods and substitution both complicate CPI measurement.

elite.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
elite.q: If official CPI inflation is 6%, but consumers increasingly substitute toward cheaper goods and product quality improves, the true cost-of-living increase may be:
elite.feedback: Substitution and quality improvements often mean CPI overstates true cost-of-living increases.

elite.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
elite.q: A student's laptop costs 25% more than five years ago, but it is faster, lighter, and has much longer battery life. What should a careful CPI interpretation conclude?
options: The full 25% price increase should not automatically be treated as pure inflation
The CPI must ignore the laptop because quality changed
