The GDP deflator counts it as unemployment
The real price definitely rose by 25%
elite.feedback: Quality improvements mean some of the price increase may reflect a better product, not just inflation.

elite.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
elite.q: Imported coffee prices rise sharply, while prices of domestically produced machinery fall. Which index is likely pushed up more directly by the coffee price increase?
elite.feedback: Imported consumer goods affect the CPI more directly than the GDP deflator.

elite.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
elite.q: Domestic firms produce fewer computers and more health care services. Computer prices fall while health care prices rise. Why might the GDP deflator respond differently from the CPI?
options: GDP deflator basket changes with output; the CPI basket is fixed
The CPI never includes health care
The GDP deflator includes imports only
elite.feedback: The GDP deflator reflects the changing composition of current production.

elite.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
elite.q: A government must update a household allowance and also convert nominal GDP to real GDP. Imported household energy gets dearer while domestic investment equipment gets cheaper. Which pairing and interpretation fit?
options: Use CPI for the allowance and the GDP deflator for GDP; the indexes can move differently
Use the GDP deflator for both because energy purchases reduce net exports
Use CPI for both because every domestic output price is in its basket
Use either index for either task because all price changes have equal weights
elite.feedback: The household payment needs a consumer-price measure, which includes imported consumer energy. Deflating GDP requires prices of domestic production, including investment goods. Their differing coverage permits divergent movements.

elite.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
elite.q: A country produces only domestic wheat and imports all oil. Oil prices rise while wheat prices are unchanged. What is most likely?
options: CPI rises more than the GDP deflator if consumers buy oil
GDP deflator rises more because oil is imported
elite.feedback: Imported oil affects consumer prices but is not domestic production, so it is not directly in the GDP deflator.

elite.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
elite.q: A stipend pays $1,800 at CPI 150. At CPI 165 it rises to $1,920. How much additional monthly pay would restore the original purchasing power, and why?
options: $180; the CPI increased by 10%, so add 10% again
$120; any increase exactly restores purchasing power
$0; the stipend already rose in dollars
elite.feedback: Maintaining the initial purchasing power requires 1,800 × 165/150 = 1,980. The actual 1,920 is short by 60. A positive nominal raise may still fall short of price growth.

elite.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
elite.q: A car cost $8,000 in the past when the CPI was 80. The equivalent current-dollar price is $28,000. What is the current CPI?
elite.feedback: 28000 = 8000 x current CPI/80, so current CPI = 280.

elite.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
elite.q: A current salary of $96,000 is equivalent to $60,000 in year-T dollars. If the current CPI is 240, what was the CPI in year T?

elite.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
elite.q: A lender expects 3% inflation and wants a 4% real return. What nominal interest rate should the lender charge approximately?
elite.feedback: Nominal interest rate ≈ real interest rate + expected inflation = 4% + 3% = 7%.

elite.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
elite.q: A loan has a fixed nominal rate of 5%. Expected inflation was 2%, but actual inflation is 6%. What happened to the real interest rate relative to what was expected?
options: It was 4 percentage points lower than expected
It was 4 percentage points higher than expected
elite.feedback: Expected real rate was 3%; actual real rate was -1%, so it was 4 points lower.

elite.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
elite.q: A lender expected a 2% real return on a fixed 7% nominal loan. Actual inflation was 2 percentage points higher than expected. Which inflation and realized real rate follow using the approximation?
options: 7% actual inflation and 0% realized real return
5% actual inflation and 2% realized real return
9% actual inflation and -2% realized real return
7% actual inflation and 4% realized real return
elite.feedback: Expected inflation was 7 - 2 = 5%. Actual inflation was 7%, leaving realized real return 7 - 7 = 0%. The two-point surprise lowers the realized real rate by two points.

elite.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
elite.q: A saver earns 3% nominal interest while inflation is 5%. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The saver has more dollars but less purchasing power
The saver has fewer dollars and less purchasing power
The saver has more purchasing power because nominal interest is positive
elite.feedback: A positive nominal return can still be a negative real return when inflation is higher.

elite.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
elite.q: Country A has real GDP per person of $20,000 and grows at 2%. Country B has real GDP per person of $10,000 and grows at 6%. Using the Rule of 70, what is the strongest long-run implication?
options: B can catch up because it doubles much faster than A
A must always remain richer because it starts ahead
B cannot grow because it is poorer
elite.feedback: A doubles in about 35 years; B doubles in about 11.7 years, so B can catch up if growth persists.

elite.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
elite.q: A country grows real GDP by 6% while population grows by 2%. Approximately what happens to real GDP per person?
elite.feedback: Real GDP per person grows roughly by real GDP growth minus population growth, or about 4%.

elite.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
elite.q: A country with rapid population growth sees total real GDP rise but real GDP per person stay flat. What is the best interpretation?
options: Output is rising, but not faster than population
Living standards must be rising quickly
elite.feedback: Living standards are better captured by output per person, not total output alone.

elite.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
elite.q: Using the Rule of 70, Country X growing at 3.5% doubles in about how many years, and Country Y growing at 1.75% doubles in about how many years?

elite.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
elite.q: Two economies have equally scarce capital and similar access to technology. One has reliable electricity and trained operators; the other has frequent outages and little training. Which evidence best limits a claim that both must catch up equally fast?
options: The complementary inputs differ, so equal capital scarcity does not imply equal realized gains
Scarce capital has a low marginal product in both, regardless of complementary inputs
Technology access proves training and infrastructure no longer matter
A country’s current income ranking fixes its future growth ranking
elite.feedback: Capital scarcity can create high-return opportunities, but skilled workers and usable infrastructure help realize them. Catch-up is conditional; equal starting capital alone does not establish equal productivity growth.

elite.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
elite.q: Output rises from 50,000 to 60,000 while labor hours rise from 10,000 to 12,500. What happens to productivity?
options: It falls from 5 to 4.8 units per hour
It rises from 5 to 6 units per hour
It stays at 5 units per hour
It rises from 4.8 to 5 units per hour
elite.feedback: Initial productivity = 50,000/10,000 = 5. New productivity = 60,000/12,500 = 4.8.

elite.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
elite.q: A country's output per worker rises from $80,000 to $92,000. What is the percentage increase in productivity?
elite.feedback: Increase = 12,000 on a base of 80,000, so productivity rises by 15%.

elite.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
elite.q: Two countries have the same real GDP, but Country A has half as many workers as Country B. What must be true?
options: Country A has higher output per worker
Country A has lower real GDP per worker by definition
elite.feedback: Producing the same output with fewer workers means higher productivity.

elite.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
elite.q: A country raises output by increasing labor force participation, but output per worker falls. What is the most precise conclusion?
options: Total production rose, but productivity declined
Real GDP cannot rise when productivity falls
elite.feedback: More workers can raise total output even while output per worker falls.

elite.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
elite.q: A government gives firms tax incentives to buy machines, funds technical colleges, and expands broadband infrastructure. Which productivity factors are targeted?
elite.feedback: Machines are physical capital, technical colleges build human capital, and broadband supports technological/infrastructure capacity.

elite.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
elite.q: Which change most clearly increases human capital rather than physical capital?
options: Workers complete coding and equipment-maintenance training
elite.feedback: Training raises worker knowledge and skills, which is human capital.

elite.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
elite.q: A country has abundant natural resources but weak education, poor infrastructure, and unstable property rights. What is the best growth interpretation?
options: Resources need skills, capital, technology, and institutions
Natural resources guarantee high living standards
Education is irrelevant if resources are abundant
GDP must equal natural resource value
elite.feedback: Natural resources help, but productivity also depends on skills, capital, technology, and institutions.

elite.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
elite.q: A new algorithm lets firms produce the same output with fewer machines and workers. Which factor best explains the improvement?
elite.feedback: A better production method is technological knowledge.

elite.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
elite.q: A country doubles its capital stock, but output rises by less than double. Which concept is most directly illustrated?
elite.feedback: Diminishing returns means additional capital raises output, but by less and less as capital accumulates.

elite.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
elite.q: A poor country receives basic tractors for farms that previously used hand tools. A rich country adds another advanced tractor to farms already full of equipment. Which investment likely has the higher marginal return?
options: The poor country's investment, because capital is scarcer
The rich country's investment, because diminishing returns never apply
elite.feedback: Capital tends to have higher marginal returns when it is scarce.

elite.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
elite.q: Which statement best connects diminishing returns and the catch-up effect?
options: Scarce capital has high returns, which fall as capital accumulates
Poor countries grow slower because every new unit of capital has zero return
Rich countries grow faster because diminishing returns help them
Catch-up occurs because inflation is lower in rich countries
elite.feedback: The catch-up effect relies on high returns to scarce capital, but diminishing returns eventually reduce those gains.

elite.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
elite.q: A government wants growth but repeatedly changes tax rules, seizes assets, and restricts courts. Which policy failure matters most?
elite.feedback: Unstable property rights reduce incentives to invest and innovate.

elite.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
elite.q: Why might openness to foreign investment raise productivity?
options: Capital, technology, management, and market links
It guarantees no domestic firms fail
It only changes the CPI basket
elite.feedback: Foreign investment can increase capital and transmit technology or business practices.

elite.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
elite.q: A country funds education but blocks firms from adopting new technologies and discourages investment. What is the likely issue?
options: Skills need complementary capital and technology
Investment is unrelated to output per worker
elite.feedback: Productivity growth usually requires complementary gains in skills, capital, and technology.

elite.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
elite.q: A country wants continuing productivity growth after a one-time equipment grant has raised capital per worker. Which package best addresses the limitation imposed by diminishing returns?
options: Maintain useful investment while improving skills, research and adoption of better methods
Repeat equal equipment grants and assume each creates a larger marginal output gain
Increase working hours and treat all additional output as higher hourly productivity
Replace training with equipment because physical and human capital cannot complement each other
elite.feedback: Additional capital can still raise output, but its marginal contribution may diminish with other inputs fixed. Skills and technological progress complement capital and support productivity growth beyond a single level increase.

elite.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
elite.q: An economy has 155 million employed, 9 million unemployed, and 96 million not in the labor force. What are the unemployment rate and labor force participation rate?
elite.feedback: Labor force = 164M; unemployment = 9/164 = 5.49%; adult population = 260M; participation = 164/260 = 63.08%.

elite.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
elite.q: An economy has 120 employed, 8 unemployed, and 72 not in the labor force. Four unemployed workers find jobs, and six people outside the labor force begin searching but do not find work. What is the new unemployment rate?
elite.feedback: New employed = 124, unemployed = 10, labor force = 134. Unemployment = 10/134 = 7.46%.

elite.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
elite.q: Adult population is 300 million. Labor force participation is 62%. The unemployment rate is 5%. How many people are unemployed?
elite.feedback: Labor force = 0.62 x 300 = 186M. Unemployed = 0.05 x 186 = 9.3M.

elite.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
elite.q: The unemployment rate falls from 6% to 5%, but employment also falls. What likely happened?
options: Some unemployed workers left the labor force
Every discouraged worker found a job
elite.feedback: The unemployment rate can fall even when employment falls if enough jobless workers stop searching.

elite.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
elite.q: An economy has 200 adults. 130 are employed and 10 are unemployed. If 10 employed workers retire and stop looking for work, what happens to labor force participation?
elite.feedback: Initial labor force = 140, participation = 70%. New labor force = 130, participation = 65%.

elite.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
elite.q: A person works 5 hours per week for pay but wants 40 hours. How is this person treated in the headline unemployment rate?
options: Counted as employed, even though underemployment is present
Counted as unemployed because they want more hours
Counted as not in the labor force
elite.feedback: The official unemployment rate counts part-time workers as employed, even if they want full-time work.

elite.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
elite.q: A survey has 84 adults working for pay, including 14 seeking more hours; 6 available jobless adults applied last week; 30 jobless adults are not searching. Which official count and limitation are correct?
options: Labor force 90 and unemployment about 6.7%; underemployment among paid workers is not in that rate
Labor force 104 and unemployment about 19.2%; add those seeking more hours to unemployment
Labor force 120 and unemployment 5%; use every adult in the denominator
Labor force 76 and unemployment about 7.9%; exclude part-time paid workers
elite.feedback: All 84 paid workers are employed, including those wanting more hours. Add the 6 active, available seekers for LF = 90; 6/90 ≈ 6.7%. The rate does not measure all of the part-time workers’ unmet demand for hours.

elite.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
elite.q: Which change would reduce the unemployment rate without improving the number of people employed?
options: Unemployed workers become discouraged and stop searching
Discouraged workers begin looking for jobs
elite.feedback: When unemployed workers stop searching, they leave the labor force and measured unemployment can fall.

elite.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
elite.q: A recession causes job loss, and some unemployed workers become discouraged. Why might the unemployment rate understate the recession's damage?
options: Discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed once they stop searching
All discouraged workers are counted as employed
The unemployment rate includes only retired people
elite.feedback: Discouraged workers leave the labor force, which can hide labor market weakness.

elite.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
elite.q: A survey classifies people as employed, unemployed, or not in the labor force. Which person is most likely misread by the headline unemployment rate as doing better than they are?
options: A part-time worker who wants full-time work
A full-time worker satisfied with their job
A retiree who does not want work
elite.feedback: Involuntary part-time workers are counted as employed, even though their labor situation is weak.

elite.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
elite.q: A recession closes restaurants temporarily, while automation permanently reduces demand for cashiers. Which unemployment types are present?
elite.feedback: Recession-related layoffs are cyclical; permanent automation mismatch is structural.

elite.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
elite.q: A worker leaves a job voluntarily to search for a better match during a strong economy. A different worker loses a job because their industry permanently shrinks. Which pairing is correct?
elite.feedback: Voluntary job search is frictional; long-term industry decline creates structural unemployment.

elite.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
elite.q: Why is cyclical unemployment not part of the natural rate?
options: It reflects short-run downturns rather than normal job search or structural mismatch
It is always caused by unions
It exists only because workers quit to find better jobs
It is another name for frictional unemployment
elite.feedback: The natural rate includes frictional and structural unemployment, not recession-driven cyclical unemployment.

elite.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
elite.q: Which worker is most clearly structurally unemployed?
options: A typist whose skills are outdated after firms switch to new software systems
A nurse moving between hospitals in the same city
A waiter laid off during a short recession
A teacher taking summer vacation but returning in August
elite.feedback: Structural unemployment involves a mismatch between worker skills and available jobs.

elite.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
elite.q: A worker has the right skills but needs time to find the right employer. Another has obsolete skills and needs retraining. What separates the two cases?
elite.feedback: Frictional unemployment is search time; structural unemployment is mismatch.

elite.commonError: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
elite.q: A wage floor is $16. At that wage, 112 workers seek jobs and firms hire 88. A demand increase raises desired hiring to 100 while the wage and labor supply stay fixed. What happens to the labor surplus?
options: It falls from 24 to 12; higher labor demand reduces the excess supply
It stays at 24 because the statutory wage did not change
It rises from 24 to 36 because firms want more labor
It disappears because any increase in demand makes a floor nonbinding
elite.feedback: Initially the surplus is 112 - 88 = 24. With hiring demand of 100, it is 112 - 100 = 12. The wage floor can remain binding even as the size of the labor surplus changes.

elite.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
elite.q: Unemployment insurance gives workers time to search, but also reduces urgency. Which unemployment type is most directly affected?
elite.feedback: Unemployment insurance most directly affects job search behavior, which relates to frictional unemployment.

elite.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
elite.q: A union wage raises pay for employed members but reduces hiring by firms. Which statement best captures the tradeoff?
options: Insiders gain while some outsiders lose job opportunities
The unemployment rate must fall to zero
elite.feedback: Union wage gains can help employed members but reduce opportunities for workers not hired.

elite.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
elite.q: A firm pays above-equilibrium wages and finds quits fall, applicant quality improves, and effort rises. Which theory explains this?
elite.feedback: Efficiency wage theory explains why above-equilibrium wages may raise productivity or reduce turnover.

elite.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
elite.q: Two economies each have 5% natural unemployment. One combines 1% frictional and 4% structural unemployment; the other combines 3% frictional and 2% structural. Which policy comparison fits these equal totals?
options: The first has more mismatch to address; the second has more scope for faster matching, holding effectiveness comparable
The same natural rate proves their underlying labor-market problems are identical
Only the second has natural unemployment because frictional unemployment is the sole component
Both can reach zero unemployment simply by ending a recession
elite.feedback: Both totals equal 5%, but the components differ. A common aggregate benchmark does not establish identical barriers or identical policy priorities. Relevant retraining and matching interventions target different components.

elite.q: A long recession causes workers to lose skills and attachment to the labor force. Why might unemployment remain elevated after aggregate demand recovers?
options: The natural rate must remain unchanged after every recession.
Cyclical unemployment automatically becomes permanent inflation.
Hysteresis may have raised the natural rate through lasting labor-market damage.
Frictional unemployment can exist only while the economy is expanding.
elite.commonError: Assuming all recession unemployment disappears without lasting effects.
elite.feedback: A prolonged downturn can create persistent skill loss or detachment that raises structural unemployment and the natural rate.

legendary.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
legendary.q: A domestic assembler sells $420,000 of new equipment, using $150,000 of imported parts and $90,000 of current domestic components. A clerk adds all three values as domestic GDP. What correction reconciles final spending with domestic value added?
options: $270,000 total domestic GDP, including $180,000 at assembly
$420,000 total domestic GDP, including $330,000 at assembly
$510,000 total domestic GDP, including $420,000 at assembly
$180,000 total domestic GDP, excluding the domestic component makers
legendary.feedback: Final spending of 420,000 less imported inputs of 150,000 yields 270,000 domestic value added. Assembly contributes 420,000 - 150,000 - 90,000 = 180,000; domestic component makers contribute the remaining 90,000. Do not count their output twice.

legendary.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
legendary.q: A firm imports $200,000 of components, adds $150,000 of domestic labor and capital services, and sells the final product domestically for $350,000. How much does this production add to domestic GDP?
legendary.feedback: Only domestic value added counts in domestic GDP. Imported components are not domestic production.

legendary.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
legendary.q: A workshop sells $560 of new furniture after buying $140 of domestic lumber. Its wage bill is $250 and rent plus interest is $90. With no other costs or taxes, which value-added and profit account is consistent?
legendary.feedback: Value added is final output less intermediate lumber: 560 - 140 = 420. Of that, wages and rent/interest absorb 340, leaving profit of 80. Subtracting wages when computing value added would remove income generated by production.

legendary.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
legendary.q: A renovation business bills households $96,000, including $24,000 of imported fixtures. It also brokers an old building for a $6,000 fee; the building sells for $310,000. Ignoring other inputs, what current domestic production and counting rule follow?
options: $78,000; count domestic renovation value and the new brokerage service
$388,000; the old building becomes current output when sold
$102,000; imported fixtures count because households bought them
$72,000; services attached to used assets must also be excluded
legendary.feedback: Domestic renovation value is 96,000 - 24,000 = 72,000. The current brokerage service adds 6,000, while the old building itself is not new output. Total current domestic production is 78,000.

legendary.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
legendary.q: A production audit reports $74 million of final sales and $6 million of new inventories. Domestic production income is $51 million in wages, $9 million in rent and interest, and unreported profit. With no imports, taxes or depreciation adjustments, which result closes both accounts?
legendary.feedback: Current production includes the unsold 6 million, giving expenditure GDP of 80 million. Wages and rent/interest total 60 million, so residual profit is 20 million. Sales alone omit inventory investment.

legendary.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
legendary.q: A used machine changes hands for $40,000 through a broker charging $2,000. A new domestic machine worth $28,000 is produced but remains unsold. An analyst counts only the $40,000 resale as this year’s GDP. What is the corrected contribution?
options: $2,000: unsold output cannot count until purchased
legendary.feedback: The resale transfers an existing asset; the newly produced brokerage service counts. The unsold new machine is inventory investment when produced. Thus current GDP includes 2,000 + 28,000 = 30,000.

legendary.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
legendary.q: A household pays $30 for a restaurant meal, including $5 of sales tax. How should this be interpreted for GDP?
options: Count the final service; the tax is not government purchases
Only the pre-tax $25 counts because taxes are never linked to GDP
Only the $5 tax counts as government purchases
Nothing counts because meals are services
legendary.feedback: GDP counts the market value of final goods and services; taxes do not turn the meal into government purchases.

legendary.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
legendary.q: An economy reports C = 46, G = 13, exports = 9, imports = 11, and GDP = 72, all in billions. A separate inventory report records 4 billion of new unsold output. What investment total reconciles the accounts, and how should the inventory figure be treated?
options: I = 15; the 4 of inventories is included within that total
I = 19; add inventories after solving the identity
I = 7; subtract inventories twice to avoid unsold output
I = 37; imports should be added when solving for investment
legendary.feedback: The expenditure identity gives I = 72 - 46 - 13 - 9 + 11 = 15. Inventory investment is one part of I, leaving 11 in other investment; it is not an extra addition after reconciliation.

legendary.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
legendary.q: A government purchases $18 million of new domestic flood barriers and pays $12 million in household benefits. Recipients spend $7 million on new domestic services and $3 million on imported goods, saving the rest. What GDP contribution and expenditure classification follow?
options: $37 million; benefits and recipient purchases both count
$28 million; imported purchases count only in C
$18 million; spending financed by benefits is excluded
legendary.feedback: The benefit payment itself is a transfer. Recipient purchases enter C = 7 + 3 = 10; M = 3 removes the imported goods. G = 18, so domestic GDP rises 18 + 10 - 3 = 25 million, without counting the transfer again.

legendary.commonError: Excluding unsold current production instead of counting it as inventory investment.
legendary.q: At the start of a year, a producer has $8 million of goods made last year. It produces $30 million this year and sells $34 million, leaving $4 million in inventory. With unchanged prices, no imports and all sales to final users, which GDP account is correct?
options: $30 million: final sales 34 plus inventory investment of -4
$34 million: sales determine the production year
$38 million: add beginning inventories to new output
$42 million: add beginning inventories to final sales
legendary.feedback: Inventory investment is the change in stock: 4 - 8 = -4. Sales of 34 plus inventory investment of -4 equal current production of 30. Selling previously produced goods does not create output again.

legendary.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
legendary.q: A revision adds $6 billion of imported household appliances to consumption and records $2 billion of previously omitted current domestic installation services. The same imported appliances were missing from M. How should measured GDP change after all corrections?
options: Rise $2 billion; imported spending cancels while domestic installation remains
Rise $8 billion; all added consumption is domestic output
Fall $4 billion; imports are subtracted without adding their spending
Remain unchanged; every correction associated with imports cancels
legendary.feedback: C rises by 8 billion and M by 6 billion. The net 2-billion increase is the newly measured domestic service. Subtracting imports removes foreign production, not the associated domestic activity.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
legendary.q: A country’s nominal GDP is $468 billion and its deflator is 130. Next year real GDP rises 10%, but nominal GDP is $475.2 billion. Which new deflator and interpretation reconcile these facts?
options: 120; real output rises while the domestic price level falls
132; nominal and real growth must move together
145.2; add real growth to the old deflator
120; the lower deflator proves real production fell
legendary.feedback: Initial real GDP is 468/1.30 = 360. It grows to 396; the new deflator is 475.2/396 × 100 = 120. Output grew despite a decline in the price index from 130 to 120.

legendary.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
legendary.q: A workshop economy makes pumps and repair visits. Base prices are $40 and $20. Current quantities are 60 pumps and an unreported number of visits; current prices are $50 and $30. Current nominal GDP is $6,000. What real GDP and deflator follow?
legendary.feedback: Pumps account for 60 × 50 = 3,000 nominal dollars, leaving 3,000/30 = 100 visits. At base prices real GDP is 60 × 40 + 100 × 20 = 4,400. The deflator is 6,000/4,400 × 100 ≈ 136.4.

legendary.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
legendary.q: Two new domestic goods have current prices of $12 and $30 and base prices of $10 and $20. Output of the first is 80 units; total real GDP is $2,400. A report calls $2,400 current nominal GDP. What is the correct nominal total and source of the difference?
options: $3,360; recover 80 units of the second good and value both at current prices
$2,880; raise all real output by the first good’s price increase
$2,400; real and nominal GDP use the same quantities, so they are equal
$4,320; current prices must be applied to the dollar value of real GDP
legendary.feedback: Base-price output of the first good is 800, leaving 1,600/20 = 80 units of the second. Nominal GDP is 80 × 12 + 80 × 30 = 3,360. The same quantities have different values at different price vectors.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
legendary.q: Nominal GDP grows 8% and the GDP deflator grows 12.5%. Population is unchanged. Which conclusion best evaluates the claim that average real production rose?
options: Real GDP per person falls 4%; nominal growth does not establish output growth
Real GDP per person falls 4.5%; subtracting rates gives an exact result
Real GDP per person rises 8%; population did not change
Real GDP per person rises 20.5%; combine both positive rates
legendary.feedback: The real-output ratio is 1.08/1.125 = 0.96, a 4% fall. With population fixed, real GDP per person falls by the same proportion. Nominal output rose only because the price increase exceeded the real contraction.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
legendary.q: An economy produces 50 units at $10 in year 1 and 60 units at $12 in year 2. Using year 1 as base, what are year 2 nominal GDP, real GDP, and the GDP deflator?
legendary.feedback: Nominal GDP = 60 x 12 = 720. Real GDP = 60 x 10 = 600. Deflator = 720/600 x 100 = 120.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
legendary.q: Nominal GDP rises 32% over two years. Real GDP rises 10% in the first year and is unchanged in the second. The deflator started at 125. Which final deflator and cumulative price change follow?
options: 152.5; subtracting growth rates gives an exact 22% price rise
150; the domestic price level rose 50% during these two years
legendary.feedback: Real GDP’s cumulative factor is 1.10. The price factor is 1.32/1.10 = 1.20, giving deflator 125 × 1.20 = 150. A level of 150 is 50% above the base year, but only 20% above the initial 125.

legendary.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
legendary.q: Two regions report real GDP per person of $44,000 and $40,000. In the first, output per hour is $40 and annual hours per resident are 1,100; in the second they are $50 and 800. Which comparison is supported without assigning a value to leisure?
options: The first has higher output per person; the second has higher hourly productivity, so welfare is not ranked
The first is more productive per hour because its GDP per person is higher
The second has higher GDP per person because it is more productive per hour
The first has higher overall welfare by exactly 10%
legendary.feedback: The products 40 × 1,100 = 44,000 and 50 × 800 = 40,000 reconcile the figures. More hours explain the first region’s higher average output despite lower hourly productivity. Neither GDP nor these hours alone values all welfare differences.

legendary.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
legendary.q: After a storm, rebuilding adds $12 million of current production while lost business activity reduces other current production by $5 million. Destroyed existing buildings were worth $30 million. Which GDP and welfare statement is defensible?
options: GDP is $7 million higher than otherwise; this does not establish a welfare improvement
GDP is $23 million lower because destroyed wealth is subtracted from current production
GDP is $12 million higher; lost current production is irrelevant
GDP is $37 million higher because rebuilding replaces the destroyed stock
legendary.feedback: The change in current production is 12 - 5 = 7 million. Destruction of existing wealth is a separate loss, not a negative item of current production. Higher measured GDP therefore does not establish higher well-being.

legendary.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
legendary.q: A country has GDP of $2T and population of 20M. Another has GDP of $4T and population of 80M. Which has higher GDP per person?
options: The first country, with $100,000 per person versus $50,000
The second country, because total GDP is larger
They are equal because both are measured in trillions
It cannot be determined without imports
legendary.feedback: GDP per person is $2T/20M = $100,000 and $4T/80M = $50,000.

legendary.q: Country A has higher market output but more pollution and inequality; Country B has more leisure and unpaid household production. Which comparison is defensible?
options: Country A must have higher well-being because its recorded market GDP is higher
Country B must have higher measured GDP after valuing every hour of leisure
GDP is useless because it measures neither legal market goods nor services
GDP compares market production, but these facts do not settle overall well-being
legendary.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
legendary.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

legendary.q: A free translation tool replaces $9 million of paid translation services. Users report more completed translations and less effort; domestic firms produce $2 million of new paid implementation services. No other output changes. Which claim is supported?
options: Measured GDP falls $9 million; the implementation services do not count
Measured GDP rises because the number of translations rose
Measured GDP falls $7 million; the value of users’ net welfare gain is not determined
Measured GDP falls $7 million, proving welfare fell by $7 million
legendary.commonError: Equates a change in market spending with the same change in total useful services.
legendary.feedback: The measured output change is -9 + 2 = -7 million. Greater use and convenience can improve welfare despite reduced market spending, but the stated information does not price the total welfare change.

legendary.q: A storm destroys productive assets, followed by a surge in rebuilding services. What distinction is essential?
options: Higher rebuilding output proves the storm created a net gain for every household
Current production can rise while lost wealth and hardship leave welfare lower
Rebuilding services cannot enter GDP because the storm destroyed assets first
The destroyed productive assets are added to current household consumption spending
legendary.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
legendary.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

legendary.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
legendary.q: A fixed basket contains 3 tickets and 2 repairs. Base prices are $8 and $18. Last year the basket cost $72. This year its CPI is 135 and each ticket costs $9. What repair price and annual inflation rate are implied?
legendary.feedback: Base cost is 3 × 8 + 2 × 18 = 60. CPI 135 implies current cost 81. After ticket spending of 27, the two repairs cost 54, or 27 each. Inflation since last year is (81 - 72)/72 = 12.5%.

legendary.commonError: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.
legendary.q: An index is rebased: the old series lists last year at 160 and this year at 176, while the new series sets last year to 100. A nominal benefit rose 6% over the period. Which comparison survives rebasing?
options: The new current index is 110; the benefit lost purchasing power
The new current index is 116; the benefit lost purchasing power
The new current index is 110; the benefit gained 6% in real terms
The new current index is 100; rebasing removes inflation
legendary.feedback: Scaling both indexes by 100/160 makes the new current index 110. Inflation remains 10%; a 6% nominal increase is smaller, so real purchasing power falls. Changing the reference base cannot erase price growth.

legendary.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
legendary.q: A basket contains 4 units of A at a base price of $6 and an unknown quantity of B at $12. Its base cost is $72. Current prices are $9 for A and $15 for B. Which CPI and next-period inflation follow if the same basket then costs $100.80?
legendary.feedback: B accounts for 72 - 24 = 48 base dollars, so there are 4 units. Current cost is 4 × 9 + 4 × 15 = 96 and CPI ≈ 133.3. The next increase is (100.80 - 96)/96 = 5%.

legendary.commonError: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.
legendary.q: A nominal hourly wage rises from $25 to $27. Basket cost rises from $500 to $540, then falls to $525 while the wage stays $27. Relative to the starting year, what real-wage change remains after both price movements?
options: About 2.9% higher; the first raise just matched prices, then prices partly fell
8% higher; only the nominal wage change matters
Unchanged; the first year’s full indexation guarantees this forever
About 2.9% lower; a later price decline reduces purchasing power
legendary.feedback: The cumulative wage factor is 27/25 = 1.08 and cumulative price factor is 525/500 = 1.05. Their ratio is 1.02857, giving about 2.9% more purchasing power. Use cumulative levels instead of adding annual rates.

legendary.commonError: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.
legendary.q: A fixed basket’s cost rises 20% in one year and falls 10% in the next. A commentator claims prices are back where they started because growth has reversed. Which cumulative index and purchasing-power statement are correct, starting from 100?
options: Index 108; unchanged dollars buy less than initially
Index 110; subtract annual rates to obtain the exact total
Index 90; only the most recent inflation rate matters
legendary.feedback: The cumulative factor is 1.20 × 0.90 = 1.08. Prices remain 8% above the starting level, so unchanged nominal income has less purchasing power. A decline does not undo an earlier rise of a different percentage base.

legendary.commonError: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.
legendary.q: A basket cost $1,200 in the base year. CPI is now 150. Last year CPI was 125. What is the basket cost now and the inflation rate since last year?
legendary.feedback: Current basket cost = 1,200 x 1.5 = 1,800. Inflation = (150 - 125)/125 = 20%.

legendary.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
legendary.q: A basket agency sees households replacing a newly expensive rail route with an existing bus route. A trial finds the cheaper travel bundle preserves the same commuting service. Which evidence supports substitution bias, and what does it fail to establish?
options: A fixed bundle overstates the cost of that service; the evidence does not quantify bias for the whole CPI
The bus is a new good; the evidence measures all economy-wide quality gains
The rail price rise is entirely a quality change; no pure inflation occurred
The change proves the whole CPI should fall because one alternative is cheaper
legendary.feedback: The same service can be maintained at lower cost by changing an existing bundle, which is the substitution mechanism. A travel example alone does not measure the full index’s bias or imply that overall prices fell.

legendary.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
legendary.q: A new pump costs 12% more than the old model and lasts 12% longer with identical annual performance and maintenance costs. Ignoring discounting, which conclusion is supported for this product, and which is not?
options: Cost per service-year is unchanged; economy-wide inflation cannot be inferred
Cost per service-year rises 12%; durability is irrelevant to quality
Cost per service-year falls 12%; equal percentage changes must be subtracted from price twice
Economy-wide inflation is zero because this product has no service-cost rise
legendary.feedback: Price per lifetime service-year changes by 1.12/1.12 = 1. The sticker-price rise alone is therefore not pure service-cost inflation for this product. Its example cannot establish the economy-wide price change.

legendary.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
legendary.q: A streaming service did not exist in the base year and later gives consumers a cheaper alternative to cable. Which CPI problems are most directly involved?
options: Introduction of new goods and substitution bias
legendary.feedback: New goods improve choice, and substitution toward them can reduce actual cost-of-living increases.

legendary.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
legendary.q: If CPI inflation is 7% but the fixed basket misses major quality gains and substitution toward cheaper goods, the CPI most likely:
options: Overstates the rise in the cost of living
Understates the rise in the cost of living by definition
legendary.feedback: Substitution and quality improvements usually make CPI overstate true cost-of-living increases.

legendary.q: A fixed basket costs 9% more, while a redesigned bundle costs only 3% more. Before concluding that substitution bias is six percentage points, what must an analyst establish?
options: The redesigned bundle preserves the relevant living standard, with comparable quality and coverage
Households bought fewer total items, regardless of the services they lost
Both bundles contain the same number of product names, regardless of quantities
The redesigned bundle is cheaper, even if it provides less value
legendary.commonError: Assumes a fixed basket fully reflects how households respond to changes in relative prices.
legendary.feedback: A cheaper bundle can reflect reduced consumption or quality rather than cost-saving substitution at the same living standard. The comparison must hold the relevant standard of living constant before interpreting the gap as bias.

legendary.q: Statisticians update baskets and adjust for quality, yet CPI still requires judgment. What is the sound conclusion?
options: CPI becomes useless once any adjustment is required
Every quality adjustment eliminates substitution bias permanently
Updated baskets make CPI identical to the GDP deflator
Measurement improvements reduce bias, but index-number challenges remain
legendary.commonError: Concludes that known index limitations make CPI useless.
legendary.feedback: CPI remains useful, while substitution, new-good, and quality challenges can make measured inflation differ from true cost-of-living growth.

legendary.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
legendary.q: An economy’s consumer basket has base spending of $40 on imported tea and $60 on domestic services. Tea prices rise 25%; services prices stay fixed. The only other domestic output is exported machinery, whose price falls 10%. With quantities fixed, which conclusion is justified?
options: CPI rises 10%; the GDP deflator falls, but its size needs domestic-output weights
Both indexes rise 25% because imports are in consumer spending
CPI rises 25%; the GDP deflator falls exactly 10%
CPI is unchanged; imported consumer prices are excluded
legendary.feedback: The consumer basket rises from 100 to 40 × 1.25 + 60 = 110, a 10% increase. The domestic deflator includes unchanged service prices and lower machinery prices, so it falls; their output weights are needed to measure the decline.

legendary.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
legendary.q: Domestic output consists of 10 machines and 100 services. Base prices are $100 and $10; current prices are $120 and $10. Consumers buy the services and imported clothing; the clothing price is unchanged. Which price-index account is supported?
options: GDP deflator 110; CPI unchanged if its fixed basket contains only those consumer purchases
GDP deflator 120; CPI rises 20% because domestic machines got dearer
GDP deflator 110; CPI must rise by the same 10%
GDP deflator 100; business equipment is not final domestic output
legendary.feedback: Base-price domestic output is 10 × 100 + 100 × 10 = 2,000; current-price output is 2,200, giving deflator 110. The stated consumer prices did not change, so their fixed basket’s CPI is unchanged.

legendary.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
legendary.q: Why can the CPI overstate inflation while the GDP deflator still moves differently for valid reasons?
options: CPI uses a fixed basket; the GDP deflator uses current output
Both measure the exact same goods but use different names
legendary.feedback: These indexes differ both because of CPI bias issues and because they cover different baskets.

legendary.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
legendary.q: A country imports most consumer goods but produces mostly capital equipment. Imported consumer prices rise while domestic capital prices fall. Which statement is most accurate?
options: CPI and GDP deflator can move in opposite directions
CPI and GDP deflator must move together
GDP deflator must include imported consumer goods
CPI must include capital equipment bought by firms
legendary.feedback: Different baskets mean the CPI and GDP deflator can diverge sharply.

legendary.q: Imported home solar panels become cheaper while domestically produced industrial turbines become more expensive. Why can CPI and the GDP deflator move in opposite directions?
options: The indexes cover different goods and use different weighting frameworks
Both indexes measure only domestic consumer purchases
The CPI excludes imports while the deflator includes them
The GDP deflator fixes a household basket while CPI tracks current output
legendary.commonError: Treats CPI and the GDP deflator as interchangeable measures of the same set of prices.
legendary.feedback: CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.

legendary.q: A household grant rises from $2,000 to $2,160 as CPI moves from 125 to 135. Nominal GDP rises 8% while the GDP deflator rises 4%. Which combined assessment uses the appropriate indexes?
options: The grant gains 8% purchasing power; real GDP rises 8%
The grant loses purchasing power; real GDP is unchanged
Both real changes are zero because each nominal value rose 8%
The grant preserves purchasing power; real GDP rises about 3.8%
legendary.commonError: Chooses an index by familiarity rather than by the purpose of the comparison.
legendary.feedback: The grant and consumer-price factors are both 1.08, preserving purchasing power. GDP requires its own price factor: 1.08/1.04 - 1 ≈ 3.8%. Matching nominal rates do not imply matching real changes with different deflators.

legendary.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
legendary.q: A grant is $2,400 at CPI 120. It is fully adjusted when CPI reaches 132, then remains frozen as CPI reaches 144. What final grant and additional payment would restore the starting purchasing power?
options: $2,880 paid; no additional payment is needed
legendary.feedback: The first adjustment is 2,400 × 132/120 = 2,640. At the final index, preserving starting purchasing power requires 2,400 × 144/120 = 2,880. The frozen payment is short by 240.

legendary.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
legendary.q: An indexed payment was $900 at CPI 100. Its purchasing power is unchanged at a later $1,260 payment, but the later CPI was lost. The next payment is $1,350 at CPI 150. Which reconstruction and comparison are correct?
options: Missing CPI 140; both later payments preserve the initial purchasing power
Missing CPI 126; the $1,350 payment buys 50% more
Missing CPI 140; the $1,350 payment buys 7.1% more in real terms
Missing CPI 150; the two nominal payments have equal dollar value
legendary.feedback: Equal purchasing power requires the lost index to be 100 × 1,260/900 = 140. The next payment deflates to 1,350/1.50 = 900 in base dollars, also preserving the initial purchasing power.

legendary.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
legendary.q: A current income of $84,000 equals $60,000 in year-T dollars. If CPI today is 210, what was CPI in year T?
A scholarship rises 15% while CPI rises 10%. Using the exact ratio and rounding to one decimal place, what is its real increase?
options: About 25.0% because the two nominal changes are added together
legendary.commonError: Compares dollar amounts from different periods without a common price level.
legendary.feedback: Put nominal amounts in common purchasing-power units before making the real comparison.
legendary.roundingRule: Use (1.15 ÷ 1.10) − 1 and round to one decimal place.

legendary.q: A pension is fully CPI-indexed, but quality gains make CPI overstate true living-cost growth. What is the likely real effect?
options: The pension must lose nominal value throughout the entire inflation-adjustment period
The GDP deflator must rise by the same amount
The pension can gain purchasing power relative to the true cost of living
legendary.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
legendary.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

legendary.q: A threshold is $40,000 at CPI 100. The contract adjusts next year using the previous year’s inflation. CPI rises to 110, then 121; by the second year the threshold has received only the first 10% adjustment. What is the shortfall from full current indexation?
options: $4,000; apply the second 10% only to the original threshold
$8,400; the threshold never received any adjustment
$4,400; the paid threshold is $44,000 instead of $48,400
$0; a one-year lag cannot alter purchasing power
legendary.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
legendary.feedback: Full current indexation requires 40,000 × 121/100 = 48,400. The lagged threshold is 40,000 × 1.10 = 44,000. The gap is 4,400; successive inflation rates apply to changing price levels.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
legendary.q: A lender charged a fixed 8% nominal rate to target a 3% expected real return. CPI subsequently moved from 160 to 172.8. What realized real rate and forecast error follow using approximate real interest?
options: 0% realized real return; inflation was 3 percentage points above expected
3% realized real return; the target guarantees the outcome
-4.8% realized real return; the CPI-point increase is inflation
5% realized real return; actual inflation was below expected
legendary.feedback: The target implies expected inflation of 8 - 3 = 5%. Observed inflation is (172.8 - 160)/160 = 8%, so realized real interest is 0%. Inflation exceeded the expectation by 3 percentage points.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
legendary.q: Two one-year accounts each credit 6% nominal interest. Account A’s year has basket costs moving from $400 to $420; B’s year moves from $500 to $540. Which real-return comparison is valid using the approximation?
options: A gains about 1%; B loses about 2%, despite equal nominal rates
Both gain 6%, since account balances rise at the same rate
A loses 14%; B loses 34%, using basket-dollar increases as inflation
A gains about 11%; B gains about 14%, adding inflation to interest
legendary.feedback: Inflation is 20/400 = 5% for A and 40/500 = 8% for B. Subtracting from 6% gives +1% and -2%. The appropriate price growth, not the nominal rate alone, determines the purchasing-power return.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
legendary.q: A lender wants a 2% approximate real return and forecasts CPI rising from 125 to 130. The resulting fixed nominal contract is signed, but CPI ends at 135. What nominal rate and realized real return follow?
legendary.feedback: Expected inflation is 5/125 = 4%, so the target nominal rate is 2 + 4 = 6%. Actual inflation is 10/125 = 8%, giving approximate realized return 6 - 8 = -2%. Use the stated approximation, not the exact Fisher ratio.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
legendary.q: Nominal interest is 12%, actual inflation is 8%, and expected inflation was 5%. What are actual and expected real interest rates?
legendary.feedback: Actual real = 12 - 8 = 4. Expected real = 12 - 5 = 7.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
legendary.q: Which statement correctly links CPI adjustment and real interest rates?
options: Both adjust nominal dollar figures for changes in purchasing power
Both are calculated from exports minus imports
legendary.feedback: Inflation adjustment and real interest rates both focus on purchasing power rather than raw dollars.

legendary.q: A fixed-rate borrower and lender expected 2% inflation, but actual inflation is 8%. The nominal rate is 7%. What happened?
options: The real rate fell from about 5% to about −1%, helping the borrower
The real rate rose from 5% to 15%, helping the lender
Both parties still received the expected five-percent real outcome because the nominal loan rate remained fixed
The nominal rate automatically adjusted to 13%
legendary.commonError: Misses how unexpected inflation changes the real burden of a fixed nominal loan.
legendary.feedback: Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real repayment burden and shifts purchasing power from lender to borrower.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
legendary.q: At the start, real GDP per person is $32,000 in Alder and $8,000 in Birch. Their persistent growth rates are 1.75% and 7%. Using the Rule of 70, which comparison follows after 40 years?
options: Alder is near $64,000 and Birch near $128,000; matching Alder’s initial level earlier was not yet catching its moving level
Both are near $64,000 because Birch began at one-quarter of Alder’s level
Alder is near $64,000 and Birch near $32,000; count only one doubling for Birch
Birch stays poorer because a lower starting level cannot be overcome
legendary.feedback: Approximate doubling times are 40 years for Alder and 10 for Birch. Over 40 years Alder doubles once to 64,000, while Birch doubles four times to 128,000. Reaching a rival’s initial level is distinct from catching a rival that also grows.

legendary.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
legendary.q: Over a decade, real GDP rises 12%, population rises 5%, and total labor hours rise 20%. Which pair best evaluates average material output and hourly productivity, to one decimal place?
options: Real GDP per person rises 6.7%; output per hour falls 6.7%
Both rise 12% because total real GDP rose
Real GDP per person rises 7%; output per hour falls exactly 8%
Real GDP per person falls 6.7%; output per hour rises 6.7%
legendary.feedback: Per-person output changes by 1.12/1.05 - 1 ≈ 6.7%; hourly output changes by 1.12/1.20 - 1 ≈ -6.7%. More total hours can raise average output even while productivity per hour falls.

legendary.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
legendary.q: Cedar reports nominal GDP of $960 billion, a deflator of 120, and 32 million residents. Delta reports $1,320 billion, a deflator of 150, and 44 million residents. Which current real-GDP-per-person comparison is supported using comparable base prices?
options: Cedar $25,000; Delta $20,000, so higher nominal total does not imply higher average real output
Cedar $30,000; Delta $30,000, so average real output is equal
Cedar $25,000; Delta $30,000, because only Cedar needs deflation
Cedar $20,000; Delta $25,000, because the larger deflator raises real output
legendary.feedback: Real GDP is 960/1.20 = 800 billion for Cedar and 1,320/1.50 = 880 billion for Delta. Divide by populations: 25,000 and 20,000 per person. The larger nominal aggregate does not settle the living-standard comparison.

legendary.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
legendary.q: A poor country grows quickly after gaining stable property rights, schools, and foreign investment. Which explanation is strongest?
options: Growth must be caused only by inflation
Poor countries grow automatically regardless of policy
legendary.feedback: Catch-up growth is more likely when institutions support investment, human capital, and technology adoption.

legendary.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
legendary.q: Real output per hour rises 10%, annual hours per employed person fall 5%, and the employed share of the population falls from 60% to 58%. Which conclusion about real GDP per person follows, assuming these cover all production?
options: It rises about 1.0%; the other two factors offset much of the productivity gain
It rises 10%; hourly productivity alone determines the exact change
It falls 7%; add the percentage and percentage-point declines
It rises 5%; the employed share does not enter output per person
legendary.feedback: Output per person equals output/hour × hours/worker × workers/person. Its factor is 1.10 × 0.95 × (58/60) ≈ 1.01017. Average output rises about 1.0%, much less than the hourly-productivity increase.

legendary.q: Real GDP per person rises, but average leisure falls sharply and pollution worsens. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: Market output per person rose, but overall well-being may have changed differently.
Living standards rose by exactly the same rate because GDP per person captures all welfare changes.
GDP per person becomes unusable whenever leisure or environmental quality changes.
Pollution and lost leisure are already fully subtracted from measured real GDP.
legendary.commonError: Treating real GDP per person as a complete measure of welfare.
legendary.feedback: Real GDP per person is useful for material output, but it does not fully capture leisure, environmental quality, distribution, or nonmarket activity.

legendary.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.q: A plant initially produces 24,000 units using 20 workers who each work 100 hours. Next period, 24 workers each work 80 hours and produce 25,344 units. Which comparison is correct?
options: Output per worker falls 12%; output per hour rises 10%
Both productivity measures rise 5.6%, matching total output
Output per worker rises 10%; output per hour falls 12%
Output per hour is unchanged because the plant hired more workers
legendary.feedback: Per-worker output falls from 1,200 to 1,056, or 12%. Total hours fall from 2,000 to 1,920; hourly output rises from 12 to 13.2, or 10%. Changes in hours per worker make the productivity measures diverge.

legendary.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.q: An economy initially produces $90 billion using 3 billion labor hours. A plan targets $108 billion while limiting total hours to 3.2 billion. What hourly productivity and increase over the initial level are required?
options: $30 per hour, with no productivity gain
legendary.feedback: Initial productivity is 90/3 = 30 dollars per hour. The target requires 108/3.2 = 33.75, or 12.5% more. Output growth alone overstates the needed productivity increase because hours also expand.

legendary.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.q: Two countries have equal real GDP per person, but one works far fewer hours per person. What can be inferred?
options: The country with fewer hours likely has higher output per hour
They must have identical productivity per hour
The country with more hours must be richer
Real GDP per person cannot be compared
legendary.feedback: Equal output per person with fewer hours implies greater output per hour.

legendary.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.q: A country’s real GDP rises 6% while employment rises 10%. Population is unchanged. Which assessment separates average material output from output per worker?
options: Output per person rises 6%; output per worker falls about 3.6%
Both fall about 3.6% because productivity declined
Output per person falls 4%; subtract employment growth from GDP growth
legendary.feedback: With population fixed, GDP per person rises 6%. Output per worker changes by 1.06/1.10 - 1 ≈ -3.6%. A productivity decline does not imply that average output per resident also declined.

legendary.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.q: Output per worker rises from $50,000 to $55,000, but real GDP per resident stays at $30,000. What must happen to the employed share of residents, assuming the measures cover the same output?
options: It falls from 60% to about 54.5%, offsetting the productivity rise
It rises from 60% to 66%, reinforcing the productivity rise
It stays at 60% because output per resident is unchanged
It falls from 50% to 45%, because wages determine employment shares
legendary.feedback: Workers/residents equals output/resident divided by output/worker. The share changes from 30,000/50,000 = 60% to 30,000/55,000 ≈ 54.5%. This accounting result does not identify why the employment share fell.

legendary.q: In GROWTH-01, two otherwise similar economies begin at A and B. Each receives the same small addition to capital per worker. Which conclusion is best supported by the graph?
options: Point A has the larger marginal output gain; convergence is not guaranteed
Point B must gain more because its current output per worker is already higher
Both economies must receive exactly the same output gain whenever capital increases by the same amount
Point A is guaranteed to overtake point B even if institutions and technology differ
legendary.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.feedback: The graph is steeper at A, so the same small capital addition yields a larger marginal output gain there; this alone does not guarantee convergence.

legendary.q: A plant automates part of production. Output rises 18 percent while labor hours fall 5 percent. To one decimal place, what happens to output per labor hour?
legendary.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.feedback: Productivity changes by (1.18/0.95)−1 ≈ 24.2%, because output rises while labor hours fall.
legendary.roundingRule: Compute 1.18 ÷ 0.95 − 1 and round to one decimal place.

legendary.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
legendary.q: A factory adds machinery but productivity barely changes. After operator training, output rises with the same machines and labor hours. A manager concludes that machines have no productive value. Which interpretation best fits both stages?
options: Training helped realize the value of complementary capital; the first stage did not show that machines were useless
Training proves all earlier spending on machines should be subtracted from GDP
The later gain must be more physical capital because worker skills are unchanged by training
The data prove training raises output equally in every factory, regardless of equipment
legendary.feedback: The second stage changes human capital while holding physical inputs fixed. Its effect can reflect complementarity between skills and machinery. A weak result before training does not identify a zero contribution from capital.

legendary.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
legendary.q: A country discovers oil but has weak courts, low education, and poor infrastructure. Why might productivity remain low?
options: Resources alone do not guarantee high productivity
Oil is not a natural resource
Education matters only in service economies
legendary.feedback: Natural resources can help, but productivity depends on several complementary factors.

legendary.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
legendary.q: Two plants initially use the same machines and hours. Plant A adopts a freely available scheduling method and raises output 8%. Plant B trains operators without changing its method and raises output 8%. What can be inferred about productivity sources?
options: A changed technological knowledge and B human capital; equal output gains do not make the mechanisms identical
Both added physical capital because output rose without more labor hours
Both changed natural resources because the gain has the same size
A’s gain is human capital and B’s is technology solely because both involve information
legendary.feedback: A new production method is technological knowledge; skills acquired by workers are human capital. Equal measured gains do not identify a common mechanism or prove the two interventions would have equal effects elsewhere.

legendary.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
legendary.q: A country builds ports, roads, and power grids while also expanding vocational education. Which factors are increased?
legendary.feedback: Infrastructure is physical capital; vocational education builds human capital.

legendary.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.q: With labor, skills and technology fixed, output at 10, 20 and 30 identical machines is 100, 160 and 200 units. A planner predicts that 40 machines must yield 260. Which assessment follows from the observed pattern?
options: The successive gains are 60 and 40; continued diminishing marginal returns would put the next gain below 40
The observed average gain is 50, so 40 machines must yield exactly 250
The capital stock doubled once, proving output must double at 40 machines
The last gain was 40, so every later ten machines must add exactly 40
legendary.feedback: Equal capital increments add 60 then 40 units while other inputs are fixed. If the diminishing-returns pattern continues, the next increment adds less than 40; the table alone does not supply an exact future output level.

legendary.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
legendary.q: A low-capital economy gets basic tools and output jumps sharply. Later, additional tools add smaller gains. Which pattern is this?
options: Catch-up effect followed by diminishing returns
CPI substitution bias followed by inflation
Frictional unemployment followed by cyclical unemployment
legendary.feedback: Capital is highly productive when scarce, but additional capital eventually yields smaller gains.

legendary.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
legendary.q: A poor country and a rich country both add $1,000 of capital per worker. Why might the poor country gain more output per worker?
options: Poor countries do not face diminishing returns
The CPI is lower in poor countries
legendary.feedback: The catch-up effect depends on higher marginal returns to capital where capital is scarce.

legendary.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
legendary.q: A country raises saving incentives, yet surveyed firms postpone equipment purchases because contracts are often unenforceable. A proposed response doubles the saving subsidy without changing courts. Which recommendation is best supported?
options: Address enforcement risk alongside finance; more saving alone may not make productive investment attractive
Double the subsidy because every extra saved dollar necessarily becomes domestic machinery
Reduce worker training because courts and skills are substitute measures of the same input
Infer that physical capital has zero marginal product because investment is currently weak
legendary.feedback: The evidence identifies insecure returns as a barrier between available funds and investment. Predictable enforcement can complement financing. The survey does not establish an optimal subsidy or prove capital has no productive value.

legendary.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
legendary.q: A government blocks foreign investment to protect domestic firms. What long-run growth cost is most plausible?
options: Less capital inflow, less technology transfer, and weaker productivity growth
Higher productivity from isolation by definition
legendary.feedback: Foreign investment can bring capital, technology, and management know-how.

legendary.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
legendary.q: A region has trained engineers and funds for new equipment, but a rule prevents firms from using improved production methods. A review proposes more of the same training while keeping that rule. Which response best addresses the stated constraint?
options: Permit useful method adoption while maintaining skills and investment; training alone may not release the constraint
Purchase equipment alone because methods cannot affect output with machines fixed
Keep the rule because a stock of trained workers guarantees continuing productivity growth
Stop all training because technological knowledge makes human capital unproductive
legendary.feedback: The constrained margin is adopting better methods. Technology, skills and equipment can complement one another; repeating one input policy while blocking another can limit the gain. This is a conditional recommendation from the stated evidence.

legendary.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
legendary.q: A policy package improves contract enforcement, funds technical training, and supports research trials. After two years, capital and skill measures rise but output growth remains modest. Which assessment best separates a coherent strategy from a guaranteed result?
options: The package targets productivity determinants; implementation, diffusion and time still matter for realized growth
The package failed in principle because research must raise output immediately
The capital increase proves the research trials caused all future growth
The modest output change proves institutions cannot affect investment incentives
legendary.feedback: The instruments address institutions, human capital and technological knowledge. These are plausible growth channels, but observed short-run output alone neither guarantees eventual success nor disproves the channels. Implementation and technology diffusion must be evaluated.

legendary.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
legendary.q: Why can population growth reduce GDP per person even while raising total GDP?
options: Total GDP may rise while output per person falls
Capital per worker automatically rises with population
legendary.feedback: Population growth can dilute capital per worker unless investment keeps pace.

legendary.q: A country saves heavily and imports machinery, yet productivity barely rises because schools are weak, power is unreliable, and contracts are insecure. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Capital alone may not deliver catch-up when complementary conditions are weak
High saving guarantees convergence even when schools, infrastructure, and institutions remain persistently weak
The country should restrict technological adoption so scarce capital continues to have a high marginal product
The catch-up effect requires poorer economies to have lower productivity growth than richer economies
legendary.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
legendary.feedback: Investment needs complementary human capital, infrastructure, technology, and secure institutions; capital alone may not deliver catch-up.

legendary.q: A government subsidizes investment for five years, raising capital per worker, but it makes no lasting change to research, education, or institutions. Which long-run caution is most appropriate?
options: The temporary subsidy guarantees a permanently higher growth rate even after capital deepening slows
Research and education matter only for short-run aggregate demand
Institutions become irrelevant once the capital stock has increased
The capital increase can raise the output level, but sustained productivity growth needs broader continuing sources
legendary.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
legendary.feedback: More capital can raise the output level, but continuing productivity growth requires ongoing gains in skills, technology, and institutions.
