legendary.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
legendary.q: A labor survey starts with 132 employed, 12 unemployed and 56 other adults. Then 4 unemployed find jobs, 3 stop searching, 5 outsiders start searching without finding work, and 2 employed retire. All job seekers are available. What are the new unemployment and participation rates?
legendary.feedback: Employment becomes 132 + 4 - 2 = 134 and unemployment 12 - 4 - 3 + 5 = 10. The labor force is 144 of 200 adults, so participation is 72% and unemployment is 10/144 ≈ 6.9%. The entering and leaving flows happen to offset in total participation.

legendary.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
legendary.q: There are 200 adults, labor-force participation is 75%, and unemployment is 8%. Next month 6 unemployed stop searching, 6 employed retire, and 4 outsiders start searching without finding work. With everyone otherwise unchanged and seekers available, which final account is correct?
legendary.feedback: Initially LF = 150, U = 12 and E = 138. After the flows E = 132, U = 12 - 6 + 4 = 10 and LF = 142. Thus U/LF ≈ 7.0% and LF/adults = 71%. A lower unemployment rate coexists with fewer people employed.

legendary.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
legendary.q: An economy has 90 employed, 10 unemployed, and 50 not in the labor force. Five employed workers lose jobs and search; five unemployed workers stop searching. What happens to unemployment rate?
legendary.feedback: Employed falls to 85. Five newly unemployed workers replace five workers who stop searching, so unemployed remains 10 and the labor force falls to 95. The rate is 10/95 = 10.53%.

legendary.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
legendary.q: A population of 200 adults is unchanged. The unemployment rate stays at 6%, while participation falls from 75% to 70%. Which employment change and interpretation follow?
options: Employment falls by 9.4; a stable unemployment rate does not imply a stable number of jobs
Employment stays at 141; a stable rate fixes employment
Employment falls by 10; every labor-force exit must be an employed worker
Employment rises by 9.4; lower participation indicates more jobs
legendary.feedback: The labor force falls from 150 to 140. Employment is 94% of each total: 141 initially and 131.6 afterward, a decline of 9.4. The unchanged unemployment rate is a ratio, not an unchanged employment count.

legendary.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
legendary.q: A jobless worker applied to three jobs last week. Another jobless worker wants work but last searched two months ago. A third works 3 hours per week but wants full-time work. How are they classified?
options: Unemployed; not in labor force; employed
Employed; unemployed; not in labor force
Not in labor force; unemployed; employed
legendary.feedback: Recent active search means unemployed; no recent search means not in labor force; any paid work means employed.

legendary.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
legendary.q: Which case makes the headline unemployment rate look better than the actual labor market experience?
options: A rise in discouraged workers and involuntary part-time workers
legendary.feedback: Discouraged and involuntary part-time workers are not fully captured by the headline unemployment rate.

legendary.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
legendary.q: A report says unemployment fell from 20 to 12 while employment rose from 180 to 184. Adult population is fixed at 250, and the only flows were unemployed people finding jobs or stopping search. Which decomposition and participation change are implied?
options: 4 found jobs and 4 left search; participation fell from 80% to 78.4%
4 found jobs and 8 left search; participation fell to 76.8%
4 left search and none found jobs; the employment rise is unrelated
legendary.feedback: The employment rise identifies 4 job findings. Of the 8-person unemployment decline, the remaining 4 are exits. LF falls from 200 to 196, so participation falls from 80% to 78.4%. Both hiring and withdrawal contributed to the lower headline rate.

legendary.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
legendary.q: Two districts have the same unemployment rate and population. One has lower participation and a larger share of employed people working part time because full-time work is unavailable. Which additional comparison is best before calling their labor markets equally strong?
options: Compare employment per adult and desired versus actual hours; the headline rate omits both differences
Compare only total unemployment; equal unemployment rates guarantee equal counts
Count all involuntary part-time workers as unemployed before applying the official definition
Exclude discouraged workers from every indicator because they are outside the labor force
legendary.feedback: Unemployment divides job seekers by the labor force. Lower participation can lower employment per adult even at the same rate, while involuntary part-time workers remain employed. Additional participation and hours evidence is needed for the broader assessment.

legendary.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
legendary.q: If measured unemployment falls because 1M unemployed workers become discouraged, while employment is unchanged, what happens to labor force participation?
legendary.feedback: Discouraged workers leave the labor force, so labor force participation falls.

legendary.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
legendary.q: A worker is laid off because a recession reduces sales. Six months later, the worker's old industry adopts technology that permanently eliminates the job type. How should the unemployment diagnosis change?
options: Cyclical at first; structural if the job type disappears
It must be natural unemployment only
legendary.feedback: Weak demand causes cyclical unemployment, but permanent skill/job mismatch is structural.

legendary.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
legendary.q: After a regional downturn ends, one group has suitable job offers but needs time to choose; another cannot meet credentials for expanding occupations. A third group has already accepted paid part-time work while seeking full-time jobs. Which diagnosis respects both cause and official status?
options: The first group is frictionally unemployed, the second structurally unemployed, and the third employed
All three are structurally unemployed because each wants a different job
The first is cyclical, the second frictional, and the third outside the labor force
All three are unemployed until they obtain their preferred full-time jobs
legendary.feedback: Normal matching among suitable jobs is frictional; a persistent credential mismatch is structural. A paid part-time job makes the third group employed under the official measure, even though underemployment may remain.

legendary.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
legendary.q: Spending and total vacancies recover after a downturn, but vacancies concentrate in licensed occupations while displaced workers lack the credentials. Which evidence would most directly strengthen a structural diagnosis over a purely cyclical one?
options: Credential training is followed by placements into the unfilled occupations while overall spending changes little
All vacancies disappear when spending weakens again
Workers have suitable offers and are briefly choosing among them
Unemployment falls only when economy-wide spending rises sharply, with no change in skills
legendary.feedback: The mismatch between expanding occupations and worker credentials points to a structural barrier. Placements after relevant training, with demand broadly unchanged, strengthen that mechanism rather than a claim based only on weak spending or ordinary search.

legendary.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
legendary.q: A worker is unemployed because moving to available jobs is too costly, even though jobs exist elsewhere. Which type is most likely?
legendary.feedback: Geographic mismatch is a form of structural unemployment.

legendary.q: A regional downturn eliminates jobs at several firms. One year later overall demand has recovered, but many displaced workers remain unemployed because growing industries require different credentials. Which diagnosis is most accurate?
options: Cyclical unemployment fell, while structural unemployment remains
The remaining unemployment must still be entirely cyclical
The recovery eliminates both structural and frictional unemployment
The remaining unemployment is frictional simply because workers are looking for jobs
legendary.commonError: Confuses persistent skill or location mismatch with temporary search or weak aggregate demand.
legendary.feedback: Structural unemployment reflects a durable mismatch between workers and available jobs, skills, or locations.

legendary.q: A city’s jobless population includes skilled movers choosing among local openings and workers whose occupation disappeared. A single faster job-listing service is proposed for both. Which prediction is best supported?
options: It must eliminate both groups’ unemployment because each can read the same vacancies
It affects only cyclical unemployment because information is part of total spending
It turns structurally unemployed workers into employed people as soon as listings are viewed
It can shorten matching for the first group; the second may also need retraining or mobility support
legendary.commonError: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
legendary.feedback: The first group faces search frictions among suitable jobs. The second faces a durable mismatch that information alone may not remove. Diagnosis should guide the intervention without assuming guaranteed placement.

legendary.commonError: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
legendary.q: In a competitive labor market, employment is 100 at the clearing wage. A binding wage floor produces labor supply of 140 and demand of 95. Assuming everyone seeking work is available and active, which comparison is correct?
options: Employment falls by 5, while the labor surplus is 45; these are different quantities
Employment falls by 45 because every person in the surplus previously had a job
Employment falls by 40, matching the increase in labor supply
There is no surplus because 95 people remain employed
legendary.feedback: Employment changes from 100 to 95, a loss of 5. The new excess of labor supplied over labor demanded is 140 - 95 = 45, including the effect of increased job seeking as well as reduced hiring. The surplus is not the number of pre-existing jobs lost.

legendary.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
legendary.q: A benefit extension lowers the cost of continued search. A simultaneous placement program improves matching. Average unemployment duration then falls. Which conclusion is warranted from these facts alone?
options: The combined outcome improved duration; it does not show that the benefit extension by itself shortened search
The fall proves benefit extensions always shorten search
The extension must have been ineffective at protecting income because duration fell
The placement program cannot matter because benefits determine every search decision
legendary.feedback: Income support can reduce search urgency while better matching shortens search. Their combined result does not isolate either effect; a credible separate comparison would be needed. The duration result also does not measure the value of income protection.

legendary.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
legendary.q: A negotiated wage rises from $20 to $24 while employment falls from 100 to 90, with hours per worker fixed. What happens to the total wage bill, and what distributional claim is justified?
options: The wage bill rises 8%; retained workers gain hourly pay while some workers lose jobs
The wage bill falls 10%; no workers gain from the contract
The wage bill rises 20%; the employment change is irrelevant
The wage bill rises 8%; this proves every original worker is better off
legendary.feedback: The wage bill changes from 20 × 100 = 2,000 to 24 × 90 = 2,160 per common unit of hours, an 8% rise. The aggregate increase does not erase the job losses; gains to retained workers and losses to displaced workers differ.

legendary.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
legendary.q: A firm considers raising wages from $18 to $21 per hour. Output per hour is expected to rise from 6 to 7 units through better retention and effort, with other unit costs unchanged. Which cost calculation and caution are correct?
options: Wage cost stays $3 per unit if the productivity forecast holds; the forecast still needs evidence
$3.50 per unit is certain because productivity cannot respond to wages
$2.57 per unit is certain because the old wage applies to the new output
$3 per unit proves the wage policy eliminates unemployment throughout the economy
legendary.feedback: The old wage cost is 18/6 = 3 per unit; the proposed cost is 21/7 = 3 if the effort/retention forecast occurs. This makes an efficiency-wage rationale possible, but does not prove the forecast or settle economy-wide unemployment.

legendary.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
legendary.q: Which policy most directly targets structural unemployment?
options: More generous unemployment insurance with no training
Changing GDP from nominal to real
legendary.feedback: Structural unemployment comes from mismatch, so retraining can help.

legendary.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
legendary.q: Which policy most directly affects frictional unemployment?
options: Job-search assistance that improves matching speed
A new GDP deflator base year
legendary.feedback: Frictional unemployment is about search and matching, so better matching can reduce it.

legendary.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
legendary.q: A recession increases layoffs, while unemployment insurance helps workers avoid immediate hardship but lengthens some searches. Which pair of concepts is involved?
options: Cyclical unemployment and frictional unemployment incentives
legendary.feedback: The recession creates cyclical unemployment; unemployment insurance affects job-search incentives.

legendary.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
legendary.q: An economy has 2% frictional, 3% structural and 2% cyclical unemployment. A recovery eliminates the cyclical component. At the same time, better matching lowers frictional unemployment to 1.5%, with structural unemployment unchanged. What actual and natural rates remain?
options: Both are 4.5%; recovery removed the cyclical component and matching lowered the natural rate
Both are 5%; recovery cannot change any observed unemployment rate
Actual is 2.5% and natural is 4.5%; subtract the cyclical decline again
Both are zero because the recession has ended
legendary.feedback: After recovery, cyclical unemployment is zero. The remaining natural rate is 1.5 + 3 = 4.5%, also the actual rate. Ending the downturn and improving normal matching are distinct channels.

legendary.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
legendary.q: Actual unemployment falls from 9% to 7%. Over the same interval, an estimate of the natural rate falls from 6% to 4%. What happens to the cyclical gap, and what claim would overstate the evidence?
options: The gap stays at 3 points; the lower actual rate alone does not show cyclical weakness diminished
The gap falls 2 points; actual unemployment determines the gap by itself
The gap rises 2 points; a lower natural rate always raises the gap by that amount
The gap becomes zero because both rates fell equally
legendary.feedback: Initially the gap is 9 - 6 = 3 points; finally it is 7 - 4 = 3. Actual unemployment fell with the estimated natural benchmark, so these numbers do not show a smaller cyclical component.

legendary.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
legendary.q: Suppose actual unemployment is 4%, natural unemployment is 5%, and inflationary pressure is rising. What is the likely labor-market interpretation?
options: Unemployment below the natural rate signals a tight labor market
legendary.feedback: Actual unemployment below the natural rate suggests tight labor markets and possible inflationary pressure.

legendary.q: An economy recovers fully from a recession, yet unemployment settles at a higher level than before because displaced workers lost skills during the long downturn. Which explanation best fits?
options: Lasting labor-market damage may have raised the natural rate
Cyclical unemployment must still equal the entire unemployment rate
The natural rate cannot change after any recession
A higher natural rate means all remaining unemployment is frictional
legendary.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
legendary.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

legendary.q: A retraining reform is expected to lower structural unemployment by 1 percentage point, but longer voluntary search raises frictional unemployment by 0.4 point. Cyclical unemployment is unchanged. Which natural-rate prediction follows, conditional on both estimates?
options: It falls 1.4 points; both changes reduce unemployment
It rises 0.4 point; structural mismatch is outside the natural rate
It stays unchanged; only recessions can move the natural rate
It falls 0.6 point; the policy effects partly offset
legendary.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
legendary.feedback: The natural rate includes both structural and frictional unemployment. Its predicted change is -1 + 0.4 = -0.6 percentage point. The net estimate is conditional on the two stated mechanisms, not a guarantee about every retraining policy.

legendary.q: Actual unemployment falls below the estimated natural rate during a strong expansion. Later it returns to the natural rate with no change in worker skills or matching. What is the best interpretation?
options: Structural unemployment must have been negative during the expansion
The return to the natural rate proves frictional unemployment disappeared temporarily
The temporary gap reflected cyclical conditions rather than a permanent change in the natural rate
The natural rate permanently fell and then rose because actual unemployment moved
legendary.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
legendary.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

easyBoss.q: Which transaction would be counted in U.S. GDP?
options: A new car produced and sold in the United States this year
A used car resold from one household to another
A parent cooking dinner at home
A stock purchase through a brokerage account
easyBoss.commonError: counts_used_goods_or_financial_transactions_in_gdp
easyBoss.feedback: GDP counts newly produced final goods and services within a country during a period.

easyBoss.q: Which of these items is included in current GDP: a new laptop, a used bike, a homemade dinner, or a stock purchase?
easyBoss.commonError: counts_nonmarket_or_resale_activity
easyBoss.feedback: The new laptop is newly produced and sold in a market. Used goods, home production, and stock trades are not counted the same way.

easyBoss.q: GDP is best defined as:
options: Final domestic production during a period
The total value of all used goods sold this year
The total value of all financial transactions
The amount of money held by households
easyBoss.commonError: counts_financial_transactions_or_used_goods_as_gdp
easyBoss.feedback: GDP measures the market value of final goods and services produced within a country during a period.

easyBoss.q: Why is a tire sold to a car manufacturer usually not counted separately in GDP when the final car is sold?
options: Counting tire and car double counts production
The tire was not produced in a market
easyBoss.commonError: double_counts_intermediate_goods
easyBoss.feedback: GDP counts final goods to avoid double counting intermediate goods already included in the final product's value.

easyBoss.q: Why does total income equal total expenditure for the economy as a whole?
easyBoss.commonError: misses_two_sides_of_each_transaction
easyBoss.feedback: For the economy as a whole, spending by buyers becomes income for sellers.

easyBoss.q: If one person’s spending is another person’s income, does every transaction increase GDP?
options: No; GDP counts current final production
Yes, every financial transaction raises GDP
Yes, all used goods sales raise GDP again
easyBoss.commonError: thinks_all_transactions_count_in_gdp
easyBoss.feedback: Income and expenditure are two sides of transactions, but GDP only counts current production of final goods and services.

easyBoss.q: Why is GDP usually studied in macroeconomics rather than microeconomics?
options: It measures total production for the economy as a whole
It measures one firm's output only
It measures only one household's choices
It tracks only one product's demand curve
easyBoss.commonError: treats_gdp_as_single_firm_measure
easyBoss.feedback: GDP measures aggregate production for the whole economy, which makes it a macroeconomic measure.

easyBoss.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
easyBoss.q: Why can GDP be measured as both total income and total expenditure?
options: Because every dollar spent by a buyer becomes income for a seller
Because income is always higher than spending
Because prices do not affect GDP
easyBoss.feedback: GDP can be measured either way because one person's spending becomes another person's income.

easyBoss.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
easyBoss.q: A household spends $500 at a local repair shop. In the income-expenditure flow, what happens to the repair shop?
easyBoss.feedback: The household's expenditure becomes income for the repair shop.

easyBoss.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
easyBoss.q: If total expenditure on final goods and services is $18 trillion, what should total income equal in the basic GDP identity?
easyBoss.feedback: Total income equals total expenditure, so both are $18 trillion.

easyBoss.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
easyBoss.q: An economist asks which item belongs in GDP. Which one counts?
options: A newly produced washing machine sold to a household
A used washing machine resold online
A gift from one household to another
easyBoss.feedback: GDP counts newly produced final goods and services.

easyBoss.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
easyBoss.q: Why is a used car sale usually not counted in current GDP?
options: The car was counted when it was first produced
Cars are never counted in GDP
easyBoss.feedback: Used goods are not current production, so they are not counted again.

easyBoss.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
easyBoss.q: A bakery buys flour for $40 and sells bread to consumers for $100. How much is counted in GDP from the final bread sale?
easyBoss.feedback: GDP counts the value of the final good, which is the $100 bread sale.

easyBoss.q: A household buys groceries, a firm buys machinery, and the government pays workers to repair roads. Which GDP components are involved?
easyBoss.commonError: puts_all_spending_into_consumption
easyBoss.feedback: Household groceries are consumption, machinery is investment, and road repair workers are government purchases.

easyBoss.q: A family buys a new refrigerator for its home. Which GDP component does this most directly enter?
easyBoss.commonError: puts_household_durable_goods_into_investment
easyBoss.feedback: Household purchases of goods and services are consumption, even when the good is durable.

easyBoss.q: A firm buys a new machine to produce more output next year. Which GDP component does this enter?
easyBoss.commonError: confuses_business_investment_with_financial_investment
easyBoss.feedback: Business purchases of capital equipment count as investment in GDP accounting.

easyBoss.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
easyBoss.q: Which formula correctly gives GDP using the expenditure approach?
easyBoss.feedback: GDP expenditure equals consumption plus investment plus government purchases plus net exports.

easyBoss.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
easyBoss.q: A firm buys a new machine to produce more goods. Which GDP component does this enter?
easyBoss.feedback: Business purchases of new capital goods are investment.

easyBoss.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
easyBoss.q: If C = 8, I = 2, G = 3, and NX = -1, what is GDP?

easyBoss.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
easyBoss.q: An economist asks how net exports are calculated:
easyBoss.feedback: Net exports equal exports minus imports.

easyBoss.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
easyBoss.q: A U.S. household buys an imported phone. What happens inside the GDP formula?
options: Consumption rises and net exports fall
GDP automatically rises by the phone price
easyBoss.feedback: Imported consumer goods raise consumption but lower net exports, so domestic GDP does not rise from foreign production.

easyBoss.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
easyBoss.q: If exports are $600 billion and imports are $750 billion, what are net exports?
easyBoss.feedback: Net exports = 600 - 750 = -150 billion.

easyBoss.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
easyBoss.q: Nominal GDP uses which prices?
easyBoss.feedback: Nominal GDP values output using current-year prices.

easyBoss.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
easyBoss.q: Real GDP is useful because it:
options: Uses current prices to preserve every change in inflation
Uses base-year quantities instead of current output quantities
Subtracts the inflation rate directly from nominal GDP
Uses base-year prices to remove inflation
easyBoss.feedback: Real GDP helps isolate changes in actual production.

easyBoss.commonError: Confusing price changes with real output changes.
easyBoss.q: An economy produces 10 units. The base-year price is $5 and the current price is $8. What is real GDP using base-year prices?
easyBoss.feedback: Real GDP = 10 x $5 = $50.

easyBoss.q: A country produces more goods this year, but some of that production replaces worn-out equipment. What does this example show about GDP?
options: GDP measures every environmental and leisure dimension of welfare
GDP excludes all replacement investment from measured current production
GDP directly reports how national income is distributed across households
GDP measures production, not all well-being
easyBoss.commonError: treats_gdp_as_perfect_wellbeing_measure
easyBoss.feedback: GDP measures market production, but it is not a perfect measure of well-being.

easyBoss.q: A country has higher GDP, but also more pollution and longer work hours. What should the student conclude?
options: Pollution and longer work hours are fully deducted from real GDP already
GDP is useless because it measures no current market production at all
GDP is useful, but it does not capture every part of well-being
Higher GDP proves every household receives exactly the same welfare gain
easyBoss.commonError: treats_gdp_as_complete_measure_of_living_standards
easyBoss.feedback: GDP is useful because income matters, but it leaves out things like leisure, environmental quality, and some nonmarket activity.

easyBoss.q: GDP rises after a natural disaster because rebuilding spending increases. What is the best interpretation?
options: GDP automatically subtracts every hardship caused by the original disaster
GDP can rise without well-being rising
Rebuilding activity is excluded whenever a natural disaster occurred first
Higher construction spending guarantees that destroyed household wealth is restored
easyBoss.commonError: assumes_higher_gdp_always_means_higher_wellbeing
easyBoss.feedback: GDP can rise when rebuilding activity increases, but that does not automatically mean well-being improved.

easyBoss.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
easyBoss.q: GDP is useful as a measure of well-being mainly because:
options: Higher production guarantees equal gains for each household
GDP measures only transfers rather than market output
People generally prefer more income and output
GDP records every environmental and leisure benefit
easyBoss.feedback: GDP is useful because income and production matter, but it is not perfect.

easyBoss.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
easyBoss.q: Why might GDP rise while well-being does not clearly improve?
options: GDP excludes every final good produced in a legal market
GDP measures only the distribution of current household income
GDP includes complete adjustments for leisure and environmental quality
easyBoss.feedback: GDP misses some important parts of well-being.

easyBoss.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
easyBoss.q: A country produces more output by making people work longer hours with less leisure. What limitation of GDP does this show?
easyBoss.feedback: GDP counts the extra production but does not fully subtract the loss of leisure.

easyBoss.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
easyBoss.q: What does the CPI measure?
options: The cost of a fixed basket over time
easyBoss.feedback: The CPI measures the cost of a fixed basket of consumer goods and services.

easyBoss.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
easyBoss.q: If the CPI rises, what does that usually indicate?
options: Consumer prices have increased on average
easyBoss.feedback: A rising CPI means the average cost of the consumer basket has increased.

easyBoss.commonError: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.
easyBoss.q: If the CPI rises from 100 to 112, what is the inflation rate?

easyBoss.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
easyBoss.q: To calculate CPI, economists compare:
options: The current cost of a fixed basket to its base-year cost
The labor force to adult population
Nominal interest to real interest only
easyBoss.feedback: CPI compares the current basket cost to the base-year basket cost.

easyBoss.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
easyBoss.q: A basket costs $200 in the base year and $250 today. What does that tell us before calculating the CPI?
options: The basket is more expensive today
easyBoss.feedback: The fixed basket costs more today than in the base year.

easyBoss.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
easyBoss.q: A basket costs $200 in the base year and $250 today. What is the CPI today?

easyBoss.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
easyBoss.q: One reason CPI can overstate the cost of living is:
options: It may miss substitution toward cheaper goods
It measures unemployment instead of prices
easyBoss.feedback: The fixed basket can miss how consumers substitute toward relatively cheaper goods.

easyBoss.commonError: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
easyBoss.q: Beef becomes expensive, so households buy more chicken instead. Which CPI problem does this illustrate?
easyBoss.feedback: Substitution bias occurs when consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.

easyBoss.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
easyBoss.q: A product becomes more expensive but also much higher quality. Why can that make CPI inflation misleading?
options: Part of the price increase reflects better quality
Quality changes are always counted perfectly
The product becomes an import automatically
easyBoss.feedback: If quality improves, a higher price may overstate the true rise in cost of living.

easyBoss.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
easyBoss.q: Which price index uses a fixed basket of consumer goods and services?
easyBoss.feedback: The CPI uses a fixed basket of consumer goods and services.

easyBoss.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
easyBoss.q: An imported coffee price rises. Which index is affected more directly?
easyBoss.feedback: Imported consumer goods affect the CPI but are excluded from the GDP deflator.

easyBoss.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
easyBoss.q: Which statement correctly compares CPI and the GDP deflator?
options: CPI uses a fixed basket; the GDP deflator uses current output
CPI tracks only exports; the GDP deflator tracks only imports
easyBoss.feedback: The CPI and GDP deflator both measure prices, but they use different baskets.

easyBoss.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
easyBoss.q: Why should dollar amounts from different years be adjusted for inflation?
options: Money's purchasing power changes over time
easyBoss.feedback: Inflation changes what a dollar can buy, so dollar amounts across time need adjustment.

easyBoss.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
easyBoss.q: A wage of $10 in the past may not be comparable to $10 today because:
options: The price level may have changed
Nominal wages are always real wages
easyBoss.feedback: The same dollar wage can have different purchasing power in different years.

easyBoss.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
easyBoss.q: A wage was $20 when the CPI was 100. The CPI is now 150. What is that wage in today's dollars?
easyBoss.feedback: Today's dollars = 20 x 150/100 = $30.

easyBoss.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
easyBoss.q: Answer the economist: The real interest rate is approximately:
options: Nominal interest rate minus inflation rate
Nominal interest rate plus inflation rate
easyBoss.feedback: The real interest rate adjusts the nominal rate for inflation.

easyBoss.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
easyBoss.q: If inflation rises while the nominal interest rate stays fixed, what happens to the real interest rate?
easyBoss.feedback: Higher inflation reduces the real interest rate when nominal interest does not change.

easyBoss.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
easyBoss.q: If the nominal interest rate is 7% and inflation is 4%, what is the real interest rate?
easyBoss.feedback: Real interest rate = 7% - 4% = 3%.

easyBoss.q: A country reports $750 billion in inflation-adjusted output and 25 million residents. Which real-GDP-per-person figure is correct?
easyBoss.commonError: Dividing by the wrong population scale.
easyBoss.feedback: $750 billion ÷ 25 million residents = $30,000 per person.

easyBoss.q: Using the Rule of 70, income growing at 3.5 percent per year doubles in about:
easyBoss.commonError: Multiplying 70 by the growth rate instead of dividing.

easyBoss.q: If population grows faster than real GDP, real GDP per person will generally:
easyBoss.commonError: Ignoring population growth when evaluating average output.
easyBoss.feedback: Per-person output falls when the population denominator grows faster than total real output.

easyBoss.q: A factory produces 900 units in 90 labor hours. What is labor productivity?
easyBoss.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
easyBoss.feedback: Labor productivity is output divided by labor hours: 900/90 = 10 units per labor hour.

easyBoss.q: In GROWTH-01, which point has both lower capital per worker and lower output per worker?
options: Both points have the same capital per worker
Neither point lies on the production curve
easyBoss.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
easyBoss.feedback: Point A is lower on both axes, so it has lower capital per worker and lower output per worker.

easyBoss.q: A company hires more workers and total output rises, but output per labor hour does not change. What happened to labor productivity?
options: It became equal to output per worker automatically
It rose because total output rose
easyBoss.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
easyBoss.feedback: Output and labor hours increased in the same proportion, leaving output per labor hour unchanged.

easyBoss.q: A worker receives a new machine that raises output with the same labor time. Which productivity input increased most directly?
easyBoss.commonError: Treats every increase in capital as producing the same output gain.
easyBoss.feedback: Providing a new machine increases physical capital per worker; with labor time unchanged, that can raise output per worker.

easyBoss.q: In GROWTH-01, why does an equal small addition to capital have greater output potential near point A than near point B?
options: Point A has more output per worker than B
The curve is vertical near B
Capital has no relationship to output near A
The curve is steeper near A
easyBoss.commonError: Treats every increase in capital as producing the same output gain.
easyBoss.feedback: The curve is steeper near A, so an equal small capital addition produces a larger additional output per worker there.

easyBoss.q: A new production method lets the same workers and machines produce more output. Which source of productivity improved?
easyBoss.commonError: Confuses technological knowledge with merely owning more machines.
easyBoss.feedback: Technology raises the efficiency with which available inputs are transformed into output.

easyBoss.q: Which policy most directly strengthens incentives for private long-term investment?
options: Secure property rights with predictable contract enforcement
Frequent asset seizure that makes long-term investment returns highly uncertain
Unpredictable contract enforcement that raises risk for firms making long-term investments
Bans on productive capital formation that prevent firms from expanding productive capacity
easyBoss.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
easyBoss.feedback: Secure property rights and predictable contract enforcement protect investment returns, strengthening incentives for private long-term investment.

easyBoss.q: Which policy most directly builds human capital?
options: Reducing access to schooling and limiting opportunities for workers to acquire new skills
Making private research illegal and restricting firms from adopting outside technologies
Replacing productive investment with longer workweeks while worker skills remain unchanged
Improving education, job training, and basic health
easyBoss.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
easyBoss.feedback: Education, job training, and basic health build workers’ human capital and can raise productivity.

easyBoss.q: Which policy most directly supports technological knowledge?
options: Increasing transfer payments without changing productive capacity
Research, innovation, and diffusion of better production methods
easyBoss.commonError: Treats a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity.
easyBoss.feedback: Research and innovation create technological knowledge, while diffusion spreads more productive methods to firms.

easyBoss.q: A worker has a part-time job but is actively searching for full-time work. How is the worker classified in official labor statistics?
options: Unemployed, because the worker wants more hours.
Employed, because the worker has a paid job.
Outside the labor force, because the job is part time.
Discouraged, because the worker is searching for another job.
easyBoss.commonError: Classifying an underemployed worker as unemployed.
easyBoss.feedback: Official employment status is based on having work, not on whether the worker wants additional hours.

easyBoss.q: A jobless adult is available to work but has not searched during the past four weeks. How is this person usually classified?
easyBoss.commonError: Ignoring the active-search requirement for official unemployment.
easyBoss.feedback: A jobless person generally must be available and actively searching to be counted as unemployed.

easyBoss.q: Which equation defines the labor force?
options: Labor force = employed people - discouraged workers.
Labor force = working-age population - employed people.
Labor force = employed people + unemployed people.
easyBoss.commonError: Including everyone in the population or excluding officially unemployed workers.
easyBoss.feedback: The labor force contains people who are employed plus people who are jobless and actively seeking work.

easyBoss.q: A recent graduate is actively searching for a first job that matches their training. Which unemployment type is most likely?
options: Structural unemployment from a persistent skill mismatch
Cyclical unemployment caused by a recession
Outside the labor force because the worker is not searching
easyBoss.commonError: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
easyBoss.feedback: Frictional unemployment comes from normal search and matching as workers move between jobs or enter the labor market.

easyBoss.q: A machinist’s occupation disappears after a permanent technology change, and available jobs require different skills. Which type is most likely?
easyBoss.commonError: Confuses persistent skill or location mismatch with temporary search or weak aggregate demand.
easyBoss.feedback: Structural unemployment reflects a durable mismatch between workers and available jobs, skills, or locations.

easyBoss.q: A restaurant cuts staff because a recession sharply reduces customer spending. Which type is most likely?
options: Structural unemployment from a permanent mismatch
No unemployment because the staffing cut is temporary
Frictional unemployment from normal job search
easyBoss.commonError: Confuses recession-driven unemployment with the natural-rate components.
easyBoss.feedback: Cyclical unemployment is the deviation associated with weak aggregate demand and business-cycle downturns.

easyBoss.q: A legal wage floor is set above the equilibrium wage. What labor-market outcome can result?
options: A surplus of workers seeking jobs
A shortage of workers because labor demand exceeds labor supply
Automatic full employment at the higher wage
No change in labor supplied or demanded
easyBoss.commonError: Forgets that a binding wage floor can leave more workers seeking jobs than firms want to hire.
easyBoss.feedback: A binding minimum wage above equilibrium can create a labor surplus: labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.

easyBoss.q: A firm pays above-equilibrium wages to reduce quits and raise effort. Which theory is being used?
easyBoss.commonError: Treats union wage setting and efficiency wages as identical mechanisms or ignores their tradeoffs.
easyBoss.feedback: Efficiency wage theory predicts that a firm may pay above-equilibrium wages to reduce turnover and encourage greater effort.

easyBoss.q: A program helps unemployed workers identify suitable openings more quickly. Which unemployment type is most directly targeted?
options: Structural unemployment from obsolete skills only
easyBoss.commonError: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
easyBoss.feedback: Frictional unemployment comes from normal search and matching as workers move between jobs or enter the labor market.

easyBoss.q: Which unemployment is included in the natural rate?
easyBoss.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
easyBoss.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

easyBoss.q: Why can a healthy economy have positive unemployment at the natural rate?
options: Every healthy economy must retain recession-driven cyclical unemployment at all times
The natural rate is a policy target chosen to match the current inflation rate
All workers between paychecks are automatically classified as unemployed
Workers still search for jobs and some skills do not match openings
easyBoss.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
easyBoss.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

easyBoss.q: Which change can lower the natural rate?
options: A short recession that increases cyclical unemployment for several months
A one-month decline in consumer confidence with no lasting matching change
Faster job matching that reduces normal search time
A temporary fall in aggregate demand that raises recession-related layoffs
easyBoss.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
easyBoss.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

mediumBoss.q: Which transaction is included in current-year GDP?
options: A used refrigerator resold by its owner.
A household purchase of corporate stock.
An unpaid repair performed by the homeowner.
A newly produced refrigerator purchased by a household.
mediumBoss.commonError: Counting asset transfers, used goods, or unpaid household work as current production.
mediumBoss.feedback: GDP includes newly produced final goods and services, not transfers of existing assets or unpaid household production.

mediumBoss.q: A bakery buys flour for $2 and sells bread to a household for $5. How much does the bread transaction add to GDP if the flour was produced this year?
options: $5, because the final sale already includes the flour’s value.
$7, because both the flour and bread sales are added.
$3, because only the bakery’s value added counts and the flour is excluded everywhere.
$2, because intermediate goods are the only production counted.
mediumBoss.commonError: Double counting an intermediate input and the final product.
mediumBoss.feedback: Counting the $5 final bread sale captures the value of the flour and the bakery’s value added without double counting.

mediumBoss.q: Why does total income equal total expenditure in the national accounts?
options: Government legally requires national income to equal national expenditure each year.
Each transaction is spending for a buyer and income for a seller.
Households always spend every dollar of income and never save financial assets.
Imports are recorded as both domestic production income and domestic expenditure.
mediumBoss.commonError: Treating the accounting identity as a behavioral claim that everyone spends all income.
mediumBoss.feedback: The same transaction is recorded from two sides: one party’s expenditure is another party’s income.

mediumBoss.q: A county buys new snowplows and sends households heating-assistance checks. Which classification is correct?
options: The snowplows enter G; the checks are transfers
Both enter G because the county pays
mediumBoss.commonError: Counts a government transfer as government purchases before any recipient buys output.
mediumBoss.feedback: Transfers redistribute income and are excluded from G; a later purchase can enter the appropriate spending component.

mediumBoss.q: A household buys an imported television. Why do C and M both change?
options: C excludes the television, while M adds its retail value
Both entries reduce GDP because the good is imported
M records a transfer from government to the household
C records the purchase, while subtracting M removes foreign production
mediumBoss.commonError: Treats the subtraction of imports as a claim that imported goods are inherently harmful or absent from spending.
mediumBoss.feedback: Imports are subtracted because imported final spending may already appear in C, I, or G and foreign production must not enter domestic GDP.

mediumBoss.q: Which pair is classified as investment in GDP accounting?
options: A pension payment plus a household appliance purchase
An imported restaurant meal plus a tax refund
A new home plus added business inventories
A used home plus a corporate bond purchase
mediumBoss.commonError: Treats only machines as investment and misses new homes or inventory changes.
mediumBoss.feedback: GDP investment includes business fixed investment, residential construction, and changes in inventories.

mediumBoss.q: Current quantity is 30 units, current price is $8, and base-year price is $5. Which pair is correct?
mediumBoss.commonError: Mixes current and base-year prices while valuing current output.
mediumBoss.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

mediumBoss.q: Nominal GDP grows 10% while real GDP grows 2%. What is the best interpretation?
options: Production rose 10% with no price change
Production rose, and prices also rose
mediumBoss.commonError: Infers output growth directly from nominal GDP growth.
mediumBoss.feedback: Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production.

mediumBoss.q: Real GDP rises from $500 billion to $525 billion. Which growth calculation uses the correct denominator?
mediumBoss.commonError: Uses the new level rather than the initial real-GDP level as the percentage-growth denominator.
mediumBoss.feedback: Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.

mediumBoss.q: Unpaid elder care becomes an otherwise similar paid service. What is most likely?
options: GDP rises although useful care changes little
GDP falls because all paid care becomes intermediate production
GDP stays fixed whenever the underlying service appears similar
Business investment rises by the full wage paid for care
mediumBoss.commonError: Equates a change in market spending with the same change in total useful services.
mediumBoss.feedback: Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently.

mediumBoss.q: Output rises while leisure and air quality decline. What can GDP alone determine?
options: The environmental loss is already netted from GDP
Market production rose; the welfare change is ambiguous
mediumBoss.commonError: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
mediumBoss.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

mediumBoss.q: GDP per person rises, but the median household’s income is unchanged. What limitation is relevant?
options: The median household must always equal the national average
Income distribution determines only the nominal price level
The average conceals how gains are distributed
GDP fails to measure any current market production
mediumBoss.commonError: Uses an average output measure to infer distribution or every quality improvement.
mediumBoss.feedback: GDP per person does not show distribution and may incompletely capture product-quality change.

mediumBoss.q: The CPI is reported as 130 and the base-year basket cost is $400. What is the current basket cost?
mediumBoss.commonError: Using the dollar difference or inverting the ratio.
mediumBoss.feedback: Current cost = 1.30 × $400 = $520.

mediumBoss.q: The CPI moves from 125 to 135. The inflation rate is:
mediumBoss.commonError: Using the 10-point change as the percentage rate.
mediumBoss.feedback: Inflation = 10/125 = 8 percent.

mediumBoss.q: If the CPI is 160, a base-year basket costing $300 now costs:
mediumBoss.commonError: Treating the index as a dollar amount.
mediumBoss.feedback: Current cost = 1.60 × $300 = $480.

mediumBoss.q: Substitution bias means consumers respond to a relative-price increase by doing what?
options: Buying relatively more of available cheaper alternatives
Stopping all purchases of every good whose price rose
Treating every new good as lower quality
Replacing the CPI with the GDP deflator
mediumBoss.commonError: Assumes a fixed basket fully reflects how households respond to changes in relative prices.
mediumBoss.feedback: Substitution bias arises when consumers shift toward relatively cheaper alternatives but the fixed basket does not fully reflect that response.

mediumBoss.q: Why can a genuinely new product make an old fixed basket overstate the cost of maintaining well-being?
options: Every new product must have a lower sticker price
New products are automatically excluded from consumer spending
The GDP deflator fixes the CPI basket immediately
The new option can expand choice and purchasing power
mediumBoss.commonError: Treats a newly available product as if it creates no gain until it enters an old basket.
mediumBoss.feedback: New goods expand choice and can improve purchasing power before a fixed basket fully incorporates them.

mediumBoss.q: A laptop price rises while speed and battery life improve. What should a careful CPI interpretation separate?
options: Quality improvement from pure price inflation
Domestic production from imported production only
mediumBoss.commonError: Treats every observed price increase as pure inflation even when product quality changes.
mediumBoss.feedback: Separate the value of quality improvement from the pure price change when interpreting cost-of-living inflation.

mediumBoss.q: A city buys domestic transit vehicles while households buy imported fuel. Which mapping is correct?
options: Vehicle prices enter the GDP deflator; imported fuel can enter CPI
Both prices enter only the GDP deflator
Imported fuel enters the GDP deflator but not CPI
mediumBoss.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
mediumBoss.feedback: Domestic transit vehicles are newly produced domestic output, so their prices enter the GDP deflator. Imported fuel bought by households is in the consumer basket and can enter CPI, but it is not domestic production.

mediumBoss.q: Domestic food-export prices rise and imported-clothing prices fall. What can happen?
options: CPI rises and the GDP deflator falls by definition
Both indexes must move together because trade is involved
The GDP deflator rises while CPI falls
mediumBoss.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
mediumBoss.feedback: Domestic food exports are part of current domestic production and can raise the GDP deflator. Imported clothing is in the consumer basket and can lower CPI, so the two indexes can move in opposite directions.

mediumBoss.q: Why can a changing mix of domestic output affect the GDP deflator more directly than CPI?
options: The deflator uses a permanently fixed consumer basket
CPI includes only domestic investment goods
mediumBoss.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
mediumBoss.feedback: The GDP deflator uses weights based on current domestic output, so a changing production mix changes its basket. CPI uses a fixed consumer basket and is not reweighted by the current mix of domestic production.

mediumBoss.q: A wage and CPI each rise 5%. What is the approximate real-wage change?
mediumBoss.commonError: Equates a higher nominal payment with a higher real payment.
mediumBoss.feedback: Compare the nominal change with the relevant price-index change to determine purchasing-power change.

mediumBoss.q: A pension is fully adjusted by the relevant consumer price index. What is the intended outcome?
options: Guarantee a real gain equal to inflation
Track prices of all domestic investment goods
mediumBoss.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
mediumBoss.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

mediumBoss.q: A past salary looks smaller only because prices were lower. What comparison corrects the problem?
options: Use the current GDP level only
Convert both salaries to a common price level
Add expected inflation to both salaries
mediumBoss.commonError: Compares dollar amounts from different periods without a common price level.
mediumBoss.feedback: Put nominal amounts in common purchasing-power units before making the real comparison.

mediumBoss.q: Why can a positive nominal interest rate still produce a negative real return?
options: Inflation can exceed the nominal rate
The nominal account balance must decline whenever consumer prices rise faster
mediumBoss.commonError: Uses the nominal rate alone to infer the purchasing-power return.
mediumBoss.feedback: For introductory approximation, real interest is nominal interest minus inflation.

mediumBoss.q: Expected inflation is used to calculate which real rate?
options: The ex post real rate calculated after actual inflation is observed
mediumBoss.commonError: Uses actual inflation to describe an expected return or expected inflation to describe the realized return.
mediumBoss.feedback: Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.

mediumBoss.q: Unexpected inflation rises on a fixed-rate loan. What happens to the real burden?
options: It leaves every real outcome unchanged
It converts the loan into an indexed benefit
It shifts downward for the borrower and reduces the lender’s real return
It rises equally for both parties and preserves the lender’s expected purchasing-power return
mediumBoss.commonError: Misses how unexpected inflation changes the real burden of a fixed nominal loan.
mediumBoss.feedback: Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real repayment burden and shifts purchasing power from lender to borrower.

mediumBoss.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
mediumBoss.q: An economist asks: why do small differences in annual growth rates matter so much over long periods?
mediumBoss.feedback: Small growth differences compound and can create large income gaps over decades.

mediumBoss.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
mediumBoss.q: Country A grows at 2% while Country B grows at 5%. What should you expect over several decades?
options: Country B's income will rise much faster if the growth rates persist
Both countries will end with the same income
Country A must grow faster because it starts slower
Growth rates do not affect living standards
mediumBoss.feedback: Higher sustained growth leads to much larger long-run income gains.

mediumBoss.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
mediumBoss.q: Using the Rule of 70, how long does it take income to double at a 5% annual growth rate?
mediumBoss.feedback: The Rule of 70 gives 70 / 5 = 14 years.

mediumBoss.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
mediumBoss.q: An economist points to two countries. Which measure is usually better for comparing average living standards?
mediumBoss.feedback: Real GDP per person is usually better for comparing average material living standards.

mediumBoss.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
mediumBoss.q: Country A has higher total GDP than Country B, but also has a much larger population. What should you check before comparing living standards?
mediumBoss.feedback: Total GDP can be misleading when countries have different population sizes.

mediumBoss.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
mediumBoss.q: Country A has real GDP of $2 trillion and a population of 50 million. What is real GDP per person?
mediumBoss.feedback: Real GDP per person = $2 trillion / 50 million = $40,000.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
mediumBoss.q: An economist asks for the core driver of long-run living standards. What is the best answer?
mediumBoss.feedback: Long-run living standards depend heavily on productivity.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
mediumBoss.q: Why does higher productivity raise living standards?
options: Workers can produce more goods and services per unit of labor
Workers automatically work fewer hours with no tradeoff
mediumBoss.feedback: Higher productivity means more output can be produced from the same labor input.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
mediumBoss.q: A factory produces 4,800 units using 600 labor hours. What is productivity?
mediumBoss.feedback: Productivity = output / labor hours = 4,800 / 600 = 8 units per hour.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
mediumBoss.q: Productivity is calculated as:
mediumBoss.feedback: Productivity is output per unit of labor input.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
mediumBoss.q: Output rises, but labor input rises even faster. What happens to productivity?
options: Productivity is unchanged by labor input
mediumBoss.feedback: If labor rises faster than output, output per unit of labor falls.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
mediumBoss.q: Output rises from 1,000 to 1,200 while labor hours rise from 100 to 150. What happens to productivity?
options: It falls from 10 to 8 units per hour
It rises from 10 to 12 units per hour
It stays at 10 units per hour
It rises from 8 to 10 units per hour
mediumBoss.feedback: Initial productivity is 1,000/100 = 10. New productivity is 1,200/150 = 8.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
mediumBoss.q: Physical capital includes:
mediumBoss.feedback: Physical capital is the equipment and structures used to produce goods and services.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
mediumBoss.q: If workers receive better machinery, what should happen to productivity, other things equal?
options: It no longer depends on output
mediumBoss.feedback: Better machinery usually allows workers to produce more output per hour.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
mediumBoss.q: A business has 10 workers and 20 machines. It adds 10 more machines while employment stays the same. What has increased?
mediumBoss.feedback: More machines with the same number of workers means more physical capital per worker.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
mediumBoss.q: Two countries use similar machines, but one invests heavily in worker education and training. Which productivity factor differs most?
mediumBoss.feedback: Education and training build human capital—the knowledge and skills workers bring to production.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
mediumBoss.q: A country expands technical training and apprenticeship programs. Which productivity factor increases most directly?
mediumBoss.feedback: Training programs increase worker skills, which raises human capital.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
mediumBoss.q: Two factories use the same machines, but one has better-trained workers. Why might that factory produce more?
options: Its workers have more human capital
It has more natural resources by definition
mediumBoss.feedback: Better-trained workers can use tools and processes more effectively.

mediumBoss.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
mediumBoss.q: Which item is a natural resource used in production?
mediumBoss.feedback: Natural resources are inputs supplied by nature, such as land, water, minerals, and oil.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
mediumBoss.q: A new drilling method allows firms to extract more oil with the same workers and equipment. Which factor changed most directly?
mediumBoss.feedback: A better method of production is technological knowledge.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
mediumBoss.q: A country discovers large copper deposits but lacks skilled workers and roads. What is the best interpretation?
options: Resources help, but skills and capital also matter
Natural resources alone guarantee high living standards
mediumBoss.feedback: Natural resources are useful, but they work best alongside skills, infrastructure, and technology.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
mediumBoss.q: A factory keeps the workforce fixed and adds identical machines. Each new machine raises output by less than the previous one. What principle is shown?
mediumBoss.feedback: With other inputs fixed, each additional unit of capital eventually adds less output.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
mediumBoss.q: A worker with no tools gains a hammer and becomes much more productive. A worker with ten hammers gains an eleventh and barely improves. What does this show?
mediumBoss.feedback: The extra hammer matters more when capital is scarce.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
mediumBoss.q: Capital per worker doubles, but output per worker rises by only 25%. What does that suggest?
mediumBoss.feedback: Output rose less than proportionally to capital, which is consistent with diminishing returns.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
mediumBoss.q: The catch-up effect says:
options: Scarce capital can produce faster catch-up growth
Growth rates are unrelated to capital
mediumBoss.feedback: The catch-up effect occurs when capital-scarce economies can gain more from new investment.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
mediumBoss.q: Why might a poor country gain more from one additional machine than a rich country?
options: Scarcer capital can have a higher marginal return
The rich country cannot use machines
The poor country has no workers
Machines count only in poor countries
mediumBoss.feedback: Capital tends to have a higher marginal product when it is scarce.

mediumBoss.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
mediumBoss.q: Country A has very little capital per worker and Country B has abundant capital per worker. If each receives the same new equipment, which country may grow faster from that addition?
mediumBoss.feedback: Country A may gain more because capital is scarcer there.

mediumBoss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
mediumBoss.q: One policy that can support long-run productivity growth is:
mediumBoss.feedback: Saving and investment can build capital and raise productivity.

mediumBoss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
mediumBoss.q: Why can higher saving support future growth?
options: It can finance investment in capital goods
mediumBoss.feedback: Saving can provide funds for investment, which builds productive capital.

mediumBoss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
mediumBoss.q: A country saves more, and firms use those funds to buy machines and build factories. Which growth channel is operating?
mediumBoss.feedback: Saving can finance investment, and investment builds physical capital.

mediumBoss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
mediumBoss.q: Property rights matter for growth because they:
mediumBoss.feedback: Secure property rights encourage people and firms to invest.

mediumBoss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
mediumBoss.q: A country has skilled workers and natural resources, but businesses fear the government may seize assets. What is likely to happen to investment?
options: Investment is likely to be weaker
mediumBoss.feedback: Weak property rights and political instability discourage investment.

mediumBoss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
mediumBoss.q: Which policy environment is most growth-friendly?
options: Secure property rights and predictable rules
Frequent asset seizure and unclear laws
mediumBoss.feedback: Growth is more likely when institutions support investment and long-run planning.

mediumBoss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
mediumBoss.q: Education supports growth mainly by increasing:
mediumBoss.feedback: Education increases human capital, which can raise productivity.

mediumBoss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
mediumBoss.q: Why can openness to trade support productivity growth?
options: Specialization plus better inputs, ideas, and markets
mediumBoss.feedback: Trade can improve productivity through specialization, competition, and access to inputs and ideas.

mediumBoss.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
mediumBoss.q: A government funds universities, public health, infrastructure, and research. What is it mainly trying to improve?
options: The resale value of old goods
mediumBoss.feedback: Education, health, infrastructure, and research can all support long-run productivity growth.

mediumBoss.q: A discouraged worker stops searching for a job while no one finds employment. What can happen to the official unemployment rate?
options: It can fall because the worker leaves unemployment and the labor force.
It must rise because employment did not increase.
It stays unchanged because discouraged workers remain unemployed.
It becomes zero because the labor force shrinks.
mediumBoss.commonError: Assuming the unemployment rate can fall only when employment rises.
mediumBoss.feedback: When a discouraged worker exits the labor force, both the number unemployed and the denominator fall, which can lower the rate.

mediumBoss.q: An economy has 900 employed people, 100 unemployed people, and 200 adults outside the labor force. What are the unemployment and labor-force participation rates?
options: The unemployment rate is 8.3 percent and participation is 75 percent.
The unemployment rate is 10 percent and participation is about 83.3 percent.
The unemployment rate is 10 percent and participation is 100 percent.
The unemployment rate is 12 percent and participation is about 66.7 percent.
mediumBoss.commonError: Using the adult population as the unemployment-rate denominator or omitting unemployed workers from participation.
mediumBoss.feedback: The labor force is 1,000, so unemployment is 100/1,000 = 10 percent; participation is 1,000/1,200 = 83.3 percent.

mediumBoss.q: An employed worker loses a job and immediately begins an active search. What happens initially?
options: Employment and labor force both rise as the search begins.
Unemployment falls because active search counts as employment.
Employment falls, unemployment rises, and the labor force is unchanged.
The worker exits the labor force despite beginning a search.
mediumBoss.commonError: Treating job loss with active search as labor-force exit.
mediumBoss.feedback: The person moves from employed to unemployed but remains in the labor force, raising the unemployment rate.

mediumBoss.q: A worker is unemployed for four weeks while comparing similar jobs in a strong labor market. Which fact most strongly supports a frictional diagnosis?
options: The worker stopped searching and left the labor force
The worker has marketable skills and needs time to find a match
The worker’s occupation has permanently disappeared
Aggregate demand has collapsed across the economy
mediumBoss.commonError: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
mediumBoss.feedback: Frictional unemployment comes from normal search and matching as workers move between jobs or enter the labor market.

mediumBoss.q: A recession ends, but workers from a permanently closed industry still cannot fill expanding jobs because their skills do not match. Which unemployment remains most directly?
options: No unemployment once the recession ends
mediumBoss.commonError: Confuses persistent skill or location mismatch with temporary search or weak aggregate demand.
mediumBoss.feedback: Structural unemployment reflects a durable mismatch between workers and available jobs, skills, or locations.

mediumBoss.q: A firm temporarily lays off workers because economy-wide spending falls, while another worker voluntarily searches for a better job. Which pair is present?
mediumBoss.commonError: Confuses recession-driven unemployment with the natural-rate components.
mediumBoss.feedback: Cyclical unemployment is the deviation associated with weak aggregate demand and business-cycle downturns.

mediumBoss.q: A union negotiates an above-equilibrium wage while a firm in another market voluntarily pays an above-equilibrium wage to reduce turnover. What do the two cases share?
options: Both can affect hiring only during recessions when aggregate demand is already weak
Both can keep wages above market clearing and reduce hiring relative to equilibrium
Both are government-mandated wage floors imposed above equilibrium in their respective markets
Both necessarily eliminate worker turnover and therefore increase employment at the higher wage
mediumBoss.commonError: Treats union wage setting and efficiency wages as identical mechanisms or ignores their tradeoffs.
mediumBoss.feedback: Unions bargain over wages, while firms may voluntarily pay efficiency wages; both can keep wages above market-clearing levels under some conditions.

mediumBoss.q: Unemployment benefits increase search time, while improved job-placement services shorten search time. What is the most careful prediction?
options: The net effect on frictional unemployment depends on the relative strength of both channels
Frictional unemployment must rise because more generous benefits always dominate any matching improvement
Frictional unemployment must fall because improved placement always dominates any change in search incentives
Only structural unemployment can respond because search incentives and matching do not affect frictional unemployment
mediumBoss.commonError: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
mediumBoss.feedback: Frictional unemployment comes from normal search and matching as workers move between jobs or enter the labor market.

mediumBoss.q: A binding minimum wage raises pay for workers who remain employed but reduces the number of low-skill workers firms hire. Which statement best captures the tradeoff?
options: Every worker gains from the higher wage because firms must continue hiring the same number of workers
Employment must rise because the higher wage brings more workers into the labor market seeking jobs
The policy changes only the nominal wage and therefore cannot alter firms’ demand for labor
Some employed workers gain higher wages while some job seekers lose opportunities
mediumBoss.commonError: Forgets that a binding wage floor can leave more workers seeking jobs than firms want to hire.
mediumBoss.feedback: A binding minimum wage above equilibrium can create a labor surplus: labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.

mediumBoss.q: Actual unemployment falls after aggregate demand recovers, while the natural rate estimate is unchanged. What most likely fell?
mediumBoss.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
mediumBoss.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

mediumBoss.q: A permanent occupational shift leaves displaced workers without skills needed in expanding industries. What is the likely effect?
options: Structural unemployment and the natural rate may rise
The natural rate must fall because some industries expanded
mediumBoss.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
mediumBoss.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

mediumBoss.q: A policy improves retraining and job matching at the same time. What is the strongest natural-rate prediction?
options: The natural rate must rise because more workers change jobs
The natural rate remains fixed by definition
The natural rate may fall as structural mismatch and search time decline
mediumBoss.commonError: Treats the natural rate as an immutable constant.
mediumBoss.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

finalBoss.q: A domestic firm produces a machine this year but does not sell it until next year. How is the machine treated this year?
options: It is excluded until a customer buys it next year.
It is counted as household consumption this year.
It is counted as inventory investment in this year’s GDP.
It is counted only if the firm imports the parts.
finalBoss.commonError: Assuming unsold output is not counted until the final sale.
finalBoss.feedback: Newly produced unsold goods enter inventories, which are counted as investment in the year of production.

finalBoss.q: A U.S.-owned factory located in Mexico produces a car. Which statement is correct for U.S. GDP?
options: The car is included because the factory has a U.S. owner.
The car is included only if sold to a U.S. resident.
The car is counted as U.S. government production.
