cyclical_unemployment.feedback: Cyclical unemployment is tied to downturns in the business cycle.

frictional_unemployment.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
frictional_unemployment.feedback: Frictional unemployment comes from workers and firms taking time to match.

frictional_unemployment.q: Why can more generous unemployment insurance lengthen some unemployment spells even while protecting workers?
options: It can reduce search urgency while providing income support
It permanently destroys worker skills by definition
It makes every unemployed worker leave the labor force
It raises labor demand above labor supply automatically
frictional_unemployment.commonError: Treating unemployment insurance as either purely harmful or guaranteed to reduce unemployment.
frictional_unemployment.feedback: Unemployment insurance protects income and may improve match quality, but more generous benefits can also reduce search urgency and lengthen some frictional unemployment spells.

structural_unemployment.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
structural_unemployment.feedback: Structural unemployment reflects mismatch between workers and available jobs.

unions_efficiency_wages.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
unions_efficiency_wages.q: Unions and efficiency wages can both create unemployment when they:
unions_efficiency_wages.feedback: Above-equilibrium wages can create a surplus of labor.

minimum_wage_surplus.commonError: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
minimum_wage_surplus.q: A binding minimum wage is set:
minimum_wage_surplus.feedback: A binding minimum wage is above the market-clearing wage.

natural_rate.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
natural_rate.q: The natural rate of unemployment includes:
natural_rate.feedback: The natural rate includes frictional and structural unemployment.

natural_rate.q: Actual unemployment is above the natural rate during a recession. Which part of the gap is not itself part of the natural rate?
natural_rate.commonError: Adding recession-driven cyclical unemployment into the natural-rate benchmark.
natural_rate.feedback: The natural rate reflects frictional and structural unemployment. Cyclical unemployment is the business-cycle deviation of actual unemployment from that benchmark.

natural_rate_not_fixed.q: Which statement corrects the claim that the natural rate is always zero and never changes?
options: It always equals cyclical unemployment in the current year.
It is permanently fixed by the central bank’s inflation target.
It includes only people who have completely stopped seeking work.
It is normally positive and can change with labor-market conditions.
natural_rate_not_fixed.commonError: Treating the natural rate as zero and immutable.
natural_rate_not_fixed.feedback: The natural rate reflects normal search and mismatch, and its level can change over time.

intermediate_vs_final_goods.commonError: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
intermediate_vs_final_goods.q: A mill sells flour to a bakery for $50, and the bakery sells bread for $120. What final value is counted if using final-goods accounting?
intermediate_vs_final_goods.feedback: Final-goods accounting counts the bread sale, not the intermediate flour separately.

income_expenditure_identity.commonError: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
income_expenditure_identity.q: If total expenditure on final goods is $21 trillion, what should total income from producing those goods be?
income_expenditure_identity.feedback: Total income and total expenditure are two sides of the same GDP activity.

gdp_counting_rules.commonError: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
gdp_counting_rules.q: Which transaction counts in current GDP?
options: A newly built apartment rented to tenants
gdp_counting_rules.feedback: Newly produced housing services count; used goods and financial transfers do not add current production.

inventory_investment.commonError: Treats only machines as investment and misses new homes or inventory changes.
inventory_investment.q: Current production remains unsold and enters inventory investment. Which GDP-measurement rule explains why it still counts?
options: Inventory is treated as a transfer from the firm
Foreign production is added before subtracting every import
Current final production is counted when produced
Used goods are counted again whenever later resold
inventory_investment.feedback: Because the goods were produced this period, they count in current GDP; the unsold amount is recorded as inventory investment.

gdp_components_identity.commonError: Classifies by the buyer label instead of the economic transaction.
gdp_components_identity.q: A firm buys a newly produced domestic machine. How is this expenditure classified in the GDP identity?
options: Classify the machine as business investment
Treat the final machine as an intermediate input and omit it
Classify the domestic machine purchase as a government transfer
Subtract the machine as an import even though it is domestic
gdp_components_identity.feedback: Classify final spending by household consumption, business/residential investment, government purchases, or net exports.

imports_exports_nx.commonError: Infers output growth directly from nominal GDP growth.
imports_exports_nx.q: The expenditure identity reports current-dollar spending. Which measure helps determine whether higher spending reflects higher prices or greater output?
imports_exports_nx.feedback: Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production.

nominal_vs_real_gdp.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
nominal_vs_real_gdp.q: Real GDP per person rises, but leisure and environmental quality worsen. Which family destination evaluates the remaining question?
options: GDP components and the expenditure identity alone
Inventory investment and unsold production accounting
Nominal GDP measured only with current market prices
Limits of GDP and welfare measurement
nominal_vs_real_gdp.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

gdp_deflator.commonError: Mixes current and base-year prices while valuing current output.
gdp_deflator.q: GDP measurement identifies current final output. Which added step makes output comparable across years with changing prices?
options: Value current quantities at consistent base-year prices
Subtract all imports from every year twice
Add transfer payments to nominal GDP
Replace quantities with current interest rates
gdp_deflator.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

gdp_wellbeing_limits.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
gdp_wellbeing_limits.q: GDP rises after a natural disaster because rebuilding increases construction. Why might well-being still be lower?
options: Rebuilding services are excluded because the disaster happened first
Destroyed homes are added to GDP as current household consumption
GDP automatically subtracts every loss of wealth and personal hardship
GDP counts rebuilding but not the original welfare loss
gdp_wellbeing_limits.feedback: GDP can rise from replacement activity even if people are worse off.

inflation_rate.commonError: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.
inflation_rate.q: If CPI rises from 125 to 150, what is the inflation rate?

cpi_calculation.commonError: Using the wrong basket cost or forgetting to multiply by 100.
cpi_calculation.q: A basket costs $400 in the base year and $500 today. What is today's CPI?

quality_new_goods_bias.commonError: Concludes that known index limitations make CPI useless.
quality_new_goods_bias.q: If CPI overstates living-cost growth because quality gains are missed, what can happen to a benefit indexed fully to CPI?
options: Its true purchasing power can rise
Its real value must fall by the CPI rate
It becomes indexed to the GDP deflator
quality_new_goods_bias.feedback: CPI remains useful, while substitution, new-good, and quality challenges can make measured inflation differ from true cost-of-living growth.

substitution_bias.commonError: Assumes a fixed basket fully reflects how households respond to changes in relative prices.
substitution_bias.q: A fixed CPI basket misses consumers’ shift toward cheaper substitutes. Which measurement design creates this bias?
options: Subtracting imports from the expenditure identity
Using actual inflation in an ex post real rate
Holding the consumer basket fixed while buying patterns change
substitution_bias.feedback: Substitution bias arises when consumers shift toward relatively cheaper alternatives but the fixed basket does not fully reflect that response.

cpi_vs_gdp_deflator.commonError: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
cpi_vs_gdp_deflator.q: Imported coffee rises in price. Which index is affected more directly?
cpi_vs_gdp_deflator.feedback: Imported consumer goods affect CPI but not the GDP deflator directly.

inflation_adjustment.commonError: Comparing nominal dollar amounts across years without adjusting for the price level.
inflation_adjustment.q: A salary was $40,000 when CPI was 100. CPI is now 160. What salary today has the same purchasing power?

real_interest_rate.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
real_interest_rate.q: Nominal interest is 9% and inflation is 5%. What is the real interest rate?

real_gdp_per_person.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
real_gdp_per_person.q: Real GDP is $3 trillion and population is 100 million. What is real GDP per person?

rule_of_70.commonError: Forgetting that doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate.
rule_of_70.q: A country grows at 4% per year. About how long does income take to double?

productivity_calculation.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
productivity_calculation.q: Output is 2,400 units and labor input is 300 hours. What is productivity?

natural_resources.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
natural_resources.q: A country discovers rare minerals used in manufacturing. Which productivity factor increased?

human_capital.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
human_capital.q: A firm trains workers to use advanced equipment. Which productivity factor rises?

physical_capital.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
physical_capital.q: Workers receive better machines but no extra labor is added. What should happen to productivity, other things equal?
physical_capital.feedback: More or better capital helps workers produce more.

diminishing_returns.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
diminishing_returns.q: A factory adds more and more machines, but each extra machine adds less output than the previous one. What is this?
diminishing_returns.feedback: Diminishing returns means each extra unit adds less additional output.

technological_knowledge.commonError: Confusing better production methods with more labor or more machines.
technological_knowledge.q: A new production method lets firms make more output with the same inputs. What improved?
technological_knowledge.feedback: Better production methods are technological knowledge.

catch_up_effect.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
catch_up_effect.q: A poor country gains basic tools and output jumps sharply. What concept does this fit?
catch_up_effect.feedback: Capital can have high returns where it is scarce.

growth_policy.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
growth_policy.q: A government improves courts, property rights, schools, and infrastructure. What is it trying to support?
growth_policy.feedback: Those policies support investment, skills, and productivity.

discouraged_workers.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
discouraged_workers.q: A discouraged worker starts applying for jobs again but does not find one. What happens?
discouraged_workers.feedback: Active job search moves the worker into the labor force as unemployed.

unemployment_rate.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
unemployment_rate.q: If 8 people are unemployed and the labor force is 160, what is the unemployment rate?

labor_force_participation.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
labor_force_participation.q: If the labor force is 150 and adult population is 250, what is labor force participation?

employment_classification.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
employment_classification.q: A person works one paid hour but wants full-time work. How are they counted?
employment_classification.feedback: Paid work means employed, even if underemployed.

labor_force_calculation.commonError: Forgetting that the labor force includes employed plus unemployed workers.
labor_force_calculation.q: Use the labor-force identity: with 90 employed and 10 unemployed, what is the labor force?

structural_unemployment.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
structural_unemployment.q: A factory job disappears permanently because of automation, and workers lack new skills. What type of unemployment is this?
structural_unemployment.feedback: Permanent skill mismatch is structural unemployment.

cyclical_unemployment.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
cyclical_unemployment.q: A recession lowers demand and firms lay off workers. What type of unemployment is this?
cyclical_unemployment.feedback: Layoffs caused by recession are cyclical unemployment.

frictional_unemployment.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
frictional_unemployment.q: A worker quits and spends two weeks finding a better job match. What type of unemployment is this?
frictional_unemployment.feedback: Short-term search between jobs is frictional unemployment.

frictional_unemployment.q: A jobless worker has actively applied for jobs this week after voluntarily leaving a suitable job. How should the case be described across measurement and type?
options: Counted as unemployed, with frictional unemployment as the likely type
Not in the labor force, with structural unemployment as the likely type
Counted as employed, with cyclical unemployment as the likely type
Not counted in labor statistics because leaving a job voluntarily prevents unemployment status
frictional_unemployment.commonError: Using the cause of unemployment to decide official employment status, or using official status without identifying the unemployment type.
frictional_unemployment.feedback: Active job search makes the worker officially unemployed; normal search after leaving a suitable job is frictional unemployment.

frictional_unemployment.q: A new job-matching service reduces the average time workers spend between jobs. What family-level implication follows?
options: Lower frictional unemployment can reduce the natural rate
Lower frictional unemployment must raise cyclical unemployment
The natural rate is fixed and cannot respond to matching
Only the measured CPI can change from better matching
frictional_unemployment.commonError: Failing to connect institutions that change search efficiency with the frictional component of the natural rate.
frictional_unemployment.feedback: Faster matching reduces frictional unemployment; because frictional unemployment is part of the natural rate, the natural rate can fall.

minimum_wage_surplus.commonError: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
minimum_wage_surplus.q: At a minimum wage, 120 workers want jobs and firms hire 90. What is the labor surplus?

unions_efficiency_wages.commonError: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
unions_efficiency_wages.q: A firm pays above-equilibrium wages to reduce quits and increase effort. What theory explains this?
unions_efficiency_wages.feedback: Efficiency wages can improve effort and reduce turnover.

natural_rate.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
natural_rate.q: Actual unemployment is 7% and the natural rate is 5%. What is cyclical unemployment?
natural_rate.feedback: Cyclical unemployment = actual unemployment - natural unemployment = 2 percentage points.
